Latvia banned the import of Russian books on September 1. That won’t get them off the shelves: booksellers say shipments will just clear customs elsewhere in the EU.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:50:07 UTC
06:50:07 KST

Latvia banned the import of Russian books on September 1. That won’t get them off the shelves: booksellers say shipments will just clear customs elsewhere in the EU.
A Latvian ban on imports of certain goods from Russia and Belarus took effect on September 1. The restrictions cover not only clothing and children’s toys but also books. Latvian authorities say the ban is meant to sever economic ties with Russia and Belarus: Latvia intends to deprive both countries of some export revenue. The ban is also aimed at combating Russian propaganda in a country where nearly 38% of the population considers Russian their native language. At Meduza’s request, Latvian journalist Roman Shmelev examines how the new law will affect Latvia’s Russian-language bookstores, which were already hit earlier this year by an increase in the value-added tax on Russian-language books.
On the last weekend of summer, one of Riga’s bookstores has few customers. A boy of about 9 walks along the shelves, reading passages to his mother from a Russian-language book on the history of ancient Rome.
“Should we get it?” the mother asks.
“Wait,” the son says. “I’m choosing between the book on Byzantium and the one on Rome. This one has a lot about politics and history; that one has more about monuments and art.”
The boy says he wants to think carefully about how to spend his savings. He offers his mother a deal: “Let me buy the book about Rome with my own money, and you buy me the one about Byzantium.”
The book on the Eastern Roman Empire costs almost 50 euros; the one on Rome is half the price. After talking it over, the family decides to put off the pricier one “until next time.” They are sure they will still be able to buy books printed in Russia after September 1.
“Why would they disappear?” asks a salesperson at MnogoKnig, Latvia’s largest bookstore chain, sounding surprised. “Selling them isn’t banned.”
How Latvia is trying to stop imports from Russia and Belarus
The book ban is part of a broader push to reduce economic ties with Russia and Belarus. In addition to European Union sanctions, Latvia has already banned imports of vegetables, fruit, grain, and animal feed.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, imports of all goods from Russia and Belarus into Latvia have fallen by more than 90%. Imports totaled 2.13 billion euros in 2022; in 2025, they came to just 193 million euros, or 0.8% of Latvia’s imports.
Latvia still imports some Russian and Belarusian food and drinks, but the authorities plan to extend the ban to these products as well. Cookies, candy, beer, and soft drinks could be next.
Latvian authorities began cutting imports from Russia and Belarus in 2024. But goods made in those countries still turn up on store shelves, brought in through other EU countries that have no such bans. The same will probably happen with books.
Even as they impose the bans, Latvian officials acknowledge that they will not make Russian and Belarusian goods disappear from shelves altogether. One of the main goals is to signal to the public that the state considers it unethical to support producers in aggressor countries.
To push businesses to drop Russian and Belarusian suppliers on their own, Latvian authorities decided to publish a list of the companies still trading with them. The hope is that those companies’ customers will take their business elsewhere.
According to Latvia’s Central Statistical Bureau, the list currently runs to 170 companies.
Will Russian and Belarusian books really disappear from stores?
Russian-language books can be found in many bookstores across Latvia — not only in Riga, but also in Jurmala, Daugavpils, and Liepaja, cities where Russian speakers make up a significant share of the population.
Rihards Jerums, who owns the small Riga bookstore Intellectual Book (Intellektualnaya Kniga), is convinced the new ban will not change his selection at all. He buys his stock from a wholesaler operating under the MnogoKnig brand, one of the biggest importers of printed matter from Russia.
The chain’s mascot is a cartoon bookworm named Fedya, whom the company’s website calls “the true guardian of the Russian word in Europe.” That’s partly true: MnogoKnig stores operate in Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Germany, and Cyprus, and legal entities with similar names are registered in Germany and Poland. Alexander Korabelnikov, a Latvian citizen, founded those companies.
Another major importer of Russian books in Latvia operates under the Polaris brand. Representatives of both companies declined to comment.
Asked by a Meduza correspondent whether shipments of Russian books would continue, employees at stores in both chains were evasive, saying the companies were “looking for a way.”
“They’ll simply clear customs in another country instead of Latvia. It’s already happening. It’s easier that way,” says Jerums. He thinks the ban “makes no sense at all”:
The European Union is a city. There’s a wall around it, and gates in the wall. One gate is called German, another Swedish, another Estonian, another Latvian. But once goods are inside the city, they travel completely freely. You can bring them in through Estonia, clear customs in Spain, and sell them in Latvia.
Arina Lindanen, who owns the Riga bookstore Vilki Books, says the ban will not change what she stocks but will complicate logistics for bookstores, since they will have to source books in other European countries. She expects prices to rise “by about 1–2%” as a result:
As far as I know, everything sold on the EU market goes through a single Latvian company. We’re all hooked up to the same pipeline. That’s bad for the market, but it’s how things turned out because of the war. I had other suppliers, but they left Russia in 2022, so we have no choice.
Lindanen says Latvian policy on Russian-language books is having a serious impact on her business: after the reduced value-added tax rate on such books was scrapped, prices rose and sales fell. “We would have had to close the store if we hadn’t found an investor,” the Vilki Books owner says.
Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže has acknowledged that the import ban could push prices higher, but she is confident that books once brought in from Russia and Belarus can be replaced with products from other countries. Booksellers are certain she is wrong: outside Russia and Belarus, they say, Russian-language classics are not printed.
“In Europe, they publish émigré literature that can’t be published in Russia. But they don’t publish the classics at all. It isn’t profitable,” Jerums says.
Lindanen says she already leans toward cheaper editions when deciding what to stock: “We’re trying to get better at choosing — to find editions where the price, the paper quality, the design, and the notes balance out so that they aren’t too expensive. Nobody is going to buy The Master and Margarita for 40 euros.”
Both Lindanen and Jerums say Russian-language classics are in high demand at their stores. “People buy a lot of Dostoevsky and Bulgakov — they’re evergreens. It’s like bread,” Jerums says. “People buy it every day — and they buy The Master and Margarita, too.”
How Latvian booksellers, readers, and security services are fighting Russian propaganda
In the early 2010s, Russian books offering “alternative” versions of history were easy to find in Latvian stores. That began to change after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, when new Russian children’s atlases started disappearing from bookstores — atlases in which state borders could be made out among the descriptions of animals and plants.
In 2024, Latvia’s State Security Service publicly acknowledged that it had held “conversations” with bookstore managers and asked them to “review the selection of books they offer.”
Jerums says customers police the shelves themselves and take action if they see books that could pass for propaganda.
“People report us to the police. There’s an anti-Putin book by Olaf Kühl, Z: A Short History of Russia, Seen From Its End. A customer saw the letter Z on the cover and filed a complaint. We had to explain ourselves to the police,” Jerums says.
The reverse happens, too: sometimes customers “ask us to order books by Margarita Simonyan or a biography of Viktor Bout.” “I wouldn’t bring those in now,” the bookseller says.
He says a bookseller cannot always keep track of everything the publishers he buys from put out, and that this sometimes leads to trouble. “Say I want to order psychology books, but that publisher might also put out Z-poetry about the Donbas. Those books automatically end up on the price list and on our website. And they shouldn’t be there,” he says.
To avoid such situations, Jerums and his colleagues at the store have had to compile their own list of “undesirable literature” to hide those books on the website. The list already runs to 470 titles, Jerums says.
Lindanen says her store, too, has deliberately cut certain Russian authors from its shelves: “I was never a fan of [the propagandist] Zakhar Prilepin, and even if I had been, we’re crossing this author out. Neither his early nor his later novels will be on our shelves.”
Meduza checked the catalogs of Latvia’s major bookstore chains and found no titles by Prilepin listed.

ICYMI: The KPMG scandal
What's it all about?
I get asked a lot about the KPMG scandal and why it's important. Here's a short recap of some of the issues.
KPMG Australia is a consulting firm, linked to a global parent.
There are four large ones in a similar model - EY, PwC and Deloitte - and like our major banks, they are known as the "big four".
There is a smaller tier of even fancier and more expensive ones: Bain, Boston Consulting Group, McKinsey & Company.
The big four have two key roles: audit and consulting. In consulting, they solve business problems.
KPMG Australia has almost 10,000 staff, and if you were a business with an issue, you could go to them or rivals to seek a solution to problems like these:
- How do we crack the Indonesian market?
- We've got immense turnover and low morale in our X division. What's going on?
- We need to get our company's emissions down. How should we do that?
The firms have lots of smart people, with experience in diverse fields.
Audit asks the hard questions
The other part of the big four is audit.
It's very important.
Auditors go into companies and government agencies and certify that the financial numbers are solid.
They ask searing questions, interrogate the spreadsheets and the staff and eventually "sign off" that the published accounts are credible and reliable.
So when you see a profit announcement, a revelation of a cost blowout on a project or an annual report, there will almost certainly be a page with the logo of a big four firm and the auditor's signature and name on it.
Weirdly, a lot of our economy runs on trust. You have to be able to trust the numbers, and auditors give you that assurance.
What went wrong at KPMG?
Well, we can't go on all day....
Essentially, a whistleblower who worked at KPMG raised serious allegations about the misuse of confidential information by extremely senior partners of the firm.
Despite raising the allegations through all the appropriate channels, the whistleblower was treated poorly. Eventually, having failed to get the allegations investigated seriously, the claims made their way to Labor senator Deborah O'Neill, who read them out in Parliament - allowing the media to report them.
What were the allegations?
They might seem minor, but the allegations were around the storage and sharing of confidential information:
- A laptop left open in a boardroom, a joke that the owner was going to lunch and another person could look at it
- A report printed off and stored in a locker, with an executive assistant being compelled to give another executive access to the documents
The best way to describe it is probably a singular example. Staff at KPMG used the confidential internal financial information from telecommunications company Optus to try and win the more lucrative account of Optus's direct rival, Telstra.
The issue is that these were the most senior leaders at the firm, who set the culture. It also trashed the reputation of the auditors and the broader firm and consulting industry, even though the overwhelming majority of people at the firms have had nothing to do with it.
What's happened since then?
After searing hearings exposed the issues, and the firm's attempt to minimise them, lots has gone on.
- The CEO, chair and a swathe of senior executives have gone
- A new CEO from a different division, John Sams, has taken over
- New chair Michael Ebeid is in place (although controversial because he was a director when the firm was busy not doing enough about the allegations - which have since been proven out)
- Hundreds of staff have been sacked, with KPMG facing a grim outlook at clients leaving or not starting congrats
- The Department of Finance has banned government agencies from new contracts with the firm until a report is completed, due this month
I hope that explains some of how we got here. Drop a comment if you have more questions.
The next hearing of the committee examining KPMG is on Friday.
We'll have more then.
KPMG grilling on Friday, but who is on the menu?
On Friday, the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services will hold a public hearing.
It's ostensibly about the "Oversight of ASIC, the Takeovers Panel and the Corporations Legislation" but let's be real: it's The KPMG Show at the moment, with the consulting firm in the frame over the misuse of confidential information and woeful treatment of a whistleblower who brought it to light.
The hearing will be in Sydney, in the Masonic Centre Corinthian Room at 66 Goulburn Street.
At this stage I do not believe there will be an internet feed, but we'll bring you the best bits.
The program for this hearing has not yet been released. We know regulator ASIC got pushed out due to the last hearing running overtime, so expect them.
Beyond that? Anyone's guess.

Economy slowing down, but will RBA be satisfied?
When it comes to GDP and inflation data, some analysts make the point that, since both sets of data are backward-looking, it can be a bit misleading to speak about them in annual terms because growth rates from a year ago don't provide much information about what's happening today.
They say one solution is to take the last six months of data and annualise it, because that gives us a better idea of what's happening right now, and Westpac's economics team has done that with today's GDP data.
For example, the data show that Australia's economy expanded 0.4% in Q2 2026, with annual growth slowing to 2.1%.
But it's a different story when you look at the last six months:
"Despite the slight upside surprise, the economy is losing momentum, with growth running at around 1.5% on a six-month annualised basis over the first half of 2026, down from around 2.8% in the second half of 2025," they say.
Having said that, they say the economy is still running a touch firmer than expected by the RBA at this point in the economic cycle.
And they say unit labour costs ticking higher in the June quarter will likely add to the RBA Monetary Policy Board's unease leading into its September meeting.

"From the 1980s this country took a series of wrong turns. Political power was centralised, economic power privatised and the country deindustrialised. "Change begins with honesty and I am not hearing much of it this afternoon. Unless we are blunt about what went wrong we will not turn things around.
"Far from 'taking back control' the combination of those policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain.
"For 40 years too many places have been drifting. Too many British high streets tell the story of this decline. People yearn to see them restored to what they once were, as the communities secretary and I heard on our visit to Ilkeston in the summer, but they see no hope if we continue on the same path with a failed economic model which does not trickle down much to places like theirs and instead allows wealth to be extracted and siphoned out.
"Britain’s water industry stands as a leaking monument to that approach — a country run in the private rather than public interest. That is now abundantly clear to voters of all parties, including the Conservative party."

With economy still growing close to trend, a rate hike remains a possibility
Marcel Thielant from Capital Economics has this to say about the GDP data:
"With GDP growth and inflation holding up better than the RBA had anticipated, the bank will probably hike rates again before long, perhaps as soon as this month.
"The 0.4% q/q rise in Q2 GDP was a touch stronger than the analyst consensus and the RBA’s forecast of 0.3%, let alone our own forecast of unchanged output.
"And due to revisions to previous quarters, the annual growth rate only slowed from 2.5% to 2.1%, leaving it above the RBA’s forecast of 1.9%.
He says it's noteworthy that public demand only rose by 2.1% over the past year instead of the RBA’s forecast of 3.6%, so that "should allay the bank’s concerns that runaway public spending is boosting price pressures".

"While the minutes of the RBA’s August meeting sounded hawkish, a rate hike isn’t a done deal yet," he says.
"After all, the labour market is now clearly loosening and revised data show that the housing downturn has accelerated.
"The key point though is that the economy is still growing close to trend, which means that the existing excess capacity isn’t being eroded. If anything, the monthly data on household spending suggest that consumption is accelerating rather than slowing.
"With inflation remaining stubbornly high, we now believe that the bank will deliver another rate hike, perhaps as soon as this month."

Key Telstra engineers on leave at time of July outage
The long-awaited report into what caused Telstra's national outage on July 8 has dropped this morning, with the investigation finding two of the telco's key engineers responsible were on mandatory leave at the time.
The outage was triggered at 2:50am after a faulty power supply was replaced and reset a timing mechanism, which resulted in a date change that flowed through the network.
It resulted in hundreds of people being unable to call Triple Zero, small businesses being unable to use EFTPOS, and stopped trains in NSW and Victoria.
The independent external review, conducted by Technology Audit Partners, found that there was "not sufficient knowledgeable staff" who could identify the error in the timing system that caused the outage, and the alarms that picked up the issue were only checked during business hours.
On a media briefing call this morning, Telstra CEO Vicki Brady accepted the findings and said the telco is focused on implementing changes to ensure the outage doesn't happen again.

Russia is secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles - report
The FT report indicates that the support continued throughout the US war with Iran, as Tehran intends to develop a new class of weapon capable of threatening US aircraft carriers
Russia has been secretly supporting Iranian missile development since 2023, according to a report in the Financial Times on Tuesday.
The goal of the program, codenamed C430L, was to help Iran develop missiles capable of taking out US Navy aircraft carriers in the Middle East.
In particular, they aimed to develop a ramjet propulsion system that would allow Iranian missiles to fly at several times the speed of sound.
Fast, low-flying missiles would give Western air defences less time to react increasing the impact of such an attack.
The transfer of advanced missile technology would have required approval from the highest political echelons in Russia, amid speculation that this was a technology exchange. Iran supports Russian drone development, and Russia supports Iranian missile development, in addition to the already existing intelligence cooperation between the two.
Leaks seen by the Financial Times showed that preparations for the deal were underway before the deal was signed in November 2023, only a month after October 7.
"Russia is trying to broaden the Ukraine war and draw the US into different theatres," said Nicole Grajewski, a professor at Sciences Po University in Paris.
The investigation also showed that the support continued throughout the war with Iran in February, and provided significant assistance to Iran during its attacks on the Gulf states.
Iran has long sought to develop a ramjet propulsion system, as far back as 2019, when then supreme leader Ali Khamenei was seen inspecting development sites. Iranian media also reported the testing of ramjet prototypes in August 2023.

As my awareness of self and world expands and deepens, I begin to better understand the sources and…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:46:49 UTC
06:46:49 KST

As my awareness of self and world expands and deepens, I begin to better understand the sources and scope of my suffering. I gradually become more aware of the simple fact that much of my ordinary experience includes various forms of suffering.
When the world seems to contradict and oppose me, I suffer from frustration or anger. When I compare my life to the lives of those who seem to be doing better than me, I suffer from envy. When memories of what I’ve lost spring to mind, I suffer from grief. When my present circumstances feel stagnant and hopeless, I suffer from despair. When I feel overwhelmed by demands and obligations, I suffer from stress. When the dangers of an uncertain future are approaching, I suffer from anxiety.
As I look more carefully at the particular forms of suffering I experience, I also start to see how these forms depend on my attachments. This is frequently a distressing process, because it means coming to terms with the broad reach of suffering. Discovering that suffering arises merely from my way of life and the structure of the society in which I live can be painful.

UK pledges additional £50 million to help contain Ebola outbreak in Congo
Sept 1 - Britain said on Tuesday it would provide more than £50 million ($67.56 million) in new funding to support efforts to contain an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where confirmed cases have surpassed 6,000 in the country's largest-ever epidemic.
• Britain allocated up to £20 million to the Ebola response in May, and the latest funding brings its total contribution to £78 million.
• The funding will support disease surveillance, frontline health workers, treatment access, infection control, community outreach and safe burials, Britain's Foreign Office said.
• British public health experts have been deployed in Congo to support the efforts.
• "As the outbreak intensifies, we are accelerating our response to match the pace and scale of the challenge," Britain's Minister for Africa Kirsty McNeill said.
• The epidemic - the second-largest and fastest-spreading on record - was caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments. REUTERS

Honduran court drops charges against former president pardoned by Trump

Honduran court drops charges against former president pardoned by Trump
TEGUCIGALPA, Sept 1 - A Honduran court has dropped charges against former President Juan Orlando Hernandez over fraud and money laundering, judiciary authorities said on Tuesday, nine months after he was freed from U.S. prison where he was serving a lengthy sentence for drug trafficking charges.
Judiciary spokesperson Carlos Silva told local media the judge concluded Hernandez was not responsible for budgetary decisions at the time of the crime and it could not be confirmed that embezzled funds had been channeled into his 2013 presidential campaign.
"Of course we expected this outcome because the case had no basis," Hernandez told supporters outside the court. "The ruling is clear. Today, this chapter of political persecution has ended."
"Those who orchestrated this operation not only wanted to see me banished from Honduras forever, never to return, but they were determined to leave my family on the street," he added, pointing to assets seized by Honduran authorities. "It was utter vandalism."
Hernandez spoke alongside his wife Ana Garcia, who sought their party's presidential nomination in 2025.
Even as Hernandez's supporters celebrated the ruling, anti-corruption groups warned the outcome could further erode Hondurans' trust in the courts and pointed to the absence of a key witness for the prosecution whose release from prison was confirmed just hours before the ruling.
Silva said prosecutors could still appeal the case.
Hernandez had returned to the Central American nation in late July, after being extradited to the U.S. in 2022 on drug trafficking charges. Two years later, he was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in U.S. prison, but was then pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump late last year.
Trump's pardon of Hernandez was announced two days before Honduras' November presidential vote, in a move widely seen as an effort to influence the country's election. Trump also said at the time he would cut funding to Honduras should the candidate for Hernandez's right-wing National Party — now President Nasry Asfura — not win the election.
After being freed from U.S. prison, Hernandez continued to face charges of fraud and money laundering in Honduras as part of a sprawling corruption investigation, known as Pandora II.
Prosecutors had accused Hernandez and other high-profile officials of diverting nearly $11 million in state funds to political campaigns between 2010 and 2013. Some of this money allegedly was used for Hernandez's first presidential campaign.
Charges have also been dropped against other high-profile officials, including former President Porfirio Lobo and ex-finance minister Wilfredo Cerrato.
Hernandez led Honduras from 2014 to 2022, a period during which the Central American nation served as a major drug trafficking route, and hundreds of thousands of Hondurans fled drug-related violence and extortion.
During that period, Hernandez abused his position as president and ran the country "as a narco-state," allowing drug traffickers to operate with "virtual impunity," according to U.S. prosecutors.
Hernandez told Reuters in an interview in late July he had no immediate plans to seek public office in Honduras but wanted to support the new government. REUTERS

Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:30:07 UTC
06:30:07 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
Rising sea levels, extreme weather and drought all remain concerns, but destabilised ice and snow at high altitudes is increasingly a threat
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Dr Zhengxu Wang is a distinguished professor at the School of Public Affairs, Zhejiang University. 
On August 26, a section of glacier collapsed at an altitude of more than 5,000 metres on the Nepalese side of the Himalayas. The falling ice and rock accelerated down a steep valley at about 50 metres per second, scouring debris and transforming into a high-speed mudslide that slammed into Gyirong Port on the Chinese side just seven minutes later.
The force of the flow largely buried and obliterated the border facilities. Hundreds of people, many of them travellers, remain missing on the Chinese side. Across the border in Nepal, entire villages were swept away, leaving hundreds dead and thousands unaccounted for.
For decades, the defining image of climate vulnerability has been the low-lying island nation, where rising seas threaten to erase entire communities from the map. That threat is real, urgent and unfinished business. However, the catastrophic mudslide that tore through the China-Nepal border forces us to look beyond the waterline and consider a more complex, multidimensional map of climate risk.
The iconic risk remains sea-level rise. It is slow, inexorable and already under way. Coastal megacities from Shanghai to Mumbai to New York are investing heavily in sea walls and surge barriers. Small island states are exploring relocation treaties and purchasing land abroad as a form of climate insurance. The very predictability of this threat has allowed societies to develop institutional responses.
The second most immediately felt climate risk is extreme rainfall and the catastrophic flooding it brings. For several years, traditionally drier places such as Beijing and large swathes of inland China have suffered disastrous floods that overwhelmed infrastructure, affecting millions and exposing the limits of urban drainage systems never designed for the intensity of rain now falling from a warmer atmosphere.
The third risk is drought. This summer, a severe and persistent drought, coupled with record-breaking heatwaves, created a crisis across much of Europe. The prolonged lack of rainfall pushed major waterways, including the Rhine, Danube and Loire, to historically low levels, disrupting river transport and forcing cargo vessels to reduce their loads. France alone faces an estimated €10-15 billion (US$11.6-17.4 billion) in heat-related losses and a projected 35 per cent drop in maize yields.
Across Europe, low river levels and wildfires have exposed unexploded ordnance from World War II that had long been submerged or buried – another stark reminder of how climate change is already profoundly affecting our lives.

Urgent need for access to Iranian sites, cautions UN nuclear watchdog
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:28:00 UTC
06:28:00 KST

IAEA calls for access to Iran nuclear sites over proliferation concerns
UN watchdog says lack of information and access to facilities to verify Iran’s nuclear material is a proliferation concern.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has called for “utmost urgency” to address the lack of access to Iran’s nuclear sites.
In a quarterly report seen by news agencies on Tuesday, the United Nations nuclear watchdog labelled its “lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of proliferation concern”.
The US has claimed preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon – an ambition that Tehran continues to deny – as the motivation for the war that it launched in March. However, Tehran has been successful in shifting the focus of the hostilities to control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway.
In particular, the IAEA report raised concerns over the lack of access to the Isfahan plant, which was targeted several times by the US and Israel over the past year or so.
In the report, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi expressed his “conviction that the long-standing problems and recurrent crises surrounding these issues must be resolved through a long-lasting, verifiable diplomatic agreement”.
However, Iran has said that access to the sites that have been struck by military action must be arranged via special arrangement.
The head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization, Mohammad Eslami, said on August 26 that the IAEA “cannot seek to inspect these centres until it develops specific criteria and protocols for inspecting sites targeted by military attacks”.
Tehran suspended cooperation with the UN nuclear watchdog following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites before saying in September 2025 it would allow the UN agency’s inspectors to return.
However, access to the nuclear sites that have been bombed has not yet been granted. Despite US President Donald Trump having claimed last year that the US had destroyed the facilities and crippled Tehran’s nuclear programme, Iran’s stores of enriched uranium remain unaccounted for.
Tehran has repeatedly denied any military ambition linked to its nuclear programme, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.
However, the IAEA, whose latest report will be discussed at its board of governors meeting from September 21-25, has reported in the past that the level of Iran’s enrichment of its uranium reserves is well above that needed for civilian purposes, although neither is it at the level of weapons grade.

Australians accused of involvement with IS look set to face trial in Iraq
In short:
About a dozen Australians accused of involvement with the failed Islamic State are set to face trial in Iraq.
Local Iraqi authorities say they have finished interrogating more than 5,700 prisoners transferred from Syria earlier this year.
What's next?
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council said the next phase was "their referral to the trial court, each according to the evidence and facts established in his or their case".
About a dozen Australians accused of involvement with the Islamic State group are set to face trial in Iraq, after local authorities said they had finished interrogating more than 5,700 prisoners transferred from Syria earlier this year.
The man known as "Dr Jihad", Perth-born paediatrician Tareq Kamleh, is likely among the group, given previous comments by Iraqi authorities about his involvement with Islamic State going beyond providing medical services.
That is despite his insistence in a recently resurfaced interview that he never pledged allegiance to the so-called caliphate.
Another member of the group may be Yusuf Zahab, now in his early 20s, who was taken to Syria at age 12.
He was captured and separated from his family after the battle of Baghuz in March 2019, when he was still a teenager, and disappeared into the Syrian jail system.
Members of his family, including his mother, were among the women who returned home to Australia in May this year, after spending years in the al-Roj refugee camp in north-eastern Syria.
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council issued a statement on Tuesday, local time, announcing interrogations of "5,704 defendants who are members of the terrorist ISIS gangs" had been completed.
It said the next phase was "their referral to the trial court, each according to the evidence and facts established in his or their case".
Evidence of crimes against Yazidi community
For the first time, the Judicial Council provided a rough breakdown of the nationalities of those involved.
It said there were prisoners from 67 different countries who were being held: 16 were nationals from Arab states, 19 from European Union members and 32 from other countries.
The bulk of the prisoners came from Syria, with 3,497 detained, while there were 474 Iraqis.
"The investigations, evidence collection, and analysis resulted in the identification of several highly dangerous individuals who had held leadership, security, religious, military, media, or other positions, or who had been involved in high-profile operations and crimes of an international dimension, including first-tier leaders within the terrorist ISIS gangs," the Judicial Council said in a statement.
"The investigations also revealed the multiplicity of roles within the organisation, which were not limited to combat activities, but also included military, security, financial, logistical, administrative, medical, technical, and media activities."
Iraqi authorities said it had uncovered evidence of crimes against the Yazidi community, a Kurdish-speaking minority IS has been described as committing genocide against.
"Six defendants were identified whose case files indicated roles directly connected to the enslavement of Yazidi women, or to their detention, transportation, sale, supervision, or benefiting from the system of enslavement established by the terrorist ISIS gangs," the Judicial Council said.
In July, the Albanese government said it would not provide assistance to "any Australian who made the horrific choice to join a dangerous terrorist organisation".
Regarding the reports about Tareq Kamleh, cabinet minister Clare O'Neil said he could "rot in jail".
Diplomats, consular staff allowed to visit citizens
The Judicial Council said it had allowed diplomats and consular staff from "several countries" to visit their citizens in jail during the interrogation process, as well as the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The ABC has contacted the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and the office of Foreign Minister Penny Wong, for details of what contact Australian officials have had with the group.
The ICRC has also been contacted for comment.
The Judicial Council said there had been insufficient evidence in some cases, leading to some prisoners being released: one Finnish national, one American citizen and seven Iraqis.
Another 457 Syrians will also be released, given a lack of evidence tying them to their alleged crimes.
The US military began transferring Islamic State prisoners held in facilities controlled by Kurdish forces in north-eastern Syria to Iraq earlier this year.
It followed moves by Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, to take back control of large swathes of the country which had been controlled by the Kurds for the best part of a decade, during Syria's bloody civil war.
Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council revealed interrogations began in February this year, and said a special courtroom had been established to allow trials to happen remotely via video link to avoid risks of transporting high-security prisoners.

BISHKEK, September 1. /TASS/. The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should expand gradually and without haste, without turning into an amorphous structure, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at a press conference following a SCO summit.

in brief
- Chanel Contos accuses social media companies of feeding misogynistic content to young men online.
- She's urging the government to replace algorithmic feeds with ones that only show posts by accounts users follow by default.
This article contains references to sexual assault.
Social media empires are being put on notice for content that promotes controlling, violent sexual acts.
Big tech companies are radicalising young men into harmful sexual acts, the founder of education and advocacy organisation Teach Us Consent is expected to tell the National Press Club on Wednesday.
Chanel Contos will say the content is pushed by bad actors who share commercial infrastructure and have identified male psychology as a market — together, they make up the "manosphere".
"Young men online seeking community, belonging, and self-improvement advice are targeted with content that blames women for their misfortune and reinstates harmful and outdated gender roles," she is expected to say.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Contos will say that boys aged between 16 and 18 are likely to be fed misogynistic content less than 25 minutes after signing up to social media.
That was true even if preferences were set to try and exclude it, according to research from Teach Us Consent.
Teens are regularly fed content suggesting women should not leave the house alone, should not work and should not be in charge of their own money.
Most harmful content starts in the wellness landscape through gym videos or motivational content.
They then promote good looks and dominance over women as markers of male worth.
Contos will tell the Press Club men who subscribe to those ideals are twice as likely to binge drink and eight times as likely to have suicidal thoughts as their peers.
They are also 17 times more likely to have hit their partner.
Australian teenage boys aged 16 to 18 are committing sexual assault against children more frequently than adults are, the Australian Child Maltreatment Study found in 2023.
Contos has previously cited media content as a driver, noting her organisation had found an explosion in peer-on-peer teen sexual violence in the past five years.
Sexual choking sparks calls for action
The federal government is currently exploring whether Australians should be able to opt out of algorithmically curated social media feeds, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek told ABC Insider's program on Sunday.
The announcement came after a 16-year-old Sydney girl's death was linked in media reports to a suspected sexual choking act — a behaviour often promoted to teenage boys through pornography and social media content.
Contos will tell the Press Club that, while the change would be positive, harsher crackdowns are needed.
She will suggest feeds should only show posts from people users follow, unless users explicitly opt out, to circumvent harmful content. Such a move would revert social media algorithms to how they were a decade ago.
"(The change) would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," Contos will say.
"It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine."
Teach Us Consent has been running a campaign promoting the change since 2025.
An open letter to the prime minister requesting an end to algorithmic feeds without an opt-out choice has been signed by more than 13,000 Australians.

BISHKEK, September 2. /TASS/. Armenia cannot be a member of both the European Union and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), despite the historic bonds of friendship with Russia, Russian President Vladimir Putin said.
"If you have decided to move toward the European Union - that is a sovereign decision of any country. We and the Armenian people are bound by historical ties of friendship, and even more than friendship. Our relationship with the Armenian people has very deep roots. But it is simply impossible to be a member of both organizations at the same time," he told reporters.
According to the Russian president, this is due to differences in phytosanitary regulations and technical standards. "We have a lot of things that are incompatible, at least today," he explained.

US may require parents to prove citizenship to get passports for their children

US may require parents to prove citizenship to get passports for their children
- The US State Department plans to require parents to prove their citizenship or immigration status when applying for their children's passports, aiming to enforce President Trump's order on birthright citizenship.
- Trump's order targets "birth tourism" and narrows birthright citizenship, but faces legal challenges after the Supreme Court ruled a previous version unconstitutional.
- Lawsuits seek to block the new order, with a federal judge expressing doubts; the Justice Department argues the challenge is premature as implementation details are still pending.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US State Department has proposed requiring parents applying for passports for their children to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status as part of President Donald Trump’s latest effort to limit birthright citizenship.
The draft guidance, reviewed by Reuters, is the first detailed look at how the State Department could enforce Trump’s Aug 6 executive order targeting what it calls “birth tourism” and broadening historical exceptions to birthright citizenship.
The White House referred Reuters questions to the State Department.
In a statement, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said that “President Trump has been unequivocal that this Administration will protect the meaning and value of American citizenship, full stop, and that includes making sure our passport adjudication process fully reflects that standard.”
Limiting birthright citizenship has been one of the president’s top priorities in his far-reaching crackdown on immigration.
The US Supreme Court ruled his previous attempt violated the country’s Constitution.
Trump’s initial executive order would have granted automatic US citizenship at birth only to children with at least one parent who was a US citizen or a lawful permanent resident known as a green card holder.
In a 6-3 ruling, the Supreme Court found the order was unlawful, with a majority finding it violated the Citizenship clause of the Constitution’s 14th Amendment.
Trump’s Aug 6 order was narrower, taking particular aim at “birth tourism,” in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship.
That order could still be blocked in court.
The new directive would withhold citizenship from children with a parent who works for a foreign government in the US, is engaged in fraud or a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or is classified as an “alien enemy.”
“The Department will require parental information and evidence of parental citizenship or immigration status as part of its determination whether the applicant is subject to EO 14418,” the State Department draft guidance reads, citing the executive order number.
If implemented, the proposal would require all parents or legal guardians to provide proof of their citizenship, such as a valid US passport or birth certificate, or evidence of their immigration status, such as an I-94 form or a legal permanent residency card, when submitting a passport application for their children.
The information would be used by the government to determine if the child qualifies for citizenship under the new order, the State Department proposal says.
Currently, parents whose children were born in the US only need to prove their parentage and present photo identification during this process.
They are also asked to check a box on the application form indicating if they are US citizens but are not required to file supporting documentation.
Lawyers pursuing class-action lawsuits on behalf of babies who would be deprived of citizenship under Trump’s initial order have asked two different federal judges to prevent his latest order from taking effect.
One of those lawsuits is before US district judge Deborah Boardman, who was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden.
At a hearing on Aug 28 in Greenbelt, Maryland, Boardman voiced scepticism about what she called Trump’s unprecedented order and allowed the plaintiffs to revise their lawsuit so she could consider whether to block it.
Justice Department attorneys have argued that a restraining order would be inappropriate and that the legal challenge was premature, as federal agencies had yet to issue public guidance on how the president’s directive would be implemented. REUTERS

news
Russia’s finance minister walked into a G20 summit for the first time since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But what did he walk out with?
Source: Meduza
- Finance ministers and central bank governors from the Group of 20 (G20) met in Asheville, North Carolina. Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended in person for the first time since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He last took part in a G20 meeting in April 2022, by video link, according to The Washington Post. That appearance drew protests from several Western countries.
- The Trump administration decided to bring the Russian delegation into the meeting, according to Politico. “We like getting along with everybody,” U.S. President Donald Trump said of the move. The U.S. Treasury Department, meanwhile, did not invite South Africa’s delegation. In late 2025, Trump said he would not grant accreditation to South African officials, citing a “genocide” against the country’s white population.
- At the summit, Siluanov met with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The two discussed Trump’s plan for ending the war in Ukraine and economic cooperation between Russia and the United States. Sources told Politico and Reuters that Siluanov tried to raise other areas of mutual interest, but Bessent cut him off and said that “nothing is possible until the war is over.”
- Officials in both countries used neutral language to describe the meeting between Siluanov and Bessent. Erin Browne, the Treasury’s undersecretary for international affairs, told Politico that Bessent “had a productive meeting with the Russian finance minister.” Russia’s Finance Ministry said the two sides had discussed “issues of Russian-American engagement on the financial track.”
- European delegations objected to the Russian minister’s visit. German Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said that he would not pose for a group photo with Siluanov, and that other European officials sided with him. Among them was Poland’s finance minister, according to Reuters. In the end, Siluanov was left out of the group photo.
- Klingbeil said he had taken the opportunity to tell the Russian finance minister “straight to his face” that Russia must end the war. “People are dying every day, we have just seen another escalation in the attacks,” The Washington Post quoted him as saying. “You cannot simply return to normality.”
- U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat, also criticized the decision to invite the Russian minister to the summit. “The Trump Admin needs to pressure Putin and his cronies, not offer them a platform,” she said. Shaheen urged the U.S. House of Representatives to pass a new sanctions bill against Russia that the Senate had already approved.
- Even so, Siluanov’s trip to the summit showed how ready Washington is to reopen high-level diplomatic channels with Moscow, according to CNBC. The Trump administration is willing to do so even over its European allies’ objections.

Albanese defends pre-COP attendance
The PM is asked about the pre-COP event being hosted by Australia in Fiji.
If you need a refresh, a pre-COP is a preparatory meeting held ahead of the UN Climate Change Conference.
The government had initially wanted world leaders to attend instead of high-ranking government officials, but there's been extensive reporting to suggest they've been unable to secure RSVPs from heads of government.
Albanese says the government had always anticipated that a pre-COP event would not attract the same level of patronage as COP itself.

Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen backs him up, stepping up to say historically, pre-COPs have not attracted heads of state.
Government tips $600 million into scheme to tackle drug smuggling in Pacific
The PM says he's discussed peace and security with leaders at the Pacific Islands Forum (which is why he is in Palau) and emphasised the need to deal with transnational crime and drug smuggling in the Pacific.
"This is increasingly an issue in the Pacific. We have rising rates of HIV, rising rates of drug usage as well, and the entry increasingly of criminal elements in the region," he says.
"Australia, tragically, is a destination for much of the drug trafficking that seeks to go through the Pacific."
The government will tip $600 million into a new Pacific scheme designed to tackle the surge of drug smuggling into the region, as my colleague Stephen Dziedzic reported this morning.
More flights between Australia and Palau
The PM says the government is supporting a doubling of flights between Australia and Palau to line up with the island's peak tourism season.
Qantas will be running the service.

"That's obviously a very important relationship for Australia, and we were able to talk about the financial system there," Mr Albanese says.
It's been busy for Albanese, who also met with leaders from the Marshall Islands, Papua New Guinea, Tonga and French Polynesia.
PM addresses Nepal tragedy
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is speaking at a press conference in Palau.
He starts with the good news that a further four Australians who were in the impact zone in Nepal have been confirmed safe today.
There are 38 Australians still missing.
"That is 38 families, 38 people who we hold grave fears for. We hope, of course, for positive news," he says.
"We're doing everything we can to work with authorities."
'Much bigger system at play' than conversations at schools: Contos
Chanel Contos was asked for her reaction to Nationals senator Matt Canavan's claim the "feminisation" of the school curriculum is a reason why young boys are turning to the online manosphere.
The consent advocate reiterates that it's not just that men and boys are seeking this content out, but it's being intentionally served to them.
"There is a much bigger system at play than kind of like the small conversations in school and that sort of thing," she says.
"Then on these online spaces I think is where we really start to get that rhetoric that conversations against about violence against women and children is an attack on men and boys. But it's truly not."
Government must act to turn off automatic algorithms: Contos
The problem, Chanel Contos says, is social media algorithms that dictate the content we see online.
She says the switch to a stream of content with no end point and users being fed content from users they don't follow was part of tech companies' focus on being addictive.
"Big tech's data about us is the basis of their profit model. They need to know our desires, our fears, what makes us aroused and what makes us insecure in order to optimise what will keep us there for longer, and to keep us going back," she says.
The solution? A mandatory "opt-in" feature for algorithms on social media platforms.
"We're not asking them to stop; we're demanding that they are obliged to clearly ask us first. And then, for us to be able to turn our algorithms on and off at will," she says.
Radicalisation of young men online an 'urgent challenge': Contos
Chanel Contos emerged on the national scene five years ago with her campaign for consent to be taught in schools.
The advocate says five years on, she now recognises consent education is "fighting an uphill battle" against an "addictive content-producing machine" preaching a contradictory message.
She calls the radicalisation of young men into misogyny online an "urgent challenge", and without immediate action, Australia risks a "generation of young men being entrenched".
"Young men online seeking community, belonging and self-improvement advice are targeted with content that blames women for their misfortune and reinstates harmful and outdated gender roles," she tells the National Press Club.
The pathway goes from something as harmless as a workout video and then takes boys and men "into the manosphere".
"Boys and men have valid concerns about the economy, and their relationships with partners and friends. From these concerns, an industry has jumped onto a market opportunity, and unfortunately, misogyny is at the heart of its business model," she says.
Algorithms 'not doing us a lot of good': Chalmers
Consent advocate Chanel Contos is about to stand up at the National Press Club.
Contos will make the case for reining in harmful algorithms, which she says are exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" content and fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia (we'll have her speech on the blog shortly).
Asked if Australia should consider whether algorithms should be "opt-in", Chalmers says it's clear that the algorithms at work are "not doing us a lot of good".
But he stopped short of backing Contos's call.
"It's hard to mount a credible argument that what we're seeing with social media algorithms is a force for good in our community and our country," he says.
Pushed again, Chalmers invoked Barack Obama as he described social media as becoming about affirmation rather than information.
"It's so divisive and it's so violent," he says.
"I think it would be hard to conclude objectively that we don't have a big problem here. Every country's got it. It's not a problem unique to us."
'No doubt' tax changes contributed to house price downturn: Labor minister
A Labor minister has admitted there's "no doubt" the government's federal budget changes have contributed to house prices falling.
Matt Thistlethwaite said interest rate hikes were the main factor putting pressure on household budgets, as well as higher living costs stemming from war in the Middle East, but he acknowledged the budget changes were adding to the downturn too.
"There's no doubt that our policies are part of a suite of reasons, but we're confident that we've got balance right because the housing market was out of control and we needed to make housing more affordable," he told News 24.
In the budget, Labor wound back capital gains tax discounts for investors and limited negative gearing to existing investments and new builds.
Thistlethwaite said the government was still confident that over the longer term, house prices would grow.
Commonwealth Bank economists yesterday downgraded their housing forecasts and now expect national dwelling prices to fall by around 9 per cent from the cycle's peak.
Asked about Thistlethwaite's remarks, Chalmers told reporters his language was "consistent" with the government's lines.
Chalmers stands by Treasury house price forecasts amid downturn
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is standing by his department's forecasts about the impact the May budget's tax changes will have on house prices.
The budget wound back capital gains tax discounts for investors and limited negative gearing to existing investments and new builds. Treasury forecast the measures would reduce house price growth by 2 per cent.
But an uptick in interest rates, paired with the changes, have been credited for prices falling in almost every capital city in August, according to Cotality.
He stressed Treasury's assumptions in the budget were over a couple of years, not a couple of months.
"It would be unusual to compare outcomes or forecasts from the first couple of months and compare that with the Treasury assumptions over a couple of years," he says.
Chalmers says it would be wrong to attribute softness in the market to "any one factor", such as the government's housing tax changes.
"House prices and auction clearance rates were already softer before the budget. And that's because, as a number of people have pointed out from outside the government, a key driver of that is interest rate movements as well as developments in the economy more broadly."
Impact of war still evident despite 'robust result': Chalmers on national accounts
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is speaking to reporters on the latest national accounts data.
Australia's economy grew 0.4 per cent in the June quarter and 2.1 per cent over the past year.
Chalmers calls this a "robust result" in really challenging international circumstances.
"The Australian economy is robust; it is resilient in the face of global uncertainty and conflict, and that's the main takeout of these, from these national accounts," he says.
He says you can see the impacts of the Middle East war are still evident.

But Antigua and Barbuda, Cabo Verde, Maldives and Timor-Leste are hardly major polluters and don't really need reminding of the perils climate change poses to island nations.
Consent advocate pushes for 'opt-in' algorithms
Consent advocate Chanel Contos is urging the federal government to pursue an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds, as it will be "too easy" for tech giants to design their way around weaker reforms.
Contos will make the case for reining in harmful algorithms, which she says are exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" content and fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia, during a speech to the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday.

In an excerpt of her speech, seen by the ABC, Contos will argue an opt-out system for algorithms would be a "first step", and she congratulates the government for seeking to address the issue.

Anthony Albanese is spending his morning meeting with leaders at the Pacific Islands Forum.
First up was Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr. Ahead of the meeting, the prime minister's office confirmed the extension of direct Qantas flights to Palau.
Qantas will increase direct flights to twice weekly between Brisbane and Koror in the peak season and extend the service through to November 2027.
The service, called the Palau Paradise Express is an agreement between the federal government and Qantas.
The government says more than 15,400 passengers have travelled to Palau since the scheme commenced in 2024.
Housing market 'cyclical': O'Neil
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil says it's clear house prices are softening, as the Commonwealth Bank warns Australia's housing downturn is deepening.
In August, national dwelling prices fell 0.9 per cent, their fifth consecutive monthly decline, according to property data firm Cotality.
That weakness prompted CommBank economists to yesterday downgrade their housing forecasts, predicting national dwelling prices will fall about 9 per cent from their peak this cycle.
O'Neil has told Seven the housing market is cyclical.
"It's clear house prices are softening around the country, and I really recognise for many Australians their house is their most important asset," she says.
"What the CommBank report also shows us is that house prices will continue to grow again, and CBA says that will happen at some stage next year."
Indeed, CommBank is forecasting prices to stabilise and begin recovering during 2027, but it says that expected recovery will be modest.
"National dwelling prices are forecast to rise around 2 per cent over 2027, and that forecast relies partly on CommBank's expectation that the RBA will cut interest rates in May and August next year."

Interior Minister Dobrindt said the perpetrators and organizers of the “hybrid attack” acted on behalf of Russia:

Foreign Minister Wadephul added:

Wadephul announced that Russia’s consulate general in Bonn would be closed on Sept. 18 and that the agreement governing the Russian House in Berlin would be terminated in response to the incident in Leipzig. He also promised continued support for Ukraine and announced tighter controls on Russian citizens entering Germany.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would respond to Berlin’s decision in standard fashion:
“Moscow will respond to all anti-Russian actions. They [the German authorities] invented a pretext. At the same time, Berlin itself is completely stained both by fueling the Ukrainian conflict and by participating in terrorist attacks against civilians… The Russian House had long been bothering them, so they were looking for something to latch onto.”

“We won’t go beyond Rossotrudnichestvo’s jurisdiction, but we wouldn’t be surprised if the principle of reciprocity affects not only the Goethe-Institut in Russia but also, unfortunately, many other bilateral initiatives.”
Russian-German intergovernmental agreements directly link the Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin (as the Russian House is officially known) to the Goethe-Institut’s work in Russia. Why Russia’s jet-powered ‘Geran’ drones are so hard to shoot down, and what Kyiv’s falling interception rate means for the future of the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:10:32 UTC
06:10:32 KST

Why Russia’s jet-powered ‘Geran’ drones are so hard to shoot down, and what Kyiv’s falling interception rate means for the future of the war
Russian forces have changed how they strike Kyiv, launching nearly continuous waves of drone attacks throughout the day rather than only at night, as they did before. The Russian army is also increasingly using jet-powered Geran drones — Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed — which fly much faster than older, propeller-driven models and are harder to shoot down.
The city has settled into an uneasy new rhythm as a result, The New York Times reported. Shopping centers and stores close several times a day because of air-raid alerts, and a growing number of residents are spending their nights in shelters. Locals believe Russia is trying to “spread chaos.” “They want people to flee Kyiv. They want to interrupt our regular life,” one resident told the newspaper.
“Right now, Russia’s tactic is to wear down Ukraine and Ukrainians — first and foremost, our people,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said on Monday that Russian forces had launched more than 1,500 drones over the previous four days, about 800 of them — more than half — jet-powered.
By comparison, Russia fired just 300 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in all of June and about 1,500 of them in July, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on technology.
Along with the numbers, Russia has changed the pattern of the attacks themselves, the BBC reported: the drones come in smaller batches than before, but more often. Russia now sends over three or four jet-powered drones, sometimes as many as 10, roughly every half hour, the BBC said.
On August 27 alone, Kyiv recorded 13 air-raid alerts lasting a combined 15 hours — a record since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Jet-powered drones are harder to shoot down because of their speed. In the winter of 2026, Ukraine was shooting down 95–98% of propeller-driven Shaheds. On August 27, Ukrainian forces shot down 88% of all drones, conventional and jet-powered alike; on August 31, just 79%.
An unnamed Ukrainian government official told The Wall Street Journal that Ukraine already has drones capable of shooting down the newest Geran models, but only a few hundred of them — far short of the thousands it needs.
Ukraine is working to develop countermeasures against jet-powered drones, and sources in the country’s defense industry told the BBC they expect Ukraine to have a counter within the next month.
As Russian strikes on Kyiv intensify, Ruslan Horbenko, a lawmaker from Zelensky’s Servant of the People party, said Kyiv and the Kyiv region could be officially designated front-line areas. The designation brings benefits including war-risk insurance, exemption from mobilization, and wage guarantees for utility workers. A government resolution to that effect has already been drafted, he said.
The war in photographs: Kyiv
Overnight, Russian forces again struck Kyiv and the surrounding region with ballistic missiles and drones, killing 12 people and injuring more than 20 across the region, according to authorities. Six of the dead were employees of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway; they were killed in a strike on a rail depot in Kyiv.

Operations resumed with a Conviasa flight to the Andean city of Valera. Flights to other domestic destinations, including Porlamar on Margarita Island and San Antonio del Tachira near the Colombian border, were also scheduled for the day.

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Violence in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is driving fresh mass displacements, complicating the response to the Ebola outbreak, UN humanitarians said Tuesday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said the hostilities are forcing people to flee their homes, and the insecurity and movement of people hamper disease surveillance and response efforts.
As of Sunday, national health authorities had reported more than 6,100 confirmed Ebola cases and nearly 2,950 deaths.
OCHA said that in Ituri province, local civil society sources reported that at least 37 civilians were killed and more than 35 people abducted during armed attacks in the territory of Mambasa on Saturday. At least 86 civilians were killed in attacks across the territory last month.
In neighboring South Kivu province, the office said its partners reported that clashes in Walungu territory have displaced at least 15,000 people since Aug. 23. Most of the displaced are sheltering with host families and need food, shelter and health care. Fighting is also forcing displacements in parts of North Kivu province.
"Despite these challenges, the UN and its humanitarian partners continue to support the authorities' response," OCHA said.
The International Organization for Migration said it has conducted nearly 23 million health screenings in the DRC and neighboring countries, helping to monitor people's movements, detect potential cases and reduce the risk of cross-border transmission.
The United Nations repeated its call on all parties to protect civilians and facilitate safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access, noting that maintaining access to communities affected by the outbreak remains critical for delivering life-saving assistance and supporting efforts to bring the Ebola outbreak under control.
UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher said "we cannot respond incrementally to an epidemic which is now growing exponentially."
Fletcher, speaking at a virtual briefing hosted by the World Health Organization, called for a sustained, large-scale operation to get ahead of the Ebola virus, adding that people need functioning health services, clean water, sanitation, food, protection and livelihoods. Above all, he said, they need trust.
"Time is not on our side. We have the experience, the tools, extraordinary people risking their lives to stop this epidemic. What we need now is political will, access, and resources. We have beaten Ebola before. And we can do it again," said the relief chief. ■

ALGIERS, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul arrived in Algiers late Monday for a visit focused on strengthening cooperation with Algeria in natural gas, green hydrogen, industrial projects and technology transfer, according to a statement from the Algerian presidency on Tuesday.
Wadephul was received Tuesday by Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, with both sides discussing ways to deepen bilateral relations and advance cooperation in areas of mutual interest, said the statement.
He also held talks with Algerian Minister of Hydrocarbons and Mines Mohamed Arkab on expanding energy sector collaboration, Algeria's Ministry of Hydrocarbons and Mines said in a statement.
The discussions focused on opportunities for German companies to provide expertise, technology and equipment for Algeria's oil, gas, petrochemical, engineering, and infrastructure projects, including seawater desalination.
The two sides also discussed cooperation in natural gas and liquefied natural gas marketing, low-carbon technologies, and the development, production, and marketing of green hydrogen and green ammonia.
For his part, Wadephul described Algeria as a reliable energy partner for Germany and expressed interest from German companies in strengthening their presence in the Algerian market and participating more actively in strategic projects. ■

Congress advances new bill to give US edge in open-source AI race with China

Congress advances new bill to give US edge in open-source AI race with China
Legislation to promote adoption of US open-source models while publicising the risks associated with using their Chinese counterparts
3-MIN READ3-MIN
8
 Listen
The US Congress on Tuesday advanced a new bill that seeks to establish American global leadership in open-source artificial intelligence, an area where China currently dominates, by promoting adoption of US open-source models and publicising risks associated with using their Chinese counterparts.
The legislation was one of several proposals marked up in the US House of Representatives targeting China amid escalating tech competition between the two countries.
Congressional committees “mark up” a proposed bill by reviewing it line by line, debating its merits and voting on changes or amendments before deciding whether to send it for a full House or Senate vote.
Introduced last week, the Open-Source AI Leadership Act, H.R. 10152, would direct the US Department of Commerce to identify barriers to adopting US open-weight models and compile data on their adoption relative to Chinese ones.
Open-weight, or open-source, models are AI models that are released freely over the internet, allowing users with the necessary hardware to download and customise them for their own use.
While leading US AI models including OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are mostly closed-source, meaning that they can only be accessed through official channels, most leading Chinese models are released as open-weight models.

Russian National Suspected in Montenegro Triple Murder Dies by Suicide After Police Standoff
A 30-year-old Russian national suspected of a triple murder at a shooting range in Montenegro committed suicide after opening fire on police officers during an intensive overnight manhunt, local outlet RTCG reported on September 1.
The suspect, Mikhail Nikolaevich Shabunin, was cornered by special police units and army helicopters early in the morning in a forest above the coastal town of Herceg Novi.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian authorities, meanwhile, are searching for convicted serial killer Andrey Kiyko, who escaped a military hospital after being recruited from prison to fight in Ukraine. Serving a 25-year sentence for multiple murders and sexual assaults, Kiyko fled a rehabilitation facility after being wounded on the front line, with officials concealing his disappearance for months before launching a public manhunt.
According to RTCG, the shooting occurred on August 31 at the “Češka Zbrojevka” shooting range near Danilovgrad. Shabunin shot and killed three unarmed employees: Podgorica residents Nemanja Kapor, 20, and Petar Globarević, 24, along with 67-year-old Danilovgrad resident Momir Radonjić, before fleeing the scene with firearms.
Following the killings, Shabunin fled in a victim’s car before taking a taxi from Podgorica to Herceg Novi, RTCG reported. Unable to pay for the ride, the suspect left his passport and phone with the driver before entering a local apartment and ultimately escaping into nearby woods, where special forces isolated him.
Police Directorate officials confirmed that law enforcement and the Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Podgorica are investigating the motive, noting that Shabunin had spent the previous several days at the shooting range, according to RTCG.
Following the incident, the Government of Montenegro declared September 1 and 2 as national days of mourning.
The incident in Montenegro follows the arrest of two former Russian prisoners in Thailand earlier this year for the murder and dismemberment of a Russian businessman. The suspects, who were pardoned for fighting in Ukraine before deserting their military units, reportedly killed the 30-year-old victim over a financial dispute.
