Xi’s Kyrgyzstan and Egypt visits put cooperation at centre of regional ties
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
00:04:17 EEST
06:04:17 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt have placed economic cooperation, infrastructure, trade and people-to-people exchanges at the centre of China’s engagement with two regions linking Asia, the Middle East and Africa.
Xi arrived in Bishkek on August 30 for a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. The trip marked his third visit to Kyrgyzstan and came as Beijing and Bishkek seek closer coordination between their development programmes.
The Kyrgyzstan visit was followed by Xi’s trip to Egypt, where China and Egypt are marking 70 years of diplomatic relations. Xi travelled to Cairo at the invitation of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi. The visit was his second to Egypt as Chinese president.
Together, the two visits presented China’s approach to relations with developing countries through investment, transport links, trade, education and coordination in international organisations.
In a written speech on arrival in Bishkek, Xi described China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation as entering a “golden period” of development. He said the two countries had built their relationship over 34 years of diplomatic ties and had developed a comprehensive strategic partnership.
The economic component formed a central part of his programme.
China has been Kyrgyzstan’s largest trading partner and source of foreign investment for years, according to Xi’s signed article published before the visit. He pointed to the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, the Bedel border checkpoint and expanding direct flights as parts of a transport network connecting the countries.
The railway has particular importance for Kyrgyzstan. Its construction gives the landlocked country another transport corridor linking it with China and Uzbekistan and, through wider networks, markets beyond Central Asia.
Xi connected infrastructure development with plans for cooperation in the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence.
“China will continue to do its best to support Kyrgyzstan in growing its economy and improving people's lives,” Xi wrote before travelling to Bishkek.
He also called for progress on the railway, modernisation of land ports and measures to make cross-border movement of people and goods easier.
The agenda fits with Kyrgyzstan’s National Development Program until 2030 and China’s 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026-2030.
Kyrgyz officials and economists said investment from China had supported infrastructure, energy and industrial projects. Tolonbek Abdyrov, professor of economics and vice rector of the International Higher School of Medicine in Kyrgyzstan, said Chinese investment had created opportunities for the country’s modernisation.
The relationship also extends beyond infrastructure.
China has established one Luban Workshop, four Confucius Institutes and 21 Confucius Classrooms in Kyrgyzstan. The two countries have also signed an agreement to establish cultural centres and have worked together on cultural heritage protection.
Two-way visits exceeded 400,000 in 2025, while 30 pairs of provinces and cities have established sister relationships.
Xi used the Bishkek visit to connect bilateral cooperation with the wider role of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.
The SCO marked its 25th anniversary in 2026. At the organisation’s summit on September 1, Xi proposed a programme centred on development, security, people-to-people relations and global governance.
He called for cooperation in trade, investment, connectivity, energy, artificial intelligence, the digital economy and green industries.
China plans to establish an international cooperation centre for AI applications for SCO countries and a China-SCO port economy cooperation centre in Tianjin. Xi also announced plans for 100 technology cooperation projects with SCO countries over the next three years.
His speech also put education and skills training on the agenda. China plans to establish a China-SCO basic education cooperation centre and continue programmes involving Confucius Institutes and Luban Workshops.
Xi presented dialogue as the basis for managing differences between countries.
The SCO should maintain the principle that countries are equal regardless of size and should address disagreements through consultation, he said.
At the SCO Plus meeting later in Bishkek, Xi expanded that argument to international governance.
“We should ensure equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all countries, regardless of their size, strength and wealth,” he said.
Xi also called for a greater role for developing economies in international institutions and said Global South countries should have greater representation in international affairs.
The SCO now brings together countries accounting for about half of the world’s population and one quarter of the global economy, according to figures Xi cited during the meeting.
His message in Bishkek centred on an organisation based on partnership rather than military alliances.
“We should stay committed to building partnerships rather than alliances, and engaging in dialogue rather than confrontation,” Xi told participants.
From Central Asia, Xi’s diplomatic programme moved to Egypt.
The Egypt visit carries a different historical context but follows a similar focus on development and trade.
China and Egypt established diplomatic relations in 1956. Egypt became the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China. The two countries are marking the 70th anniversary of those ties this year.
Before his arrival, Xi published a signed article in the Egyptian newspapers Al-Ahram, Al-Akhbar and Al-Gomhuria.
“This time, I look forward to renewing the friendship and working together with President El-Sisi to explore ways of cooperation and map out a new blueprint for deepening the China-Egypt comprehensive strategic partnership,” Xi wrote.
Economic cooperation has expanded through trade, industrial investment and infrastructure.
Egypt is one of China’s trading and investment partners in the Arab world and Africa and was among the earlier participants in Belt and Road cooperation.
One centre of that relationship is the China-Egypt Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone, which Xi and El-Sisi promoted during Xi’s previous state visit a decade ago. Chinese companies have also participated in projects including the Central Business District of Egypt’s new administrative capital and the country’s electric light rail network.
Agricultural trade provides another area of cooperation.
Xi pointed to Egyptian oranges entering the Chinese market under China’s zero-tariff policy for African countries that maintain diplomatic relations with Beijing. The measure gives Egyptian agricultural producers access to China’s consumer market while expanding the range of African goods entering the country.
Xi linked future cooperation to Egypt’s Vision 2030 and China’s current five-year development programme.
China has an industrial base, capital, technology and equipment, while Egypt offers resources, a population of more than 100 million and access to markets across Africa, the Middle East and the Mediterranean.
The two governments see those factors as a basis for further cooperation in manufacturing, infrastructure, technology and trade.
“We need to pursue mutual benefit and win-win cooperation and set a benchmark for joint development,” Xi wrote in his article for Egyptian media.
Education and cultural links also form part of the relationship.
Egypt was the first Arab and African country to sign a cultural cooperation agreement with the People’s Republic of China. Chinese is now taught in more than 40 Egyptian secondary schools, while vocational education programmes involving China operate in the country.
Tourism has added another link. The Grand Egyptian Museum has become a destination for Chinese visitors, while an Egyptian civilisation exhibition at the Shanghai Museum drew demand for tickets in China.
Xi called for more cooperation in education, tourism, science, technology, health, sport and archaeology.
The Egypt visit also gives Beijing and Cairo a forum for discussion of regional conflicts and international institutions.
China and Egypt support Palestinian national rights and a political settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Both governments also advocate a larger role for developing countries in international decision-making.
Those positions connect Xi’s message in Cairo with the one he delivered in Bishkek.
In Kyrgyzstan, he called for equal participation in global governance and stronger representation for the Global South. In his article for Egyptian media, he called on China and Egypt to coordinate on peace, development and multilateral affairs.
The two visits also show how China is linking bilateral relationships with wider regional frameworks.
Kyrgyzstan occupies a position on China’s western border and forms part of transport routes across Central Asia. Egypt controls the Suez Canal and connects Africa, the Middle East and the Mediterranean.
China’s cooperation with Kyrgyzstan therefore centres in part on overland connectivity. Its cooperation with Egypt includes industrial development, maritime trade and access between Asian, African and European markets.
Xi’s programme also linked Kyrgyzstan with the SCO and Egypt with China-Arab and China-Africa cooperation.
In his Egyptian article, he described Egypt as an important participant in both frameworks and called for further implementation of China-Arab cooperation programmes and China’s partnership actions with African countries.
The state visits come as China places the Global South at the centre of its international agenda.
Xi used his SCO speeches to argue for sovereign equality, multilateral decision-making and development cooperation. He called for technology and development gains to reach countries at different income levels and for work to narrow digital and artificial intelligence gaps.
“We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides,” Xi told the SCO Plus meeting.
The practical measures announced in Bishkek included technology projects, education programmes and new cooperation institutions.
In Kyrgyzstan, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway remains one of the most visible examples of that approach. In Egypt, the Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone, transport infrastructure and construction projects provide comparable examples of long-term economic engagement.
Xi placed people-to-people contacts alongside those investments.
In both countries, his statements referred to education, cultural exchange and contacts between younger generations as elements of relations that extend beyond government agreements.
The Kyrgyz and Egyptian visits also have symbolic weight because of their anniversaries.
Kyrgyzstan is marking 35 years of independence. China and Egypt are marking 70 years of diplomatic relations. The SCO is marking 25 years since its creation.
Xi used those milestones to set out the next stage of China’s partnerships.
In Kyrgyzstan, his message focused on closer economic integration, transport links and the SCO’s future. In Egypt, he focused on industrial cooperation, trade, cultural exchange and coordination between China and the Arab and African worlds.
“For 70 years, China and Egypt have stood by each other rain or shine,” Xi wrote before the Egypt visit. He said the two countries were beginning a new stage of cooperation based on their previous agreements and development programmes.
His message in Kyrgyzstan carried the same emphasis on continuity.
China, Xi said, was ready to work with Kyrgyzstan to advance cooperation and create new prospects for bilateral relations.
From Bishkek to Cairo, the agenda puts infrastructure, trade, technology, education and diplomatic coordination at the centre of China’s ties with Kyrgyzstan and Egypt.

House passes stopgap bill that pauses changes to federal science grant-making process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:02:06 UTC
06:02:06 KST

A Trump administration effort to give political figures control over a large swath of U.S. science funding is off the table until at least December.
On Tuesday members of the House of Representatives voted 370-48, with 14 members not voting, to adopt a Senate appropriations bill that will continue funding federal agencies until December 11.
In August, as part of the stopgap measure, the Senate agreed not to adopt proposed rule changes from the Office of Budget Management that would give politically appointed bureaucrats authority over federal research grants. If implemented, these changes would break from the current system, in which independent panels of peer reviewers, experts in the field, assess grant requests for funding from the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation and other governmental agencies.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The proposed rule changes have met an outpouring of opposition from the scientific community. Thousands of researchers, including several Nobel laureates, used the public comment period on the proposal to say it would politicize research and destroy U.S. leadership in global science.
The question of whether the proposed rule changes will go further could hinge largely on the outcome of the midterm elections, which will be held in November: Democrats, who are currently favored to win control of the House, have broadly opposed the changes.

Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
Published September 1, 2026last updated September 2, 2026
What you need to know
Below is a roundup of the top headlines on the Iran war and other developments in the Middle East region on Tuesday, September 1, 2026.
- US military says it has launched strikes on Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)
- US President Trump described the strikes as 'large and powerful'
- Iran said the US would 'regret' the latest attacks
- Jordanian military says it intercepted Iranian missiles in Jordanian airspace
- Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq's Kurdistan region also targeted by Iranian attacks
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Iran reports 11 civilian deaths in US strikes
Separate US attacks in southwestern Iran have killed 11 people and injured dozens more, Iranian state media reported on Wednesday.
In Hormozgan province, which straddles the Strait of Hormuz, four people, including a child, were killed after shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a residential home in the costal city of Kuhestak where a wedding was taking place, according to the Iranian Red Crescent. More than 50 people were reported injured.
AFP news agency reported a video shared by an Iranian government account showed extensive debris and damage at what it said was the site of the wedding in Sirik country.
"This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a statement, pointing to previous attacks including a strike on a girls' school in Minab in February that killed 160 people.
Elsewhere, officials in Khuzestan province further to the north said US missile attacks on three locations in the province killed seven people and injured eight.
US officials did not directly address reports of the strike on a wedding, but US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians."
WATCH: Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?
Six months into the Iran war, US military leaders are warning of stretched forces and depleted weapons stockpiles. Does the US have the resources to keep fighting?
Iran's Revolutionary Guards say US bases targeted in Iraq's Kurdistan region
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had launched strikes on US bases with drones and missiles in Erbil, Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, according to state media.
State-run IRNA reported that the IRGC said they had "carried out a coordinated missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil" and had destroyed a maintenance facility, warehouses and the "guidance system of a US surveillance aerostat."
The claims cannot be independently verified. The US military has not yet commented on the matter.
Air alert sirens sound in Bahrain, Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones
Sirens warning of potential aerial threats sounded in Bahrain early on Wednesday amid the latest escalation between the US and Iran.
Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said in a post on X: "A danger is present. The Ministry of Interior calls upon citizens and residents to adhere to calm, head to the nearest safe place, and follow the news through official channels, to safeguard public safety.
Bahrain is home to a major US naval base where the 5th Fleet is headquartered and has previously been targeted by Tehran.
Kuwait, another US ally in the Mideast region, also said it repelled attacks by "hostile" Iranian drones.
US military says it completed strikes on targets in Iran
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that its latest wave of strikes against Iranian military targets has been completed.
"U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a statement.
It went on to say that the strikes came after "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
CENTCOM said there were currently 50,000 US military personnel operating in the Middle East.
Jordan's military says Iranian missiles intercepted
The Jordanian Armed Forces said that 10 ballistic missiles launched from Iran had been intercepted, while another three landed in remote areas.
"Jordan's air defence systems engaged 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them, while three missiles fell in remote areas away from populated centres," a Jordanian military statement stated. Jordan added that no casualties had been reported.
Earlier, US President Donald Trump said that the latest strikes on Iran had been in response to Iranian missile launches at US targets on Monday and attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.
"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.
"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."
He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."
US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back
The United States has launched fresh strikes on targets in Iran as hostilities once again flare up.
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."
"The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump warned.
Earlier, Trump told US broadcaster Fox News that US forces had struck Iranian radars.
“They tried to rebuild their radar because they can’t see anything,” Trump told Fox. “We waited until it was almost built and then we hit it."
An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, located around 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.
Welcome to our coverage
The US military announced it has launched new strikes on targets in Iran. Iran has vowed retaliation.
The Iran war has been fought intermittently for the past 6 months and with the latest round of hostilities, there doesn't appear to be an end in sight to the conflict that is having major global economic repercussions.
Stay with us for updates and analysis on unfolding events in both Iran and the wider Middle East region.

"This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a statement, pointing to previous attacks including a strike on a girls' school in Minab in February that killed 160 people.
Elsewhere, officials in Khuzestan province further to the north said US missile attacks on three locations in the province killed seven people and injured eight.
US officials did not directly address reports of the strike on a wedding, but US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians."

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that its latest wave of strikes against Iranian military targets has been completed.
"U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a statement.

"Jordan's air defence systems engaged 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them, while three missiles fell in remote areas away from populated centres," a Jordanian military statement stated. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.
"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.
"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."
He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."
US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back
The United States has launched fresh strikes on targets in Iran as hostilities once again flare up.
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."
"The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump warned.

An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, located around 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Italian arms dealer sentenced to 18 months in U.S. prison for supplying ammunition to Russia in violation of sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:55:04 UTC
05:55:04 KST

On Aug. 24, a federal court in the Eastern District of New York sentenced Manfred Gruber, a 61-year-old Italian citizen and former commercial director of an Italian arms company, to 18 months in prison for conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws. Gruber pleaded guilty to the charge on March 30.
According to the U.S. Justice Department, Gruber organized the illegal export of more than $540,000 worth of U.S.-made ammunition produced by a Nebraska company and another supplier in Tennessee, routing it through JFK International Airport in New York. The shipments were declared for export to Italy, where the ammunition was required to remain as per official documents. Instead, prosecutors said, the cargo was routed to Russia via Kyrgyzstan.
The case also involved Sergei Zharnovnikov, the owner of a Kyrgyz arms distributor, who previously pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 39 months in prison. A key piece of evidence consisted of correspondence found on Zharnovnikov’s phone in which the men discussed breaking up shipments of 100,000 rounds into smaller orders in order to avoid attracting the attention of customs officials.
Joseph Nocella, Jr., the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said Gruber had been “held accountable for his scheme to send military‑grade ammunition to Kyrgyzstan before reexporting the ammunition to Russia to support its war effort.”
Gruber had served as commercial director of Bignami S.p.A., which bought ammunition for sniper rifles from Nebraska-based Hornady Manufacturing under a U.S. export license, then rerouted the shipments to Russia through Kyrgyzstan, bypassing permit requirements that the ammunition remain in Italy. The Insider previously identified Gruber’s business partners.
From 2022 to 2024, Russian companies including Arsenal, Artemida, Ve-Kasa, Promtekhnologiya, and Tetis received Hornady ammunition. In 2023, Politico Europe found evidence that Hornady ammunition had been used by snipers from the Wagner Group, the Russian state-funded private military company co-founded by the late Yevgeny Prigozhin. The Insider later found that the company’s ammunition was being used by snipers from the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade of Russia’s Pacific Fleet.
Gruber’s case is not an isolated incident. In August 2025, U.S. authorities seized more than $250,000 and dozens of weapons components and accessories after arresting Maxim Larin, a 44-year-old U.S. citizen from Plantation, Florida who owned several small American companies selling firearms parts. On Aug. 25, 2026, the U.S. attorney’s office for the Eastern District of New York accepted Larin’s guilty plea on charges of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the attempted violation of the Arms Export Control Act.
According to prosecutors, Larin and an accomplice in Russia organized shipments of weapons components to Kazakhstan, including trigger mechanisms for semiautomatic firearms, charging handles, and laser rangefinders of the sort used by snipers and artillery spotters.
The investigative bureau Tri Trace Investigations found that from 2009 to 2014 Larin had owned the Russian gun store Shooter’s Shop. In 2012, before leaving the Russian business, he also opened a gun store in the United States. Larin’s former Russian store continues to operate under the iShooter brand. The store’s website has an “international shipping” section listing Express Mail Shipping as its logistics partner. The store’s current owner, Albert Goncharov, is also listed as an employee of Larin’s U.S. company.

Deported Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ‘ashamed’ of support for Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:49:02 UTC
05:49:02 KST

Milo Yiannopoulos, the British far-right commentator who was arrested last week by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Louisiana and deported to the United Kingdom, has broken his silence about the experience, saying that “for the first time I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified”.
Yiannopoulos on Tuesday appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored, a YouTube show presented by Piers Morgan, the British broadcaster and media personality. Yiannopoulos, 41, described the experience in the US as “humiliating and disorientating”, “physically degrading” and “frightening”.
He also said that he was “ashamed” of his previous support for Donald Trump, who has pursued an agenda of mass deportation throughout his second presidency.
“I didn’t really understand the physical reality of how institutionalized the brutality is in America,” he said. “It’s like everybody that’s arrested is an MS-13 gang member, and it hurts a lot more than it looks like on television.”
His remarks came just days after he was deported from the US, after being arrested on Thursday by ICE officers at New Orleans airport.
In a statement last week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, said Yiannopoulos had “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.
Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Trump before he first became US president in 2016. He is a former editor of Breitbart News and later worked to help the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, explore a presidential run in 2024.
The homeland security department said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.
In the Piers Morgan interview, Yiannopoulos disputed the government’s account and denied previously overstaying a visa. He said he is married to an American, and claimed he held a green card that he was “renewing on a two-year basis”.
The Guardian has contacted homeland security and the White House for comment on Yiannopoulos’s remarks.
Yiannopoulos also said that while he was detained, “no one would tell me anything” – a common complaint from people held in ICE custody.
“I don’t think I’ve ever been frightened like that before” he told Morgan. “I think maybe in the past I’ve been a little bit blasé when people talked about their trauma, a little bit cavalier when people talked about stuff kind of lingering with them, but I get it now … I wouldn’t wish it on anyone.”
Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had been supportive of Trump’s crackdown on immigration.
In one post, he wrote: “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering. It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”
In another post, Yiannopoulos had said that California “needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.
During Tuesday’s interview, Yiannopoulos said of his past support for Trump: “If I had any clue that anything remotely like this was even possible, I would never have gotten involved in supporting Trump in the first place and I’m very ashamed that I did.”

MH-139 Reaches Initial Operational Capability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:48:07 UTC
05:48:07 KST

The Air Force’s new nuclear security helicopter, the MH-139A Grey Wolf, achieved initial operational capability in August—a significant milestone in the service’s effort to replace its Vietnam War-era UH-1N Hueys but years later than originally planned.
In an Aug. 31 release, Air Force Global Strike Command said it declared IOC for the Grey Wolf on Aug. 10. IOC occurs when a system can be fielded and maintained by some of its operational units. In the case of the MH-139, that’s the 40th Helicopter Squadron at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.
More units will soon follow. The 37th Helicopter Squadron at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo., opened a new operations facility to support the MH-139 on Aug. 14, setting the stage for helicopters to arrive there in the coming weeks. After that, the 54th Helicopter Squadron at Minot Air Force Base, N.D., is next up to get the Grey Wolf helicopters.
The Air Force first awarded Boeing a $2.4 billion contract for the MH-139—based on the civilian Leonardo AW139—in 2018. It was the first time the service had procured a helicopter directly, and it was the first major acquisition program for Global Strike Command. The first aircraft was delivered in December 2019, and the goal was to achieve IOC by 2021.
The need for the Grey Wolf was and is driven by the aging Huey fleet, whose average age is now past 50 years old. Air Force security forces use the helicopters to patrol and escort convoys around sprawling intercontinental ballistic missile fields that cover a combined 33,600 square miles. The MH-139 can fly farther, faster, higher, and with more weight than the UH-1N.
Originally, the Air Force planned to buy up to 84 Grey Wolves and use them not only for nuclear security, but also for aircrew survival training and contingency response in the Washington, D.C., area, where the 1st Helicopter Squadron flies the Huey.
But the program was beset by delays: Federal Aviation Administration certification presented one holdup, a swath of testing problems emerged, and there were even concerns that the helicopter risked not meeting operational requirements.
The Air Force revamped its plans in 2024, cutting the planned fleet size to 42 aircraft, all for ICBM security, but that drove costs up, triggering a “critical” cost breach and congressional notification under the Nunn-McCurdy Act.
Since then, however, the program has bounced back on several fronts. Congress included $210.3 million in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last July to procure an extra six MH-139s, and in its fiscal 2026 budget, the Air Force increased its objective to 56 aircraft. House lawmakers have since followed by voting to authorize four additional aircraft in their version of the 2027 defense policy bill, which is still well short of becoming law.
Operational test and evaluation, which began in January 2025 and was led by the 550th Helicopter Squadron at Malmstrom, wrapped up in June 2025. A pair of MH-139s flew their first operational mission in January 2026, escorting an ICBM convoy at Malmstrom about 100 miles out and back.

Staving off crisis, Israeli banks reach agreement to keep working with Palestinian counterparts through 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:45:11 UTC
05:45:11 KST

Israel's next government will need to find a solution that will allow Israeli banks to continue working with their Palestinian counterparts after a deal was reached to continue services until the end of 2026, a senior Bank of Israel official said on Tuesday.
Two Israeli banks had been set to halt working with Palestinian banks — Israel Discount Bank opens new tab on September 1 and Bank Hapoalim opens new tab in a month — due to concerns over the risks of associating with possible terrorism financing and money laundering. But after negotiations with the Finance Ministry, the banks have agreed to delay severing ties until the end of 2026, Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Andrew Abir said.
"Then, it will be an issue for the new government to decide who should be carrying on that burden of the business of correspondent banking with Palestinian banks," he told Reuters. "The deadline has been pushed off."
Discount and Hapoalim have been providing correspondent services with Palestinian banks through a series of indemnity waivers signed by Israel's finance minister.
The current minister, Bezalel Smotrich, oversees the waiver mechanism that enables cooperation between Israeli and Palestinian banks. He is against a Palestinian state and has been opposed to signing waivers but has relented on that issue several times due to U.S. and Israeli government pressure.
The waiver lets Israeli banks process shekel payments for services and salaries tied to the Palestinian Authority without the risk of being charged with money laundering and funding terrorism. Without it, Palestinian banks would be cut off from the Israeli financial system.
The Palestinian Monetary Authority estimates that Discount and Hapoalim process 51 billion shekels ($17 billion) a year in transactions for the PA while 90 percent of Palestinian trade — such as food, fuel and medicines — passes through Israel.
"The long-term solution is to get a permanent agent who will provide correspondent bank services between Palestinian and Israeli banks, whether that's Bank Hapoalim and Discount continuing or whether it's a government company that will take over for them. But some form of permanent player to carry out correspondent banking needs to be settled upon," Abir said.
In July, Yahya Shunnar, governor of the PMA, said that over the past decade the PA had built up its anti-money laundering framework to international standards. The United States and the UK, he said, assessed that the PA's "counter-terrorism financing practices meet or exceed international standards when the concern raised is financial integrity risks."
When asked whether the PA could shift to another currency other than the shekel, Abir said it was not likely since "the Palestinian economy is so interlinked with the Israeli economy that, for all purposes, the shekel is the obvious choice of currency that they use."

Austria offers Vienna as venue for Ukraine peace talks
Austria's Chargé d'Affaires and Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, Stefan Pretterhofer, made the statement during the UN General Assembly's general debate on the "Situation in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
"Austria is ready to offer its good offices and host talks in Vienna – on the war in Ukraine and the broader question of the European security architecture," Pretterhofer said.
According to him, the United Nations and the OSCE – both with headquarters in Vienna – could play an important role in the implementation of a ceasefire or a broader peace agreement..
The diplomat called a ceasefire the immediate priority.
"Austria calls for a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire. It should open the way to negotiations between the parties on a just, lasting and comprehensive peace based on the UN Charter and international law," he said.
Austria also emphasized the inviolability of international law and the sovereignty of states, stressing that it is unacceptable to consider illegal occupation and violations of a country's sovereignty as legitimate means of pursuing politics.
Pretterhofer also drew attention to the humanitarian consequences of the war and called for the return of unlawfully transferred and deported civilians, including children, and for international monitors to be granted access to the temporarily occupied territories.
In his address, the Austrian representative also noted that the humanitarian effects of the war extend far beyond Ukraine. In particular, attacks on Black Sea ports and commercial vessels disrupt agricultural exports. This is driving up global food prices, with the greatest impact on countries least able to cope with such consequences.

Expressing deep concern over developments in "the Middle East and around Iran", the SCO member-states including India reiterated the bloc's condemnation of military strikes on Iranian territory that resulted in numerous civilian casualties and significant damage to Iran's economy, said the Bishkek Declaration.India also joined other member-states in expressing condolences over the death of former Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei.This was the second time that the SCO denounced the strikes on Iran after the West Asia war started on February 28, the first in an early March standalone statement that called the attacks unacceptable. India had endorsed that statement too, even though bilaterally it has not explicitly condemned the attacks on Iran the way it has missile and drone strikes on the GCC countries.
India also joined other member-states in expressing condolences over the death of former Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei
However, unlike the Tianjin Declaration last year that too condemned the June 2025 US and Israeli strikes on Iran, the Bishkek Declaration did not name the US and Israel."Such actions violate the principles and norms of international law and the UN Charter and create serious risks to international peace, security and stability," said SCO's Bishkek Declaration.India and others backed Iran's sovereignty and territorial integrity, advocating a resolution to the conflict solely through political and diplomatic means.
In this regard, they welcome all efforts aimed at de-escalating the situation in the region and, as the declaration said, noted that the only possible way to ensure peace and stability in the Middle East is a comprehensive and just settlement of the Palestinian question.PM Narendra Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the margins of the SCO summit in Bishkek on Monday and backed expansion of bilateral economic ties with Tehran, while the Iranian president sought India's help to end the war. After distancing itself from a statement by SCO in June last year condemning Israel's strikes, India has signed on to joint documents by the bloc censuring US-Israel military action against Iran.The Declaration reflected a major Indian concern as it strongly condemned terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, emphasised that "double standards" in the fight against terrorism are unacceptable, and called on the international community to combat terrorism, including the cross-border movement of terrorists.It called for the UN playing a central role by fully implementing relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy in accordance with the UN Charter and the principles of international law to jointly combat all terrorist groups."Member States, reaffirming their firm commitment to combating terrorism, separatism, and extremism, emphasize the inadmissibility of attempts to exploit terrorist, separatist, and extremist groups for selfish purposes. They recognize the leading role of sovereign states and their competent authorities in countering terrorist and extremist threats," said the Declaration.Significantly, targeting use of economic sanctions by the West, the leaders came out in support of an open, fair and non-discriminatory multilateral trading system focused heavily on the framework established by the WTO, while slamming unilateral coercive measures.
"Member States oppose unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to the UN Charter and other norms of international law, the rules and principles of the World Trade Organization, that are detrimental to the interests of ensuring international security, including its food, energy and humanitarian components, and that have a negative impact on the global economy," said the Bishkek Declaration.

UN slashes food aid for occupied West Bank and Gaza amid funding shortfall
International aid organisations are struggling for money as the United States has led a sharp cut in Western donations.
The World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that it is being forced to halve the scope of its assistance in the occupied West Bank due to funding issues.
The United Nations agency said on Tuesday that critical financing constraints mean it must pull back on assistance, reducing its support for 400,000 people to 200,000. International aid organisations across the globe have been struggling for money as the United States has led a sharp cut in support, with other Western nations also reducing donations.
Starting this month, food assistance provided to families in the West Bank in the form of cash, vouchers, food, livelihood programmes and nutritional services will be cut, the WFP said in a statement. A lack of funding is also affecting the WFP’s operations in Gaza, it added.
The UN agency estimates that 900,000 people are food insecure in the West Bank. Its Country Director for Palestine, Shaun Hughes, said the WFP is “prioritising the most vulnerable while cutting assistance to others despite widespread needs”.
In Gaza, the WFP supports 1.5 million people, “including one million who receive monthly food assistance,” it noted.
The agency’s spokesperson for the Palestinian territories, Claire Nevill, told The Associated Press that the agency has started reducing its cash assistance to around 75,000 families in Gaza.
The WFP said the cash value of its assistance for 375,000 people in the Palestinian enclave had been reduced by 40 percent in July.
The world’s leading authority on food insecurity, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, said in July the situation in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in parts of the Palestinian territory last year, but warned conditions were still at crisis levels.
The WFP said it needs additional funding of $386m over the next six months to serve around two million food-insecure people across Gaza and the West Bank.
“We urge the international community to act immediately and step up support for Palestinians,” Hughes said.
The UN launched its 2026 appeal for aid by asking for just half the amount it said it needed, despite humanitarian needs globally being at an all-time high.
UN data showed that the US remained the biggest fund provider in 2025, despite the cuts implemented by US President Donald Trump, but its share shrank from more than one-third of the total to 15.6 percent.

“Russian airspace will effectively be closing”: Zelenskyy warns airlines Russian skies are no longer safe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:40:03 UTC
05:40:03 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines, insurers, and other aviation stakeholders on 1 September that Russian airspace is becoming increasingly dangerous as Ukrainian drones operate deeper inside the country.
The warning comes as Ukraine has increasingly carried out long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia, targeting military, energy, industrial, and other infrastructure. Russian authorities have repeatedly reported temporary airport closures and flight disruptions during drone attacks as part of air defense measures.
“We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine does not intend to threaten civilian aviation or civilian aircraft, but warned that the growing presence of drones over Russia means airlines must account for the risks.
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said.
Zelenskyy accused Russian authorities of failing to properly inform airlines about the risks, saying they have not adequately communicated the growing danger posed by drones in Russian airspace.
“Although the Russian authorities are not properly informing people about this, Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” Zelenskyy said, arguing that Russia’s war against Ukraine is making its own airspace unsafe.
Zelenskyy warned that the growing scale of Ukrainian drone operations over Russia will have to be factored into aviation risks. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
He called on foreign ambassadors in Ukraine and Russia to relay the warning to their governments, and said Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry and other institutions would provide international organizations with information about the risks to Russian airspace.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine closed its skies in 2022. Russia has kept flying
The warning highlights a stark difference between the two countries. Ukraine has kept its airspace closed to civilian aviation since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The risk is familiar to Ukraine. Russian forces have repeatedly attacked Ukrainian airports and aviation infrastructure during the full-scale invasion, making the continued operation of civilian aviation impossible.
Russia is also responsible for the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over occupied eastern Ukraine, which killed all 298 people aboard, showing the danger Russia’s military activities can pose to civilian aviation.
Russia, meanwhile, has continued operating major airports and regular passenger flights despite Ukrainian drones increasingly reaching deep into its territory. EASA has warned that Russian air defenses responding to Ukrainian drone and missile attacks could pose risks to civilian aircraft, including through misidentification, particularly around major airports.
Russian airports increasingly disrupted by Ukrainian drones
Russian authorities have repeatedly restricted or suspended flights at Moscow and other airports during Ukrainian drone attacks. The disruptions have generally come as Russia activates air defenses against drones targeting military, energy, industrial, and logistics infrastructure.
Russia has also moved toward broader restrictions on civilian aviation. In June, Russia imposed new restrictions on light aircraft around Moscow and neighboring regions, while regular passenger and charter flights remained exempt.
The result is a growing disruption to Russian aviation even as Moscow continues to keep its main passenger airspace open: Ukrainian drones are not being used to target civilian aircraft, but their increasing presence is making normal aviation operations more difficult and forcing Russia to restrict or suspend flights during attacks.

Congress Passes Short-Term Funding Bill, Putting DOD’s $1.5T Budget Ask on Hold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:39:04 UTC
05:39:04 KST

With 30 days to go before the end of fiscal 2026, Congress passed a continuing resolution Sept. 1 to extend current spending levels through Dec. 11—putting on hold the Pentagon’s request for $1.5 trillion in spending authority.
The House of Representatives and Senate had previously passed continuing resolutions, or CRs, with different end dates, but the House agreed to the Senate’s timeline in a 370-48 vote on Sept. 1. President Donald Trump is expected to sign the bill into law.
Under a CR, some or all of the federal government is funded at the previous fiscal year’s levels.
As military and civilian leaders frequently note, CRs typically don’t allow for new programs to start, delaying contracts and slowing training events. Yet CRs are now the rule, and years when the military has a budget on time are rare. According to the Government Accountability Office, this will be the 38th time in 50 years that the Defense Department will begin the fiscal year with a temporary spending measure.
But this year’s impact could be greater than most, because of the scale of increase the Pentagon is seeking. The Pentagon’s budget request for ’27 is $1.5 trillion, but by extending the baseline 2026 budget, it will be working with budget of $838.5 billion, 44 percent less than it wanted.
Funding included in 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last summer by a Republican-only majority using a process called reconciliation is not covered by the CR. Because most of the funding for the Golden Dome for America missile defense shield was included in the reconciliation bill, the program now faces a crisis. Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein warned last month that “a CR doesn’t help me under Golden Dome because I don’t have a topline to fall back to.”
The Air Force’s F-15EX program faces a similar conundrum. Its fiscal 2026 procurement was almost entirely funded through reconciliation; under the CR, it will start 2027 with a topline of $115 million, less than 5 percent of the $2.65 billion officials asked for.
Congress appears unlikely to approve the Pentagon’s full $1.5 trillion request, which the White House divided into two parts: $1.15 trillion through the usual appropriations process and $350 billion through the reconciliation process.
House appropriators advanced a base spending measure in June with $1.07 trillion for defense, but their Senate counterparts have yet to agree on a topline. And neither chamber has made any meaningful movement on the $350 billion reconciliation request.
The House did approve the framework for a much smaller reconciliation package, including just $60 billion for defense, but lawmakers say that money is meant to address supplemental needs to replenish the department for costs associated with the Iran war, rather than 2027 budget asks. Some top Republicans have suggested they will try for another reconciliation bill after the midterm elections to address the ’27 budget, but it’s unclear if they will be able to get even the current package across the finish line because of intraparty disagreements about how to pay for it.
Defense budget watchers have told Air & Space Forces Magazine they remain extremely skeptical about the outlook for the wished-for $1.5 trillion budget. Byron Callan of Capital Alpha Partners suggested in a recent newsletter that the base budget for 2027 may not clear Congress “until spring 2027,” six or more months late.
That would leave defense officials little time to obligate all that money. In years with longer CRs, the GAO has noted, “activities and programs can face bottlenecks, such as with the capacity of contracting offices to solicit and issue contracts or the ability of vendors to complete projects.”

UN says Nepal flood debris tops 2.2M tonnes as deaths, missing mount

2026-09-01

mer

The UN said Tuesday that Nepal’s flood response was entering a new phase as deaths and missing people mounted and preliminary assessments put debris at more than 2.2 million tonnes.
“Our colleagues tell us that the response to last week’s flash floods is entering a new phase, with authorities intensifying relief efforts and recovery operations,” UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told a news conference.
Dujarric said authorities had recovered more than 1,000 bodies, while 3,900 people remained unaccounted for.
“Nearly 12,000 have been rescued so far,” he added.
“Nearly 3,500 people are now living in 27 displacement sites across the hardest-hit districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa,” Dujarric said.
Many are sheltering in schools, disrupting children’s education, he added.
Citing the UN Development Programme, Dujarric said a preliminary assessment estimated that at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris had been left along the most affected river system.
That included approximately 556,200 tonnes of building debris, based on satellite assessments covering more than 2,300 damaged buildings, he said.
The floods also damaged energy infrastructure, knocking out 11 hydropower stations and one solar plant, representing about 431.1 megawatts of capacity, according to Dujarric.
He said 15 hydropower projects under construction, which would have added another 470 megawatts, were also damaged.
Dujarric said access remained the main challenge, with more than 40 bridges destroyed and sections of the main highway blocked.
Remote communities were relying on army helicopter flights for supplies, he added.
Dujarric also warned of growing public health risks from “overcrowded shelters, contaminated water and damaged health facilities.”
He said the conditions put people, particularly women and children, at greater risk of disease during the monsoon season.
Official data from Nepal and China showed Tuesday that the death toll from flash floods and mudslides in the Himalayan border region had surpassed 1,050.
The data showed more than 4,000 people, including hundreds of foreigners, remained missing.

Why Is Nepal So Vulnerable to Flooding?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:24:28 UTC
05:24:28 KST

Catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet is laying bare the risks mountain villages stand to face amid human-induced global warming.
Maheshwar Dhakal, Nepal’s climate change chief in the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment explicitly blamed climate change for the flooding, while the country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal urged world leaders to undertake a "global effort" to tackle climate change.
"We'd ask the world... to take climate change as one of the major challenges that Nepal and its citizens face, and this has to be a global effort," Khanal said. "We request the global community to come together and preserve the Himalayan ecosystem."
The death toll from catastrophic flooding at the Nepal-Tibet border has now surpassed 1,000, with more than 4,000 people still missing.
The country has seen a number of deadly climate events and natural disasters in recent years. Landslides and flooding devastated the region in 2012 and 2017, meanwhile in 2015, a 7.8 earthquake killed close to 9,000 people and triggered more than 20,000 landslides across 14 districts of Central and Western Nepal.
While it’s too early to know exactly how climate change might have contributed to this August’s disaster, experts say that as our planet continues to warm extreme weather events are only going to become more frequent—especially in climate vulnerable nations like Nepal. The United Nations has warned that millions of people in the Himalayan region face severe risks from future glacial floods in the coming years.
Why is Nepal so vulnerable to extreme flooding?
Nepal has a complex topography—ranging from low-lying planes to some of the world’s highest peaks. Last week’s flooding was triggered by a landslide, which caused a glacier to fall, sweeping rocks and melted water into a number of villages downstream.
“These landscapes up in the high Himalayas are very dynamic,” says Göran Ekström, professor of earth and environmental sciences at Columbia University. “There's a lot of erosion going on. There were landslides there before there was global warming, but global warming has been speeding up that erosional process, and so everything is happening faster, including the number of big landslides up there.”
Over the decades, economic activity has concentrated in riverbank towns and villages below—putting those growing communities at risk.
“Economic development has increased along the rivers. Tourism has expanded. A growing number of hydropower facilities have been built,” says Rajiv Ghimire, lecturer at the University of Michigan’s school for environment and sustainability.
That means that the area where the floods occurred has become far more populated than it once was. “They have always had these flooding events,” says Ekström. “It's just that now we have a lot more people and infrastructure in these steep valleys. What 100 years ago maybe would have killed dozens of people now kills hundreds of thousands of people.”
How can Nepal prepare for future climate disasters?
Nepal lacks early warning systems that might have made evacuations easier. Mathias Vuille, professor of atmospheric and environmental sciences at the University at Albany, SUNY, notes that, in Switzerland, a landslide and glacial collapse buried a small village last year—but only one person was killed thanks to warning systems.
“We know about the threat, and we're not completely helpless,” says Vuille. “We can adapt, and while we can't prevent the process from occurring, we can limit the impacts again, mostly by setting up these warning systems, and having the right plans in place.”
Ghimire stresses the necessity of thinking about the climate risks when it comes to building in the future. “Himalayan mountains are fragile, so we need to anticipate situations like this as we are building infrastructure,” he says.
Adaption measures will only become more important in a warming world. Nepal produces less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet is among one of the most climate vulnerable nations in the world. The Himalayan region is warming nearly twice as fast as the global average, leaving Nepal vulnerable to more crises in the face of retreating glaciers and thawing permafrost.
“When we take away the glaciers, we are disturbing the steady state of equilibrium that has existed,” says Ekström. “So for places like Nepal and other places around the world…where the glaciers are disappearing, they are having more landslides because glaciers have been stabilizing the landscape. So we should expect more of these events.”

Kokkinakis formally withdrew from the season's last grand slam after being unable to take the court for his scheduled first-round clash with Spanish wonder boy Rafael Jodar because of an ankle sprain.
The Australian suffered his latest injury in Cincinnati two weeks ago and has been racing the clock to be fit for the Open ever since.
He ran out of time and, after a decade battling endless back, shoulder, abdominal, knee and arm injuries, Kokkinakis admits he is losing patience.
"It is a possibility for sure," the 30-year-old told AAP when asked if his US Open career might be over.
"I'm not going to say never. The thing is, I feel like the tennis part, I've still got a lot of good tennis left in me.
"On the limited matches that I've played, I've shown that I'm more than good enough to still compete and then beat some good players.
"But, to be honest, I'm sick of going into tournaments not feeling like I can do it physically and everyone asks me how my body is."
The 30-year-old used — or "wasted" — the fifth of nine injury-protected ranking entries available to him to make the US Open draw.
The one-time Roger Federer slayer now plans on continuing his recovery and trying to be fully fit for the Australian summer.
"I want to go into it being confident in myself and, if I do win, give myself a chance to back up and try and play again," Kokkinakis said.
"That's always the thing. So it's about feeling strong in myself.
"I'll definitely obviously give the next Aussie a crack and see where I'm at after that."

It said German authorities blamed Russia without presenting evidence and announced sanctions over what Berlin called Moscow’s “escalating hybrid attacks.”
The measures include closing Russia’s Consulate General in Bonn by September 18 and terminating a 2011 Russian-German agreement covering cultural and information centres, which includes the Russian House in Berlin.
The Russian ambassador rejected the allegations, calling the measures an “unprecedented escalation” in bilateral relations and warning they would have consequences for which Germany would bear full responsibility.
“He emphasised that the hastily concocted provocation at Leipzig Airport serves exclusively the goals of the Kiev regime, the militaristic wing of the European political class, and the magnates of the military-industrial complex interested in fuelling the Ukrainian conflict,” the statement said.

“Both the Russian House and our Consulate General in Bonn have long been harassing the ruling elite. Now they've come up with a pretext. Well, they'll get a fitting response,” she emphasised.

Desalination crisis explained: what shut the plants, and could Israel run out of water?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:12:06 UTC
05:12:06 KST

A large share of Israel’s water now comes from seawater desalination, a field in which the country is considered a global pioneer. But since Saturday, most of Israel’s major Mediterranean desalination plants have been shut down because of unusually turbid seawater, forcing authorities to cut water supplies to farmers in the Negev and ask municipalities to stop watering public gardens.
For now, officials say household water supplies are not expected to be significantly affected, although disruptions have already been reported in some places, including Be'er Sheva.
So what caused the shutdown, how much water is Israel losing and why can microscopic algae disable some of the country’s most important infrastructure?
How much water does Israel use?
During a typical summer day, Israel consumes about 3.9 million cubic meters of water, including agricultural use.
The shutdown of the desalination plants created a potential shortfall of roughly 85,000 cubic meters per hour. In practice, cuts to agricultural water supplies amounted to about 300,000 cubic meters a day.
Danny Sofer, acting head of national water company Mekorot, said the system was forced to rely heavily on Israel’s natural water sources after five desalination plants stopped operating.
“Because five desalination plants stopped working, we activated our entire natural water system, which brings us to about 90% of our summer supply capacity,” he said.
“In winter, nobody would have noticed the problem, because consumption is about 50% of the summer level. In summer, we cannot fully overcome it.”
Which desalination plants shut down?
Israel operates six large Mediterranean desalination plants: Ashkelon, Palmachim, Sorek A, Sorek B, Ashdod and Hadera. Of those, only Hadera remained operational during the disruption. Israel also has a desalination plant in Eilat.
Sorek A and Sorek B briefly returned to operation Monday night before the Water Authority announced Tuesday morning that they had been shut down again. Energy Minister Eli Cohen later said Sorek A and Palmachim would be restarted.
What caused the shutdown?
A preliminary investigation by researchers at Israel Oceanographic and Limnological Research points to a bloom of microscopic algae, apparently originating near the Nile Delta.
Satellite images showed large algal blooms in the area, while eastern Mediterranean currents can carry material northward and eastward from the Nile toward Israel.
“It would not be surprising if something that bloomed in the Nile Delta also reached southern Israel,” said Alon Zask, CEO of Israel Oceanographic and Limnological Research.
He noted that Ashkelon, Israel’s southernmost Mediterranean desalination plant, was the first to shut down, fitting that possible pattern.
The problem is that the algae are extremely small and may pass through the filters used at the entrances to desalination facilities.
Algal blooms are a natural phenomenon influenced by weather, sea currents and the amount of organic material in the water. They generally develop over time before collapsing, after which the organic matter they produce decomposes.
Scientists, however, cannot always determine why a particular bloom emerges at a specific place and time.
What kind of algae are they?
Prof. Tamar Guy-Haim of the National Institute of Oceanography said researchers believe the organisms belong to a group known as picophytoplankton.
“We are in the preliminary stages of characterizing the algae,” she said, adding that researchers are working with Prof. Edo Bar-Zeev of Ben-Gurion University.
“We believe it is probably cyanobacteria, small photosynthetic bacteria that are a natural part of the ecosystem and form the base of the food web.”
Researchers have not yet identified the exact species and are awaiting molecular test results.
The algae are not believed to be toxic through food or contact, and beaches have therefore remained open.
How does desalination actually work?
Desalination removes dissolved salts from water to produce water suitable for drinking, agriculture and other uses.
Modern Israeli plants largely rely on reverse osmosis. In the process, salty water is pushed at very high pressure through membranes that allow water molecules to pass while blocking salts.
About half of the seawater entering the system becomes desalinated water. The remainder becomes concentrated brine and is discharged back into the sea.
Technological advances in membrane performance and energy recovery have sharply lowered the cost of reverse osmosis, making it far more energy-efficient than older evaporation-based methods.
The Water Authority says water produced by Israel’s seawater desalination plants is of very high quality and must meet standards stricter than basic drinking-water requirements before entering the national system.
Who is being hit hardest?
For now, farmers in southern Israel are bearing the brunt of the shortage.
Growers were told to stop using desalinated water for irrigation, and some say their taps have effectively run dry.
Roy Yosef, a farmer from Be’er Milka who has grown tomatoes and cherry tomatoes for 15 years, warned that even a short interruption could destroy crops in the Nitzana region.
“Never before have they shut off agricultural water,” he said. “We are the main suppliers of tomatoes in Israel for the holidays.”
“Twenty-four hours without water can already cause irreversible damage. More than that? The entire crop dies.”
Doron Hevel, another Be’er Milka farmer who grows about 65 dunams of tomatoes and cherry tomatoes, described the situation as “a survival event.”
“We are at the peak of the season,” he said. “A medium-sized farm invests about NIS 2 million in the ground, and there will be no way to get that money back.”
Was Israel warned this could happen?
Yes.
A State Comptroller report published in November 2024 found that between 2007 and the end of 2023, there were 14 incidents in which seawater contamination forced desalination plants to stop production.
Shutdowns lasted anywhere from several hours to five days.
About 57% of the incidents were caused by microbial contamination, 29% by fuel and oil pollution and 14% by turbidity linked to storms and an earthquake.
The comptroller recommended that the Health Ministry conduct periodic surveys of algal toxins and other toxins released into the water, and develop a plan for coping with such events.
Can future shutdowns be prevented?
Experts say probably not completely.
Prof. Edo Bar-Zeev of Ben-Gurion University’s Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research said Israel needs contingency systems capable of keeping water production running during exceptional events.
“In my opinion, it is impossible to completely prevent events like this,” he said. “What must be done is to prepare backup solutions in advance.”
He warned that the current episode could be a preview of a much more severe threat: a large oil spill.
“This event is only a teaser for similar events that could happen in the future, especially oil incidents,” Bar-Zeev said. “A major oil spill will happen. The only question is when.”
Such an event, he warned, could shut desalination plants for much longer, potentially for months.
“Oil reaching the desalination plants would be a tragedy,” he said. “There is currently no contingency plan for that scenario either. The current contingency plan is simply to take the switch at the desalination plants and turn it off.”

Japan Modifies ASM-3 Anti-Ship Missile to Destroy Air Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:10:24 UTC
05:10:24 KST

Japan is likely to modify the ASM-3 supersonic anti-ship missile into an ultra-long-range air-to-air missile for intercepting aerial targets.
The Japanese Ministry of Defense announced its plans to procure air-to-air missiles for 2027 in a budget document.
Converting the anti-ship missile into an air-to-air interceptor is intended to create a means of countering long-range enemy aircraft — such as long-range radar detection aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, and strategic bombers.
Thanks to its ramjet engine, the upgraded air-to-air version of the missile will be capable of reaching an estimated range of 400-600 km.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries began developing the basic ASM-3 anti-ship missile in 2003 to replace the obsolete ASM-1 and ASM-2.
The development program lasted more than a decade, and in 2017, test launches from the decommissioned destroyer Shirane confirmed the new weapon’s performance characteristics.
However, the initial version of the missile, with a range of 200 km, never entered serial production because the Japanese Ministry of Defense deemed this range insufficient to penetrate modern naval air defense systems and demanded upgrades.
As a result, an improved version, the ASM-3A, was developed; by reducing weight and optimizing fuel consumption, its range was increased to 400 km or more.
In its basic anti-ship version, the ASM-3 is 6 meters long, has a body diameter of 350 mm, and a total launch weight of approximately 940 kg.
The missile is equipped with a penetrating high-explosive warhead weighing about 150 kg, designed to engage medium- and large-displacement surface ships.
The primary platform for the ASM-3 family of missiles is the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s F-2 fighter jets.
It should be noted that, starting in 2027, the Japanese Ministry of Defense will begin the procurement process for AARGM-ER anti-radar missiles to counter Chinese air defense systems.

Large
Instead of granting the discharge, IAF initiated a court of inquiry
NEW DELHI: The principal bench of Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) has converted the order of dismissal of a non-commissioned IAF officer, who confessed to being gay, into a routine discharge.The bench, headed by Justice Rajendra Menon and Justice Rasika Chaube, ruled that substituting dismissal with routine discharge prevents lasting career stigma for the ex-officer seeking employment outside the armed forces.The non-commissioned IAF officer, who had served about 10 and a half years, had applied for a compassionate premature discharge in 2024 to settle down with his partner, disclosing his relationship in an application.Instead of granting the discharge, IAF initiated a court of inquiry. The inquiry concluded he had breached discipline and risked national security by entering into a relationship with a foreigner. The court of inquiry also found him guilty of travelling abroad (Thailand and Sri Lanka) without permission. He was subsequently dismissed from service earlier this year.
He then approached AFT principal bench not to challenge IAF's disciplinary right, but to request "dismissal" be changed to a "discharge" so he could seek future civilian employment.
The bench held that while dismissal is warranted when rules are breached, exceptions must be considered in this case. "The respondents could have granted discharge to the applicant, but in the garb of maintaining discipline they dismissed him. The effect of both is identical inasmuch as the respondents do not want the service of the applicant."

Canada’s Carney says US must ‘start being serious’ to resolve trade dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:08:25 UTC

Canada’s Carney says US must ‘start being serious’ to resolve trade dispute
Carney and Trump continue to trade barbs amid ongoing threats against Canadian sovereignty and economic disputes.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has reprimanded the United States for what he describes as a flippant approach to the ongoing trade dispute between the two countries.
On Tuesday, Carney hit back against a series of insults and disparaging remarks from US President Donald Trump and his officials, saying that talks can proceed once Washington takes a more serious approach to the issues at hand.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3With the US and Canada locked in a trade war, fears of a recession lurk
- list 2 of 3Ontario’s Doug Ford prods Trump with sign rejecting ‘Lake America’ name
- list 3 of 3Google Maps renames Lake Ontario after Trump’s decree on ‘Lake America’
“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa. “It’s not constructive, but that’s their democracy.”
The Liberal Party leader’s remarks come as tensions flare once again between the US and Canada, which have historically had tight relations.
But Trump’s second terms have caused those ties to fray. Since returning to office in 2025, Trump has imposed a series of tariffs on Canadian products, prompting retaliatory actions.
The latest round of tariffs came on August 22, when negotiations between the two countries fell through.
As a result, 50 percent tariffs were imposed on roughly $20bn worth of Canadian goods. Canada has pledged to respond with tariffs on US goods, worth roughly the same dollar amount, starting on September 8.
In the aftermath of the failed negotiations, Carney blamed the impasse on last-minute US demands.
He accused the Trump administration of seeking to limit Canada’s ability to cement trade deals with other countries and of requesting changes to laws protecting Canada’s French language and culture.
Carney also said Trump’s team attempted to push an asymmetrical deal that would damage Canada’s industries.
“Canada’s a sovereign state. We will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals with,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday. He added, “Of course, we’re not going to accept those terms.”
The trade war between the two countries has prompted a surge of nationalism in Canada.
A June poll from the research firm Abacus Data found that national pride surged 12 points in two years, reaching 77 percent this year.
Carney has faced pressure not to yield to US demands. In addition to imposing steep tariffs, the Trump administration has also pushed Canada to cede its sovereignty and become a “51st state” within the US.
Trump has also taken symbolic actions designed to assert US dominance over the two countries’ shared border region. On August 27, the US president signed an executive order directing federal entities to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.
“They are one of the worst countries in the world to deal with,” Trump said of Canada in a recent radio interview.
Other cabinet-level officials in the Trump administration have echoed Trump’s remarks disparaging Canada.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the news outlet CNBC that Canada’s economy is ill-equipped to handle a trade war with the US, and he blamed Carney for escalating the situation.
“Well, I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are,” Bessent said on Monday.
Of Carney, he added, “He came to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump agenda. He was 20 points behind in the polls. And then he started this. And it’s unfortunate that he’s not doing what’s best for the Canadian people.”
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, meanwhile, posted an image of two female Canadian cadets on social media, in an apparent effort to mock the country’s armed forces.
“This is real,” he wrote beneath the image of the two women, alongside an emoji of the Canadian flag.
Hegseth, a former TV host, has frequently castigated efforts to include women, LGBTQ people and racial minorities in the military as “woke” distractions from the US military’s core mission.
When reporters asked Carney to respond to such messages, he replied that such comments were “beneath” the officials’ office.
“Our plan has always been standing up for Canada, first and foremost, here at home,” Carney said.
