Russian investigators drop murder case against Putin-linked businessman Ilya Traber, partner Vladimir Danilenko, and two others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:45:04 UTC
04:45:04 KST

Russian investigators drop murder case against Putin-linked businessman Ilya Traber, partner Vladimir Danilenko, and two others
Vladimir Danilenko, a longtime partner of St. Petersburg businessman Ilya Traber, has been released from pretrial detention, according to sources cited by the St. Petersburg-based news outlet Fontanka, the business news outlet RBC, and the state news agencies RIA Novosti and TASS.
Danilenko, like Traber, had been suspected of involvement in the 2020 murder of St. Petersburg businessman and municipal deputy Alexander Petrov, known as the “boss of Vyborg.”
According to Fontanka, the case against Danilenko was dropped due to his lack of involvement in the murder.
In addition, the Investigative Committee dropped the cases against everyone named in the Petrov murder investigation, sources told RBC and Fontanka. Investigators found contradictions in the testimony of former prisoner of war Igor Lykov, which was “inconsistent,” RBC’s sources said. The case had been built in part on that testimony.
Besides Traber and Danilenko, Fontanka said, the case named Alisultan Nadirbegov and Said Saladinov, both natives of Dagestan, whom investigators believed had carried out Petrov’s killing. Everyone named in the case is now entitled to exoneration and compensation for the emotional distress and financial losses caused by their time in custody.
Ilya Traber is a businessman considered to have been close to Russian President Vladimir Putin early in the latter’s career in St. Petersburg. In the 1990s, he controlled the port of St. Petersburg and the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal — the largest oil-products transshipment facility in the Baltic region.
Traber was detained on June 17 on suspicion of involvement in Petrov’s murder. He was taken to Moscow the same day, and a court ordered him held in pretrial detention. His longtime business partner, Vladimir Danilenko, was sent to a detention center soon afterward. In late August, the Investigative Committee dropped the case against Traber “due to his complete lack of involvement” in the murder. He was released from custody and returned to St. Petersburg.

Silicon Valley fascism is waging war on democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:43:41 UTC
04:43:41 KST

analysis
The Nerd Reich wants to 'destroy' democracy, and its mask has slipped
"Billionaires have become radicalised against democracy," the American independent journalist Gil Durán tells the ABC.
"We have to realise how much power we have, and to stop being tuned out from the very real threat we face from a billionaire class that has gone off the edge of sanity into an altered reality.
"But we also need to realise where we're at, how we got here, and who's paying for it all.
"It's not just Trump anymore. It's a regime. And it's a regime that is funded and supported and strengthened by the oligarchs of Silicon Valley."
That is Durán's warning to Australians.
He was speaking to the ABC about his new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy.
It describes how tech billionaires and venture capitalists in the US have cultivated a virulently anti-democratic ideology for decades and how they're using technology to remake today's world, with consequences for everybody.
And it is resonating with American readers, debuting as an instant New York Times bestseller after its release on August 18.
"America has been revealed as highly vulnerable to destruction," the book explains.
"Pushing it to the brink wasn't particularly difficult. It required only enough wealthy and influential people who were willing to fund it, or at least go along with it quietly.
"Democracy's enemies specialise in long-term strategies, and they have enough money to operate in perpetuity; they are scheming for global control."
Replace democracy with corporate dictatorship
We're all short of time.
We appreciate books that help us quickly understand the ideas driving contemporary politics and the technological future of countries like the United States and Australia.
And this book is one of them.
Loading...
It tells the story of how anti-democratic, anti-government, and aggressively anti-tax ideas were fused and incubated in Silicon Valley in the 1980s and 1990s, and how strange books like The Sovereign Individual (1997) inspired a generation of new tech entrepreneurs to build the technology to start undermining national governments and their currencies.
It reveals how decades ago, influential figures in Silicon Valley began describing democracy as a flawed operating system that had to be replaced by a corporate dictatorship.
It explains how, back in 1999, Peter Thiel (the co-founder of PayPal and Palantir) was predicting that official Washington DC would be too dumb to understand the encryption technology that was emerging out of Silicon Valley at the dawn of the millennium, and that "incredible technological forces" were pushing the world in the direction of digital currency and limited government.
It records how some female journalists, like Paulina Borsook, sounded the alarm early about the toxic culture emerging from Silicon Valley's chatrooms in the 1990s, but the mainstream US tech press dismissed and ridiculed them.
Borsook's book Cyberselfish (2000), which fell out of print, is now being called "prophetic" and is being republished this month, after 26 years.
And it details how Silicon Valley billionaires want to carve up the world into thousands of tax-free "economic zones" and create their own sovereign jurisdictions.
Foreign Correspondent's recent story on Próspera, the "libertarian utopia" on a Caribbean island off the coast of Honduras, is part of the same story of Silicon Valley's yearning to "exit" the world we live in.
Loading...
A philosophy of 'exit'
Ultimately, Durán's book describes how a lot of the behaviour and investment decisions of Silicon Valley's influential venture capitalists in recent decades can be explained by their philosophy of "exit".
That is, it explains how they want to "exit" (i.e. abandon) democracy, with its laws and regulations and fiat currencies, and create new forms of government and new jurisdictions (in space, the ocean, on land, and in the cyber world) that use digital currencies.
"It doesn't make sense for these billionaires, the most successful and wealthy people in our society … to be investing in this massive disruption like this unless they are zealots who believe it's time to completely collapse the world order," Durán told the ABC.
"In my book, I tell the story of this idea, that that's exactly what they see as necessary and inevitable."
And the same names keep popping up in the book.
Names like Peter Thiel, Curtis Yarvin, Elon Musk, Marc Andreessen, Mark Zuckerberg, Balaji Srinivasan, Sam Altman, and JD Vance, among others, many of whom spent years in Silicon Valley's cauldron.
They would create culturally potent companies like PayPal, Palantir, LinkedIn, Tesla, Uber, Lyft, Airbnb, Facebook, Instagram, and Amazon, and technologies like Bitcoin and Coinbase.
"In 2025, the tech industry revealed its true face," Durán writes.
"Devoid of any moral scruples or loyalty to democratic principles, many of Silicon Valley's most well-known figures chose to openly ally themselves with a president who would soon, with their help, check every box in the authoritarian playbook.
"Instead of filing lawsuits against the administration, tech giants lavished him with money and support.
"As his administration carried out a shock-and-awe effort to destroy the pillars of American democracy, the most powerful and prominent figures in tech stood behind him," he writes.
An open enemy of democracy
Durán writes simply and clearly.
He is a former opinion editor for The Sacramento Bee and editorial page editor for The San Francisco Examiner.
He is an independent journalist who runs The Nerd Reich, a newsletter about "tech authoritarianism, billionaire extremism, the Network State and the meta politics of California".
Politically, he used to work as a press secretary for California's Democratic governor Jerry Brown and he served as Kamala Harris's communications director when she was California attorney-general.
But he does not hold back criticism of US Democrats.
"Democratic leaders continue to operate as if the tech sector has not become an open enemy of democracy itself," he writes in the book.
"They speak of AI and billionaires and crypto in flattering and friendly terms, no doubt hoping to remain beneficiaries of campaign checks from tech billionaires.
"While the champions of tech fascism see the Republican Party as the best vehicle for its hopes, they also understand the inherent corruptibility of the Democratic Party, which also serves its wealthy donors more than it serves anyone else."
We can have billionaires or democracy
The final chapter of his book is a call to arms.
"We can have billionaires, or we can have democracy. We cannot have both," he writes.
And he tells the ABC that the growing backlash in the United States against data centres and AI shows people do not like the future tech billionaires have been forcing on everyone.
He said normally in US politics new technology would be promoted in terms of how many jobs it would create, not destroy, but that wasn't the story that these tech companies had been telling investors.
"The oligarchs of Silicon Valley have done their best to terrify everybody, and so what's happening right now is absolutely logical and rational and reasonable," he said.
"The data centres are viewed, I think, as a physical manifestation of billionaire power on the land that's become this bogeyman, this monster, this alien invasion that arrives in your community to suck up your water and pollute your air and eat up your land, all for the promise that it will fuel a technology that will kill your job and possibly wipe humanity off the face of the planet.
"What's not to love?" he jokes grimly.
And he said data centre protests in the US had become a focal point for regular people from all walks of life to come together as a community to fight billionaire power and learn what was happening in neighbouring counties.
"The billionaire city in Solano County, for instance, Republicans are even more opposed to it than Democrats are," he said.
"Similarly for crypto. Some of Trump's most fervent supporters got completely robbed by putting money into these crypto schemes, so on a very personal level they know that this is bad.
"We're seeing movements like "Purge Palantir" to get Palantir out of our government, our cities, our hospitals and stores.
"And then there's "DeFlock", which is pushing back against "Flock" cameras [automated licence plate readers] and the new surveillance state where everything will somehow be safe and secure by all of us being under surveillance.
"People are waking up."

Putin meets Pashinyan for the first time since Armenia’s latest election and asks him to choose soon: the EU or the EAEU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:43:02 UTC
04:43:02 KST

Putin meets Pashinyan for the first time since Armenia’s latest election and asks him to choose soon: the EU or the EAEU
Russian President Vladimir Putin met with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek. It was their first in-person meeting since Armenia’s parliamentary elections in June.
During the meeting, Putin again raised the subject of Armenia’s push to join the European Union. He called it “the country’s legitimate right,” but said it “creates complications, including those stemming from membership in the Eurasian Economic Union.”
Putin said that “the sooner Armenia decides on the question of joining the EU, the better,” because “Moscow needs to understand how to build the relationship going forward.”
Putin also renewed his proposal to “give the people of Armenia a say on joining the EU.” Russia and its allies — Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan — had previously demanded that Armenia hold a referendum on whether to remain in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). In response, Pashinyan said at the time that Armenia was abandoning the idea of holding a referendum on EU membership.
Putin and Pashinyan last met in early April, when the Armenian prime minister traveled to Moscow. During that Kremlin meeting, Pashinyan spoke about democracy and freedom of speech, saying that in Armenia, unlike in Russia, “social media is 100% free.” In early June, Armenia held parliamentary elections in which Pashinyan’s Civil Contract party won with more than 49.7% of the vote.
In recent years, Pashinyan has consistently pushed for closer ties between Armenia and the European Union. Moscow has responded that it considers simultaneous membership in the EU and the EAEU impossible. Pashinyan, for his part, has said that Armenia will keep working within the EAEU “until the choice between the European Union and the Eurasian Economic Union becomes unavoidable.”
The two countries also disagree over membership in the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). Pashinyan himself said in late August that he “would be very glad” if Armenia were expelled from the CSTO.

Tucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:41:48 UTC
04:41:48 KST

Authorities in Tucson, Arizona, are investigating a shooting outside a gay bar that left three people dead as a possible hate crime.
The shooting occurred shortly after midnight on Monday in the parking lot of Venture-N, according to Tucson police. The suspect, identified by police as 44-year old Ousman Ceesay, allegedly killed 42-year-old Vincent Anthony Siqueiros and 33-year-old Cameron Davis Capara.
Tucson police said Ceesay, who had suffered gunshot wounds, later died after being transported to a local hospital.
In a news release, Tucson police said: “Initial evidence suggests that the suspect confronted the victims in the parking lot of the business.
“After confronting Mr Siqueiros and Mr Capara, the suspect shot them. There is no known active threat to the community. The suspect was in possession of a note with several LGBTQIA+ associated businesses written on it.
“The Tucson police department is currently investigating this homicide as a hate crime. The investigation remains active and ongoing.”
Tucson police chief Monica Prieto said in a statement: “We recognize this incident may cause fear and pain within our community. Tucson is, and always has been, a diverse community where people of different backgrounds, identities and experiences call this city home. We are committed to ensuring every member of our community feels safe, valued and welcomed.”
Speaking to the Tucson Sentinel, Tucson resident Peter Loya, who frequents Venture-N, said he was acquainted with Siqueiros, whom he had known for approximately 20 years, and Capara, who was newer to the bar.
Describing Siqueiros, Loya said: “He’s always just been a thoughtful, considerate person, always looking for the best in people. You could always have fun with him.”
Drew Fellows, a friend of Capara, described him as a “revolutionary” photographer who was “always with a people-first mentality”.
“He always fought for and believed in a better future, for himself, for his community and, most importantly, for everybody,” Fellows told the Tucson Sentinel.
Tucson mayor Regina Romero called the shooting “a direct and devastating attack on our LGBTQ+ community, another senseless act of gun violence”.
“This tragedy serves as yet another painful reminder that homophobia is still rampant in our country. We must implement smarter policies to prevent mass shootings and keep our communities safe. Easy access to firearms and Arizona’s weak gun safety laws continue to put all of us at risk,” Romero added.
In June 2016, 49 people were killed and 58 others were injured in a mass shooting at Pulse, a gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida, making it the second-deadliest mass shooting in US history.
A 2020 study published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances found that LGBTQ+ people in the US are 2.7 times more likely to be victims of violent crime than cisgender, heterosexual people.

I was told I was born with bad genes. I believed it and ended up in jail at 14

A man diagnosed with psychopathic traits, parents concerned about their children's violent behaviour, and guests who grew up believing they were bad. Are some of us born bad, or is harmful behaviour shaped by experience? How do nature and nurture influence our choices and morals? Watch Insight episode Born Bad? on SBS On Demand.
This article references sexual abuse, self-harm and suicide.
I remember playing with a dollhouse on the floor of a psychiatrist's office as a seven-year-old while my adoptive mother spoke to the psychiatrist about me having "bad genes". One week earlier, I'd set fire to my younger sister's bed.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
My parents adopted me at birth after being told that they couldn't conceive naturally. Three months later, Mum was pregnant; and before I'd turned four, they'd had four biological children.
I felt like the outsider, being the only adopted child, and I acted out — I'd scream, throw and break toys. I burnt my sister's bed (while she was not in it), rationalising that if she had nowhere to sleep, they'd have to get rid of her — not me.
We moved around a lot as kids due to my dad's work. I went to seven schools and lived in about 11 houses across four states by the time I was 14. I felt dislocated in both place and self.
Dad called me a wild cat and said he wished they'd never adopted me. I came to believe there was another girl inside me called Wild Cat. She had lit the fire. She did the bad things.
At 12, some older boys sexually abused me. From then on, I'd vanish from myself sporadically — losing sense of time and place. I also went from being a straight-A student to a struggling one.
I ran away from home, trying to escape the boys. The police brought me back after dark. My parents were frantic, thinking I'd been kidnapped. I told them what the boys had done.
Running away
When I was 13, my parents sent me to my grandmother's farm in Gippsland, Victoria, to live with her and my great-uncle after I had run away. My grandmother loved and supported me and believed in me; she was convinced I would grow up to be a teacher.
On my first day at my new school in Gippsland, I went to write my name, and instead of writing Sandra, I wrote Sandie, which I had never been called before.
It wasn't intentional; Sandra just didn't exist anymore — after the boys who abused me said vile things to me using that name.
I haven't called myself Sandra since.
Dad and the family soon transferred to a new town. I visited them for a holiday when I was 13, and because they were being kind to me, I chose to stay.
But I underestimated my resentment and anger towards them, and I started wagging school, shoplifting, and throwing tantrums — like I had when I was small.
A friend and I soon decided to run away when I was 14. We slept in an old railway shed and stole cheques we found in a trunk. We were caught and sent to juvenile detention.
That was the end of my high school education; I had only completed one year.
Going to jail
I was in juvenile detention with girls who had far more violent backgrounds, including a murderer. But there were also some like me who had wagged school.
Back then, I thought I was the problem.
I didn't read the file until years later, but one of my juvenile case notes implied that because I'd come from a "respectable" family, "they had done their best" with me. Another referred to me as a "cunning, devious girl"; I had also been labelled with a "character defect" that was not treatable.
I'd bounce from enjoying jazz ballet or typing to throwing a bedhead at the juvenile detention centre's superintendent and talcum powder around a dormitory. I'd hurl verbal abuse at people and physically harm myself.
After nine months, I was released and sent home.
I hated being back with my parents, and I had no friends. Because I'd been locked up, no one wanted their children near me. I just stayed in my bedroom; I felt like a prisoner even though I wasn't locked in there. I was screaming the whole time and even burnt my bra. I tried to kill myself a couple of times.
My mother was kind and was trying her best, but my parents couldn't cope, and I was returned to juvenile custody on a welfare complaint of being an uncontrollable child.
All up, I spent two years in the system and escaped three times.
'I vowed never to steal again'
At 16, my life began to change.
After being released, I lived with a kind friend of my mother's, who had visited me every week with chocolates when I was in prison.
The trouble was: I was still a thief.
I got caught shoplifting, and my mother's friend convinced me to get a job so I wouldn't be locked up again.
So, I found work as a mail girl in a solicitor's office and moved to a boarding house near the city.
Soon after that, I lost a close friendship with a girl I'd been locked up with after I was nearly caught stealing again. She was 18 and turning her life around.
Heartbroken by the people I'd hurt and lost, I vowed never to steal again, and I patched up my relationship with my adoptive family.
Teaching in prisons
Fourteen years later, I was a sole parent living in Woolloomooloo in Sydney when I decided to go to university; this led me to be a counsellor with NSW Health.
Later, I worked as a teacher in a men's prison for 14 years.
Ironically, my first prison job was teaching anger management. Who would have thought?
And I also taught the men life writing, a genre exploring lived experiences and memories.
When you're a prison teacher, you teach the whole person — not their crimes. Active listening is vital, not judgement; judgement puts up barriers.
The courses I taught required students to be open about themselves. It was important to me that they felt heard.
'No one is born bad'
I was in my 50s, when I asked for and read my juvenile records. It stripped my humanity, my soul, reading these comments in my middle age. It was like I just stripped bare and my trauma wasn't mentioned.
They were wrong to say that there was no hope for me. They were wrong that I was born bad.
That lost girl is still a part of me, though. I sometimes hear her voice in my head and the screams of Wild Cat.
I still dissociate, and time dissolves.
No one is born bad ... But if you tell a child they’re bad, they’ll believe it.
For most of my life, I fled the child versions of myself, but after years of therapy I have learnt to soothe them — to remind them I'm an adult and looking after them.
No one is born bad; it's always an interaction between the person and the environment.
But if you tell a child they're bad, they'll believe it.

Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ as MapQuest downloads surge
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Issued on: Modified:
Lake Ontario is now appearing as “Lake America” on Google Maps for US users, following Donald Trump’s executive order to rename the lake. Canadians still see “Lake Ontario”, while users elsewhere see both names. But the change is far from universal: Apple Maps and MapQuest continue to use Lake Ontario. MapQuest has remained defiant against the move and since surged to the top of the US App Store download charts.
Google says it made the change to align its maps with the US government’s Geographic Names Information System, or GNIS, which has officially adopted “Lake America”. Depending on where you are and which map you use, it can be “Lake Ontario”, “Lake America”, or both.
Google Maps has implemented the change, but only for users in the United States. In Canada, the lake remains “Lake Ontario”, while users elsewhere, including here in France, can see both names.
Apple Maps and MapQuest continue to call the lake “Lake Ontario”. MapQuest has gone a step further, publicly rejecting the change and saying it will not rename the lake, a move that has seen its popularity surge. A 30-year-old pioneer in the internet mapping game, MapQuest has since topped the Apple's App Store download charts in the US.
The dispute comes amid already strained relations between the United States and Canada, as Donald Trump continues to escalate his trade confrontation with his northern neighbour. He's used social media to promote the new name, sharing AI-generated images that mock Canada and celebrate “Lake America”. One depicts Canada geese with Trump-style blond hair appearing to defend the lake, while another shows Trump replacing a “Lake Ontario” sign with one bearing his preferred name.
In Canada, the decision has been met with dismissal and ridicule. Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded by putting up a large sign overlooking the lake's shores, reading “Lake Ontario now and always” in both English and French.
Trump’s attempt to influence geographic names is not unprecedented. Last year, he ordered the Gulf of Mexico to be renamed the “Gulf of America”. Google subsequently adopted the new name for US users, while retaining “Gulf of Mexico” elsewhere.
US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said Trump has contacted Apple directly about complying with the order. Whether Apple eventually follows Google’s lead remains to be seen.
Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.

orphea: a playable 13-key electronic piano that fits into your pocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:35:14 UTC
04:35:14 KST

Orphea is a compact 13-key electronicpiano developed by Pianni to examine how far a conventional keyboard can be reduced while retaining its physical and musical functions. Measuring only slightly larger than a modern smartphone, the instrument combines a standard chromatic black-and-white key layout with physical pressable keys, polyphonic playing, octave controls, built-in speakers, headphone output, MIDI connectivity, and USB-C charging.
The current prototype spans one chromatic octave, from C to C, across 13 physical keys. Dedicated octave controls extend the playable pitch range without increasing the instrument’s footprint. This configuration allows the keyboard to retain the arrangement and tactile interaction of a conventional piano within a significantly reduced format.
A conventional keyboard layout in a compact format
Orphea addresses limitations found in many ultra-portable keyboards, which often reduce their dimensions by removing black keys, replacing physical keys with touch surfaces, limiting polyphony, or depending on an external device for sound. Pianni retains the chromatic black-and-white layout and physical key mechanism while integrating the electronic components required for independent operation.
Built-in speakers allow the instrument to produce sound without additional equipment, while a headphone output supports quiet practice. MIDI connectivity allows Orphea to function as a compact controller for external software and hardware, extending its use beyond the integrated sounds.
The instrument has gone through multiple prototype and engineering iterations focused on key feel and mechanical behaviour, enclosure geometry, internal electronics, speaker placement, and portability. Its enclosure uses a compact molded plastic body intended to balance low weight and durability with the physical interface of a conventional piano.
Orphea is a compact 13-key electronic piano by Pianni
Orphea mini piano acts as a portable musical sketchbook
Orphea is designed as a portable musical sketchbook rather than a replacement for a full-sized piano. Its reduced dimensions allow it to be carried in a small bag and used in situations where a traditional keyboard would be impractical, including while travelling, outdoors, at a desk, or during quiet practice.
The reduced keyboard has also been tested against different levels of musical complexity. Pianni founder and pianist Jordan Daniels has used the prototype to play simple melodies as well as more complex repertoire, including a three-voice Bach fugue, testing the extent to which the compact format can support polyphonic playing. The project is currently being refined towards production and is preparing for launch through Kickstarter.

Israel’s multiple wars see finance, defence ministries clash over spending

Israel’s multiple wars see finance, defence ministries clash over spending
Spiraling costs of Israel’s conflicts deepen rift between finance and defense ministries ahead of budget decisions.
Israel’s Ministries of Finance and Defence have clashed over the spiralling costs of Israel’s multiple and ongoing wars in the region, which are adding pressure to the government’s budget.
The Israeli military has warned that if the dispute is unresolved it could jeopardise the security of the country.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Lebanese president calls on Greece for help pushing Israel on ceasefire
- list 2 of 4Israeli forces raze West Bank homes as EU weighs ban on settlement goods
- list 3 of 4Palestine weekly: Israel’s rightwing campaigns on anti-Palestinian abuses
- list 4 of 4Israeli strikes on Gaza kill at least five, including children
Since the war on Gaza began in October 2023, Israel has entered its longest period of sustained conflict in its history.
Israeli forces are deployed in Lebanon and Syria as they continue to occupy the Gaza and the West Bank, and are prepared for further conflict with Iran.
Israeli military Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir warned that these costly conflicts are being undertaken with “empty coffers.”
The Israeli government has attempted to inject a further 15 billion shekels ($5bn) into the military, the Israeli news website YNet reported, increasing the 2026 defence budget to 184 billion shekels ($60.8bn). The defence funding is a near-record in the country’s history, second only to the 188 billion shekels ($62.2bn) spent on defence during the first year of its genocide in Gaza.
Tensions between Israel’s defence and finance ministries have been building for some time, with the two sides divided over the scale and management of military spending.
In late August, YNet News reported that the dispute was likely to continue even after the additional funding had been approved.
Senior finance officials rejected the military’s claim that it was “on the edge of the abyss” and warned that meeting its demands could push military spending to nearly one-third of the country’s entire state budget, the Israeli media outlet added.
“Everything costs money. Their only mode of operation is using military force, as we’ve seen in Lebanon, Syria, Gaza and Iran, but they never seem to want to talk about paying for it,” Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.
“It costs. The hardware, the ammunition, the soldiers, and the benefits if they’re injured,” he said. “It all needs paying for, which is something they rarely seem to want to discuss.”
Complicating the picture is the fragmented nature of Israeli politics, said Makelberg. Politicians compete for small and often uncompromising parts of the electorate that are often unwilling or unable to see beyond their own interests.
That was especially true for Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, whose far-right Religious Zionist Party might not pass the electoral threshold to sit in the next Knesset.
“Smotrich is in an uncomfortable position. On the one hand, he needs the support of these hardcore nationalists who demand more expenditure on the military and their occupation of the West Bank. On the other, as minister of finance, he has to pay for it,” he said.
Blame games
Briefings from within the Israeli military have blamed foot-dragging from the Finance Ministry for a number of potential spending cuts. This includes a sharp reduction in reserve forces in the Northern and Southern Commands, while the West Bank Division will be maintained at current levels despite heightened tensions and security warnings after a wave of settler pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied territory.
The military has also warned that it will significantly scale back intelligence gathering, where operations rely on costly technologies. At the same time, the military has warned that it will need to prepare for a possible escalation with Iran and other threats, including the Houthis in Yemen and pro-Iranian Shia militias in Iraq. All of this will require continuous costly training and adequate stocks of spare parts and munitions.
“Struggling departments often blame the Ministry of Finance for their own problems, much in the way that the government of developing countries sometimes blame the IMF [International Monetary Fund],” said Michael Ben-Gad, a professor of economics at City St George’s, University of London said.
“The Ministry of Finance will make sure the army’s funded. Most of the people in the ministry have family in the army and/or served themselves.”
The political difficulty, especially close to an election, is to be seen to oppose the army.
“Smotrich can either pay now and raise taxes after the election, or pay now and then criticise the next government for doing just that,” Ben-Gad said.
Future wars
Few ministers are showing any appetite to curb Israel’s military endeavours, despite the warnings of “empty coffers”. In the occupied West Bank, the Israeli army has announced it is preparing a widescale deployment to stem the unrestrained settler violence that many in the government, including Smotrich, have been accused of encouraging.
At the same time, Israel is preparing for an escalation in the conflict with Iran. Billions of dollars are being spent to replenish munition supplies that were expended in both the last war with Iran and Israel’s neighbours.
“It’s like a rule of nature. Every year, the Israeli army asks for more money and every year the Ministry of Finance will impose a cut of around one to two percent across all other departments to pay for it,” Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg told Al Jazeera.
“We’re seeing a fresh military doctrine develop where the Israeli army is establishing front lines in enemy territory, with what they call ‘dead zones’ behind it,” he said.
Not one of the frontrunners in October’s election was questioning the wisdom of that tactic.
“If this is the new doctrine, then it could be an expensive one, as those frontlines are going to need to be replenished with both manpower and equipment,” Flaschenberg said.
“There might be disagreements over how that capacity is eventually deployed, but not the doctrine of building it up.”

Australia bucks a years-long winter sickness trend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:33:12 UTC
04:33:12 KST

IN BRIEF
- COVID-19 cases are down 56 per cent on last year, despite infections beginning to rise again over the past fortnight.
- Experts are pointing to population immunity and a more stable virus.
Australia appears to have avoided the winter surge in COVID-19 cases seen in previous years, according to a recent report.
Federal surveillance data shows 64,357 COVID-19 cases have been reported so far this year, 56 per cent fewer than the 146,232 cases recorded over the same period in 2025.
The latest figures paint an unusual picture of Australia's COVID-19 landscape, with infections remaining well below last year's levels even as cases begin to tick upwards across the community.
"In contrast to previous years, national data in 2026 to date do not yet show a clear winter peak," the Australian Centre for Disease Control said in its latest respiratory surveillance report.
Experts says changing virus behaviour and population immunity are possible explanations.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Where has the winter wave gone?
Professor Catherine Bennett, chair of epidemiology at Deakin University, said the absence of a clear winter peak was significant.
She said Australia's experience reflected a population that had gradually developed greater immunity to the virus through previous infections and vaccination.
"When you have variants that stay in circulation for a longer period of time, more people have had their immunity naturally boosted against that variant, and that then keeps infection rates down," she said.
Bennett said having fewer major changes in the variants circulating than earlier in the pandemic may be helping people's existing immunity provide greater protection against severe infection.
Rather than a substantially different variant emerging every few months in Australia, the same dominant variant was continuing to circulate, allowing immunity in the population to remain "primed".
Have COVID-19 patterns changed?
Epidemiologist professor Adrian Esterman told SBS News that the pattern of COVID-19 outbreaks had changed significantly over the past few years.
"We aren't actually seeing waves anymore, or if we do have waves they're very small ones," he said.
Esterman said smaller increases in cases now tended to coincide with the emergence of a variant that was better able to transmit or evade existing immunity.
The experts said that a major change to the virus' genetics could still trigger a larger wave, but said there was currently little evidence of one developing.
"Unless there's a huge genetic shift in the virus ... that's the only thing that could disrupt things and cause another wave," Esterman said.
Fewer cases detected
The sharp fall in reported cases raises the question of whether fewer Australians are getting COVID-19, or if fewer infections are being detected.
Reported COVID-19 cases are only a proportion of all infections, meaning surveillance data cannot capture every person who contracts the virus.
But Bennett said she believed the lack of a winter peak was broadly consistent with what was being seen in other measures of COVID-19 severity.
She pointed to hospitalisation data showing COVID-19 was now causing less severe disease among younger and healthier adults than earlier in the pandemic.
At the same time, she warned that there were still important gaps in Australia's understanding of the virus, particularly in relation to the longer-term consequences of infection.
Why immunity could be making a difference
Bennett said repeated exposure to COVID-19 may now be giving many people protection against severe illness without necessarily preventing them from becoming infected.
People may therefore experience very mild infections that are never detected, or fight off infections without becoming noticeably sick.
Bennett and Esterman told SBS News that if the same variants continue circulating, people who have previously encountered them may have enough immunity to prevent infections from producing the large rise in cases Australia has seen in previous winters.
"It's sort of keeping our immunity levels primed up naturally," Bennet said.
But she said that protection is not evenly distributed.
Bennett said older people and those who are immunocompromised may not develop the same strength of immune response from previous exposure, which is why vaccination remains important for those groups.
What happens as we head into spring?
According to the latest federal surveillance report, COVID-19 cases have started increasing again over the past fortnight.
But neither expert believes the rise signals the start of another major wave.
Bennett said the increase needed to be watched, particularly for evidence of a new variant gaining a foothold.
She said a new variant could potentially produce a summer surge, but there was currently no strong trend suggesting that was happening.
Esterman similarly expects the virus to continue producing relatively small increases in cases rather than the large, distinct waves seen earlier in the pandemic.
Could this become the new normal?
The absence of a winter peak does not mean COVID-19 has disappeared, or that future winters will necessarily look the same.
Both experts said that while Australia's 2026 experience could represent an important shift in the way COVID-19 behaves as an endemic respiratory virus, a significant change in the virus could alter the current pattern.
Bennett said the combination of declining transmission, population immunity and a more stable virus had put Australia in a much stronger position than it was in the early years of the pandemic.
"It's very unusual but an important sign that our population-level immunity is still evolving and maturing and putting us in a much better position to cope with an endemic disease like COVID-19."
And if the current trend continues through the warmer months, she said Australia could be entering its quietest 12-month period of COVID-19 transmission in years.
"If we can get through summer without another wave, then that will be the best 12 months we've had for a long time with COVID-19."

West lacks adequate defence against drone swarms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:30:49 BST
04:30:49 KST

Western militaries do not currently have an adequate defence against the autonomous drone swarms that could emerge as unmanned warfare moves beyond systems requiring individual human pilots, General David Petraeus has warned in an address to the House of Lords, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Speaking on 1 September, Petraeus argued that the war in Ukraine is demonstrating a change extending well beyond the adoption of drones themselves. He described a battlefield in which large numbers of relatively expendable unmanned systems are linked with sensors, software, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence and increasingly rapid targeting processes, while military technology and tactics are being modified continuously during combat.
Petraeus said: “Much of the discussion has understandably focused on individual technologies—unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, precision strike, battle management systems, and others. Each matters. But the principal lesson is larger: the very concept of warfare is changing.”
He continued: “We are witnessing the convergence of technological, operational, industrial, and organizational change into an entirely new way of conducting war. Information is collected, analyzed, disseminated, and acted upon at unprecedented speed. Sensors and battle management systems are connected to vast numbers of attritable unmanned systems capable of precision effects across every domain.”
Petraeus said commercial innovation was also moving directly onto the battlefield, with software, hardware and operational methods adapted during fighting and an increasingly close relationship developing between military operations and the industrial base.
The former US commander said remotely controlled systems are already changing the role of conventional formations by taking over tasks previously performed by personnel in some of the most exposed parts of the battlefield.
He said: “And remotely operated unmanned systems on the ground, in the air, and at sea are increasingly displacing humans from many of the most dangerous functions of front-line combat and profoundly changing the role of traditional combined-arms formations.”
Petraeus also made a strong claim about the scale of drone employment in Ukraine, telling peers that remotely piloted systems now account for the overwhelming majority of Russian casualties and that established land systems are operating under persistent threat from surveillance and precision weapons.
He said: “Those changes will encounter fierce resistance from advocates of existing force structures and legacy systems, many of which are becoming extraordinarily vulnerable on the battlefield we see in Ukraine. Remotely piloted systems, employed there in enormous numbers, already inflict the overwhelming majority of Russian casualties. Tanks and artillery increasingly operate only under extraordinary threat from ubiquitous surveillance and precision strike.”
His warning went further with the development of fully autonomous systems. Petraeus argued that removing the requirement for an individual human pilot for each platform would allow unmanned formations to increase dramatically in size, potentially producing swarms considerably larger than those possible with today’s remotely operated systems.
He said: “And the advent of fully autonomous systems in the months and years ahead will represent another profound development. Removing the constraint imposed by the number of human pilots will make possible unmanned operations at vastly greater scale—including swarms for which we presently possess no adequate defense.”
Petraeus argued that military advantage would consequently depend on institutional adaptation as well as technical development, particularly the ability to incorporate battlefield lessons rapidly into doctrine, force design, training and acquisition.
He said: “In this environment, decisive advantage will belong not simply to those who innovate technologically, but to those whose institutions learn faster than their adversaries. Warfare is becoming a continuous competition in institutional learning and adaptation—the ability to identify lessons, incorporate them rapidly into doctrine, force design, procurement, training, and leader development, and repeat the process before the adversary catches up.”

Burnham promised hope. Reality is already getting in the way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:30:27 UTC
04:30:27 KST

LONDON — Britain’s new prime minister spent his first statement to parliament promising to “bring back hope.” Over 204 minutes he demonstrated just how many of those hopes could ultimately be dashed.
Taking 125 questions in the Commons Tuesday, Andy Burnham made, hardened or reiterated a dizzying flurry of commitments that would radically alter the British state — if he manages to see them all through.
The man who became PM just 43 days ago suggested he will scrap Britain’s first-past-the-post voting system before 2034 if a majority of parties pledging reform — such his own Labour Party plus the centrist Liberal Democrats — win “consensus” at the next general election, due by 2029. He hinted that he could cap individual U.K. donations to political parties or block those from abroad entirely in future (though as POLITICO revealed, he has declined to do either in the short term).
Advertisement
He pledged to shake up England’s privatized water sector as part of a “10-year plan” this fall. He promised to impose his predecessor Keir Starmer’s social media ban on under-16s “at pace.” He repeated his long-held vows to radically reform the social care system, move powers and officials out of Whitehall, release public land for a wave of house-building and “end” rough sleeping — while still bringing down the welfare bill. “Working together to build a new sense of optimism around the country, we can make this next decade better than the last,” he said.
The parliamentary chamber began to empty, MPs turning to other duties and their bladders, as the hardiest stayed behind in the hope they would extract yet another commitment from the prime minister.
As the session wore on, Burnham hinted he could one day scrap England’s system of local taxation, which is based on property valuations from 1991. In the third hour he even promised to save Jodrell Bank, a locally-beloved cluster of deep space radio telescopes near Manchester that has had its funding cut.
The new prime minister was not offering a free-for-all and, like any minister, swerved more invitations to commit policy than he accepted. He insisted he will make tough choices.
Yet he is also enjoying a practical by-effect of being a new leader: He hasn’t yet had to disappoint all the people he will eventually disappoint.
Rhetoric vs. reality
The 125 questions he took showed that the difficulties and trade-offs that come with power are already coming into view.
Advertisement
Burnham dropped a hint that he could raise defense spending to 3 percent of GDP by 2030 — a key demand of his chief finance minister, John Healey, when he quit Starmer’s government earlier this year as defense minister. Burnham said he had appointed Healey “precisely because” of his arguments on defense.
Yet both men have pushed back any decision to a spending review in 2027, and will not face easy choices; the U.K.’s long-term borrowing costs are their highest since 1998, and Burnham declined to rule out tax rises in Healey’s fall budget. On paper, the position did not move on Tuesday.
The tension was summed up in Burnham’s promise to bring “much more substantial change as promised in [our] 2024 manifesto.” Healey last week put the same thing very differently, saying it was a “continuity of a Labour government with a change of leader.”
Contradictions are already emerging within Burnham’s approach.
The new prime minister wants to keep his focus more domestic than Starmer’s, but said he will head to the COP31 climate summit this November. He also promised a statement “very shortly” responding to Israel’s E1 settlement project in the West Bank, which he said “could imperil, if not end, the two-state solution.” That statement will strain relations with Israel and could do so too with Donald Trump, who Burnham is hoping to meet on a U.S. trip in late September.
He said the recent mass fatalities in Nepal, caused by falling glacier ice, were “what the climate crisis looks like.” But with energy prices rising, Burnham hinted his government will soon approve at least one of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas projects in the North Sea.
Advertisement
Not even the Commons theatrics were immune. Moments after he pledged to avoid point-scoring, Burnham pointed some jabs at the 49-day premiership of former Tory PM Liz Truss.
Past is precedent
Elsewhere, Burnham’s promises to change the way things are done in Britain are butting up against reasons why they were done that way in the first place.
The PM told MPs that Brexit had inflicted “a decade of low growth” and promised to get closer to Brussels ahead of an EU-U.K. summit in the fall. Yet like his predecessor he will be bound simultaneously by the EU’s red lines and his own. Burnham has chosen to continue Labour’s 2024 pledge not to rejoin the single market or customs union.
He appeared tearful when he promised to invest “all” his political capital into reforming the social care model, but even that cannot happen fast thanks to the complexity of the system; his intervention has been to bring forward a review from 2028 to 2027.
He promised to be “relentless” in bringing in more “public control” of the water industry, but as POLITICO reported, his officials are still wading through all the ownership models and could apply several at the same time.
He left the door open to banning all overseas donations to U.K. political parties (saying “we can come back to these issues” before 2029), and to imposing a cap on individual donations (“we do need to go further,” he added). But unions worry their donations to Labour would be imperiled by a cap, and Burnham punted any action to an ongoing taskforce on democracy rather than accepting amendments to a bill this week.
Advertisement
He also left the door open to reforming the council tax system, but made clear that he already knows the danger in expending too much political capital. (When Conservative PM Margaret Thatcher last tried major reforms in 1990, there were riots in the streets; the successor system dating to 1991 has remained ever since.) “I don’t think I can go all that way today [… but] a council tax system based on 1991 valuations is not going to deliver fairness across the country,” he said. “We need to proceed with consensus if we can.”
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of presiding over “a government swerving all over the place” that is obsessed with Thatcher’s legacy of privatization. “He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s,” she said.
For many of his own Labour MPs, Burnham is saying what they want to hear — at least for now. “The grasp of detail is impressive,” said one, granted anonymity to speak candidly.The statement was “good,” said another. (The adulation is not universal; a third Labour MP confessed: “I’ll be honest, I was doing emails and forgot.”)
But as Starmer retreats from parliament — the former PM announced Tuesday that he will stand down from the Commons entirely — MPs are turning their full focus to his successor. At some point, they and the public will expect the many promises to be fulfilled. The question is when they decide that point has arrived.

Spain Signs First Contract to Supply Artillery Components for K9 Wheeled Self-Propelled Howitzer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:28:17 UTC
04:28:17 KST

South Korean company Hanwha Aerospace has signed a contract with Spain’s Indra Sistemas to supply K9 Thunder self-propelled artillery systems.
The agreement provides for localized production of the howitzers in Spain, rather than direct import of finished equipment, according to Maeil Business.
The Korean side will provide the platform and key technologies, while Indra will manufacture the chassis, control systems, and components at its plant in Gijón.
The cost and timeline of the contract have not been officially disclosed due to commercial confidentiality, but the deal is estimated to be worth over €450 million.
The procurement is part of a large-scale program to modernize the Spanish Army’s self-propelled artillery, with a total value of €4.5 billion, which includes the purchase of 128 tracked and 86 wheeled self-propelled howitzers.
News of the development in Spain of a new wheeled self-propelled howitzer based on components from the South Korean K9 Thunder first emerged this past spring.
Spanish experts plan to borrow the main components of the loading and fire-control systems, which have already been tested on the tracked prototype. The vehicle’s primary armament will be a 155-mm gun with a 52-caliber barrel. This will allow for the standardization of ammunition use with allies.
To achieve a firing range of over 40 km, the military is considering options for using an even longer barrel.
Due to the integration of Korean automation technologies, the crew size for each vehicle will be reduced to three service members.
Instead of a specialized chassis, the developers will use a military truck platform with an 8×8 or 10×10 wheel configuration.
Militarnyi previously reported that the U.S. subsidiary Hanwha Defense USA, signed an agreement with the U.S. Army to supply a prototype of the K9MH wheeled self-propelled howitzer.

Spanish government approves €309 million aid package for Ceuta amid migrant crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:27:31 UTC
04:27:31 KST

Spain's Economy Minister said the aid package represents a 'shock response' designed to meet the demands of social organisations and the city government.
The migrant crisis in Ceuta continues to dominate Spain's political agenda.
The Council of Ministers on Tuesday approved an extraordinary funding package worth €309 million for the autonomous city, aimed at safeguarding jobs, supporting businesses, strengthening security and ensuring public services.
Government spokesperson Elma Saiz presented the measures alongside First Vice-President Carlos Cuerpo and Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres. The announcement came on the eve of a demonstration in the city that has exposed divisions in the PSOE and prompted Podemos to call a separate anti-racism rally.
The package, Cuerpo explained, amounts to around 16% of the city's GDP over the four remaining months of 2026.
The money is divided into four areas: €21 million for healthcare, education, justice and water treatment; more than €90 million for defence and the national security forces; €118 million for humanitarian care of unaccompanied migrant minors; and €80 million in direct support for businesses, incentives for trade and tax cuts.
Cuerpo, who also serves as Economy Minister, said the aid package represents a "shock response" designed to meet the demands of social organisations and the city government.
He said that the main aim of the decree was "to give confidence" to both companies and workers.
Cuerpo also stressed that, before the migration crisis, Ceuta was going through a "period of economic dynamism" that had helped to correct some of the "structural deficits" the city had struggled with for decades.
Direct aid for businesses and the self-employed
Of the €80 million allocated for businesses, €36.6 million is earmarked for direct support: €5,000 per self-employed worker and between €10,000 and €150,000 per company, depending on turnover.
Applications can be submitted from Monday 14 via the Tax Agency website, with the first payments aiming to arrive in early October.
The government has estimated that the measure will benefit 2,600 self-employed workers and 1,400 companies. This is supplemented by €14 million in consumer and tourism vouchers, €1 million for the Plan Ceuta Exporta, and another €1 million to promote the city as an international tourist destination.
The package also includes permanent measures: Corporation Tax relief rises from 50% to 60% for companies in Ceuta and Melilla that maintain their activity and jobs, alongside improvements to personal income tax (IRPF) for the self-employed, totalling €12 million.
Employers' Social Security contributions are to be subsidised from 50% to 75% for permanent contracts linked to training, at a cost of €12.2 million over four months.
The government will also set up an ICO-backed loan guarantee scheme worth up to €50 million, introduce exemptions for companies that make use of the job retention scheme (ERTE) and provide an extraordinary benefit for self-employed workers who are forced to stop working.
The president of the Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, warned of the seriousness of the situation a month ago, when the Government approved a first package of €168 million euros for the territory.
Vivas reiterated this in a new text, published by PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, in which he denounced an "attack on its territorial integrity" and described a city "overwhelmed and on the brink of collapse."
Vivas calls for Spanish unity on Ceuta Day
Vivas has also addressed Spaniards across the country in a message marking Ceuta Day, which is celebrated on 2 September, amid the fallout from the migrant crisis.
In his letter, Vivas called for national unity and solidarity and thanked people for the support shown to Ceuta in recent weeks.
"Ceuta has lived through its toughest month this August," he added in the text, in which he described recent events as "an unprecedented outrage" against the territory.
But whatever happens, he insisted that the city would "never" be abandoned.
A Ceuta Day overshadowed by crisis
Vivas also acknowledged that this year's 2 September celebrations would be different from those of previous years.
However, in his view, the situation the city is facing has made this day "particularly significant" and has presented an opportunity to strengthen ties and unity among Spaniards.
The president also referred to the rallies scheduled for 8 pm in municipalities across Spain following a call by the Spanish Federation of Municipalities and Provinces (FEMP).
He stressed that these demonstrations were not intended to serve partisan interests and are "not marked by political colours or ideologies."
Their purpose, he said, was to send a message of unity and support to Ceuta.
Another of the key messages in the letter is that the defence of Ceuta goes far beyond the territory itself.
"The cause is not exclusively Ceuta's; it is the cause of all Spain," he said, linking the defence of the city to protecting territorial integrity and democratic values.
"We have never stopped feeling you at our side," Vivas continued, while also expressing gratitude for the support shown towards the city during "its most difficult moment."
He added that such displays had been "a source of encouragement and hope" and had helped send Ceutans a clear message: "We are not alone".

Reacting to reports that Russian national Denis Kulanin remains in detention after he was pardoned by the president on 28 August, and amid concerns that he could be deported to Russia, Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Deputy Director, said:
“Denis Kulanin has publicly opposed Russia’s war against Ukraine and expressed support for Aleksei Navalny – both of which are regarded as crimes and punishable by prison in Russia. The Georgian authorities must ensure that he is not deported to Russia, where in the current climate of severe repression of anti-war dissent, he could face a real risk of arbitrary prosecution and imprisonment, torture or other ill-treatment.”

The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin can effectively seek international protection, including to leave voluntarily for a safe third country.”
The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin can effectively seek international protection, including to leave voluntarily for a safe third country
Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia Deputy Director
Background
On 1 September, Denis Kulanin was due to leave Georgia voluntarily for Armenia, after his lawyers submitted his flight ticket, passport and boarding pass to the court and the Temporary Accommodation Centre where he is held, following his pardon by the president on 28 August. He was one of nine people pardoned in connection with protest-related convictions. He had been serving a two-year prison sentence imposed on 4 June 2025 for damaging a police vehicle during a protest in Tbilisi on 28 March 2025.
Following his pardon, Tbilisi City Court placed him in the Temporary Accommodation Centre of the Migration Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs pending a further court hearing on his deportation from Georgia. This has deprived him of an opportunity to leave Georgia for Armenia voluntarily and raised concerns that the authorities are planning to hand him over to Russia instead.

IAEA urges access to Iran's nuclear sites with 'utmost urgency'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:25:16 UTC
04:25:16 KST

The UN nuclear agency has said in a confidential report that the lack of access to key nuclear sites in Iran "needs to be addressed with the utmost urgency".
"The agency's lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of proliferation concern," the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said in the report, according to AFP on Tuesday.
The IAEA has not had access to some key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28. The IAEA has repeatedly urged access.
IAEA head Rafael Grossi "again expresses his conviction that the long-standing problems and recurrent crises surrounding these issues must be resolved through a long-lasting, verifiable diplomatic agreement", the report said.
‘Widespread impression’
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday vowed to match any US move to return to a June deal aimed at ending their war.
The deal, meant to set the stage for final peace talks, has collapsed as both sides accused each other of violating its terms.
Prior to US strikes in June 2025, the IAEA calculated that Iran possessed approximately 440 kilogrammes of uranium enriched to 60 percent, which is close to the 90 percent needed to make a bomb and well above the 3.67-percent limit set by a 2015 now-defunct agreement with Iran.
Since June 2025, the fate of this stockpile has remained uncertain.
Grossi said in June that the "widespread impression" was that the stockpile remains where it was before June 2025, near to the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant.
In the report, to be discussed at an IAEA board of governors meeting next week, the IAEA said it was "concerned" about the lack of access to the Isfahan plant.
Israel and the United States have long accused Iran of wanting to build a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied having any military nuclear ambitions, insisting on its right to the technology for civilian purposes.

Putin transfers third major foreign asset to a Rostec-linked company that was created just a year ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:25:05 UTC
04:25:05 KST

Vladimir Putin has placed the assets of an Italian electrical equipment manufacturer under the temporary management of Razvitiye Stroitelnykh Aktivov (RSA), a Rostec-linked entity that, since its founding less than a year ago, has already been the beneficiary of three such presidential decrees.
The third asset in a year
RSA has taken over Dielectric Cable Systems (DKC), the Russian business of Italy’s Adventus International S.r.l. According to the company’s website, DKC JSC is one of the largest manufacturers of cable support systems and low-voltage equipment in Europe. Last year, DKC reported net profit of around 9 billion rubles ($111 million).
It is not the only profitable asset to have been transferred to Razvitiye Stroitelnykh Aktivov in the past year. In addition to DKC, the company has also taken over:
- the Russian assets of Danish group Rockwool, which owned four plants producing thermal and acoustic insulation materials in Russia
- the Russian business of Dutch Akzo Nobel, a paint manufacturer.
Notably, RSA is a relatively young company. According to available data in the corporate data platform SPARK, it was established in September 2025 and received its first foreign asset — the Danish one — just before New Year’s, a little more than three months later.
A little-known company and businessman from Ufa
Nothing is known about the founders of RSA (that information is hidden in SPARK). There is also no information about its staff. The company ended its first partial year of operation with a loss of around 160,000 rubles ($1,843). Its sole listed employee is CEO Timur Rustemovich Amirov, a 33-year-old native of Bashkortostan.
In data examined by The Insider, Amirov's employment history since 2016 includes work at the Development Corporation of the Republic of Bashkortostan. In July 2021, for example, he had food delivered from Yandex Eats to his workplace at 46 Tukayev Street in Ufa — the same address as the corporation and of the Bashkortostan government.
Amirov built his career with the help of his father, Rustem Amirov. From 2020 to 2021, the elder Amirov headed Ufa’s municipal Specialized Department for the Repair and Maintenance of Artificial Structures (SURSIS), and before that he had spent more than nine years running Bashkortostan’s Road Maintenance Enterprise No. 104. The elder Amirov also made headlines, but in connection with a criminal case involving the abuse of office related to irregularities in equipment procurement. In April of this year, a court sentenced him to two years in prison (albeit on a suspended sentence).
Another curious detail about the younger Amirov is his black Tesla Model Y bearing the patriotic license plate S999VO. The plate previously belonged to a Chevrolet Niva operated by the public amenities service of Ufa’s Oktyabrsky District. In spring 2022, the Niva was bought by its current owner, who transferred the plate to his electric car. In 2026, the Tesla bearing the “SVO” plate was photographed on the streets of Moscow.
The business activities of the 33-year-old Amirov have developed beyond just Ufa. He is a beneficiary of the Leningrad Region-based LLC Cirkut, which trades in electrical equipment, and until 2024 he was a co-owner of the St. Petersburg-based trading company Spetsmash. None of this, however, would seem to have prepared him to take control of a multibillion-ruble business comprising the assets of foreign companies.
The Rostec trail
Earlier this year, The Bell offered its own answer to the question of who might ultimately benefit from the activities of RSA. Citing a source close to the Russian government, the outlet wrote that Rostec structures are behind Razvitiye Stroitelnykh Aktivov. Another source told The Bell that when RSA was taking over the assets of Danish company Rockwool, he saw a letter bearing Putin’s instructions that the business be transferred specifically for the benefit of Rostec, which is headed by longtime Putin associate Sergei Chemezov.
The Rostec theory is also supported by the business activities of the younger Amirov’s previous employer, the Development Corporation of the Republic of Bashkortostan (KRRB), which works with investors in the region on turnkey projects, helping them with paperwork, site selection, information support, and other matters.
Rostec has several key manufacturing enterprises in the region. These include NPO Stankostroenie in Sterlitamak and the Kumertau Aviation Production Enterprise (KumAPP), part of the Russian Helicopters holding company. When cooperation with Russian Helicopters was just getting underway in the region, the Bashkortostan government set up an interagency commission whose members included representatives of the Development Corporation of the Republic of Bashkortostan.
The corporation also operates several industrial parks in the republic and the Alga Special Economic Zone, often serving as a link between businesses and the regional authorities. Timur Amirov’s younger brother, Almaz Amirov, is listed as the corporation’s deputy director for capital construction.

Through the institutionalized and resolute implementation of the Makkah Agreement, the three countries will provide essential contributions to regional peace and stability.

“Human Safari” Terror in Kherson—Russian Drone Hits Taxi, Injuring 2 Young Girls
Five people, including two children, were injured after a Russian drone struck a taxi in Kherson on September 1, the Kherson Regional Military Administration reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to regional authorities, the attack occurred at around 1:40 p.m. in the city’s Korabelnyi district. Three adults and two children were injured in the strike.
The two children, girls aged 11 and two, suffered concussions, blast injuries, and closed head injuries. The 11-year-old also sustained shrapnel wounds to her abdomen and legs.
The taxi driver, a 46-year-old man, and two women aged 32 and 36 were also injured. All three were diagnosed with concussions, blast injuries, and closed head injuries. The girls’ mothers additionally suffered shrapnel wounds to their legs.
All five victims were hospitalized and remain under medical supervision. Regional authorities described their conditions as moderate.
The September 1 strike follows a deadly Russian drone attack on civilian transport in Kherson less than two weeks earlier. On August 19, Russian forces struck a civilian minibus with an FPV drone, killing four people and injuring at least five others, according to Yaroslav Shanko, head of the Kherson City Military Administration.
That attack also occurred in the city’s Korabelnyi district, at approximately 8:50 a.m. The victims included three women aged 89, 71, and 63, as well as a 69-year-old man. Local authorities said the oldest victim was one month away from her 90th birthday.
Kherson has also faced continued Russian attacks on its critical infrastructure. On August 26, Russian forces hit the Kherson Combined Heat and Power Plant (CHP) with a guided aerial bomb, significantly damaging the facility, according to Ukraine’s state-owned energy company Naftogaz.

Hakainde Hichilema sworn in as Zambia’s president after disputed election
Incumbent is inaugurated with his main rival in last month’s election jailed and the courts shuttered.
President Hakainde Hichilema has been sworn in for a second term as Zambia’s president following his victory in disputed elections.
As Hichilema was inaugurated at the National Heroes Stadium in the Zambian capital Lusaka on Tuesday, his main rival in last month’s election was in detention, accused of treason as allegations of vote rigging persisted.

Leaders and dignitaries from several countries, including the United States and China, flew in for the ceremony, during which the president pledged to rule with equality.
“We receive your support with humility and with a clear understanding of the responsibility it places upon our shoulders. To those who chose other candidates or other parties, we say with equal sincerity: We have heard you,” Hichilema said.

Addressing thousands of jubilant supporters as he was sworn in, Hichilema pledged to continue improving Zambia’s economy. He oversaw the restructuring of the country’s debt during his first term, while also attracting international investment and reducing inflation.
Hichilema’s running mate, Mutale Nalumango, was sworn in as vice-president at the same ceremony.

Pentagon Issues Contracts to Boost Manufacturing Capacity for Space Systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:17:45 UTC
04:17:45 KST

The Pentagon is moving forward with plans to invest in manufacturing capacity for the space industrial base, awarding multiple contracts in recent weeks to companies who supply key space components and subsystems as well as firms with innovative manufacturing technology that’s ready to scale.
The Defense Innovation Unit, a Pentagon technology hub designed to help funnel promising commercial capabilities to the military at scale, awarded other transaction agreements in July and August to two companies through its Adaptive Space Manufacturing and Integration Scale project. The effort aims to leverage commercially available tools and adaptive manufacturing processes to kick-start higher production rates across the space industrial base.
ALL.SPACE, a firm owned by York Space Systems, was one of those recipients. The company said in an Aug. 31 statement that it will demonstrate on-demand production of its Hydra satellite communications terminal with the goal of producing hundreds of units per month and potentially thousands per year.
“This award reflects a fundamental shift in how defense capabilities are being fielded,” ALL.SPACE Chief Operating Officer Rod McCurdy said in a statement. “Hydra was designed to deliver resilient connectivity across multiple networks and orbits, and this effort provides an opportunity to demonstrate how those capabilities can be delivered at the pace required by next-generation space and defense architectures.”
A second company, Freeform Future Corp., received a contract in July to scale its production of key propulsion and structural hardware. Earlier this year, the company unveiled a laser-based additive manufacturing platform called Skyfall, which it says will significantly expand its production.
Separate from the DIU awards, the Pentagon announced Sept. 1 it would invest $11.4 million in Stellant Systems, a company that makes vacuum tubes that can amplify certain radio frequency signals. In a statement, the Pentagon said it would use Defense Production Act funds to support qualification of the company’s space-based amplifier and to boost production rates, which it says “will greatly reduce schedule, cost, and performance risks to U.S. government satellite programs.”
The Space Force is preparing for a sizable increase in the number of satellites it operates. Deputy Chief of Space Operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements Gen. David N. Miller Jr. said in May that the service’s five-year budget projection includes “thousands” of satellites. Those will fall across a number of mission areas, including space-based moving target indication, data transport, missile warning, and space domain awareness.
In May, the Space Force awarded more than $4 billion to SpaceX to build out a new Space-Based Air Moving Target Indicator constellation and another $2.3 billion contract to field satellites as part of its Space Data Network program. It’s also planning to launch new fleets of surveillance and reconnaissance satellites starting in 2029. The service hasn’t said how many spacecraft these constellations will include, but officials have said hitting these numbers will require significant expansion of current production capacity.
“If a company is nominally making 10, we want you to be prepared to make 40,” Space Systems Command Commander Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant said in April. “We want industry to make the investments in capitalization and facilitization, and in return you’re going to get these large production contracts.”
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink has said he’s interested in awarding multiyear procurement contracts for both aircraft and satellites. He told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the goal is to give industry the demand signal it needs to make investments in its manufacturing capacity.
“When the future is uncertain, it’s hard for industry to make those investments to either modernize their facilities or do what they need to do to get to the production capacity we need,” Meink said. “So those long-term deals are a huge part of that.”
