"Explosions were heard again in Bandar Abbas city and Qeshm island," Iranian state television reported, adding that blasts were also heard on Lavan island, home to one of Iran's Gulf oil export terminals.
Oil prices rose in the wake of the latest attacks with US crude up by as much as 5%.
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."
US President Donald Trump said the strikes, which he described as "large and powerful," were retaliation for "failed" Iranian attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the firing of "eight missiles" towards a US military base in Jordan, all of which he claimed were shot down.
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump wrote in his latest social media threat. "But it will not be the biggest attack of them all. That is waiting in the wings."
Iran: IRGC vows to respond to US strikes

Pezeshkian, speaking after the US and Iran had already resumed exchanges of fire for the first time in over a month, accused Washington of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms.
Pezeshkian was speaking on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he also met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday.
Putin reportedly told Pezeshkian that Russia stood in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries would maintain their economic relationships despite the current turbulence.
Pezeshkian thanked Putin and criticized the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries.

Rescue package to help vulnerable families care for children at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:44:50 UTC
03:44:50 KST

Rescue package for in-home child care to ensure vulnerable families can access support
In short:
The federal government has announced an $11 million rescue package to shore up the in-home childcare sector.
Earlier this year the ABC revealed the sector was on the verge of collapse, with about 1,000 vulnerable children at risk of losing care.
What's next?
The sector says the support package is "monumental" but has warned big challenges remain for it to reach its potential.
Australia's in-home childcare sector has welcomed an $11 million federal government rescue package, but there is criticism some operators will gain more generous support than others.
In-home care is designed to support families who cannot access mainstream child care, because they live in remote areas, work nights or care for children with complex medical needs, serious disability or child protection concerns.
Earlier this year, the ABC revealed anger from vulnerable families as services came close to shutting down.
In an interview with ABC News, Minister for Early Childhood Education Jess Walsh said in-home care was "an absolutely vital service".
Senator Walsh recently met one-year-old Cece and her mother, Jennifer, who lived south of Sydney.
Cece was diagnosed with a rare medical condition and doctors recommended she avoid mainstream child care.
"Initially, it was like, 'My God, what are we going to do?'" Jennifer said.
"In today's society, my husband and I both need to work and I love my job and I love what I do."
Jennifer described the program as "game-changing", allowing her to return to work while Cece was cared for by a qualified educator at home.
However, the sector has shrunk significantly in recent years, due to higher costs and unique challenges of delivering early learning in family homes, making the program out of reach for many.
The sector was excluded from a government subsidy scheme introduced in 2024 to cover a historic 15 per cent pay rise for long day care workers.
That meant families had to pay more for in-home care to cover the wage increase themselves.
More than 70 per cent of families in the scheme reduced their hours or withdrew because they could not afford to absorb the rising costs.
The federal government has come under pressure in Senate estimates from the Liberals, Greens and crossbenchers who warned children could be put at risk if the in-home care sector collapsed.
Senator Walsh announced the $11 million support package after hearing from many families including Cece and Jennifer's.
The package includes $5 million for Sustainability Support Grants, $3.4 million to deliver a 15 per cent pay rise to in-home care employees and $2.7 million in further grants for operational support for the sector.
"The in-home care sector is quite unique," Senator Walsh said.
"We wanted to make sure that we knew that the pay rise would be able to be passed on and when we were confident about that we extended the pay rise to the in-home care sector."
Relief package 'monumental' but some workers will miss out
Nicole Morgan, president of the Australian Home Childcare Association (AHCA), has been an in-home care provider for 19 years and described the announcement of the sustainability grants as "monumental".
She said she had been on the cusp of closing in June as it was no longer financially viable to continue operating.
"[The grant] meant that I was able to stay in the program. Not only me, but several other in-home care service providers that were going to close as well and not be working in the new financial year, have remained open."
While all have welcomed the sustainability funding, some operators are angry the worker retention payment, to cover pay rises for carers, is not available to contractors, who make up 70 per cent of the in-home care sector.
That means just five of the 21 agencies qualify for the worker retention payment, which has been available to long day care operators since 2024.
Ms Morgan warned the impact could be "catastrophic".
"We feel the inequity has created a division within the sector that is really unfair," she said.
"What we might find is that those educators will leave those providers. Those families will not be able to afford the cost of care and those providers, therefore, will close," she said.
Senator Walsh said providers employing staff as contractors were still being supported.
"Our In-Home Care Sustainability Support Grants provide tailored support to this specialised sector, and can be used, in line with the grant guidelines, to help providers retain contractors.
"The Worker Retention Payment is also available where providers and educators choose to move from a contractor to an employee model."
Long-term future for home care still to be resolved
Ms Morgan said the in-home care program was "massively underutilised", operating at about 35 per cent occupancy due to the extra costs associated with delivering care in the family home.
She said there were currently 1,370 children accessing the program, with the potential for the program to help 3,200, under the government cap.
Over the past decade, the sector has shrunk from about 70 providers to 21.
Three separate reviews from the federal government, Productivity Commission and consumer watchdog have identified affordability as a barrier to access.
Another and wider-ranging federal government review is underway, which the sector hopes will ensure it is "sustainable" and "viable" into the future.
"The childcare subsidy needs to reflect the cost of care for in-home care and the differences that we have," Ms Morgan said.
Senator Walsh foreshadowed the sector receiving further support after the review was completed.
"The Service Delivery Price Project is due later this year and will provide important input into our plans for universal early education and care, including future support for the In-Home Care sector," she said.

Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:43:38 UTC
03:43:38 KST

An explosives-laden drone aimed at a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport was part of a Russian state operation, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on 1 September.
Germany has moved from suspecting foreign sabotage to formally blaming Russia for the Leipzig attack. The finding has prompted diplomatic and security measures against Moscow while the criminal investigation continues.
Police investigations, the attack pattern, and intelligence findings established Russian responsibility, Dobrindt said. The drones' configuration, components, explosives, and detonation systems resembled those used in other Russian hybrid operations—covert sabotage and disruption below the threshold of open war—and in Russia's war against Ukraine, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said.
The first drone, carrying explosives, was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft on the evening of 4 August and defused. Investigators believe a DHL freighter may have collided with a second drone while aborting its landing after the airport closed; that drone was never recovered. A third drone was found on 14 August in a field at Kabelsketal, where investigators subsequently discovered roughly 50 grams of suspected military explosive.
Leipzig/Halle is an international freight hub used by Ukrainian Antonov aircraft and NATO's strategic airlift program, through which allies charter heavy transport aircraft to move oversized military cargo.
Berlin will close the Bonn consulate on 18 September, end the operating agreement for the Russian House, a Moscow-backed cultural center, tighten entry controls for Russian nationals, seek to add more targets to EU sanctions lists, and pressure Russia's shadow fleet—opaquely owned tankers used to move Russian oil outside Western restrictions. Wadephul also summoned the Russian ambassador. Russia's Berlin embassy will remain open.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Interfax that Moscow would respond to Germany's “anti-Russian action,” without specifying how.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance stood in full solidarity with Germany, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described Berlin's measures as a strong response.
Dobrindt said Germany expects further Russian hybrid attacks. The Leipzig incident follows a widening campaign of suspected Russian sabotage across Europe, including a 2024 incendiary-device attack at the same airport that Western security officials suspected Russian intelligence organized.
How the Leipzig attack unfolded
Euromaidan Press reported on 12 August, citing Die Zeit, that footage showed an explosives-laden quadcopter striking the wing of a parked Ukrainian Antonov An-124 before falling without detonating. The article also noted that a US Defense Department official told CNN that Washington assessed the drone belonged to Russian intelligence.
On 25 August, EP reported, citing Tagesschau’s NDR/WDR/SZ investigation, that investigators had expanded the case to three drones and found the third with suspected military explosive nearby in Kabelsketal, 10 days after the original attempt.

Social media algorithm opt-in would curb 'manosphere', says advocate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:43:18 UTC
03:43:18 KST

Algorithm opt-in best way to stop big tech serving manosphere content to young men, says advocate
In short:
Chanel Contos is warning tech giants could design their way around weaker attempts to rein in harmful social media algorithms.
The Teach Us Consent chief executive used a National Press Club speech to further her push for algorithmic feeds to be "opt-in".
What's next?
The federal government is considering giving users greater control over content served online, while draft digital duty of care laws are due to be released later this month.
Consent advocate Chanel Contos is urging the federal government to pursue an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds because it will be "too easy" for tech giants to design their way around weaker reforms.
Ms Contos made the case for reining in harmful algorithms, which she said were exposing young people to misogynistic manosphere content and fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia, during a speech to the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has backed giving Australians more control over the content they are served online but has stopped short of backing the algorithm opt-in model proposed by Ms Contos.
"In response to community concern about the impact of algorithms, we are considering options to ensure people have greater control over what they receive on their devices," Mr Albanese said.
In her speech, Ms Contos argued an opt-out system for algorithms would be a "first step" and congratulate the government for seeking to address the issue.
"However, opt-in algorithms would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," she said.
"This is crucial, and the detail in any reform will determine its success."
Algorithms are the automated systems used by social media platforms to decide which posts, videos and other content a user sees and in what order, based on factors such as their behaviour and apparent interests.
Ms Contos, who is the founder and chief executive of advocacy group Teach Us Consent, launched the "fix our feeds" campaign, which calls for the government to mandate an "opt-in" for algorithms, in December last year.
Labor has since indicated an interest in addressing the broader issue to further complement its laws banning Australians aged under 16 from holding any social media account.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said "deliberately opaque" algorithmic recommender systems had allowed social media companies to influence Australian culture "for better or worse".
"Online harm has real-world consequences," she said.
"If we want to prevent harm, we must fix platforms that reward it."
Digital duty of care next on Labor's agenda
Ms Wells has been developing a digital duty of care, which would be a legal obligation on online platforms to proactively identify and reduce foreseeable risks of harm to their users.
It reverses the current situation that relies mainly on users reporting harmful content after something has gone wrong.
An exposure draft of the legislation is due to be released later this month, with Ms Contos describing the "overall strength" of those reforms as "critical" to their success.
Loading...
"It is too easy for big tech to design schemes that appear as structural reform but actually suit them just fine," she said.
In her speech, Ms Contos linked algorithm-driven harm to the "uphill battle" schools are facing in their attempts to teach consent to young students.
Ms Contos said a yearly class had "little hope" of changing the attitudes responsible for the current culture of sexual violence in schools while an "addictive content producing machine" simultaneously targeted teens with a "contradictory message".
How algorithms fuel the manosphere
She outlined how "manosphere" is not simply a broad term describing online communities that hold male supremacy ideologies, but a money-making venture facilitated by algorithms.
Ms Contos said young men online seeking community, belonging or self-improvement advice are "targeted" with content that blames women for their "misfortune".
This content also reinstates "harmful and outdated" gender roles, like the idea women should not leave the house without their male partner, hold jobs or earn their own money.
"Boys and men have valid concerns about the economy, and their relationships with partners and friends," she said.
"From these concerns, an industry has jumped onto a market opportunity, and unfortunately, misogyny is at the heart of its business model."
Ms Contos described how young men engaging in "harmless" workout or motivational videos are "very quickly" served content promoting the idea that emotional control, material wealth and dominance "especially over women" are "markers of male wealth".
She pointed to research showing men who subscribe to those sorts of beliefs are twice as likely to binge-drink, six times as likely to problem gamble and eight times as likely to have suicidal thoughts.
They are also 17 times more likely to have hit their partner, according to the Man Box study.

Government agrees €92.5 billion budget with €12.4 billion deficit
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:39:30 EEST
03:39:30 KST

Finland’s government has agreed a €92.5 billion budget for 2027, including a €12.4 billion deficit, tax cuts and about €1 billion in additional spending savings.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the government had completed its final budget negotiations of the parliamentary term in one day and argued that the economy had returned to growth.
“We have now got Finland back on its feet,” Orpo said at a press conference after the talks.
Finance Minister Riikka Purra said the government would continue with spending reductions agreed earlier. Savings next year include cuts to organisation grants, integration spending and public administration.
Total spending cuts included in the budget amount to about €4.8 billion before taking account of other expenditure increases and tax reductions, according to figures presented by Purra.
The government will also proceed with previously agreed tax changes. Corporate tax will fall from 20% to 18%, while income tax for low- and middle-income earners will be reduced. Purra said the combined tax reductions amount to about €1.7 billion.
The government will abandon a planned tax benefit for data centres. It will also allow municipalities to introduce a voluntary tourist tax under new framework legislation.
Debt servicing costs remain a major pressure on the budget. Interest expenditure is expected to reach €4.4 billion next year, compared with less than €1 billion in 2022.
Purra said higher debt levels and increased interest rates had driven the increase. Defence, security and health and social care costs are also adding to spending.
The government also agreed additional funding for shelters, forests, the justice system, sports facilities and measures to combat African swine fever.
Orpo said the government expected employment to improve during the autumn as economic growth continued.
The opposition criticised the package.
Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela said the budget failed to address Finland’s unemployment problem and attacked the corporate tax cut.
She also criticised reductions in funding for social and health organisations and higher health care client fees, arguing that the measures would place more pressure on low-income households.
The government rejected calls for further fiscal tightening during the budget talks. Orpo said the coalition had already agreed almost €1 billion in additional adjustment and wanted to focus on growth and employment.
Purra said further action would follow if required by the European Commission.

How Coles and NSW Police busted an Apple gift card tampering scam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:38:13 UTC
03:38:13 KST

How Coles and NSW Police busted an Apple gift card tampering scam
It is a movement of the hands barely visible on the grainy CCTV.
A man standing in front of a rack of colourful gift cards reaches into his pockets and, in several reaching motions, places cards back on the supermarket racks.
It is one of the moments Coles's fraud team captured while building a case against the man last year, alleging he was tampering with Apple gift cards in its supermarkets.
The ABC can confirm the man was later convicted for the incident, after Coles worked with police to monitor the man, originally from Taiwan, and eventually bust him with a haul of tampered cards.
"Gift card tampering and fraud is an evolving challenge affecting retailers and customers both in Australia and internationally," the supermarket said to ABC News in a statement.
"Coles takes the issue extremely seriously."
Loading...
What is gift card tampering?
An ABC investigation this week revealed supermarket customers nationwide were reporting gift card tampering, with the issue possibly linked to a wider global scam.
Homeland Security in the US has been investigating this issue for several years, with Project Red Hook linking it to money laundering in China, human trafficking and even murder.
"All of America's top 20 retailers were being affected," lead investigator Adam Parks said.
"Young Chinese nationals were being interdicted and arrested while taking cards off the rack, blank cards off the rack, taking them away from the store."
Mr Parks said the organised crime they found had a network of people dedicated to taking apart the cards, stealing their codes, and then returning them packaged back in store.
"Once they were put on the rack, then an unwitting consumer would go and would purchase those cards, and put funds on the cards," he said.
"And then [the] Chinese organised crime syndicates were able to spend the card before the unwitting consumer was [able to]."
As well as the CCTV footage supplied to ABC News, Coles captured the man on numerous other occasions at supermarkets around Sydney in March and April 2025, court documents show.
In some security video, the man was seen taking gift cards from the supermarket's aisles, while in others, like the one ABC has witnessed, he was seen returning them.
Security staff then went down the supermarket aisle and noticed numerous Apple cards worth hundreds of dollars had been tampered with, and some stock had gone missing from the shelves.
After an internal investigation, Coles contacted the police.
Loading...
How the arrest unfolded
In April, officers attached to Campsie Police Area Command started covertly tracking their suspect.
Phone mapping records show the man regularly travelled to regional New South Wales, Goulburn and the Southern Highlands, with police suspecting he was also tampering with cards there.
Police obtained a warrant and searched the 32-year-old man's home in Eastwood, in Sydney's western suburbs, on May 9, 2025.
They found a bag containing 47 iTunes gift cards in bundles of five labelled with Post-it Notes.
The cards ranged from $100 to $500 in value, and there were nine more in his car.
Police said he told them outside of the interview that he was hired by an unnamed criminal syndicate, according to the court documents.
After arresting him, police alleged that he handled 61 Apple and iTunes gift cards worth more than $10,000.
He was charged with five counts of dishonestly obtaining financial advantage and two counts of dealing with property proceeds of crime of less than $100,000 and less than $5,000.
He was then refused bail after police said there was a risk of "interfering with witnesses and tampering with or fabricating evidence".
The man was eventually convicted on July 22, 2025, and received a 15-month suspended prison sentence and a two-year community corrections order.
The ABC has been unable to reach the man for comment.
Trouble 'joining all the dots'
While the case highlights that gift card tampering is happening in Australia, private investigator Ken Gamble says "joining the dots" nationally might take more work.
The Australian Federal Police and the financial crimes regulator AUSTRAC both said this was not their domain.
"This is not a matter for the AFP," a spokesperson said.
And the authority that handles complaints about financial products, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA), said it had limited scope over gift cards.
"It's definitely theft, but it would be one law enforcement would give a very low priority to because of the monetary value," Mr Gamble said.
"Unless they join all the dots here and they can see that this is done in great volume, [then] you're not going to get law enforcement to put the resources in.
"And that's the problem. That's why this type of crime is potentially something that could become very prolific in Australia."
Apple changed its gift card packaging in early 2025 to make it harder to open. The tech giant defended the measures as a way to prevent tampering and declined multiple requests for comment.
Coles said stopping the crime took more than just the supermarkets and police.
"Coles works in conjunction with other retailers, gift card and brand partners, and law enforcement agencies to share relevant information and support investigations into suspected gift card fraud," the company said.
"We know that there is no single measure that will eliminate gift card fraud, and this isn't an issue that can be solved by retailers alone. It requires cooperation across retailers, gift card providers and law enforcement."

What can the German 'Dragon' submarines do?

One especially challenging area has been defending against Houthi attacks on Eilat, given that when the navy helps shoot down threats, it must contend with an extremely small zone of defense so as not to invade Egyptian or Jordanian airspace – or it would need to coordinate with those countries if necessary.
The submarine deal dates back many years and has been part of the navy’s strategic modernization effort.

Mathematician discovers how to fold the smallest origami doughnut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:37:10 UTC
03:37:10 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly math newsletter that’s delivered to your inbox every Tuesday afternoon. Sign up today and read it first.
How can you create a doughnut-shaped surface from a flat sheet of paper? The most elegant solution is probably to use the art of paper folding called origami. Mathematician Richard Schwartz of Brown University wanted to find out how to achieve this feat in as few steps as possible.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA, Schwartz presented his result: the paper must be folded at least 24 times. This creates 16 triangles that intersect at eight vertices. For his proof, he used computer simulations and methods of analysis. He also consulted artificial intelligence—and a hallucination by the program almost undid his efforts.
Creating a Curve from Something Flat
That a doughnut shape—called a torus by mathematicians—can be formed from a single folded sheet of paper is by no means a given. In fact, you have to curve a sheet of paper to form a doughnut-shaped surface: first, it is rolled into a cylinder, and then the two open ends are brought together. This last step cannot be done without creating creases, however. The same is true when trying to form a sphere from a sheet of paper. But the principles of origami come to the rescue. Through folding, it becomes possible to create certain curves from a flat sheet of paper. In this way, you can form a torus, though not a sphere.
The first examples of such a construction were determined by mathematicians Yuri Burago and Viktor Zalgaller in 1960. In the decades that followed, experts constructed various types of origami tori, all composed of triangular shapes. The vertices of the triangles, which meet at the corners (also called vertices), must have an angle sum of 360 degrees. Most recently, in 2025, researcher Vincent Tugayé constructed an origami torus with only nine vertices. Schwartz then wondered whether this value could be further reduced.
The mathematician, who had previously proven the shortest origami Möbius strip dimensions, was able to prove that a torus with only seven vertices is impossible. “The proof was quite simple,” Schwartz says, “so I was surprised that no one had presented it before.” As he demonstrated, a curvature is necessary to form a torus from triangles with only seven vertices—something that cannot be achieved using pure origami folding techniques. Then arose the question of whether it was possible to construct an origami torus with eight vertices or whether Tugayé had already found the optimal solution.
Schwartz initially tried to demonstrate that an origami torus of eight vertices could not exist, as he had for a torus with seven vertices. But he failed. So he looked for examples of such structures.
His first goal was to determine how many different ways triangles could be arranged on the sheet in the eight vertex case. In other words, how many folds are theoretically possible? To simplify things, he asked ChatGPT this question. The AI chatbot told him there are thousands of possible solutions and linked to a website where the answer should be available. “I found that very discouraging because I didn’t want to work my way through thousands of patterns,” Schwartz says. So he briefly abandoned the project.
But the topic wouldn’t let him go. He started going through the various arrangements of triangles with a pencil and paper. “It seemed highly improbable that there could really be thousands of different solutions,” Schwartz says. “I finally looked at the website linked by ChatGPT, and it turned out there were only seven possibilities!” From these arrangements, the mathematician picked out the ones that looked most promising. One of them reminded him of the solution to the origami Möbius strip puzzle.
Using a computer program, he then tried to fold the possible arrangements of triangles to create a torus—and succeeded. The result resembles a doghouse more than a doughnut. But from a mathematical perspective, it was exactly what he was looking for: a ring-shaped structure with a hole.
“The most difficult part of the study was probably debugging the computer programs,” Schwartz says. “Whenever you’re working with computer-aided mathematics, you have to be absolutely certain that the program is telling you the truth.” He estimates that the final proof, by which he demonstrated the existence of an origami torus with eight vertices, accounted for only about 10 percent of his time.
But with that, the smallest origami doughnut has now been found. Schwartz hasn’t folded it from real paper yet, however, citing his skill in origami: “I’m terribly bad at it.”

Iran’s worsening economic crisis raises questions over Tehran’s willingness to compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:37:07 UTC
03:37:07 KST

Images emerging from Iran in recent days showing vehicles waiting in long lines to refuel are another indication of the severe economic crisis facing the country – one of the most serious Iran has experienced in decades.
The rial has continued to collapse against the US dollar, recently falling below the threshold of 2 million rials to the dollar on the open market. Soaring inflation, growing difficulties in importing and exporting goods, and a dramatic decline in oil exports are increasingly being felt on the streets of Iran.
The latest figures underscore the scale of the deterioration.
Even senior Iranian officials have acknowledged the severity of the situation. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said the country’s foreign trade has contracted by about 35% due to US sanctions and disruptions to maritime trade.
The World Bank estimates that Iran’s economy contracted by 2.7% during the Iranian fiscal year that ended in March 2026, and has warned that the current conflict could further weaken the economy.
“The main problem is inflation,” Dr. Raz Zimmt, director of the Iran and Shi’ite Axis Program at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Jerusalem Post. “The official inflation rate is more than 80%. But what is even more interesting is the price of basic goods, particularly food, which has increased by between 120% and 180%.”
Can Iran outlast America's blockade on Hormuz?
The most immediate threat to Tehran’s finances is the US blockade, which is disrupting Iran’s ability to export oil and other goods.
For years, Iran has relied on tankers known as the “shadow fleet” and on intermediaries to continue selling crude oil – primarily to China – despite US and European sanctions. The system allowed Tehran to maintain a significant flow of foreign currency despite the sanctions.
In recent weeks, however, Iran’s crude oil exports have reportedly plunged to approximately 220,000-255,000 barrels per day in August, compared with around 2 m. barrels per day in March.
The sharp decline is putting additional pressure on Iran’s ability to obtain foreign currency at a time when it needs it more than ever.
At the same time, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that the US administration will impose sanctions and severe penalties on any country that enables Tehran to obtain foreign currency.
At the start of the war, Iran tried to circumvent the pressure through alternative trade networks, offshore oil storage, ship-to-ship transfers, barter arrangements, and transactions in currencies other than the dollar.
But these mechanisms are becoming increasingly difficult to operate as Washington expands its sanctions and implements its “D-Day” campaign targeting Tehran’s financial and banking system.
The central question is no longer simply whether Iran’s economy can survive the sanctions. It is how long Tehran can absorb the cumulative impact of its economic problems – and whether the pressure will ultimately push the regime toward an agreement with the US.
Dr. Zimmt estimates that despite the difficult economic situation, which he expects to deteriorate further, there are currently no clear signs that the economic crisis is translating into protests capable of threatening the regime’s stability.
“There is a difficult economic situation, there is inflation, but it is not unbearable at this point,” he said. “We still don’t see anything that can be defined as a loss of control or a collapse. Not at all.”
Expert tells 'Post': Nothing suggests Iranian regime's loss of control
He also said that reports of widespread hunger in Iran do not currently reflect the situation on the ground.
“The situation is certainly difficult, but there is no hunger as a phenomenon. This is still not a situation that can be defined as a collapse,” he continued. “Inflation is very worrying; there is no doubt about that. But over the past week or two, there has been some stabilization. It is still considered extremely high, around 80%, but it has stopped rising.”
In his assessment, this means the regime may still be able to weather the pressure for some time.
“I don’t get the impression that this is a matter of days or weeks,” he said.
At the same time, Zimmt noted that the regime itself is preparing for the possibility of renewed protests, and warned that if demonstrations do erupt, the Iranian authorities could respond even more harshly than they have in the past.
Despite the mounting pressure, Zimmt cautioned against assuming that Iran will necessarily capitulate to US demands.
One of the central problems, he said, is that the Iranians do not believe that concessions on their part would necessarily guarantee an end to the war. History, he added, shows that economic pressure alone is not sufficient to force Tehran into a compromise.
“Economic pressure is bringing them very close to the point of decision,” Zimmt said. “But in order for them to make a decision in the desired direction, they need to be offered something that would also allow them to come out without being humiliated – to save face.”
Zimmt also warned of the possibility that Washington could fall into a “misconception” of its own, overestimating the degree of pressure it is exerting on Tehran and concluding that the Iranian regime is on the verge of surrender.
“The sense of hubris and self-confidence that characterized the Iranians in recent months is now somewhat characterizing the Americans,” he said. “I’m not sure that they themselves are not now trapped in some kind of misconception that if we just continue doing this, it is only a matter of time before the Iranians surrender.”

Political language has become a weapon against the truth and Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:36:49 UTC
03:36:49 KST

In my childhood – not that long ago – we believed Americans were modest and plain-spoken – and Canadians, even more so. Soviet Communists were the Orwellian liars, creating ministries of truth masking atrocities with ten-dollar words.

Nepal’s deadly debris avalanche is a warning for the rest of the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:36:40 UTC
03:36:40 KST

The death toll from the catastrophic floods that swept through parts of Nepal and Tibet last week has risen beyond 1,000 people, while thousands of people remain missing. Among them are hundreds of workers believed to be stuck inside large underground tunnels connected to hydroelectric power plants. As the rescue mission continues, researchers warn that disasters like this could become more common all over the planet as a result of climate change.
Part of what made this disaster so deadly was its suddenness. Experts believe it was likely caused by a large landslide on the mountain Langtang Lirung that included a chunk of glacier. It sent hundreds of millions of tons of ice, rock and other debris hurtling down the slopes to the villages below. The avalanche traveled nearly 100 kilometers (about 62 miles), according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
And while it’s too early to say whether this event was caused by rising global temperatures, the trend is clear: Earth is getting warmer, and that will make disasters like this worse and more common. The rest of the world should be on notice.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Understanding why climate change is making such events more likely is important. Generally, in high-altitude environments such as mountain ranges, permafrost—basically, frozen soil—holds sediment and rocky material together. When it thaws, it can cause cracks in the rocks that make a violent break more likely.
“It's essentially preconditioning the glacier and the rock for potential collapse or a landslide,” says Regine Hock, a geoscientist at the University of Oslo.
At the same time, the world’s glaciers are shrinking because of the warming planet. This weakens the ice’s “buttressing” effect on the surrounding slopes, which in turn make those rocks more unstable, Hock says. Excess melted water can also create lubrication, more easily triggering a slip, she says.
What that means is that, in principle, a mountain landslide can happen anywhere that those conditions exist, Hock says. That could be in the Himalayas or in South America or in the Cascade Range in the Pacific Northwest or on the slopes of Alaska. “Wherever you have similar conditions, like warming, destabilizing of the rock, thawing of permafrost and steep slopes, you can have these mass movements,” she says.
But pinpointing the exact risk to any specific village, town or city is difficult. For one, it’s hard to know when a mountain or glacier might crack. Determining that involves having a deep understanding of the land’s features, as well as tracking possible triggers such as earthquakes, says Ben Orlove, an anthropologist who studies climate risks at Columbia University.
The equation also needs to factor in any mitigation efforts—say, early warning systems—to reduce risk and the local conditions where people live. In 2025, for instance, the Tracy Arm landslide in Alaska was so powerful that it produced a tsunami of nearly 500 meters. But because Alaska is so sparsely populated, no one was killed.
There are ways to reduce some of the risks of high-mountain hazards. Local officials can, for instance, work to prevent spills from “glacial lake outburst floods,” lakes formed by melting glaciers. Many of these lakes are not dangerous, says Olivier Gagliardini, a professor at Grenoble Alpes University in France, but if one’s walls are “not strong enough,” they can burst. In France, for example, officials have drained glacial lakes to head off potential flooding, Gagliardini says.
In other cases, evacuation is the only option, Gagliardini adds—that is certainly true for a glacial collapse or landslide on the scale of what happened in the Himalayas.

Russia Turned Crimea Into a Missile Launchpad; Ukraine Is Now Dismantling It. Here’s How
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:34:12 UTC
03:34:12 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Turned Crimea Into a Missile Launchpad; Ukraine Is Now Dismantling It. Here’s How
As Ukraine works to isolate Crimea from Russia and disrupt logistics on the southern front, its strikes on the peninsula serve as a form of proactive air defense, eliminating Russian missiles and drone salvos at their source before they can be used against Ukrainian cities.
Across 40 relentless days and nights between late June and early August, Ukraine launched a sweeping long-range campaign to paralyze Russian oil refining, cripple arms production, and neutralize shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov—all to pressure Moscow toward peace.
Strikes hit key economic targets feeding the Kremlin's war chest, sending dual-use Wildberries logistics centers over 1,700 kilometers away in Yekaterinburg up in smoke. Eleven of Russia's largest oil refineries were also set ablaze, with hits reaching a record 2,500 kilometers into the interior, causing widespread fuel shortages and emergency rationing nationwide.
However, Ukraine’s strikes are also delivering a major blow to Russia’s ability to strike Ukraine from Crimea and hold on to the peninsula.
Why Crimea matters for Russia’s air campaign
Beyond deep strategic economic strikes, Ukraine's campaign relied heavily on "middle strike" drones to dismantle Russian supply chains and air defenses. Nowhere was this more evident than across temporarily occupied Crimea.
Thanks to Ukrainian efforts to hit Russian air defenses, they have been able to exploit gaps better and strike missile and drone launch sites. It is what Tomáš Nagy, an air defense expert and analyst at GLOBSEC, called “passive air defense,” which means that “you harden everything that you can harden, you mobilize whatever you can mobilize, and yes, you strike the capabilities of the other side to create vulnerabilities. And the best that the Ukrainians can do is to try to cripple [Russian] production capacity as much as possible.”
"It all started with Crimea, and it will end with Crimea,” a former Norwegian Defense Attaché to Ukraine, Hans Petter Midttun, told us. He underscored the peninsula's ultimate role in Russia's war against Ukraine.
"Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 had a dramatic and immediate positive effect on Vladimir Putin's popularity and perceived legitimacy among Russians," he said, adding that it served as "one of the most important turning points in his domestic political standing".
Polling tracked this shift directly, showing Putin’s trust and approval for the general direction of the country jumped notably by August of that year, while overall approval for Putin reached 86% by September.
For years, "Crimea was perceived as the 'unsinkable aircraft carrier', essential for Russian power projection in the Black Sea and beyond," while also enabling full Russian control over the Sea of Azov, Midttun said. "Ukraine has turned a strategic trophy into a strategic liability. The campaign aims to make Russian operations from Crimea unsustainable. Every Russian military installation on the peninsula–airfields, naval bases, logistical hubs, sensors and weapons–is today within range of Ukrainian missiles and drones.”
If Crimea is liberated, Putin will likely fall.
Hans Petter Midttun
Former Norwegian Defense Attaché to Ukraine
Ukraine has managed to scale up its drone launches against Russia in both occupied territories and Russia itself, which is redefining the war.
“In the first 16 days of August, the reported rate rose to at least 480 per day,” said Midttun. “With the seven-day average reaching about 540 by 16 August. Russia is presently unable to effectively protect itself against Ukrainian missiles and drones.”
What is Ukraine's active (or proactive) air defense?
While one of the main goals of targeting Crimean infrastructure has been disrupting Russian supply lines, the campaign serves a vital secondary role: proactive air defense.
“Crimea is well within range of southern Ukraine,” said Midttun. “It reduces Ukrainian warning time and ability to counter incoming threats. The maritime domain further increases Ukraine’s defensive challenges, making it hard to locate air defense threats." That geography makes Crimea particularly valuable as a launchpad for Russian missile and drone attacks.
Crimea gives Russia a platform to project its military power from the south, creating what Midttun described as a “near omni-directional” threat and preventing Ukraine from concentrating its forces in the north and east.
To counter this, Ukrainian mid-range strikes degrade threats directly at their launchpads.
How Ukraine targets Russian missile launch infrastructure
Under Operation Crimean Power Switch Off, Ukrainian drone waves methodically degraded Russia's launch capabilities across the peninsula, striking a key forward staging hub and suppressing the daily barrage directed at Ukrainian civilians, cities, and critical infrastructure.
Specifically, Ukrainian strike networks have targeted six distinct pillars of Russia's Crimean military infrastructure:
- Air defense—S-300/S-400 launchers, Pantsir-S1 point-defense batteries. This weakens Russia’s defense of military sites.
- Missile launch sites—the aforementioned S-300/S-400 launchers, which Russia can use to fire surface-to-air missiles in a secondary ground-attack role, as well as Bastion launch sites used to fire Zircon and Oniks missiles. Striking these systems can reduce missile salvos targeting Odesa, Mykolaiv, and southern frontline positions at the source.
- Drone networks and launchpads—Dzhankoi Orion drone relay systems, Cape Chauda Shahed staging grounds, UAV command infrastructure. This targets the infrastructure used to stage, launch, and control Russian drones. In the same coordinated waves that neutralized two S-400 batteries, Ukrainian strikes also destroyed Shahed and Geran drone storage depots.
- Radars and tracking arrays—96L6 target acquisition radars, Okhotnyche radar shelters, Nebo complexes. This strips Russian forces of real-time air and maritime tracking, blinding target-coordination networks.
- Forward aviation hubs—Belbek, Saky, Dzhankoi, and Hvardiiske airbases: Suppresses tactical jet sorties by striking airfield hangars. This destroys ammo/fuel depots and forces strike aircraft to evacuate further inland.
- Military grid infrastructure—Tavriyskaya TPP, 330 kV Simferopol/Sevastopol substations, Kuban-Crimea power bridge. This cuts high-voltage power to bases, forcing air defense batteries and radars onto fragile backup generators.
What Russia uses in Crimea to launch attacks against Ukraine
Tracking every launch from Russian-occupied Crimea is difficult. While no single public source provides a complete picture, UNITED24 Media compared reports from Ukrainian threat-monitoring channel Monitor with official Ukrainian Air Force data to identify changes in Russia's use of Crimea as a launchpad.
Between January and August 12, Monitor’s tracking data recorded at least 35 confirmed missile launches across 17 distinct dates and 14 explicit drone launch episodes originating from the peninsula. Ukrainian Air Forces data shows the number of missiles is significantly higher, as Monitor tracks attack launches as they occur, not after; by August, Monitor observes a decrease in ground launches after the 40-day campaign.
Iskander, Zircon, and Oniks missiles were used repeatedly from January through to July. That surge saw a massive spike in attacks from Crimea at the height of the 40-day campaign—mostly from air-launched Kh-56/69 missiles, though ground launches also continued. However, combining the Monitor and Ukrainian official data, it shows that in August, the attacks drop, with four specific instances of Oniks missile launches by August 27, consisting of 8 confirmed missiles. In addition, there is one attack with Iskanders from the Crimea/Black Sea region, though it is unclear if it came from Crimea.
If we compare the types of attacks from Crimea, UAV attacks generally increase in July from the previous two months, but drop by mid-August. At the start of the year, in January, the majority of attacks were from ballistics, yet this number had dropped.
Oniks missiles continue to be launched from Crimea. In August, they were the majority of verified ground-launched missiles recorded from the peninsula in the combined dataset. Originally designed as anti-ship cruise missiles, Oniks can also be used against land targets. The shift in type of missile, and the volume, shows that Ukraine has made an impact on Russia’s ability to use Crimea as a missile launchpad.
Why Crimea is a key part of Ukraine's defense strategy
Further strikes on Russian launch infrastructure could constrain Crimea’s role as a platform for attacks on Ukraine even more. While Crimea remains a crucial launchpad for Russian drones and missiles, further degrading its potential to launch strikes yields multiple strategic benefits.
Midttun listed the key impacts:
- Opens the Black Sea for maritime trade and activity
- Allows Ukraine to relocate forces and capacities towards Belarus and Russia
- Increases the protection of Ukrainian citizens and critical infrastructure
- Creates the precondition for the forthcoming liberation of the Crimean Peninsula
The operation “Logistics Lockdown” is not only affecting Russia’s ability to sustain operations from Crimea but also the Russian occupation forces in the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, says Midttun.
“During the last three months, Ukraine has destroyed an average of 13,456 trucks monthly across all sectors,” he said. “A majority of these, however, are destroyed in the south. Road and rail bridges are being destroyed at scale.”
Targeting such a crucial launchpad and eliminating weapons systems before they can fire eases pressure on the southern front. Odesa, Mykolaiv, and other southern cities stand to benefit most directly because of their proximity to the peninsula.
These operations put pressure on Russia’s forces across the occupied south. If Russia cannot transport troops, supplies, and military vehicles without a major risk, then they cannot reinforce and are less able to conduct large-scale offensive operations.
These strikes also divert Russian resources, forcing Moscow to either protect its military equipment on the peninsula by relocating it or transfer air defense systems from elsewhere—weakening Russian defenses on other parts of the frontline.
Further degrading Russia’s ability to launch Oniks missiles could reduce the missile threat to Odesa and southern Ukraine—protecting civilians, supporting frontline forces, and securing Black Sea grain corridors.
What does Ukraine need to increase and repeat these results?
In a recent interview, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Magyar” Brovdi revealed that his forces are operating at just 14% of full capacity, but could strike seven times as many military targets in Crimea if pledged Western funds arrived faster.
This operational constraint aligns directly with Midttun’s assessment that production readiness is not the issue, but financial backing: "Ukraine lacks the economy to ramp up its missile and drone production. That’s the only thing stopping Ukraine from increasing the scale and scope of the campaign."
Western support must increase to allow Ukraine to expand its impact and replicate these tactics across other fronts, Midttun said. Russia’s invasion is part of a broader hybrid war against Europe—one that will only escalate if Ukraine is forced to operate under persistent material constraints.
Another way to boost Ukraine’s capabilities beyond its own territories would be allowing Starlink use over Russian territory. Ukraine’s ability to use Starlink over Crimea enabled it to strike a wide range of Russian military targets across the peninsula. However, even with the impressive long-range strikes, the satellite system could be more impactful if it eased the transfer of communications to drones.
President Zelenskyy recently said that Ukraine has a “window of opportunity” to end the war, because of its many advantages on the battlefield and in the skies. Operations that degrade Russia’s military infrastructure in Crimea are part of that broader effort.
Empowering Kyiv to degrade Crimean launchpads and set the conditions for the peninsula's eventual liberation is not just a battlefield tactic; it directly fortifies wider European security.

The Palestinian Education and Higher Education Ministry warned on Tuesday that Israel is systematically targeting education in occupied East Jerusalem to “erase national identity,” including by imposing its curriculum and barring teachers from schools.
On Monday, the Palestinian Jerusalem Governorate warned that, with the start of the academic year on Tuesday, Israel would begin imposing the Israeli curriculum on more than 45,000 Palestinian first- and seventh-grade students at schools run by the Israeli municipality in Jerusalem.
Earlier Tuesday, several private schools in Jerusalem, including Christian schools, went on strike as the new academic year began, protesting Israeli authorities’ failure to issue entry permits to teachers from the West Bank working at those schools.
In a statement, the Palestinian Education and Higher Education Ministry said developments concerning Israeli practices targeting education in Jerusalem were part of a “systematic and ongoing” campaign against the educational process.
It stressed that Palestinian students’ right in Jerusalem to education and to study the national curriculum is an “inalienable right guaranteed by international conventions and agreements.”
The ministry said Israeli authorities had prevented a number of male and female teachers and education staff from reaching their schools, particularly Christian schools, due to the failure to renew their entry permits.
It added that this prevented education staff from reaching their schools, directly affecting the regular start of the academic year.
The ministry said Israeli measures had also affected schools run by the UN Agency for Palestinian Refugees and the national curriculum, in addition to preventing the construction of school buildings.
It called on the international community to take urgent action and exert pressure to halt these measures.
The ministry affirmed that it would continue following up on the issue with relevant parties and work to ensure the regular provision of education in Jerusalem schools and protect Palestinian students’ right to education.
Israel requires Palestinians from the West Bank to obtain special permits to enter occupied East Jerusalem, including for work, education, medical treatment and worship. The issuance of these permits is subject to strict restrictions and security procedures, and not all applicants receive them.
Since October 2023, Israel has obstructed the issuance of permits for Palestinian workers from the West Bank, including teachers, amid the genocide it has been carrying out in Gaza.
In January 2026, the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, passed a law banning the employment in the Israeli education system of teachers who obtained their academic degrees from institutions affiliated with the Palestinian Authority.
According to an earlier report by Israeli newspaper Haaretz, implementation of the law directly affects the availability of teachers in occupied East Jerusalem, where around 6,700 teachers work in the city’s Arab education system, at least 60 percent of whom hold bachelor’s degrees from Palestinian academic institutions.

Ukrainian schools hear air-alert wails instead of the first-bell welcome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

As Ukrainian schools open, students hear air raid sirens instead of the first bell
A boy stands near the site of a heavily damaged residential building following a Russian strike in Kyiv, Ukraine on Sept.1, 2026. (Vladyslav Musiienko / AFP via Getty Images)
Thousands of Ukrainian children mark a milestone on Sept. 1 by stepping into a new world of classrooms and learning, with the "first bell" ceremony traditionally marking this transition.
Yet this year, the "first bell" was forced underground as Russia pounded Kyiv with aerial attacks for the sixth consecutive day, as across the country, hundreds of thousands of pupils see their school life disrupted by Russia's full-scale war.
Nataliia Maievska, the director of a secondary school with an emphasis on bilingual studies, Lyceum No. 257 "Syniozernyi," in Kyiv's northwestern neighborhood, said it was a very bittersweet day.
While glad that her school was able to hold the ceremony in some capacity, she feels for the seven-year-old first-graders whose experience was tainted by the event.
Around 88 new students joined the lyceum's student body of around 1200.
"They will remember this. Because these are the moments that are remembered for a lifetime," said Maievska.
Lessons amid the sound of sirens
Just as the new students were settling into their classrooms, an air raid siren interrupted their first-ever lesson. Without panic, perhaps already used to the sound, the children took each other's hands and walked down to the underground shelter with their new class.
The loud wail of air-raid sirens, sounding more than 10 times a day, leaves the city paralyzed for up to 14 hours on some days.
Kyiv authorities announced on Aug. 31 that learning may need to start in a hybrid format to ensure maximum safety. Schools are told to prepare for all possible scenarios — from teaching in shelters to teaching completely remotely.
"It is impossible to provide full-fledged education for this school in the shelter today," said Maievska. While the school's shelter can accommodate all its students and staff, there is not enough space to fit hundreds of desks and boards to "imitate" a proper classroom atmosphere.
"Our children are already a little used to it, you can see it in their eyes."
The number of enrolled first-graders decreased by 10% compared to last year, according to Iryna Borzova, a member of the Ukrainian parliament's Youth and Sport Committee.
The lawmaker noted that while 2.2 million students are expected to learn in person, up to 800,000 children are likely to adopt a hybrid model, with lessons split between in-person attendance and online study.
About 200,000 students, mainly in the front-line regions, will have to study completely remotely, said Borzova.
For first-grade teacher Olena, this was an unusual first day of school. Instead of speaking to her students in front of the class, she was trying to keep the children safe in the shelter as an air alert interrupted their first-ever class.
However, she feels confident that these students will adapt.
"Our children are already a little used to it; you can see it in their eyes," says Olena.
Despite the sleepless nights, the constant threat of Russian attacks, and the difficult first day of school, Kyiv authorities estimate that almost 94% of first-year students attended school today.
Across the city, 412 schools started the school year. While most opened their doors physically, 11 of them had to experience the "first bell" fully online.
Much remains uncertain about the upcoming school year. Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine will enter its fifth year in a few months, but Ukrainians continue to adjust.
"There is nothing that can force us not to study, not to work, not to endure," added Maievska, looking at the year ahead with resolve.

Some institutions were evacuated, but as of the time of publication, no explosive devices had been reported found.
Leningrad Region governor Alexander Drozdenko claims that dozens of schools, kindergartens, hospitals, and other social facilities received threats. He called what happened an “information terrorist attack.” According to him, the “enemy” is trying to sow panic by disrupting Knowledge Day — the traditional first day of school on Sept. 1. Drozdenko did not specify, however, who exactly sent the messages or how he arrived at the conclusion that there was a single organizer behind the threats.
In Tatarstan, medical institutions under the regional Health Ministry began receiving anonymous emails starting at 8:00 a.m. The hospitals underwent a partial evacuation but returned to normal operations after inspection. In the Altai Krai, patients and staff were evacuated from the regional diagnostic center, and the anti-terrorism commission reported a wave of threats against social, administrative, and educational institutions.
Authorities in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug stated that after the buildings had been inspected none of the threats had proven to be actionable. Bomb threats against schools, kindergartens, and hospitals were also received in the Perm Krai, the Kemerovo and Orenburg regions, and the Zabaykalsky and Krasnoyarsk krais. There has still been no evidence presented publicly indicating that the geographically dispersed threats came from the same sender or group of senders.
Meanwhile, several museum venues in Moscow suspended operations. The Pushkin Museum announced a temporary closure and canceled tours for a period of four hours, the Museum of the East closed its main building until approximately 1:00 p.m., and the Museum of Moscow and all its branches stopped admitting visitors until 2:00 p.m. The ROSIZO branch on Petroverigsky Lane also suspended the exhibition “Art Behind Closed Doors: Leningrad Apartment Exhibitions of the 1960s–1980s.” The Pushkin Museum, the Museum of the East, and ROSIZO cited “technical reasons,” while the Museum of Moscow cited “reasons beyond our control.” None of the institutions officially linked the closures to the wave of bomb threats.
The mass sending of false threats has happened in Russia before. In February 2020, unknown individuals reported bomb threats against more than 1,500 sites in Moscow in a single day, including schools, hospitals, courts, and every metro station in the city’s network. No bombs were found, but around 8,000 people had to be evacuated.
Also in 2020, at the request of the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office, Roskomnadzor blocked access to Protonmail after the Federal Security Service (FSB) claimed its servers had been used to send threats to 830 sites. The FSB had previously blacklisted the Startmail service, which it claimed had been used to send more than 1,000 bomb threat emails targeting over 16,000 sites. Russian security agencies have not yet named the parties responsible for the current wave of messages.

Britain's shop price inflation hits two-year high in August: BRC

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

03:30:38 KST

LONDON, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Britain's shop price inflation rose to a two-year high in August as higher energy, input and commodity costs fed through prices, data from the British Retail Consortium (BRC) showed Tuesday.
Shop prices rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in August, accelerating from 0.9 percent in July, according to the BRC.
Food inflation accelerated to 2.8 percent from 2.2 percent in July, while non-food rose to 0.9 percent from 0.2 percent.
"The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed," said Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the BRC.
"In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage," she said.
Dickinson said the months ahead will remain challenging for households, as rising bills put further pressure on budgets and retailers faced persistently high operating costs that limited their ability to absorb further increases without impacting investment, jobs and prices.
She called on the government to address business costs, including business rates, packaging costs and employment taxes, to support growth and help contain the cost of living. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Xi calls for SCO to strive for higher quality development, promote better global governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:30:31 CST
03:30:31 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers an important speech during the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhai Jianlan)
BISHKEK, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Tuesday that China is ready to work with all parties to continue to strive for higher quality development, and make the global governance system more just and equitable.
Xi made the remarks in his speeches at the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the "SCO Plus" meeting held in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
PUTTING DEVELOPMENT FIRST
This year marks the 25th founding anniversary of the SCO. Xi said that over the past 25 years, the most significant achievement of the organization has been its gradual transformation into a new type of regional cooperation organization that spans the largest geographical area, represents the largest population, and possesses enormous development potential in the world.
The SCO's most important experience for cooperation is that it has found the right way of coexistence featuring non-alliances, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party, while bringing countries in the region together to build a common home, he added.
At the crossroads concerning the future of humanity, the SCO should shoulder its historic responsibility and take the initiative in steering the course of history, he said.
Xi put forward a four-point proposal at the summit, calling on the SCO to stay committed to putting development and the people first, taking security as a key goal, and promoting dialogue and consultation.
The SCO, Xi said, should champion a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, consolidate cooperation in traditional areas such as trade and investment, connectivity, energy and resources, and expand cooperation in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence (AI), digital economy, green industry and green mining.
China will develop an international AI application cooperation center with fellow SCO countries, establish a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin, and implement 100 technological cooperation projects with other SCO countries in the next three years, he said.
The SCO should pursue coordinated measures to tackle traditional and non-traditional security threats, Xi said, adding that the organization must prevent external forces from interfering in internal affairs, endangering political security, and undermining regional stability.
China stands ready to work with all parties to act on the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and support the early opening of the SCO's four security centers, so as to upgrade the capacity of member states in responding to security threats and challenges, Xi said.
According to Alexey Mukhin, director general of the Centre for Political Information in Moscow, the outcomes of the SCO summit demonstrated that all member states are focusing on development and security priorities, and working together to address threats and challenges and promote long-term development through effective mechanisms within the SCO framework.
This not only serves the common interests of all parties, but also contributes to improving regional and global governance, Mukhin said.
China stands ready to work with all parties to implement the Global Civilization Initiative, Xi said, adding that China will host SCO forums on innovation and sustainable development, on people-to-people friendship and on friendship cities, as well as establish a China-SCO basic education cooperation center.
The SCO should always advocate that all countries, regardless of their size, are equal, and that regional affairs should be discussed by all countries to bridge differences and build consensus, properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation, and meet common challenges through multilateral collaboration, Xi said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers an important speech during the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhai Jianlan)
ADVANCING GLOBAL GOVERNANCE
At the "SCO Plus" meeting, Xi called on the SCO to shoulder the responsibility of the times and work together to advance a more just and equitable global governance system, as well as an equal and orderly multipolar world.
In his address, Xi noted that the trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible, and multipolarity, independent choice of development paths, and greater democracy in international relations are the right way forward.
Xi said that in recent years, the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power. As an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs, he said.
Xi said that as a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world, in which sovereign equality and mutual respect should be upheld as fundamental principles, balance, order and the rule of law as essential requirements, multipolarism, dialogue and consultation as key pathways, and mutual benefit, win-win cooperation and universally beneficial and inclusive development as the way forward.
"Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law, and work together to tackle global challenges," Xi said.
China, as a major country, has set an example in this regard and played a leading role, said Seun Sam, a policy analyst at the Royal Academy of Cambodia.
"Major countries taking the lead in abiding by international law can have a demonstrative effect, help safeguard the sovereignty and interests of small countries like Cambodia, promote mutual trust among countries, and achieve peaceful coexistence," he said.
Xi called on countries to promote the common values of humanity, advance the rule of law in international relations, restore the authority and vitality of the United Nations, and improve the coordination and efficiency of global and regional multilateral mechanisms.
"We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations," Xi said.
Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University, said that with its deep experience in multilateral cooperation, the SCO has developed mature practices for transcending differences, building consensus and fostering cooperation.
It enables countries with different political systems, cultural traditions and interests to engage in equal dialogue and practical cooperation, precisely what is needed to build a more just and equitable global governance system, Ulmasov said.
Highlighting the role of the SCO, Xi put forward three proposals for the organization to advance common prosperity, promote the development and rise of the Global South, and guide the reform and improvement of global governance, to make greater contributions to an equal and orderly multipolar world.
As an important pillar of South-South cooperation, the SCO should carry forward the Shanghai Spirit, strengthen and expand the "SCO Plus" partnerships, and jointly speak up for peace, foster synergy for development, build bridges for cooperation, and pave the way for win-win outcomes, Xi said.
"Let us take the people-centered and action-oriented approach, jointly advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world, make global governance more just and equitable, and build a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said. ■
Chinese President Xi Jinping shakes hands with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. Xi attended the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) held here on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Wang Ye)

Emergency services responded to and extinguished 13,463 fires during this period, including 239 major fires in forested areas, Khalil Meshri, head of operations and follow-up at the Civil Protection Department, was quoted as saying.

The fire was eventually brought under control through coordinated ground and Tunisian Air Force aerial operations.
Despite extensive environmental and material damage, civil defense officials said no casualties were reported.

John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Apple Inc.'s leadership transition took effect Tuesday, with John Ternus succeeding Tim Cook as chief executive officer and Cook becoming executive chairman of the company's board of directors.
Apple's updated leadership page lists Ternus as CEO and a member of the board, while Cook is now listed as executive chair.
Apple announced the succession plan on April 20, saying the transition had been unanimously approved by its board and followed a long-term succession planning process. Cook remained CEO through the summer and worked closely with Ternus on the transition. As executive chairman, Cook will continue to assist with certain aspects of the company, including engagement with policymakers around the world.
Cook, who joined Apple in 1998, became CEO in 2011 and led the company for about 15 years. During his tenure, Apple introduced new product categories including Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple Vision Pro, as well as services ranging from iCloud and Apple Pay to Apple TV and Apple Music.
Apple said in April that under Cook's leadership, its market capitalization had grown from approximately 350 billion U.S. dollars to 4 trillion dollars, while annual revenue had risen from 108 billion dollars in fiscal 2011 to more than 416 billion dollars in fiscal 2025.
In a public letter to the Apple community, Cook reflected on his 15 years as CEO and said the transition was "not goodbye." He described Ternus as a brilliant engineer and thinker who had spent 25 years helping build Apple products.
Ternus joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became a vice president of Hardware Engineering in 2013 and joined the executive team as senior vice president of Hardware Engineering in 2021.
He has overseen hardware engineering across a range of Apple products and played a key role in the introduction of iPad and AirPods, as well as multiple generations of iPhone, Mac and Apple Watch.
In his April statement, Ternus said he had spent almost his entire career at Apple, had worked under Steve Jobs and had Cook as his mentor. He pledged to lead the company according to the values and vision that have defined Apple for half a century. ■

BELGRADE, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- High-level representatives from across the Global South gathered in Belgrade on Tuesday to mark the 65th anniversary of the first conference of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), reaffirming support for multilateralism, sovereign equality and respect for international law amid heightened global tensions.
The commemorative meeting at the Palace of Serbia brought together more than 30 delegations, including representatives of the movement's current leadership Troika -- Azerbaijan, Uganda and Uzbekistan -- as well as countries with longstanding ties to NAM.
The meeting opened with addresses by Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic and Ugandan Vice President Jessica Alupo, who spoke on behalf of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, as Uganda currently chairs NAM.
Vucic described NAM as an important pillar of multilateralism and warned against what he described as selective approaches to international law.
Delivering Museveni's address, Alupo said the movement emerged in responseto the rigid ideological divisions and polarization of the Cold War and stressed the continuing importance of independent and balanced international cooperation.
She described NAM as "the correct response by sections of the people of the world to the narrow-mindedness that had emerged."
Several representatives from Africa, Asia and Latin America also emphasized themes of strategic autonomy and stronger cooperation among countries of the Global South.
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama called for "positive neutrality" and proactive diplomatic engagement, urging Global South countries to translate their collective weight into concrete diplomatic results rather than align with competing power blocs.
Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud highlighted South-South cooperation and multilateralism in addressing transnational challenges, including terrorism and climate vulnerability.
Other participants included Angolan Foreign Minister Tete Antonio, Lebanese Defense Minister Michel Menassa, Indian Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju and Cuban First Deputy Foreign Minister Gerardo Penalver Portal.
The meeting came 65 years after the first NAM conference, held in Belgrade from Sept. 1 to 6, 1961, which brought together leaders of countries seeking to remain independent of the rival blocs of the Cold War.
Serbia, which is not a member of NAM but has observer status, has sought to preserve the diplomatic legacy of the 1961 conference and maintains relations with Global South countries. ■
