Israel’s newest submarine INS Drakon heads home from Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:56:43 UTC
01:56:43 KST

Israel’s sixth submarine, INS Drakon, has begun its voyage from Germany to Israel and is expected to arrive within weeks, the IDF and Defense Ministry announced Tuesday.
A send-off ceremony was held this week at the TKMS shipyard in Kiel, marking the end of years of joint Israeli-German planning and construction and the start of the submarine’s journey home.
INS Drakon is the third and final submarine in the Dolphin-class AIP series purchased by the Defense Ministry for the Israeli Navy. According to the IDF, it incorporates advanced technologies designed to expand the Navy’s operational flexibility, range and endurance for years to come.
The Israeli flag was raised aboard the submarine at the ceremony, formally marking the start of its voyage to Israel.
Its departure was accompanied by a large-scale security operation led by the Defense Ministry’s Security Department together with German security forces. A state ceremony is planned at Haifa Naval Base once the submarine arrives.
Israeli Navy commander Vice Adm. Eyal Harel said the Drakon, together with three future Dakar-class submarines, would form a central part of the future of Israel’s submarine fleet.
“They will bring more advanced capabilities, greater operational range, longer endurance on missions and significant operational power,” Harel said.
He added that the submarine’s crews would operate “covertly, in the dark and in silence, far from home,” often in circumstances in which only those on board would know what was happening around them and would bear responsibility for critical decisions.
The send-off ceremony was also attended by Rear Adm. Amir Chimney, head of the Israeli Navy’s Technology, Logistics and Material Command; Zeev Landau, head of the Defense Ministry’s Procurement Directorate; Israeli Ambassador to Germany Ron Prosor; German Navy chief Vice Adm. Jan Christian Kaack; and representatives of the Navy, Defense Ministry and TKMS.
Landau described the submarine as “the most advanced and complex weapons system in the IDF” and said its delivery reflected the strategic partnership between Israel and Germany.
He said the two countries were now discussing additional joint projects that could expand cooperation into new areas of development and production.
Prosor said the submarine’s delivery demonstrated the depth of ties between Jerusalem and Berlin and their cooperation in confronting shared strategic challenges.
TKMS CEO Oliver Burkhard said the Drakon’s departure marked the successful completion of a complex program built on years of trust, technological expertise and shared responsibility.
“Israel is an important partner for us in the maritime arena,” Burkhard said, adding that cooperation would continue with the future Dakar-class submarines.

Gifts for Uzbekistan's president
Modi gifted president of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev a marble inlay decorative plate, featuring floral and foliate motifs in blue, green and red set into polished white marble. The craft is particularly associated with Agra in Uttar Pradesh and reflects generations of Indian artisan skill.

The tea represents the heritage of Kangra Valley in Himachal Pradesh, where cultivation dates back to the 19th century.Another gift was a sandalwood Shata Tantri Veena, popularly known as the Santoor, a many-stringed instrument associated with Jammu and Kashmir.
Its resemblance to Uzbekistan's traditional Chang was highlighted as a link between the musical traditions of the two countries.
Modi also presented Mirziyoyev with the original handwritten scoresheet of Uzbek Grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov from the 2025 FIDE World Cup final in Goa. Sindarov defeated China's Wei Yi to become the youngest FIDE World Cup champion and qualify for the 2026 Candidates Tournament.
Gifts for Uzbekistan's prime minister
Uzbekistan Prime Minister Abdulla Aripov received a marble inlay decorative plate, showcasing India's traditional stone-inlay craftsmanship and intricate floral designs.
He was also gifted a marble inlay casket with a Banarasi silk stole. The white marble casket carries floral patterns created with coloured stones, while the blue Banarasi silk stole features a paisley zari design, bringing together craft traditions from Agra and Varanasi.
Gift for the President's spouse
PM Modi gifted Uzbekistan president’s spouse and first lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva, a marble inlay casket paired with a Banarasi silk stole, blending Agra’s stone craftsmanship with Varanasi’s weaving heritage. The floral marble work and blue paisley zari design reflected India’s artistic traditions.
Gift for the President's daughter
Modi gifted the daughter of Uzbekistan's president a fine silver brooch featuring a floral bouquet in an ornamental basket. The piece incorporates openwork, latticework, leaves, blossoms, green cabochons and clear stones.
For the prime minister of Kyrgyzstan, Modi presented a Dokra artwork depicting a pair of traditional musicians. The handcrafted pieces use India's traditional lost-wax metal-casting technique.Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan's president was gifted a Ladakhi Tsug-dul blanket, a traditional woollen textile from Ladakh featuring geometric, floral and stylised motifs.
A 10-volume English translation of the Mahabharata by Bibek Debroy was also presented to the president.Together, the gifts showcased India's regional crafts, artistic traditions, literature and cultural heritage while underscoring the longstanding cultural affinities between India and Central Asia.

Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
Is it a bird? Is it a plane? Is it a well-timed ploy to ramp up defense spending? Germany's evidence-free claim that a drone found lying between Ukrainian cargo planes on the canopy of Leipzig/Halle airport is part of a pattern.
Last year's late-autumn drone sighting hysteria that swept across Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium, was used by the bloc to amplify and entrench an anti-Russia stance that has seen it throw hundreds of billions it cannot afford into weapons and a war its chosen side cannot win.
Tens of millions of Euro has since been spent on the back of a 'scare' that has been shown to have been irrational, exuberant and driven by vested interests.
The most bizarre national security scare in recent European history began at Copenhagen’s Kastrup Airport on September 2 last year. According to Denmark’s Frihedsbrevet news site, an airport employee told her supervisors that she saw two drones approach the area “stealthily,” adding that “they are big. They are not toys.”
The airport was temporarily shut down, and within hours, reports of a similar drone incursion came in from Oslo, Norway.
“I can only say that this is in my eyes a serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at the time. “I cannot in any way deny that it is Russia.” Her Norwegian counterpart, Gahr Store, came to a similar conclusion. “Russia has violated Norwegian airspace on three occasions this spring and summer,” he claimed. “We cannot determine whether this was done intentionally or due to navigation errors. Regardless of the cause, this is not acceptable.”
“It is clear we are witnessing a pattern of persistent contestation at our borders,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. “Our critical infrastructure is at risk. And Europe will respond to this threat with strength and determination.”
Open-source investigators insisted that the sightings were a hoax from the outset. Sleuths on the Metabunk forums concluded that the ‘drone’ seen at Kastrup Airport in the above footage was actually a small single-engine plane. FlightRadar24 data showed one such plane – a Socata TB-20 Trinidad – passing over the airport’s main runway twice at the time of the sighting.
Where were drones spotted?
Nevertheless, panic spread across northern Europe as drones were supposedly spotted at the following airports, military bases, and infrastructure sites in the following days and weeks:
- September 23: Aalborg Airport, Denmark
- September 24: Aalborg Airport, Billund Airport, Sonderborg, Esbjerg and Skrydstrup airports, Denmark
- September 25: Billund Airport, Denmark; Thyssenkrupp factory, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany; University Medical Center, Kiel, Germany; Bundeswehr base, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany
September 26: Karup Air Base, Skrydstrup Air Base, Jutland Dragoon Regiment base, Denmark
- September 27: Orland Main Air Station, Norway
- September 28: Bronnoysund Airport, Norway; Borris Camp, Denmark
- October 2: Munich Airport, Germany; Elsenborn-Butgenbach Air Base, Belgium
- October 3: Munich Airport, Germany
- October 31: Berlin-Brandenburg Airport, Germany
- November 2: Bremen Airport, Germany; Kleine Brogel Air Base, Belgium
- November 6: Gothenburg Airport, Sweden; Brussels Airport, Antwerp Port, Belgium
- November 9: Liege Airport, Doel Nuclear Power Plant, Belgium
- November 22: Volkel Air Base, Netherlands
- December 1: In the Irish Sea off Dublin, during Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s arrival by plane
Police across northern Europe received thousands of additional drone reports from civilians. In Denmark alone, nearly 6,000 reports of suspected drones were filed.
Did the drones even exist?
Not only is there no proof that Russia was connected with these sightings, there is no evidence that any drones were present at all. No wreckage has been recovered, no perpetrators have been identified, and no footage of the drones exists, except for the video from Copenhagen that apparently shows a light aircraft.
Despite being certain that Denmark was under “hybrid attack,” Mette Frederiksen acknowledged in late September that there could be an “alternate explanation” for the sightings. Six months later, six government sources told Denmark’s TV2 that they don’t “have any technical evidence to support that Denmark was subjected to a hybrid attack with drones.” Frihedsbrevet’s sources came to a similar conclusion, with the airport employee who reported the initial sighting admitting that she could have been mistaken.
Airport management still insist that drones were present in the area on September 22, but police have not acknowledged any drones, only “reports” of drones.
Danish troops reportedly opened fire on a drone over Borris Camp on September 28. According to an investigation by TV2, the only aircraft operating in the area at the time was a turboprop passenger plane. The Danish military, if TV2’s reporting is correct, nearly shot down a civilian aircraft over a false alarm.
After interviewing witnesses and reviewing surveillance footage, Norwegian police closed their investigation on November 6, stating that they were “unable to confirm or deny whether drones were actually observed on the night of September 23.”
German police have not been able to confirm any drone activity; Dutch officials have identified no threat, with internal documents stating that there was “no indication of sabotage or attacks on vital objects.” Dutch and Belgian authorities have found no credible basis for panic, with Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken issuing a half-apology last month for attempting to pass off a video of a police helicopter as evidence of nefarious aerial activity.
Did they just lie?
Out of every country involved, Denmark’s leaders were most insistent that Russia was behind the spate of sightings. Frederiksen, Defense Minister Troels Lund Poulsen, and Justice Minister Peter Hummelgaard all described the incidents as “attacks,” despite nothing being attacked and no attackers being present.
“I consider it a new reality that Denmark and Europe are under more violent and frequent hybrid attacks,” Frederiksen said in a televised address on September 25. “And even though the authorities cannot conclude who is behind the hybrid attacks…there is primarily one country that poses a threat to Europe's security – and that is Russia.”
The flood of tips and reports from the public can be written off either as mass hysteria, or – more charitably – as a natural reaction from Europeans primed by their politicians and media to believe that Russia is planning an all-out war on the continent. As for why Frederiksen would stoke this fear, however, some clues can be found in her actions.
At the time, Denmark was just over a year into an historic rearmament program. After a €5.4 billion military budget hike in 2024, Frederiksen announced last February that defense spending would be increased from 2.4% to 3% of GDP by 2030 (since increased to 3.5%). By late 2025, Denmark had purchased hundreds of armored combat vehicles, signed contracts for new air defense systems, increased annual conscription numbers, and, for the first time in its history, introduced compulsory military service for women.
Denmark, she said last February, needs to undergo a “massive rearmament,” because “We don’t know what [Russian President Vladimir Putin] is planning, but we know that he and Russia are in the process of rearming.”
Frederiksen referenced this rearmament again in her September address, declaring that “the events of recent days only emphasize how important it is.”
Denmark held the EU’s rotating presidency at the time, and Frederiksen added that the alleged drone threat would be made front and center when EU leaders met in Copenhagen the following week, and that she would push for “the establishment of an actual drone wall.”
The EU’s drone wall
Frederiksen kept her word. Published on October 16, the European Commission’s ‘Defense Readiness Roadmap’ stated that a ‘European Drone Defense Initiative’ – the so-called “drone wall” comprising sensors and interceptors – would be operational along the bloc’s eastern borders with Russia and Belarus by 2027.
🚨🇪🇺 “We need to act now”Ursula von der Leyen now wants to build a “Drone Wall” on the Eastern Flank of Europe to protect from the alleged Russian Aggression. pic.twitter.com/UAGH93fKRc
— Concerned Citizen (@BGatesIsaPyscho) October 1, 2025
Drones continued to dominate the agenda at a European Council summit in Brussels in December. “The European Council strongly condemns all recent hybrid attacks against the European Union and its Member States,” read a statement released after the meeting. “In the light of Russia’s and Belarus’ intensified hybrid campaign, it calls for accelerated efforts to strengthen resilience, protect critical infrastructure, and…decisively ramp up Europe’s defense readiness by 2030.”
None of this is to suggest that Denmark orchestrated the drone panic to justify its remilitarization, or to sell the EU’s “drone wall.” Both initiatives were already underway at the time. Instead, it illustrates how Danish and EU officials saw an opportunity not to let a crisis go to waste, and kept the drone threat alive even as their own police forces, to put it mildly, struggled to substantiate it.
Belgium's very own drone crisis
Frederiksen wasn’t the only national leader who saw an opportunity amid the panic. Remember Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken? After police hotlines were flooded with more than 550 reports of drones between September and December, Francken bypassed the standard bidding process to authorize the purchase of €50 million worth of drone detection and jamming systems.
An investigation by Belgium’s VRT broadcaster has since found that none of the reports of drones were credible, and Francken has been hammered by the opposition for sharing an image of a ‘drone’ over Brussels Airport that turned out to be a police helicopter. VRT found that the defense ministry ignored warnings from Belgium’s Inspectorate of Finance and purchased detection antennas at an inflated price, and Francken is now the subject of an inquiry by the Brussels Public Prosecutor's Office.
The debacle is reminiscent of the Agusta-Dassault affair. During the 1980s, defense contractors Agusta and Dassault paid the equivalent of €4 million in bribes to secure no-bid contracts for AW109 transport helicopters and electronic warfare equipment. Once exposed, the scandal led to the criminal conviction of Belgian Defense Minister Guy Coeme and Foreign Minister and NATO Secretary General Willy Claes.
So did Russian drones spook the EU?
Nearly eight months after the first ‘drones’ were spotted over Copenhagen, the crisis is still being milked across Europe. In early May, long after the threat had been debunked in Denmark, Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands, the Dutch defense ministry announced that it would acquire approximately 900 “electro-optical aiming devices” for use against UAVs, “without prior announcement due to the urgency of a crisis situation.”
Questioned by the Belgian parliament in April, Francken insisted that there is “no other plausible explanation” for the reports other than Russian drones, and that the only way to prove or disprove this is to invest in drone defense technology. “As long as you don’t have the means to detect and neutralize drones, it stands to reason that you cannot immediately produce physical evidence,” he told lawmakers.
The Dutch and Belgians aren’t letting a lack of evidence stop them from pursuing the defense deals that they wanted from this crisis, and the EU is unlikely to step in and pump the brakes.
The EU's censorious and paranoid media industry is the perfect environment for fake news to fester, as long as it suits the bloc. Remember, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's claims of “GPS jamming” hitting her plane on a trip to Bulgaria last September, and how, despite it being roundly debunked within days, it has been allowed to fester to serve her political agenda.
Anti-Russian hysteria is the animating political force in the EU, and the bloc’s leaders clearly aren’t going to let police and media investigations, or common sense, put a stop to the show.

Swinney sticks with pledge to cap prices on basic foods in Scotland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:52:44 UTC
01:52:44 KST

John Swinney insisted on Tuesday he still planned to introduce a legally binding price cap on bread, milk and other essential food items in Scotland despite fierce opposition from farming and business groups.
Unveiling the Scottish National party’s programme for government – the equivalent to the king’s speech – the first minister said he wanted to give “families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices”.
Swinney also announced commitments to restructure local government and NHS boards, introduce a misogyny bill to crack down on violence against women and girls, and set a £2 price limit on bus fares in the west of Scotland. He confirmed his government would pilot a minimum income for artists.
But the proposals to limit essential food and drink prices have faced intense criticism from industry groups, which have described the policy as “unnecessary” and a “potty gimmick”.
On Monday, 23 food, drink and farming organisations published an open letter arguing that markets were already working to deliver the best possible prices and a cap could increase the cost of household goods.
“Scots benefit from western Europe’s most affordable grocery and food supply market,” the letter read. “A statutory cap would not address the root causes of elevated food prices: rising production, refrigeration, and distribution costs. Supply chain shocks after Covid and conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have pushed up fertiliser, fuel and energy costs.”
The SNP committed to introducing price controls by the end of the year in a manifesto published before Holyrood elections in May, framing the scheme as a health measure. Similar initiatives have been implemented in Hungary and Croatia and the UK government encouraged supermarkets to consider voluntary price caps on foodstuffs in May.
The Scottish government did not specify which essentials would be covered by the law in a consultation paper published on Tuesday, although Swinney has said that between 20 and 50 products would be included, such as rice, cheese and eggs. Any limit would cover only retailers that make more than half of their annual turnover from groceries, have more than 250 employees and make more than £250m a year.
“It is our ambition, and intention, to put more money in families’ pockets, building on what is already the most generous cost of living support package anywhere in the UK,” Swinney told Holyrood on Tuesday. “Today we have also begun a formal consultation on the legislation that will introduce a legal price ceiling on a basket of essential food items, giving families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices.”
There is uncertainty over whether any price cap on food and drink essentials would even be legal. The Scottish government is planning to introduce the policy under devolved health powers. But critics say it would clash with post-Brexit internal UK market rules to stop regulatory divergence between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Scotland is facing growing pressure on its finances. The Scottish government estimated last year that there would be a near-£5bn gap in its finances by the end of the decade, with experts warning that difficult choices await over how to fund healthcare, schools and other parts of the public sector.
In his five-year programme for government, Swinney announced a major change to the structure of NHS Scotland, reducing the number of health boards from 14 to two. He described the shake-up as “the most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era”.

To Secure the Natuna Sea, Indonesia Needs More Than New Ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:52:00 UTC
01:52:00 KST

Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing is one of Southeast Asia’s most persistent maritime security challenges. Indonesia, the owner of the region’s largest maritime area, has expanded patrols in its most contested waters, added community surveillance, and expanded international partnerships to address the threat. As the world’s largest archipelagic country, maritime security is one of Indonesia’s most demanding defense domains. And at its current stage, Indonesia needs significant help.
The North Natuna Sea, which lies along the southern portion of the South China Sea, is a hotspot for commercial fishing. Home to over 750,000 tons of fish stock, is among the areas where China’s sweeping South China Sea claims overlap Indonesia’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). Yet despite stepped up maritime law enforcement by Indonesia’s Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries (KKP), illegal activities – including, but not limited to, IUU fishing – continue.
Indonesia is not starting from zero. Since the 2019-2020 confrontations near the Natuna Islands, the government has expanded the Indonesian Navy and Maritime Security Agency (Bakamla) patrol programs, incorporated fishermen and community surveillance into maritime surveillance through the Kelompok Masyarakat Pengawas (POKMASWAS) program, and distributed communications equipment to selected fishermen communities. Yet these initiatives remain unevenly distributed and insufficiently connected to the agencies responsible for verification and enforcement.
Indonesia still faces substantial capacity limitations. In 2025, only three of the seven KKP patrol vessels assigned to the broader WPPNRI 711 area could reach the North Natuna Sea. Even when the KKP is able to catch IUU fishing boats in the act, there aren’t enough dock space or facilities to store impounded vessels and accommodate the crew. Jakarta began addressing those shortages this July by announcing ten new Class I surveillance vessels and an expansion of the PSDKP pier in Batam, which will become the principal base for operations in WPPNRI 711.
Indonesia’s partners have likewise invested in its maritime capacity. Japan, for example, through a 9.053 billion yen grant (USD $56.57 million) is funding an offshore patrol vessel for Bakamla, scheduled for delivery in 2028. Other Japanese programs have trained Bakamla personnel in boat operations, maritime law enforcement, criminal investigations, and instructor development. Australia’s current strategic partnership plan with Indonesia provides for fisheries surveillance cooperation, maritime domain awareness information sharing, technical training, coordinated patrols, and desktop exercises.
In early August, at the Southeast Asia Cooperation and Training exercise in Singapore, Indonesian personnel joined representatives from 15 other Indo-Pacific countries in practicing the real-time transfer of sensor data and vessel-contact information among operational centers, patrol aircraft, and ships. Days later, Bakamla hosted Malaysian and Singaporean coast guard personnel for a trilateral exercise in the Riau Islands covering cooperation in the Natuna Sea. Bakamla Chief Vice Admiral Irvansyah subsequently proposed expanding that model to other ASEAN countries.
However, a shared regional maritime security architecture is only reliable as the national systems that feed information into it. Exchanging satellite tracks, radar data, or participating in joint exercises are meaningless if fishermen’s observations are unable to reach Indonesia’s national surveillance and enforcement system in time.
In June, local Indonesian fishermen spotted foreign vessels conducting IUU fishing in the North Natuna Sea within Indonesia’s EEZ. The fishermen reported the sighting to patrol officers, and Indonesia’s Navy deployed the KRI John Lie-358 warship on extended patrol the following day. By the time the warship searched the area the following morning, however, the vessels had disappeared.
Government Regulation No. 13 of 2022 already provides for an integrated national maritime security and safety information system, alongside joint and coordinated patrols. Bakamla Regulation No. 2 of 2024 goes further, directing the system to improve connectivity among maritime information sources, accelerate the transmission of information about security incidents, and support more effective patrols. The legal foundation exists, but Indonesia still needs to develop a standardized operational procedure to ensure that reports reach the appropriate enforcement asset without losing critical hours along the way.
Bakamla’s command-and-control center should maintain a joint reporting and coordination process with designated liaison officers from KKP, the Indonesian Navy, the Water Police, and relevant local authorities. This center would be responsible for interagency communication and assignment, acting as a dedicated maritime desk manned through a single radio frequency and hotline for fishermen to report to.
Jakarta should also create a Natuna-wide inventory to accurately identify key needs and distribution gaps and ensure that resources are given to those who need it most, both from a domestic perspective and as a reference point for allies when investing in resources. Capitalizing on the Prabowo administration’s recent investments in the Natuna Red and White Fishing Villages, these new hubs could act disbursement centers for communication materials while conducting training for basic vessel identification guidance and report standardization.
Indonesia’s partners should organize their assistance around this chain. Japanese-organized training could help develop watch officers and instructors capable of processing contact reports and integrating the new Bakamla vessel into joint operations. Australian information sharing and desktop exercises could test the full sequence from a fisherman’s initial report to verification and deployment. Future exercises should measure reporting, verification, and response times – not simply whether participating agencies can exchange data.
Once the system functions domestically, Indonesia can make it the foundation for regional cooperation. The next exercise with Malaysia and Singapore should begin with a simulated report from a fishing vessel, require Indonesian agencies to verify and task a response, and then test the transfer of the contact if the suspected vessel crosses into another country’s jurisdiction. Indonesia could subsequently use its position as secretariat of the 11-country Regional Plan of Action to Combat IUU Fishing to promote a common contact-report format and standardize procedures for transferring verified vessel information across borders.
More patrol vessels will give Indonesia greater reach. They will not matter, however, if those vessels continue arriving after the target has disappeared. The measure of progress would be straightforward: how much time passes between a fisherman spotting an intrusion and an Indonesian agency directing an asset toward it?
The Prabowo administration should make the North Natuna Sea the pilot for answering that question, directing its current maritime defense agencies into a single reporting chain with a common response protocol and measurable targets. Japan and Australia should focus their assistance on the communications equipment and personnel training that chain requires, while regional exercises test whether it works under operational conditions. Regional maritime domain awareness will remain incomplete until information from the first observer can reliably trigger action by the final responder.

Germany blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport

Germany blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
Berlin says it will shut down a Russian consulate and take other actions, citing ‘hybrid attacks’ by Moscow
The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures.
The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on August 4 and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger.
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilising European nations.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are “known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine”. He said the device pointed to “a high degree of technical expertise” and painstaking planning, but carrying out the plan appears to have been left to “low-level” agents.
Dobrindt told reporters that intelligence points to “people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities”, though he didn’t specify which ones. “Taken together, the police investigations, the pattern and intelligence findings prove a Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig airport.”
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that “with the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership decided deliberately to do significant damage again to our already massively burdened bilateral relationship”. He said the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective September 18. The Russian House cultural centre in Berlin also will be closed, though that may take some time.

EU will never recognize occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian

EU will never recognize occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian
EU Ambassador to the United Nations Stavros Lambrinidis said this during a General Assembly debate on the situation in Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“Crimea, Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia are Ukraine. The European Union will never recognize as lawful any attempt by Russia to annex Ukrainian territory. We do not recognize the forced Russification of people and their communities, nor the results of any illegal so-called elections organized by the Russian occupation administration in the temporarily occupied territory of Ukraine,” Lambrinidis said.
He said Russia’s occupation was aimed not only at controlling territory but also at destroying the daily lives, rights and identity of Ukrainians living under Russian rule. Despite being denied access, the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine have documented Russia’s actions in the occupied territories, he added.
“Russia’s goal is clear: it seeks to alter the demographic composition of the territories it occupies, including through the forced transfer and deportation of civilians, including children. This is illegal. It is shameless. And it is disgraceful,” Lambrinidis said.
He reaffirmed that the EU would continue providing political, financial, economic, military and diplomatic support to Ukraine as it exercises its inherent right to self-defense, while addressing humanitarian needs and supporting diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Russia must end its “illegal war of aggression and occupation” of Ukraine, accept an immediate, unconditional and comprehensive ceasefire, and engage in negotiations aimed at achieving a just and lasting peace in accordance with international law and the UN Charter, Lambrinidis said.
He also called on Russia and Belarus to end the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children, which the UN Commission of Inquiry has found to constitute war crimes. He urged an end to the illegal adoption of Ukrainian children and called for the immediate, safe and unconditional return of all children unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred from Ukraine.
Read also: Around 6,000 Ukrainian Civilians May Be in Temporarily Occupied Kherson Region – Lubinets
Lambrinidis further called for the release of political prisoners and civilians arbitrarily detained by Russia and for stronger international monitoring of human rights and humanitarian conditions in the occupied territories. He urged Russia to provide UN human rights mechanisms with immediate and unhindered access, including to places of detention.
Lambrinidis delivered the statement on behalf of the EU and its member states. North Macedonia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Liechtenstein, Andorra and Monaco also joined the statement.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the UN General Assembly is debating the situation in Ukraine’s territories temporarily occupied by Russia. The issue has been on the Assembly’s agenda since 2019 and covers the political, security, humanitarian and human rights consequences of Russia’s occupation.

SCO challenges West as diverse group of nations pursues multipolar future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:51 UTC
01:49:51 KST

The summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which represents almost half of the world’s population, ended with an aim to signal the rise of a global powerhouse challenging the West. Yet the SCO's diversity also revealed significant disagreements and divergent interests.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), a diverse group aiming to balance the West’s global influence, has called for a more representative and fairer multipolar world order as its summit in Kyrgyzstan ended on Tuesday with a run of headlines.
The 25th gathering of the 10 members — China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan — brought together regional leaders as “dialogue partners” from Central Asia, the Caspian region, the Middle East and wider Asia in a broad forum of meetings to address a rapidly changing multipolar world, even amid significant disagreements and often diverging interests.
The Iran war and Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine defined the summit’s focus, with disruptions in global supply lines and emerging alternatives through Central Asia and the Caspian, as well as the rapid geopolitical shockwaves and realignments they have generated.
In a surprise moment with global impact, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin directly, on live television, to end his war against Ukraine.
"Every single day spent in war pushes humanity backwards, ” Modi said unexpectedly to a visibly tense Putin. “We need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities.”
“This is very important for all of humanity," Modi added.
"We have to move in that direction, which is also essential for the welfare of humanity. It is humanity’s call to resolve all issues peacefully as soon as possible," the Indian premier told the Russian president.
"This is India’s message — the message from the land of Gandhi, the land of Buddha: a message of peace, a message of humanity."
Putin did not reply to Modi, but in a speech later at the summit said that "today, 1 September, is the day World War II began."
"We must do everything to exclude from world practice any provocation of armed conflicts," Putin added. Russia’s war in Ukraine is now longer than World War II in duration.
In another snub for the Kremlin, a bilateral meeting between Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping produced no progress on a Siberian natural gas pipeline that Moscow urgently needs as the country’s infrastructure and economy reel from continuous Ukrainian strikes on key energy targets across Russia.
The Russian president however received the public gratitude of his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian, who thanked Putin "for your positions at every stage.”
Putin said that Russia is providing Iran with assistance and “supplying the needed goods,” and that “Russia stands in solidarity with the people of Iran, who are defending their interests. He further said he "admires their courage and steadfastness” in their fight against the US and Israel.
"Today we are experiencing an erosion of the foundations upon which international order is built," Pezeshkian said.
"If such actions are met with no effective response from the international community, what state can be certain that its sovereignty and security will be protected in the future against the use of force?"
The Iranian delegation pushed for maximum results at the SCO summit, with Pezeshkian also meeting his Azerbaijani, Indian and Pakistani counterparts, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his counterparts from China, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Russia.
China and Turkey laud multilateralism
China, which sees the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organisations like the G7, has recently shown it wants to expand the organisation's scope and influence, while Russia and Iran joined the summit to build relations with non-Western partners and seek support and recognition.
In his speech at the summit, China’s Xi said the SCO should “foster an environment of universal security,” while criticising “hegemony, unilateralism, and protectionism” which run “counter to the tide of history.”
Xi further urged the SCO leaders and partners to “shoulder the responsibility of the times,” as multipolarity is an “irreversible trend” and that “dominance by just one or several countries, or bloc politics are not true multilateralism.”
Turkey, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region, viewing its partnership in the organisation as part of a balanced foreign policy that maintains its traditional ties with the West through NATO while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan told the summit that the SCO is “a rising star in every field” and that with its “3.5 billion people and $35 trillion in gross domestic product (it) is an indispensable element of a multipolar order."
Calling the SCO a “complement to the UN,” Erdoğan said the organisation “has a structure that aligns with our multidimensional foreign policy centred on regional ownership,” adding that “as Türkiye, we are taking responsibility for resolving conflicts around us through dialogue and diplomacy.”
Erdoğan highlighted one of the new thrusts of the SCO summit participants: alternative transport and energy corridors, as the war with Iran disrupted traditional avenues.
"We believe that the organisation can play a role not only in ensuring peace and stability, but also in establishing uninterrupted and secure transportation corridors, which are vital for the prosperity of our peoples, and in areas such as energy supply security," the Turkish president said.
Billions in Central Asia and Caucasus projects
The leaders of Central Asia and the South Caucasus pushed relentlessly during the summit to maximise the economic opportunities for their regions as the Iran war and wider Middle East disruptions place them at the forefront of new global trade and connectivity solutions.
Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Premier Nikol Pashinyan held a new round of their peace talks in Bishkek, with Aliyev saying “the South Caucasus is becoming a zone of peace.”
Pashinyan said transport corridors and regional connectivity are now developing toward the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev told the summit that trade among SCO countries has reached $1 trillion and that much more remains to unlock the full potential of cooperation and resource use.
Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed establishing a bank for inter-regional projects, natural resource management, digital services and healthcare.
Mirziyoyev agreed with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to raise bilateral trade from $18 billion in 2025 to $30 billion in the coming years through a portfolio of joint investment projects and industrial cooperation.
"The existence of multiple centres of political influence is an important condition for advancing a political pluralism on the international stage," Tajikistan's President Emomali Rahmon said.
New security centre approved
Away from the diplomacy, the summit closed Kyrgyzstan's year as chair with a package of institutional decisions. Leaders signed the Bishkek Declaration and a protocol amending the SCO's Founding Charter, which Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev said would create the basis for a more flexible bloc.
On security, members approved the rules for a Universal Centre for Countering Security Challenges based in Tashkent and an anti-drug centre in Dushanbe.
A unit to fight transnational organised crime will open in Bishkek under that centre, the first permanent SCO body on Kyrgyz soil.
Members also agreed to complete consultations "in the shortest possible time" on a long-discussed SCO development bank, with a view to signing its founding document, although they concluded no deal in Bishkek.
Leaders adopted further documents on artificial intelligence, climate, energy and information security, a declaration on nuclear safety, and a decision to develop cooperation with the African Union.
Kyrgyzstan said it held around 200 events during its chairmanship, more than 50 of them in the country itself, and marked the anniversary by naming a 4,050-metre peak in the Ala-Archa range "SCO Peak".
Pakistan now takes the chairmanship and will host the next summit in Islamabad.

Brig.-Gen. Rahman Moghaddam, the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)'s special operations unit, Unit 4000, began planning operations in the Strait of Malacca and the Bangka Strait, two waterways essential to global trade, and ports in Indonesia and China, Iran International reported on Tuesday, citing several informed sources.
Moghaddam was previously believed to have been killed during Israeli strikes on March 4. The day after reports of his death were published by Israeli media, two drones were launched by Iran towards Azerbaijan. The strikes were reported by CNN to be in retaliation for Moghaddam's killing in an attack believed to have been carried out from Azerbaijani territory.
Informed sources have told Iran International that Moghaddam survived the attack and commands Unit 4000, heading a unit responsible for assassinations and sabotage operations against Iran's opponents outside its borders.
IRGC recruits operatives in East Asia
The IRGC began recruiting non-Iranian operatives long ago to facilitate maritime terrorism operations in East Asia, allowing it to deny responsibility if operations were exposed, according to Iran International.
Moghaddam sought to recruit non-Iranian Shi'ite operatives in Thailand through Seyed Momen Saketicha, a senior figure in the Thai Shi'ite community. Saketicha participated in negotiations with Hamas in Tehran two years ago over the release of 31 Thai hostages held in Gaza.
Iran attempted to pressure Thailand into removing 40,000 Thai workers from Israel in exchange for the hostages' release.
In addition to attempting to recruit Thai operatives, Unit 4000 focused its attention on Indonesia, with Moghaddam using two Indonesian clerics to help recruitment, according to Iran International's report.
Three Unit 4000 recruits from Indonesia have been allegedly hired to carry out maritime sabotage operations in East Asia.
Iran threatens to expand war into Indian Ocean, Mediterranean Sea
Two months ago, Mohsen Rezaei, adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told CNN that if the war and US naval blockade were not lifted, Iran would expand the war into the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.
IRGC Quds Force commander Brig.-Gen. Esmail Qaani said in a televised interview that the IRGC had additional maritime targets beyond the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.
The Strait of Malacca has been repeatedly raised in discussions of the oil trade in recent months. As the shortest maritime route between Middle Eastern energy exporters and East Asian markets, roughly 29% of global seaborne oil trade passed through the strait during the first half of 2025.
Disruptions in Hormuz and Malacca would put pressure on two major energy supply routes from the Middle East to Asia.
While the Bangka Strait, located between Sumatra and Indonesia's Bangka Island, does not have the same global importance as Malacca, it forms part of the region's shipping network. An interruption there could intensify pressure caused by any potential disruption in Malacca.
Iran's target list also includes Tanjung Priok Port in Indonesia and the Ningbo Zhoushan and Shanghai ports in China, according to Iran International.
Hezbollah member Pando Yudahvinata, who was expelled from an Indonesian university before traveling to Tehran and being recruited by security organizations, is one of the three operatives the IRGC has hired, Iran International wrote. Yudahvinata was responsible for a failed suicide attack against the Israeli Embassy in Bangkok 32 years ago. His name has also been linked to a series of bombings in Sri Lanka.
He and two other Indonesian citizens, Ardianta Mutoha and Mohammad Hossein, traveled to Tehran for training to prepare for covert operations at ports and waterways in East Asia, according to the report.

Third consecutive cut: Bank of Israel lowers interest rates to 3.25%, following economic review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:19 UTC
01:49:19 KST

The Bank of Israel (BoI)'s Monetary Committee cut the interest rate by 0.25% to 3.25% on Tuesday.
This comes amid a backdrop of a relatively moderate inflation rate and rapidly growing gross domestic product (GDP) in recent months and constitutes the third consecutive interest rate reduction in the past 12 months.
While uncertainty in the economy remains high, Israel’s risk premium continued to remain at levels similar to those prevailing before the October 7 massacre, and the shekel’s exchange rate with key global currencies remained without significant change.
The committee’s policy focuses on price stability, support for economic activity, and market stability, BoI said.
“The interest rate path will be determined according to developments in inflation, economic activity, geopolitical uncertainty, and fiscal developments,” BoI noted.
Israel’s Consumer Price Index remained unchanged in June and rose by 0.3% in July. Inflation over the past 12 months stood at 1.5% in July, below the midpoint of BoI’s target. According to forecasters’ assessments and one-year-ahead expectations from most sources, inflation is expected to remain near the midpoint of BoI’s target range in the coming months.
Shekel relatively stable in global monetary trade
Since the last decision to cut Israel’s interest rate in July, the shekel appreciated by 0.6% against the US dollar, depreciated by 1% against the euro, and depreciated by 0.1% in effective nominal terms.
BoI’s Monetary Committee estimated that the inflation environment will continue to be affected by geopolitical developments and energy prices, the risk premium and exchange rate, demand developments and supply constraints, alongside fiscal developments.
Israel’s Central Bureau of Statistics’ national accounts data for the second quarter of 2026 indicate a growth of 15.4% in annual terms compared with the first quarter of the year, and an increase of 6.2% as compared with the fourth quarter of 2025.
This, together with revisions to previous CBS data, narrowed the gap from the long-term growth trend to approximately 0.8%.
Israel's economy sees ramifications of war with Iran after Operation Roaring Lion
Growth in the second quarter of 2026 was affected by rapid growth in all GDP components and partly reflects recovery from the damage in the first quarter against the onset of Operation Roaring Lion, which began when Israel carried out intense airstrikes on Tehran on February 28.
However, excluding the activity of Israeli companies abroad, GDP in the second quarter was 3.8% higher than in the fourth quarter of 2025.
The labor market in Israel continues to be tight, according to BoI data, with a slight increase in participation rates and broad unemployment.
In July, employment rates for Israelis aged 25-64 stood at 78.9%, and the participation rate stood at 81.3%. The rate of those temporarily absent due to reserve military service remained stable at 0.5%. The broad unemployment rate among the 25-64 age group stood at 3.2%, similar to before the operation began, and the job vacancy rate rose slightly to 4.5%.
Additionally, the rate of nominal wage increases in the second quarter stood at 6.2% compared with the previous year, largely influenced by increases in minimum wage and in the public sector, while wages in the private sector, excluding hi-tech businesses, rose by 5.4% from March to May.
However, geopolitical tensions, including war with Iran, led to a surge in energy prices and disruptions in supply chains. The price of a barrel of Brent oil rose by about 25% to $90, and European gas prices reached their peak since the outbreak of Operation Roaring Lion.
Within Israel’s housing market, the availability of apartments for sale remained stable, data showed.
BoI said that a summary of the monetary discussions held by the committee will be published on September 15, and the next interest rate decision will be published on October 21, less than a week before the slated Knesset elections on October 27.

California Legislature passes SB 1387, advancing recognition of Jewish identity as ethnicity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:09 UTC
01:49:09 KST

The California Legislature gave final approval to Senate Bill 1387, placing the state on the verge of becoming the first in the nation to formally recognize Jewish identity as an ethnicity alongside its religious classification in state law on Monday.
During the final hours of the legislative session, the Assembly overwhelmingly passed the measure with a 62-0 vote, followed shortly by the Senate concurring on a 38-0 vote. The bill now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk, where it awaits a signature or veto ahead of the September 30 deadline.
Authored by Sen. Henry Stern (D-Sherman Oaks) and sponsored by the advocacy group Jewish California, SB 1387 requires state agencies collecting demographic data on ancestry or ethnic origin to include a separate category for Jewish identity.
Proponents emphasize that the shift will ensure Jewish Californians are accurately represented in state datasets tracking hate crimes, public health metrics, and educational outcomes.
Advocates point to data from the Pew Research Center’s 2020 study of American Jews, which revealed that 52% of respondents view ancestry as essential to their Jewish identity and 55% point to culture, while only 36% define it purely through religion.
California's data collection historically hasn't reflected its multifaceted identity
Despite this multifaceted identity, California’s institutional data collection systems have historically lacked a mechanism to reflect it.
“SB 1387 makes sure that we are seen and included when the state counts ethnic communities, a national first,” said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California. “Good data makes good policy, and this bill means hate crime reports, health surveys, and education data will finally reflect who we actually are.”
Bocarsly also credited Stern’s leadership, the backing of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, and the coalition of 59 Jewish organizations that championed the legislation.
Under the bill’s provisions, participation will be entirely voluntary for individuals, and the new demographic option will be added without altering or removing existing religious data categories.
Data to remain strictly aggregate to address privacy concerns
To address privacy concerns, the legislation mandates that all published data remain strictly aggregate and explicitly prohibits using the collected information to establish individual registries or for law enforcement and immigration enforcement purposes.
The statutory requirements are scheduled to take effect in January, 2029, with the first formal reports slated for publication beginning January, 2030.
The landmark legislation underscores California’s role in setting potential precedents for state-level demographic accounting.
With SB 1387’s passage, all six bills sponsored by Jewish California during this legislative cycle now sit awaiting final action from Newsom, alongside measures establishing 100-foot safe zones around houses of worship, enhancing K-12 protections against antisemitism, reforming voter guides to exclude hate speech, combating campus disruptions, and securing care for Holocaust survivors.

What do the Altalena and the Heritage Ministry have to do with the approaching elections? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:49:05 UTC
01:49:05 KST

On the night between Sunday and Monday last week, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Heritage Minister Amichai Eliahu (both from Otzma Yehudit) announced that the remains of the Altalena – an Irgun ship which had brought weapons and immigrants from France to Israel, and on June 22, 1948, had been shelled by the IDF off the shore of Tel Aviv – had been found complete at a depth of 503 meters, 27 kilometers from the shore.
In July 1949, the Israeli Navy had towed what remained of the damaged ship 24 km. off the coast of Jaffa.
The Altalena was originally a 4,500-ton American World War II tank landing craft, converted by the Irgun to carry around 930 immigrants (most of them holocaust survivors) and Irgun personnel, and 4,500 tons of armaments, originally meant for Irgun fighters, and after the establishment of the state on May 15, 1948, to be shared with the newly founded IDF.
The Altalena departed from Marseilles in France on June 11 – 10 days after Irgun leader Menachem Begin signed an agreement with one of prime minister David Ben-Gurion’s assistants, Yisrael Galili, to disband the Irgun and integrate its fighters into the newly founded IDF.
At the time, Begin claimed that he had tried to put off the departure of the Altalena from France, but was ignored by the Irgun people there, and that after it had been sunk (at Ben-Gurion’s order), had done everything in his power to prevent civil war from breaking out, especially after it became known that 16 Irgun members and three IDF soldiers had been killed during the event.
The Altalena reached the shore of Kfar Vitkin, north of Tel Aviv, on the evening of June 20. The immigrants were all taken off the ship, and local members of Irgun managed to unload around 40% of the arms on board.
But then, due to disagreements with the IDF that deteriorated into mutual shooting, the ship departed for Tel Aviv on June 21 – with Begin on board.
On June 22, after the disagreements were not resolved, Ben-Gurion ordered the shelling of the ship. When the ship began to burn, and after everyone else was evacuated, Begin agreed to jump into the water.
From Ben-Gurion’s point of view, the whole affair happened because now that the State of Israel had been officially declared, there was to be only one sovereign power in it, which was to hold a complete monopoly over the holding and use of arms. There were to be no militias in Israel.
This assertion had practical ramifications for both the Irgun and the Palmah (the separately run, elite combined strike forces established several years earlier within the Hagana), both of which were finally obliged to give up their arms and separate command systems, and integrate fully into the IDF.
Ben-Gurion and Begin's relationship
In addition, Ben-Gurion did not trust Begin, and feared that he might instigate a revolt against his newly formed government. The order to shell the Altalena came after all other efforts to get the Irgun to surrender failed.
Begin believed that Ben-Gurion’s goal was to kill him, and that this was the main reason he had decided to shell the Altalena with him on board.
Though Begin accepted the sovereignty of Ben-Gurion’s government, he was divided with him over most policy issues, and suspected that the members of the Irgun and Lehi would continue to be discriminated against in the Mapai-governed state (as they were, to a certain extent).
And what does all this have to do with the approaching elections?
Though it is unclear what exactly is meant by “heritage” in the name of the Heritage Ministry, established as a separate ministry after the 2022 elections – whether it has to do with the heritage of the State of Israel as a whole, including its Arab citizens, only with the heritage of its Jewish population, or only with the heritage of specific sections of the Jewish population – Ben-Gvir and Eliyahu had no qualms about getting the Heritage Ministry to deal with this particular issue.
Most likely, Ben-Gvir did not have the elections in mind when he instructed Eliyahu to start searching for the exact location of the Altalena about a year after Israel’s 37th government was formed.
However, he did believe that the whole affair was part of the heritage of the Israeli Right, and that pulling the Altalena out of the sea and putting it on display on land would help give this feeling a concrete dimension, while pointing a scolding finger at the Left.
This issue has already been picked up by right-wing circles and Channel 14, and hurled in the direction of the “just not Bibi” camp, in connection with the approaching elections.
Furthermore, Ben-Gvir and Eliyahu had no qualms about embracing an issue with which the Likud is more directly connected historically than the Kahanist Otzma Yehudit.
Their decision to announce the finding of the Altalena by means of the Otzma Yehudit spokesperson around two months before the elections, and later on to hold a press conference at the Irgun Museum in Tel-Aviv, without involving Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in advance, was undoubtedly connected to the growing tensions between Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu.
These tensions are primarily over the latter’s statements that his goal is to form a “wide Zionist government” after the elections, and his efforts to get Otzma Yehudit to run again together with Religious Zionism’s leader, Bezalel Smotrich, in the coming elections.
Netanyahu managed to delay Otzma Yehudit’s press conference by half an hour by giving a separate photographed statement on the finding of the Altalena outside the hall where the press conference was to be held. His statement was directed at the voters, from a different perspective than that of Ben-Gvir and Eliyahu.
He stated that, “I undertake to extract [the Altalena] from the bottom of the sea so that it will serve as a concrete symbol for our generation and also for future generations: a concrete symbol to one simple command – never to a fraternal war!”
Netanyahu was obviously alluding to Begin’s efforts back in June 1948 to prevent his followers from instigating a civil war in reaction to the sinking of the Altalena.
However, it is doubtful whether the Altalena will ever be lifted from the bottom of the sea; first of all, because such a project cannot be performed by Israel on its own, and will cost tens or even hundreds of millions of shekels.
The Heritage Ministry required the services of a special Italian vessel equipped with specialized sensors and advanced survey systems for a single day, at the cost of one million shekels, just to find the Altalena. Furthermore, marine experts believe that the Altalena is likely to fall apart if moved due to corrosion.
Given the many real and urgent issues in almost all spheres of Israel’s existence and its citizens’ lives that ought to be dealt with in the election campaign, the Altalena affair is little more than a red herring within this context.
The writer has written journalistic and academic articles, as well as several books, on international relations, Zionism, Israeli politics, and parliamentarism. From 1994 to 2010, she worked at the Knesset Library and the Knesset Research and Information Center.

Christian school official says strike in East Jerusalem to continue over Israeli entry restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:47:25 UTC
01:47:25 KST

Abdel Raouf Arnaout, Sahin Demir, and Lina Altawell
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
- Israeli restrictions are ‘form of pressure’ to stop schools relying on teachers from West Bank, Richard Zananiri tells Anadolu
A Christian school official in occupied East Jerusalem said Tuesday that a strike by Palestinian private schools, including Christian schools, will continue as around 40% of teachers and staff remain without Israeli permits to enter the city.
Richard Zananiri, director-general of Al-Mutran School in East Jerusalem, told Anadolu that Israeli authorities issued some permits late Monday night, but not all of them.
He said private schools had taken a unified position to continue the strike until all teachers and staff receive permits, stressing that schools could not operate normally while part of their staff remained unable to reach their workplaces.
Zananiri described Israel’s failure to issue entry permits to teachers as a “purely political measure” aimed at separating the occupied West Bank from East Jerusalem.
“Students, parents and teachers had been waiting for the start of the new school year, including the return of school movement, the ringing of the bell and the morning lineup, but the lack of permits prevented that,” Zananiri said.
He said the permit issue is not new, noting that the same problem happened last December and caused schools to declare a strike.
“Teachers coming from the occupied West Bank need permits to cross Israeli checkpoints and enter Jerusalem,” he added, describing the restrictions as “a form of pressure on us to stop relying on teachers from the West Bank.”
“Those teachers are part of Jerusalem’s education system, especially amid shortages in some specializations, with around 25% to 30% of teachers at Al-Mutran School coming from the occupied West Bank,” he added.
He noted that Jerusalem schools as a whole have around 120,000 students.
Earlier Tuesday, private schools in occupied East Jerusalem, including Christian schools, began a strike as the new academic year started, protesting Israeli restrictions on teachers and staff living in the West Bank.
Israel requires Palestinians in the occupied West Bank to obtain special permits to enter occupied East Jerusalem, including for work, education, medical treatment and worship.
Jerusalem’s schools fall into three main categories: private schools, most of which are Christian; schools run by the Islamic Waqf Department; and schools affiliated with the Israeli municipality and Education Ministry.
In January 2026, the Knesset passed a law banning the employment of teachers who obtained their academic degrees from institutions affiliated with the Palestinian Authority in the Israeli education system.
According to a previous report by Haaretz, the law directly affects the availability of teachers in occupied East Jerusalem, where around 6,700 teachers work in the Arab education system, at least 60% of whom hold bachelor’s degrees from Palestinian academic institutions.

GlobalWafers Co (環球晶圓), the world’s third-largest silicon wafer supplier, said yesterday that advanced packaging wafers are expected to make a substantial revenue contribution this year following limited contribution last year, driven by their production ramp-up.
The company started delivering samples of 310x310mm square silicon wafers to customers for verification earlier this year, with the products designed for panel-level packaging applications and expected to enter volume production this year. GlobalWafers also produced a prototype of a larger 510x510mm wafer, it said.
“Silicon wafers, or wafers made on other materials, are playing an increasingly important role in semiconductor [production] as technology evolves generation by generation,” GlobalWafers chairwoman Doris Hsu (徐秀蘭) said.
Photo: CNA
“Wafers not only serve as the substrate for building dies and micro devices... They could also play a role in advanced packaging,” Hsu said.
A part of GlobalWafers’ revenue this year would come from advanced packaging wafers, she said.
In addition to square silicon wafers, silicon carbide wafers and transparent silicon carbide wafers are options for advanced packaging applications, Hsu said.
“The overall sentiment is exceptionally positive,” Hsu said.
The company has created a comprehensive range of wafers tailored for 3D packaging applications, including specialized silicon on insulator (SOI) wafers for silicon photonics, as well as wafers for devices, interposers and carriers. GlobalWafers supplies 12-inch SOI wafers to make high-end optical waveguides for silicon photonics, it said.
Hsu is optimistic about the global semiconductor wafer industry, saying the industry should grow at a double-digit percentage each year over the next two years as chipmakers expand capacity amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
“It is not just the beginning of another new cycle. AI is driving a structural shift in silicon and other semiconductor segments, leading to a stronger demand for semiconductors beyond silicon,” she said.
The growth also stems from wafer price hikes, she said.
GlobalWafers has concluded price negotiations with some customers and signed long-term supply agreements, and the trend is moving toward a “positive” direction, she added.
GlobalWafers said utilization rates are high across its production lines, reflecting strong order momentum. Customers are willing to secure capacity years in advance, the company said.
GlobalWafers in July secured a 10-year supply agreement with Micron Technology Inc, along with US$500 million in strategic funding from the US memory maker.

Lionel Messi on Monday said he was retiring from international soccer after leading Argentina to a second successive FIFA World Cup final in July.
The 39-year-old forward who won the World Cup in 2022 and dragged his nation to the final in the US only to lose to Spain, said the decision had been painful.
“It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul but I understand that it is the right time,” Messi wrote on Instagram.
Photo: Reuters
“I swear I always gave everything, not just in the last few years when we won everything but before that too, and I always fought and gave my all for this shirt,” he added.
Messi led Argentina to World Cup glory four years ago by winning the final against France in a penalty shoot-out in Doha, but his side lost 1-0 to a superior Spain side in the final in East Rutherford, New Jersey.
Following the death of his father, Jorge Messi, last month, Lionel Messi had said he had “serious doubts” about continuing to play soccer of any sort for “much longer.”
“I don’t know what I’ll do without you, I don’t know how to go on. I just played football, and now I have serious doubts about continuing to do so for much longer,” he said then.
Lionel Messi’s contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.
In this year’s finals, Lionel Messi inspired Argentina to another final by scoring eight goals and provided two assists in the dramatic late comeback against England in the semi-finals.
However, the dream of lifting the trophy again proved one match too far as the South Americans lost to Spain in the MetLife Stadium.
Lionel Messi was pictured in tears after receiving his loser’s medal.
He said afterward that the pain of defeat was “immense” and that it would “take a long time for this wound to heal.”
In his statement on Monday, the eight-time Ballon d’Or winner said it was time for a new generation of Argentina players to take up the torch.
“I love, I loved and I will always love being on the national team,” he wrote. “I gave everything I had, I have nothing more to give, and besides, there are some very talented young players coming up behind me who deserve to be there.”
Argentine President Javier Milei simply posted on social media: “Thank you very much, incredible man.”
First called up in 2005 by Jose Nestor Pekerman as an 18-year-old, Lionel Messi would go on to play 207 times for Argentina and become the country’s leading scorer, with 125 goals.
He also won two Copa Americas in 2021 and 2024 during his 21-year international career.
Yet, prior to the trophy-laden later years, Lionel Messi did not hold the place in Argentine hearts reserved for other national idols such as Diego Maradona or Pope Francis.
After moving to Catalonia at 13 to join Barcelona, Lionel Messi could have represented Spain, but chose Argentina.
His long-time teammate Angel Di Maria, also a 2022 world champion, on Monday paid homage to Lionel Messi for this choice and his impact on the national team.
“We will be forever grateful to you for being Argentinian and for having taken Argentina to the top of the world,” Di Maria said.
“For having chosen to be Argentinian when you could have chosen something else. Thank you for everything.”
For Ernesto Godoy, a 38-year-old teacher in Buenos Aires, Lionel Messi’s retirement from international soccer marks “the end of an incredible career, a sportsman of a caliber rarely seen.”
“There was Maradona, then a void, then Messi, and now we’re going to experience that void [again], life without Messi, just as Argentina did without Maradona,” he said of the player who hangs up his shirt assured of his place in the Argentine pantheon.

EDITORIAL: Taiwan grows its future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:47:01 UTC
01:47:01 KST

Taiwan is betting heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) as a pillar of its competitiveness. President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration plans to spend more than NT$40 billion (US$1.26 billion) next year on 10 major AI projects and train at least 500,000 AI professionals by 2040.
The ambition goes beyond expanding AI applications across industries. The government wants to boost Taiwan’s technological sovereignty and resilience by developing capabilities including sovereign AI and low Earth orbit satellite communications.
Lai spoke about the kind of adaptability Taiwan needs on Monday as he met with the VIS Mars robotics team. After Turkish customs detained the team’s equipment on their way to a tournament in Istanbul, the students borrowed tools to build a replacement robot from discarded parts, with which they won four matches.
Fostering talent in emerging technologies could do far more for Taiwan than simply make it more competitive. It could help diversify an economy heavily dependent on semiconductors while giving Taiwan greater control over technologies that would shape its economy and national security.
The AI industry is entering a period of rapid expansion as businesses and governments pour money into data centers, AI models and computing infrastructure. Gartner projects that revenue from AI-processing semiconductors would grow at a 26.8 percent compound annual rate through 2030, driven by demand for AI accelerators. The expansion is moving beyond AI training into inference, agentic AI and AI-enabled devices, all of which require substantial computing power.
Taiwan is well positioned to benefit. It accounts for more than 60 percent of global foundry revenue and more than 90 percent of leading-edge chip manufacturing, making it indispensable to the semiconductor supply chain. Its electronics industry is a major producer of AI servers and related equipment. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co in July said that demand related to AI remained “extremely robust” and projected its revenue for this year to grow by about 40 percent in US dollar terms.
However, manufacturing the hardware that powers AI should be only the beginning. Taiwan should cultivate the software engineers, researchers and entrepreneurs capable of developing the platforms and applications that run on that hardware. Building those capabilities domestically would allow Taiwan to capture more of the value generated by the AI boom while creating a more complete and resilient technology ecosystem.
There is a significant national security dividend. A strong domestic AI industry would reduce Taiwan’s reliance on foreign technology in areas that could become critical during a crisis. Domestically developed AI could help the military analyze intelligence, identify threats, improve surveillance and accelerate battlefield decisionmaking. It could assist researchers and defense companies in developing more effective weapons systems and strategies.
That matters because a conflict with China would place extraordinary demands on Taiwan’s ability to process information quickly and operate independently. AI cannot replace human judgement, but the ability to rapidly analyze enormous quantities of data and identify patterns could give Taiwan valuable time to respond to threats. Building that capability at home would make it less vulnerable to disruption or restrictions due to foreign technology.
Taiwan has long dreamed of creating its own Silicon Valley. The rise of AI makes that goal more plausible than it has been in decades. Taiwan already possesses many of the ingredients: world-class semiconductor manufacturing, a sophisticated electronics industry, strong universities and an increasingly ambitious technology sector. The missing piece is a deeper ecosystem connecting hardware with software, research, start-ups and investment.
If Taiwan can grow that ecosystem, it could attract some of the world’s best AI students, researchers and engineers, while giving talented Taiwanese more reason to remain at home rather than taking their expertise abroad. More talent would generate more innovation, which would attract more investment and create more opportunities for talent — a cycle that could transform Taiwan from a place that makes the chips powering the AI revolution into a place that helps create the revolution itself.
Taiwan has already demonstrated that it can become indispensable to the world’s technology industry. The next challenge is to ensure that its greatest technological strength is not simply making the machinery of the future, but developing the people and ideas that would determine how that machinery is used.
If Taiwan succeeds, its AI strategy could become much more than an economic diversification project: it could improve the nation’s technological independence, deepen its global importance and give it another tool with which to defend its future.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
