UN rapporteurs concerned over targeting of MEP Rima Hassan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:11:32 UTC
01:11:32 KST

Breadcrumb
UN rapporteurs raise serious concerns over harassment of European parliament member Rima Hassan
Five UN special rapporteurs have expressed their “grave concern” over the harassment of French-Palestinian European parliament member, Rima Hassan, adding that she has been targeted due to her political and human rights activism.
The rapporteurs raised the alarm over the matter in an official letter sent to the French government, with the correspondence highlighting the “numerous legal prosecutions” filed against Hassan, and noting that such moves mark a growing trend by French authorities to supress pro-Palestine voices.
This official letter also comes following a request from Hassan and her legal team to document the violations and pressure she is facing.
According to details in the letter, which was sent in June, French authorities were given until the end of August to provide an official response before the document was made publicly available online.
The UN Special Rapporteurs, whose mandate involves freedom of opinion and expression, said: “These measures may constitute political and judicial harassment against Hassan and may form part of a growing trend by the French authorities to supress voices defending the rights of the Palestinian people”.
In their letter, the experts also raised concerns over “several human rights violations,” including the right to privacy, freedom of expression and non-discrimination.
The left-wing France Insoumise party, to which Rima Hassan belongs, welcomed the UN experts’ intervention, describing it as “an important political warning about the erosion of the rule of law in France and the use of the judiciary as a tool to suppress political debate.”
The party, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, called on the government to address the concerns highlighted in the letter and stop exploiting anti-terrorism legislation to hinder democratic discourse.
The developments come as Hassan is due to appear before a French court in Paris on 19 and 20 October to stand trial on charges of “glorifying terrorism.”
The legal action stems from a formal referral by the French interior minister over a post the lawmaker shared on her X account in late March, where she made mention of Kozo Okamoto, one of the perpetrators of the 1972 Tel Aviv airport attack that resulted in 26 deaths. The post was later deleted.
The decision to place Hassan under pre-trial detention on 2 April sparked widespread backlash, with the lawmaker denouncing press leaks hinting at the presence of synthetic drugs in her bag, claims which were later refuted by investigations.
Hassan previously told The New Arab that her trial was “a political process” involving “the instrumentalisation of the judiciary and the distortion of counter-terrorism laws for the purposes of political repression.”
She said that, over the past two years, she had faced 16 legal proceedings, six police summonses and more than 45 hours of questioning in total.
She further said her case was part of what she described as a “growing dynamic of repression against voices expressing solidarity with Palestine” in France.
She pointed to an increase in legal proceedings, security interventions against student activism, and the banning of conferences and seminars related to Palestine.
Hassan also said that in her view, defending Palestine has now become grounds for security and judicial scrutiny, as well as media smear campaigns.

Russians likely building base in Crimea to store uncrewed surface vessels – OSINT

Unknown Publisher

Russians likely building base in Crimea to store uncrewed surface vessels – OSINT
Russian forces have begun constructing a base in temporarily occupied Crimea where they are likely planning to store the Russian military's uncrewed surface vessels (USVs). Analysts from the OSINT project CyberBoroshno published a satellite image showing the construction work.
Source: OSINT project CyberBoroshno
Details: The analysts identified newly built boathouses on the shore of Lake Donuzlav near the settlement of Novoozerne. Such structures are designed for the repair or storage of vessels.
CyberBoroshno analysts said they had not yet observed Russia actively using USVs.
However, they noted that the construction of such infrastructure suggests that Russia is likely at the testing stage and is preparing a base for the future deployment of this type of vessel.
Lake Donuzlav is located on the western coast of the Crimean Peninsula. It is connected to the Black Sea by an artificial navigable channel dug in the 1960s.
Background: Oboronka previously reported that the Russian fleet is expected to receive more than 150 uncrewed surface vessels in 2026, while the state order could increase to 230 units.

Russian Serviceman Tells Schoolchildren to Learn the Kalashnikov So “the Whole World Speaks Russian”
A Russian serviceman who fought in Moscow’s war against Ukraine told schoolchildren in Krasnoyarsk to study the Kalashnikov assault rifle so that “the whole world would speak Russian” during an opening school ceremony, The Moscow Times reported on September 1.
The remarks were made during a traditional first-day-of-school gathering at Lyceum No. 11 in the Siberian city, according to video published by local outlets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“As one politician said, if you want the whole world to speak Russian, learn how the Kalashnikov assault rifle works,” the serviceman said, quoting the late nationalist politician Vladimir Zhirinovsky.
He then congratulated the students and made a hand gesture associated with Wagner Group mercenaries.
“Jambo to everyone. Victory will be ours,” he added.
According to Russian outlet Ostorozhno, Novosti, the speaker was Alexander Klaus, who joined Russian forces in August 2023 and served as a machine gunner.
Klaus has said he participated in assaults around Avdiivka, Pisky and Vodiane in occupied eastern Ukraine before suffering a severe arm injury. He underwent five operations, was discharged from military service and later returned to Krasnoyarsk.
Local media reports indicate that Klaus has since become a regular participant in so-called patriotic events aimed at Russian schoolchildren and young people.
At a forum for students in Krasnoyarsk’s Central District in October 2025, Klaus encouraged young Russians to sign military contracts after completing compulsory service and go to war, describing such a decision as a “heroic act.”
He has also participated in a “Lesson of Courage” at a Krasnoyarsk vocational college, part of a broader system of state-backed events that increasingly expose Russian students to military themes and narratives surrounding Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
At the same time, Klaus has publicly acknowledged struggling to readjust to civilian life.
In an interview with Russian media NIA-Krasnoyarsk, he said he intended to return to the war despite having been medically discharged, potentially serving as either a medic or machine gunner.
Previously, Ukrainian officials reported the first documented case of a child listed as missing in the official “Children of War” registry later being identified as a serviceman in the Russian armed forces.
The case involves Oleksandr Mustyatse, a native of the village of Krynky in the Kherson region.

Russia Has Hit 4,650 Ukrainian Schools and Education Facilities, Destroying 423
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:05:07 UTC
01:05:07 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Has Hit 4,650 Ukrainian Schools and Education Facilities, Destroying 423
Russian attacks have damaged 4,650 educational facilities across Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion, with 423 destroyed completely, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said on September 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The figures were released as Ukrainian schools, colleges, and universities began a new academic year.
“Since the beginning of the full-scale war, 4,650 educational institutions have been affected by Russian shelling, and 423 have been completely destroyed. These are thousands of classrooms, lecture halls, laboratories, and spaces where Ukrainian children and young people were supposed to study,” Lubinets said.
The damage to education infrastructure has forced institutions across Ukraine to adapt their operations, including through remote learning and the relocation of students to other facilities.
Lubinets also reported that his office had received 644 education-related appeals in 2026 alone. They concerned access to education, children’s safety, university and school admissions, remote learning, institutional reorganizations, bullying, discrimination, and other issues.
“Therefore, today we are talking not only about the beginning of the academic year. We are talking about what Ukrainian education should look like during the war and what needs to be done to ensure that the right to education remains real for every child,” Lubinets said.
Ukraine’s education system entered the new academic year on September 1 under continued Russian attacks, with schools and universities using in-person, remote, or mixed formats depending on local security conditions.
In Kyiv, a Russian drone attack disrupted the first day of classes, forcing some students to begin the school year in shelters or join lessons online during an air raid alert.

US Army Secretary Driscoll resigns amid Hegseth tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:05:00 UTC
01:05:00 KST

U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation, the White House confirmed Monday, following reports of mounting tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Asked about a Wall Street Journal report that Driscoll had resigned, White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly did not deny it.
"Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army," Kelly said.
She cited his "outstanding leadership" during U.S. military operations, "restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more."
She added: "The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War."
If accepted, Driscoll's resignation would mark the latest departure of a senior leader in the U.S. military under President Donald Trump's administration.
A former law school classmate of Vice President JD Vance, Driscoll had reportedly benefited from their friendship within the administration, but clashed with Hegseth.
The most senior Democrat on the Senate's Armed Services Committee, Jack Reed, laid the departure's blame at the defense secretary's feet, saying, "I do not welcome Secretary Driscoll's resignation... It is far past time for President Trump to recognize the lasting harm that Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense."
An Army veteran who served in Iraq, Driscoll ran unsuccessfully for Congress in 2020 and later advised Trump's 2024 reelection campaign.
With the Iran war entering its seventh month, the resignation could effectively leave the Army without permanent civilian or uniformed leadership.
Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff General Randy George in April and has yet to nominate a permanent successor.

Russian air attack interrupts lessons on first day of school in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:04:55 UTC
01:04:55 KST

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy marked the start of the academic year with children at a Kyiv Oblast school rebuilt after Russian forces destroyed it in 2022, before an air attack forced their first lessons into the shelter on 1 September 2026, the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said.
Knowledge Day, Ukraine’s traditional start of the academic year, fell during the full-scale invasion for the fifth time. Russia’s war now determines whether children can learn alongside their classmates: local security and shelter access govern classroom returns, while about 200,000 pupils near the front will remain fully remote.
Around three million pupils began the 2026–2027 academic year, including roughly 240,000 first-graders, 10% fewer than a year earlier, Member of Parliament Iryna Borzova of the Verkhovna Rada’s Committee on Youth and Sports told Ukrinform. Most will learn in person or through a blended format, but some 200,000 children near the front will study entirely online, she said.
More than 82% of school pupils and preschoolers can access shelters, Education Minister Andrii Butenko said. The government has allocated UAH 6 billion this year to expand access to shelters and other educational safety infrastructure.
Russian forces destroyed the school Zelenskyy visited in March 2022. It reopened only last autumn with a shelter and backup power, according to the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration.
Zelenskyy said Russia had spent the preceding two weeks attacking infrastructure partly to disrupt the start of the academic year.
Ahead of Knowledge Day, Kyiv Oblast Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko advised schools in high-risk communities not to hold mass opening ceremonies. Each school was to decide whether to proceed based on the security situation in its community.
“First and foremost, there must be safety,” Tkachenko said. If a ceremony went ahead, he recommended holding it directly in a shelter where possible. For events outside shelters, attendance was not to exceed the capacity of the nearest protective facility, and schools were told to avoid large gatherings of pupils, parents, and staff.
How Russia’s invasion has devastated Ukrainian education
Ukraine’s 2026 Knowledge Day began after six consecutive days of Russian attacks on Kyiv and its surrounding region, culminating overnight in a massed missile and drone strike. Eight people were killed, and seven were injured, including three children, while civilian infrastructure was damaged across five Kyiv districts.
Russia’s invasion has turned school safety and reconstruction into central parts of Ukraine's education policy. By September 2024, more than 3,500 educational institutions had been damaged and nearly 400 destroyed, with the World Bank estimating that almost $14 billion would be needed to rebuild them.
Attacks on Ukraine’s energy system have also left classrooms without heat or electricity, forcing prolonged holidays and renewed distance learning.

How climate change threatens Europe’s nuclear renaissance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:03:32 UTC
01:03:32 KST

The Cattenom nuclear power plant, where a reactor was shut down as a precaution in August due to low river flows. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — European governments are planning to fight climate change with a major expansion of nuclear power. Global warming, however, is fighting back.
The continent’s ambitions for boosting atomic power generation, a central part of government efforts to meet net-zero goals and rising electricity demand, collided this summer with the effects of climate change.
Wilting heat waves and worsening drought plunged European river levels to record lows in August, depriving nuclear plants of the water needed to cool their reactors. The resulting shutdowns and production cuts prompted some governments and companies to question whether their multi-billion-euro plans to build new plants should be adjusted to account for the rising threats of climate-related disasters.
Advertisement
“Climate change is making nuclear power more and more unpredictable,” said Per Högselius, a professor of technology history at Sweden’s KTH Royal Institute of Technology.
The consequences of this summer’s extreme weather conditions have been dramatic.
Bulgaria’s sole nuclear plant throttled supply. Romania blew up a rock to keep the water flowing but was eventually forced to shutter both of its reactors. Hungary narrowly avoided shutting down its only nuclear plant, which provides half of the country’s electricity, but slashed production by three-quarters. In France, a record number of reactors had to halt or cut output.
Even when enough water is available, rising river temperatures sometimes force a shutdown due to rules preventing power plants from releasing the warmed water to protect local wildlife. Switzerland shut off one reactor for that reason in June.
Drought isn’t the only problem. Increasing wildfires, storms and floods can also pose threats to nuclear power plants."We are clearly going to see this more and more frequently," Högselius said of the shutdowns and production cuts.
That trend raises questions about Europe’s ambitious plans to reverse its long decline in nuclear power generation. A large coalition of European Union countries wants to boost the bloc’s nuclear power generation by 50 percent by midcentury, while the United Kingdom has plans to quadruple its capacity over the same period.
Advertisement
The risks seen across Europe this summer come as nuclear power experiences a comeback in popularity. Across the globe, nuclear generation could triple by 2050, fueled by a growing desire for homegrown electricity, rising power demand and decarbonization efforts. In the United States, the Trump administration wants to quadruple nuclear capacity by 2050, in part to account for the explosion of power-hungry data centers.
Europe, the fastest-warming continent, is particularly exposed to climate risks because many of its reactors were built along inland rivers or depend on cooling ponds that are vulnerable to drought.
“The temperature increases within Europe have been among the highest in the world,” said Brent Wanner, head of the power sector unit at the International Energy Agency. “So Europe would see some of these impacts first.”
Jellyfish washed up on the beach in front of the Gravelines nuclear power station on Aug. 12, 2025. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Also … jellyfish invasions
Europe’s nuclear fleet was constructed for a different climate. “Almost all nuclear power plants were designed in the 1970s, 1980s,” Högselius said.
That’s also the case for reactors in many other parts of the world, though the risks differ from continent to continent.
“Over 70% of installed capacity in operation or under construction is in three regions — Eastern North America, Western and Central Europe and East Asia — all of which will face a wide variety of climate hazards in the future, including extreme heat conditions, heavy precipitation, coastal and river floods and tropical cyclones,” the International Atomic Energy Agency wrote in 2022.
Advertisement
Around 15 percent of reactors worldwide depended on freshwater sources that faced significant strain from warming in 2022. It’s expected to rise to 25 percent over the next 20 years, the IAEA says.
Drought is an acute problem in South Asia and Europe, increasing the risk of production disruptions. European reactors, “particularly in the South of France, could see the largest percentage increases in consecutive dry days,” the agency writes.
Reactors that draw water from lakes or the sea rather than rivers aren’t as vulnerable to drought, but they face other challenges.
Nuclear infrastructure in North America and East Asia, for example, is exposed to rising threats from cyclones and other storms, the IAEA warned. In the longer term, rising ocean levels could jeopardize atomic plants on the coast, particularly in the U.S. and Japan.
Then, there are the jellyfish: The gelatinous animals thrive in warmer waters, multiplying into large coastal swarms that sometimes clog up pumping systems at nuclear power plants — as happened in France this summer.
The frequency of outages is higher in the summer than winter and has increased with every decade since 1990, according to IAEA data.
Advertisement
The International Energy Agency has also been tracking the impact of climate change on power infrastructure, Wanner said, finding that longer-lasting extreme weather events are adding strain to power systems.
Most systems are designed for heat waves that last a few days or a week, Wanner said. “But if it’s over two weeks, three weeks or a month, that’s much harder. That’s a much bigger stress on the system.”
Adjusting to a warmer world
This summer’s extreme events haven’t prompted a rethink of Europe’s nuclear ambitions — but it’s leading governments to adjust their planning and prompting companies to invest in measures to make reactors more resilient.
Workers and machinery on the banks of the Danube near the Paks Nuclear power plant on Aug. 18, 2026. | Attila Kisbenedek/AFP via Getty Images
France’s state-owned nuclear giant EDF said in a statement that it’s planning to spend €4.3 billion by 2040 to adapt its plants to the effects of climate change.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is reconsidering expansion plans for the nuclear power plant that teetered on the verge of a shutdown, citing a cooling system that he said is unfit to deal with the reality of global warming.
Romania’s energy ministry said in a statement that the drought hasn’t changed minds about the country’s nuclear expansion plans, but that it “reinforces the importance of ensuring that future projects are appropriately assessed against a broad range of climate, hydrological, environmental and energy-system conditions.” The Bulgarian and Hungarian ministries did not respond to requests for comment.
Advertisement
The emerging risks may also prompt governments to search for less vulnerable sites to build the next generation of nuclear reactors — potentially complicating an already difficult process. One senior French official said that water availability “is one of the key factors” determining where a plant is built.
There are signs countries and industry are already taking the new reality into account.
“The vast majority of new constructions are on coastal sites,” said the IEA’s Wanner. “It’s actually already kind of being structurally addressed.”

Russia's Starlink copycat has failed so far, but still threatens Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:02:04 UTC
01:02:04 KST

Russia's homegrown Starlink rival has suffered a fresh setback, with an entire batch of satellites failing to reach orbit — but even a partially working system could still sharpen Russian strikes on Ukraine.
None of the 16 satellites Russia launched on 19 July as part of its Rassvet programme, Moscow's attempt to build its own version of Starlink to guide the drones and missiles it has used against Ukraine for more than four years, have reached their planned orbit, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), citing data from live satellite tracker N2YO.
Most of the satellites are sitting at altitudes of 300 to 400 kilometres, "well short of the intended 870-kilometer operational altitude for the Rassvet satellites," the report said.
At least two satellites appear to be heading for reentry into Earth's atmosphere.
Those flying at lower altitudes face greater atmospheric drag, burn through fuel faster and have shorter operational lifespans than those flying higher, meaning the affected satellites are unlikely to last as long as Russia had planned, even if they stabilise.
Satellite internet has become central to how both sides fight this war.
Ukraine's access to Starlink has let its forces fly reconnaissance and strike drones, coordinate artillery and stay connected in areas where Russian strikes have destroyed ground infrastructure.
The stakes involved are not abstract. Since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) has verified at least 16,874 civilians killed and 51,173 injured, as of the end of July.
HRMMU said in a report published on 13 August that July 2026 was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since March 2022, with at least 437 killed and 2,610 injured, driven by a sharp rise in aerial bombardment and glide bomb attacks alongside continued long-range missile and drone strikes on cities far from the front line.
The mission's monthly reports also recorded successive records for short-range drone casualties near the front in April and May.
A functioning Rassvet constellation would extend Russia's ability to direct strikes over greater distances and with greater precision, which is why the programme's repeated failures matter well beyond the technical details.
A troubled launch record
Of the 16 Rassvet satellites launched on 24 March, 12 reached their intended altitude of 550 kilometres and remain there, according to the report.
Those satellites already give Russian forces two daily windows of connectivity with ground terminals, lasting up to 90 minutes in total over Ukraine.
Moscow appears to be rushing the programme to compensate for the loss of Starlink access. Ukraine's defence ministry said in early February that Starlink terminals being used illicitly by Russian forces had been deactivated after Kyiv and SpaceX moved to a "whitelist" system restricting the network to verified terminals.
"Russia may have been unprepared to accelerate constellation deployment at this pace and will likely face additional delays," the ISW report said.
But the threat has not gone away. ISW warned that the existing satellites "may allow Russian forces to conduct more precise strikes against Ukraine using remotely controlled unmanned systems" during the windows when connectivity does work — a reminder that Russia does not need a fully functioning constellation to keep inflicting harm, only a partially working one.
Falling short of scale
Bureau 1440, the Russian aerospace firm developing the satellites, has said it plans "dozens" more launches to deploy hundreds more satellites.
Serhii Beskrestnov, then an adviser to Ukraine's defence minister, said on 31 May that Russia would need at least 200 to 250 satellites in orbit to achieve continuous, stable connectivity, and that Moscow was unlikely to hit that target in the near term.
The report attributed Russia's bottleneck to its reliance on the Soyuz-2.1b, "a costly and scarce asset."
The country has carried out only six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches across all space and commercial missions since 2022, a tempo that ISW said would allow for "a maximum of 128 Rassvet satellites per four years," and only if every launch succeeded and none were diverted elsewhere.
So far, only 37.5% of launched Rassvet satellites have reached a sustainable operational altitude.
Ukraine targets the supply chain
Ukrainian forces have also gone after the infrastructure behind the programme, in an apparent effort to slow a system that would extend Russia's ability to deliver deadly strikes in Ukraine.
Ukrainian forces struck the Progress Space Rocket Center, which produces Soyuz-type launch vehicles, overnight between 14 and 15 August.
A further strike was attempted against the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on 23 August, two days before Russia launched a Soyuz-2.1b vehicle reportedly carrying a GLONASS-K1 satellite, part of Russia's GPS alternative.
Both Rassvet batches were launched from Plesetsk, and the report concluded that Ukrainian strikes "threaten not only Russia's limited supply and production of launch vehicles but also the scarce launch infrastructure to place satellites into orbit" — infrastructure that, if it succeeds, will make Russia's war on Ukraine much more lethal.

Scott Ritter: The CIA never comes to Russia in peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:01:53 UTC
01:01:53 KST

Scott Ritter: The CIA never comes to Russia in peace
CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow last week.
What we know: Ratcliffe met with Sergey Naryshkin, the director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. This has been confirmed by Naryshkin himself, who described the meeting as “routine.” We also know that the US spy chief did not meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The meeting took place, there is nothing unusual in this,” Naryshkin stated afterwards. “In the practice of special services, meetings of managers, personal meetings or online are part of our work. So, the meeting with John Ratcliffe is a working format.”
Naryshkin refused to state what issues were discussed, explaining that they were within the competence of the intelligence services. “And the competence of the intelligence services is such a rather delicate and special thing,” the Russian spy chief said.
What we don’t know: literally anything else.
Rumors abound about additional attendees, as well as the agenda – or lack thereof – that was pursued by Ratcliffe during a meeting which appeared to be anything but routine. But the fact is, any meeting between Ratcliffe and Naryshkin, given the nature of the times we live in, could never be described as “routine.”
A quick reminder: John Ratcliffe’s CIA is currently at war with Russia. Literally.
Ratcliffe assumed his current position on January 23, 2025. Prior to this, he did a short stint as national intelligence director during the last year of Trump’s first term in office. He was a Texas congressman for a few years, as well as a small-town mayor and acting US attorney for the Eastern District of Texas.
He is a politician, not a spy.
But he is fully cognizant of the CIA’s secret war against Russia, having been fully briefed while serving as DNI. As a member of Congress, Ratcliffe was a leading policy maker on national security issues serving as a member of the House Intelligence and Homeland Security committees.
Any effort to portray him as some sort of “innocent abroad” fails on the face of the facts.
The CIA has always been at war with Russia. During the Cold War, Moscow Station (the name of the CIA’s operation center based out of the US Embassy) was literally the front line of the spy-versus-spy antics taking place between the US and the Soviet Union.
The CIA headed up Operation Cyclone, a massive paramilitary-driven effort to create a Vietnam-like quagmire for the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The goal of Operation Cyclone was to kill Russians.
I worked with people who were directly or indirectly affiliated with Operation Cyclone. ‘Kill more Russians’ was literally their mantra.
There was a time when the CIA hired genuine Russia-area experts. The analysts who populated the Office of Soviet Analysis (SOVA) in the Directorate of Intelligence at the height of the Cold War were some of the best experts on the Soviet Union imaginable.
I know because I worked with them. From 1988-1990, I received two classified commendations from the director of the CIA for my analytical work involving the Soviet Union. I was considered by the CIA leadership to be a top-notch Soviet analyst.
In 1992 the CIA actively recruited me for an analytical position within the predecessor to SOVA, the Slavic and Eurasian Office. I was brought in for a high-level interview, after which I was informed that the CIA would be passing on my application. When I asked why, I was told that I was too married to old school thinking about Russia – in short, I was a ‘Sovietologist’.
The CIA was looking for people who could imagine Russia ‘differently’. What this meant was divorcing oneself from the mindset that Russia (i.e., the Soviet Union) was a peer-level opponent worthy of respect (my view), and instead adopting a stance that Russia was a defeated foe that needed to be kept down by any means necessary.
In the 1990s, the CIA’s task was to use Boris Yeltsin as an agent of influence to weaken Russia and facilitate foreign control over its resources. The CIA actively infiltrated every aspect of the Russian economy and used ‘soft power’ resources funded by the likes of the National Endowment for Democracy and overseen by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) to hijack Russian democratic institutions and Russian social life, especially through media-related activities.
The CIA also was very active in working to break Russia up into more manageable fiefdoms, each ruled over by a CIA-controlled lackey. The Russian-Chechen conflict was a primary example of this activity.
When Boris Yeltsin stepped aside in favor of Vladimir Putin as Russia’s president on New Year’s Eve 1999, the CIA immediately made it its task to undermine Putin and replace him with someone from the Yeltsin camp willing and able to do the CIA’s bidding.
Putin’s resistance and resilience as a Russian leader operating independent of CIA control helped shape a new generation of Russophobes in the United States. The first generation were the ‘new Russian’ thinkers that replaced the old school ‘Sovietologists’ at the end of the Cold War. To them, Russia was a playground for which to launch experiments on economic and political domination with absolutely zero regard to the price being paid by the people of Russia.
This generation of Russophobes simply detested Russia and the Russian people, failing to attribute any normative human value to their lives. Millions of Russians lost their lives as a result, and tens of millions of others suffered greatly.
Michael McFaul, the former US ambassador to Russia, falls into this category. So, too, does Fiona Hill. And Beth Sanner. People whose educational background and Russian experience pre-dates Putin, people who know the truth about Russia but opted instead to embrace the hegemonic policies of superpower singularity and work to weaken and destroy Russia.
But Putin’s stubborn hold on power, despite concerted efforts by the CIA to oust him (think Navalny), led to the birth of a new generation of Russophobes, so-called ‘experts’ whose only claim to relevance is their undying hatred of Putin and everything Russian.
It is this generation that has gravitated to the upper levels of the CIA’s analytical community, and who openly hate all things Russia. People like Andrea Kendall-Taylor and Julia Gurganus.
It is this openly Russophobic CIA that John Ratcliffe oversees.
His relationship with Julia Gurganus is both instructive and illustrative of the sickness that pervades the CIA when it comes to Russia. Gurganus was the National Intelligence Officer for Russia back in 2016-17, at the height of the Obama-era Russiagate scandal that tried to make the case of collusion between then-candidate Donald Trump and Russia to steal the 2016 presidential election from Hillary Clinton.
Gurganus helped manufacture the intelligence that underpinned this false allegation. She was a vociferous critic of Trump, so much so that the CIA quietly exiled her to a think tank position during Trump’s first term in office.
When Trump was reelected, Ratcliffe oversaw the whitewashing of Gurganus’ role in falsely accusing Trump of collusion, leading to the elevation of Gurganus as the senior CIA briefer onboard Air Force One as Trump flew to Alaska to meet with Putin in August 2025. That’s right – Ratcliffe purposefully cleansed Gurganus of her anti-Trump credentials so she could personally brief the president before his meeting with Putin.
Tulsi Gabbard, in her role as DNI, exposed Gurganus as an anti-Trump operative and had her security clearances revoked, but not before the damage was done.
There was a time when the CIA’s Directorate of Operations Russia House was home to living legends. People like Milton Beardon, who helped run Operation Cyclone and was chief of the Soviet/East European Division at the time the Soviet Union fell. Gardner Hathaway and Berton Gerber, who ran some of the most successful CIA spying operations from Moscow Station in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
And Murat Natirboff, another legendary Russian hand who led the Moscow Station during the Nicholas Daniloff affairs in the 1980s. Natirboff is instructional in this regard. His father was an officer in the Russian White Army which fought the Bolsheviks during the Russian Civil War. Natirboff hated the communists. But he loved Russia. He was held in very high regard by the Soviet officers of the KGB which faced off against him during his tour in Moscow.
I can personally attest to Murat’s feelings toward Russia – I met him after he left Moscow in 1988, where we spoke about my experiences in Votkinsk as an INF Treaty weapons inspector.
The CIA no longer employs people of this caliber in its operational work regarding Russia. Gone are the days of the Russian romantics – people who took the time to learn about their enemies to bring to life Sun Tzu’s classic observation: “If you know your enemy as yourself, you need not fear the outcome of a hundred battles.”
The present-day Directorate of Operations is overrun with paramilitary operatives, men (and women) who cut their teeth during the heyday of the post-9/11 ‘Global War on Terror’, where they oversaw secret wars in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, and Iran.
They take their cue from veterans like Tom Sylvester, a former Navy SEAL who worked in the CIA’s Special Activities Branch as a Ground Branch operative. Tom headed the CIA’s efforts in Ukraine post-2022, when the Special Military Operation began. His job was literally to kill Russians.
People like ‘Santa Claus’, the nickname of the CIA’s Kiev Station Chief who sent Ground Branch to Ukraine post-2014 to train the Ukrainian intelligence special operations forces on how best to kill Russians.
Veterans of the CIA’s drone assassination programs now advise the Ukrainian drone operators on how to kill Russians and destroy Russian infrastructure.
In December 2025, the CIA helped direct Ukrainian drones toward a residence in Valdai where Putin was staying.
Yes – John Ratcliffe’s CIA tried to kill the Russian president. The CIA denies Putin was the target, but the data from the guidance chips extracted from Ukrainian drone debris appears to suggest otherwise.
Today, the CIA is knee-deep in the business of killing Russians. They continue to guide Ukraine’s expanded drone warfare campaign targeting Russia. And Russians.
This is John Ratcliffe. This is the organization he leads. So, when people reflect on the recent visit by Ratcliffe to Russia, never lose sight of his primary mission.

Sydney’s beaches enter the drone age to get swimmers back in the water after spate of shark attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:00:07 UTC
01:00:07 KST

“Hey Taha, what’s the visibility like?” shouts a man with a towel slung over his shoulder.
“Uh, nice,” says Surf Life Saving New South Wales drone operator Taha Kafil-Hussain.
“Good?” the man asks.
“Very good,” Kafil-Hussain assures him.
Thanking him, the early morning swimmer turns and heads down the steps to Coogee beach.
Kafil-Hussain, who Guardian Australia has joined on his early morning shark surveillance flight, says: “When they’re local, they just want to see what the weather, what the water looks like, [if there’s] anything scary.”
The 22-year-old has been flying drones for SLS NSW for four years, but only at Coogee beach for a matter of weeks. Before a shark attack on 34-year-old Sydney teacher and mother Leah Stewart in June, drone surveillance was not permitted at Coogee because it lies directly under the flight path from Sydney airport’s east-west runway.
In an interview with 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, Stewart described the horror encounter with a four-metre white shark, after which her left arm was amputated, as “like fighting a dinosaur”. The attack, one of a series of high-profile incidents in Sydney in the past 12 months, has prompted the state government to massively ramp up its shark mitigation program.
Under a $34m initiative by the state government which rolled out on 1 July, 38 of Sydney’s ocean beaches, including Coogee, now receive dawn-to-dusk drone monitoring year round.
Seventy NSW beaches in total are part of the dawn-to-dusk program, while others will benefit from increased surveillance throughout the summer and school holidays. From Tuesday, surveillance hours increased, running from 6.15am to 5pm each day for the start of spring, as daylight increases.
When Guardian Australia meets Kafil-Hussain in mid-winter, he arrives at 6.30am to throw up a marquee, before checking a radio to determine which direction the planes are flying in (drone surveillance at Coogee has been allowed with special permission from the airport).
Not long after, the drone takes off in a whir of plastic from a miniature landing pad, rising 60 metres into the air before heading out to sea. During each 20-minute flight, Kafil-Hussain rakes the bay in sections from left to right, backwards and forwards, leaving a chequerboard pattern on his control screen.
He says he’s looking for “anything moving in a different way than normal”.
“Anything moving against the flow of water, anything that looks a little bit long – anything alive, really.”
He pauses when he thinks he’s spotted something, to zoom in. “Looks like seaweed,” he says.
University of Sydney shark policy expert and associate professor Christopher Pepin-Neff agrees that “drones are the best technology that we have at the moment”.
But they say there are “important caveats that we need to give to the public”.
“On days that are windy, if the shark is too small, the drone operator is not going to be able to see a shark if it’s there.
“I’m slightly nervous that, in the absence of [a] large public education campaign, we have the possibility that we’re going to scare the shit out of people,” says Pepin-Neff.
With more drone surveillance comes more regular shark sightings. The NSW government says there have been more 750 sightings and more than 200 intervention actions by Surf Life Saving NSW since 1 July.
Shark listening stations are now tracking 1,698 white sharks, 938 tiger sharks and 374 bull sharks – the “target sharks” which are most frequently involved in serious shark bites.
Kafil-Hussain says he has seen more bull and tiger sharks than whites, and has raised the alarm a few times, most recently for a bronze whaler – involved in rare attacks – which he initially thought was a target shark.
If it’s early and he’s on his own, raising the alarm means making the call to clear the water himself – otherwise he shares what he has seen with lifeguards and they make the decision, with the time from spotting a hazard to fully clearing the water about two or three minutes.
The SLS drones have a speaker attached to them, allowing him to communicate directly with surfers and swimmers.
It’s a technology familiar to followers of the Instagram account Drone Shark App, run by Jason Iggleden, who has been using a drone since 2018 to surveil beaches including Bondi, Tamarama and Bronte.
Videos on the account show an enormous seal barrel-rolling through the water and a swirling vortex of Australian salmon, while in another a whale lingers beneath a kayaker in Tamarama.
“I just had a bit of a vision to help … with getting people out of water with sharks, and just showing them the beauty of what’s out there,” he said.
The licensed and insured drone flyer, who continues to work independently, now passes on any sightings to SLS NSW. He is a firm believer in the drone surveillance, saying the ability to spot target sharks grows with experience.
“I don’t think you really need to consider much more than drones, to be honest,” he says.
Pepin-Neff is supportive of other non-lethal technologies, such as SMART drum lines. They say a trial of new artificial intelligence detection software on drones will take the pressure off humans to discern between more and less dangerous sharks. But their message on controversial measures such as shark nets, here to stay on NSW beaches, and culling, is unequivocal: “They do not work.”
‘Not a perfect solution’
Kafil-Hussain, who drives each day from his home in Parramatta, has now flown drones at most Sydney beaches, from Palm beach in the north to Cronulla in the south. Every beach is different – he sees turtles, dolphins, the occasional whale. Coogee is home to a wobbegong, a low-swimming carpet shark which does not hunt humans but can attack if threatened.
“He’s not around. He’ll pop out eventually,” says Kafil-Hussain.
When Guardian Australia visits the beach, arriving before sunrise, it is already heaving with eastern suburbs dog walkers, swim clubs and surfers. Just weeks after the attack on Stewart, Kafil-Hussain says numbers at the beach have only been growing.
Pepin-Neff says the drone program will “restore confidence” ahead of a busy summer, but there is “no silver bullet”. “Drones are a great tool but they’re not a perfect solution.”
Pepin-Neff swims at fully enclosed beaches, like Marrinawi Cove in Barangaroo, but their advice for those that swim at unenclosed beaches is: “Swim between the flags.”
“The ocean is the wild and we need to treat the beach like the bush.”

Gabapentin prescriptions are rising in addiction treatment despite weak evidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:00:02 UTC
01:00:02 KST

Doctors are increasingly prescribing the nerve pain medication gabapentin to patients undergoing treatment for substance use disorders, even as researchers note a lack of strong evidence supporting this practice. At the same time, patients using the drug without a prescription account for nearly double the rate of those who have a formal prescription, though this unprescribed use appears to be slowly declining. These patterns were detailed in a large study recently published in Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
Gabapentin is originally approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration to treat partial seizures and specific types of nerve pain. In clinical practice, physicians routinely prescribe the medication “off-label,” meaning they use it to treat conditions outside of its approved uses. For patients in substance use treatment, doctors often recommend gabapentin to help ease withdrawal symptoms. Clinicians also prescribe it to manage co-occurring issues such as anxiety, insomnia, and chronic pain.
Many medical professionals have traditionally viewed gabapentin as a safe alternative to medications with high potential for addiction, such as opioids and benzodiazepines. Medical literature evaluating gabapentin’s effectiveness in treating substance use disorders remains sparse. Reviews of past research show mixed results regarding the drug’s ability to reduce heavy drinking or opioid withdrawal. Medical trials have shown no benefit for treating cocaine or methamphetamine use disorders.
Despite this limited evidence, national prescribing rates for gabapentin have climbed steadily over the past two decades. Public health monitoring systems have simultaneously tracked a rise in nonmedical use of the drug, particularly among individuals with a history of substance use. People taking gabapentin without a prescription often report doing so to self-medicate for pain, sleep problems, or withdrawal symptoms. Others use it seeking euphoria or attempting to enhance the effects of other substances.
Psychiatry researcher Matthew S. Ellis of Washington University in St. Louis led a research team to investigate these dual trends. The researchers wanted to identify how often gabapentin was being used with and without a prescription inside substance use treatment centers. They also sought to understand the demographic traits, medical diagnoses, and other drug use patterns associated with gabapentin consumption. Penn Whitley and Steven D. Passik of the testing laboratory Millennium Health co-authored the paper.
To track these patterns, the researchers designed a retrospective study analyzing patient data gathered over an eight-year period. They examined 206,161 urine drug test results collected between January 2016 and October 2023. These tests came from patients aged 18 and older at 2,053 substance use treatment facilities across all 50 U.S. states. The researchers selected one test per patient based on their earliest specimen collection date.
The laboratory analyzed the urine specimens using a technique called liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. This process separates the individual chemical components in a sample and measures their mass to identify specific drugs. The researchers looked for the presence of gabapentin alongside a range of other prescription and illicit drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, fentanyl, heroin, and alcohol. They then compared the laboratory results against the medication lists provided by the clinics to determine if the patient had a documented gabapentin prescription.
Following this data collection, the researchers applied statistical models to assess the relationship between gabapentin use and various patient characteristics. They evaluated age, sex, insurance type, and clinic location. The models also accounted for specific medical diagnoses, such as alcohol, opioid, or sedative use disorders, as well as psychiatric conditions like mood disorders and anxiety.
The analysis revealed that 5.9 percent of the total sample had a documented prescription for gabapentin. Over the course of the study period, the prescribing rate nearly doubled, rising from 3.9 percent in 2016 to 7.6 percent in 2023. Prescriptions increased across all categories of substance use disorders. Patients with a sedative use disorder saw the highest prescribing rates by the end of the study period.
Certain demographic groups were more likely to receive a gabapentin prescription. Patients aged 55 and older had the highest likelihood of being prescribed the medication compared to young adults. Women were more likely to receive a prescription than men. Medical conditions including anxiety, mood disorders, insomnia, and pain were also highly associated with receiving a gabapentin prescription.
The data showed a different trajectory for patients taking the medication without a doctor’s guidance. The researchers identified gabapentin use without a prescription in 11.3 percent of the total sample. This rate was nearly double the proportion of patients who were formally prescribed the drug. Unlike the upward trend in prescribing, the rate of unprescribed use steadily decreased over time, dropping from 15.2 percent in 2016 to 9.9 percent in 2023.
Unprescribed gabapentin use shared several demographic similarities with prescribed use, occurring more frequently in older adults and patients with Medicare or private insurance. People diagnosed with an opioid or sedative use disorder were highly likely to use gabapentin outside of a prescription. Patients with psychiatric diagnoses like anxiety and mood disorders were also more likely to engage in unprescribed use.
The researchers found a strong association between unprescribed gabapentin use and the presence of other drugs in the patient’s system. Detection rates for all analyzed drug classes were higher among individuals taking gabapentin without a prescription compared to those with a prescription. Cannabis was the most frequently detected substance in both groups. Among patients without a gabapentin prescription, the detection of fentanyl increased from 12 percent to 29 percent during the study period.
The study design relies on urine drug tests submitted to a single national laboratory, which may not represent the entire population of individuals in substance use treatment. The accuracy of the prescription data also depends entirely on the medication lists provided by the treating clinicians. If a doctor failed to record a patient’s gabapentin prescription on the test order form, that patient’s authorized drug use would be incorrectly categorized as unprescribed.
The measure of unprescribed use in this study operates as a proxy for nonmedical use, but it may undercount the true scope of the issue. Patients who possess a valid prescription might still engage in nonmedical use by taking the drug in higher doses or at different frequencies than directed. Urine testing alone cannot distinguish between a patient following their doctor’s orders and one misusing their own prescription. Patients might also consume gabapentin unknowingly if it is mixed into the illicit drug supply as an adulterant.
Future research will need to explore the specific origins of gabapentin prescriptions for patients in substance use treatment. It remains unknown whether addiction specialists are prescribing the medication directly or if patients are receiving it from outside healthcare providers for unrelated conditions. Researchers also hope to investigate whether high rates of polysubstance use among these patients reflect intentional mixing of drugs or a broader symptom of gaps in treating multiple co-occurring illnesses.
The study, “Use of gabapentin with or without a prescription in substance use treatment settings: A national analysis of urine drug testing data, 2016 – 2023,” was authored by Matthew S. Ellis, Penn Whitley, and Steven D. Passik.

The universe may have been building rocky planets almost from the start
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

The universe’s first rocky planets may have gotten their start astonishingly early — perhaps only 100 million years after the Big Bang.
Explosions of some of the universe’s first massive stars could have created isolated pockets rich enough in dust and elements like iron and carbon to form the building blocks of planets, a new computer simulation suggests. The simulation produced enough rocky building material to potentially make several Earth-sized planets, and there was water available in the young stellar system that could have made it to the planet just a bit later, researchers report August 19 in Astrophysical Journal Letters.
“Habitable worlds, in principle, could have formed billions of years earlier than previously thought, even before the first galaxies formed,” says astronomer Daniel Whalen, of Portsmouth University in England. “These simulations really go to the real true origin of life in the universe.”
Researchers had previously tried to understand when planets formed using large-scale computer simulations to figure out when enough of the heavy elements — such as carbon, oxygen, and iron — would have accumulated. But Whalen and colleagues wanted to take a more detailed look at the most element-enriched regions in the early cosmos — debris fields left behind after the universe’s first giant stars exploded as supernovas. Because these regions would have had higher heavy element content than the universe overall, maybe they could have formed planets much earlier, the astronomers thought.
The researchers used the simulations to track the evolution of debris from a type of supernova called a pair instability supernova, which can create 100 times the sun’s mass of heavy elements. The simulations showed the debris mingled with gas in the early universe, eventually collapsing to form a small new star surrounded by a dusty disk. In the disk, the researchers found planetesimals — small rocky bodies a few meters to kilometers across that are the embryos of planets. Notably, some planetesimals formed at the right distance from the star to have liquid water.
“The study would indicate that all the way up back almost to the very beginning there may have been conditions for life being set in place,” says astrophysicist Jarrett Johnson of the Los Almos National Laboratory in New Mexico who was not involved with the new study. “Just because there are planets forming doesn’t mean there’s life, of course, but the ingredients are being put in place pretty much as early as they possibly could be.”
It’s possible that some of these earliest planets could still exist, Whalen says. The star that formed in the simulation was around 70 percent the mass of the sun, making it very long lived. If one of those such systems made it into the Milky Way, they could easily be identified as ancient systems based on their chemical makeup.
“[Finding one] is well within the realm of possibility,” Whalen says.
He and his colleagues are now working to simulate the next stage of the planetesimals growth to see what types of planets they ultimately form. They’re also interested in looking at what might happen around a different type of supernova thought to be more common in the early universe. But even the first results are inspiring astronomers to ask new questions.
“I think it opens up the window to think about what could have happened in the 13 billion years plus since those first planets formed,” Johnson says. “The studies suggest that we probably should consider that more carefully.”

Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
- Published
Germany has said Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig's airport.
A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, on 4 August.
It failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty, and investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. A third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe" and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.
Putin did not provide evidence for the accusation.
Meanwhile, the Russian embassy in Berlin said the allegation that Russia was responsible was "absurd".
Dobrindt said examination of the equipment used along with intelligence findings proved Russian involvement in the attack.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who was standing beside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the contract for the Russian House in Berlin will also be terminated - which many observers have said has been used for espionage and to spread Russian propaganda.
He also announced tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and vowed to increase pressure on Moscow's shadow fleet - old tankers used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Wadephul said he had summoned Russia's ambassador to Germany, Sergei Nechayev. He was seen arriving at the foreign ministry shortly after the announcement.
Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for Russia's foreign ministry, said Moscow would respond in a "mirror-image" fashion to Germany's measures while the Russian embassy described the measures as an "unprecedented escalation in Russian-German relations".
"Berlin is sponsoring terrorism", Zakharova told the German Press Agency in reference to its military and economic support provided to Ukraine.
There have been previous suggestions that the Goethe-Institut in Moscow would have to cease operations if the Germans went through with closing Russian House.
Security experts had speculated that Russia may have been responsible, however Russia has always rejected claims of involvement.
Leipzig/Halle Airport in the east of the country is used by Germany's military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo.
The head of Nato, Mark Rutte, said the organisation "stands in full solidarity with Germany".
"The evidence is clear. And I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response," he wrote on X.
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression. We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security."
She added that the EU was preparing additional sanctions against Russia.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russia was "escalating tension across the whole region". Polish prosecutors are investigating whether foreign intelligence services were involved in a fire at a factory making drone components on Monday.
Meanwhile, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail."
Germany is one of several Nato member states to have reported drone sightings at airports, military and industrial sites over the last year.
Berlin has until now been tight-lipped about who may have been behind the Leipzig attack, except to say "foreign powers" may have been involved.
US media had already reported that American officials had linked the incident to Russia.
Berlin has warned that the country is the "daily target" of hybrid warfare, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned last week that those who carried out hostile acts against Germany would "pay a price".
The government is looking to boost the powers of its intelligence services, which have long been criticised as relatively toothless, to counter such threats.
Germany is a key backer of Ukraine with Merz forthright in his support for Kyiv.
However an MP in Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) party said the measures so far taken against Russia "fall far short of what is required" and Moscow "just laughs" when its ambassador is summoned.
"From a self-proclaimed leading nation, I expect courage and resolve, not self-deterrence and appeasement," said Roderich Kiesewetter.
It is not hard to imagine why Ukrainian cargo planes at a key German logistics hub might be in Moscow's sights.
But this announcement comes at a delicate moment for Merz's government.
A key state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could propel the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) into power at a state-level for the first time.
The AfD, which is Germany's biggest opposition party, wants to stop sending support to Ukraine and reopen ties with Russia.
In a separate development, German police said they were investigating the discovery of improvised explosive and incendiary devices at a power substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday.
A power line was damaged, which caused a temporary outage. It is not known who planted the devices.

Nationwide restrictions on mobile phone use in Poland’s primary schools and preschools took effect Tuesday as students returned for the new academic year.
Under the new rules, primary school pupils are prohibited from using mobile phones and similar electronic devices during lessons, breaks and other school activities, Polish broadcaster TVP World reported.

Brussels says €90 billion loan for Ukraine is enough for now amid growing doubts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:57:01 UTC
00:57:01 KST

The longevity of the EU's €90 billion support loan for Ukraine is in serious doubt as Russia escalates the war and drives up material costs. Brussels says the financial plan remains sufficient "for the moment".
The European Commission is reluctant to reopen the sensitive debate on financial support for Ukraine, despite growing doubts about whether the €90 billion loan agreed by leaders last year will last until the end of 2027, as originally conceived.
Brussels intends to disburse €45 billion this year and €45 billion next year. So far, €3.2 billion in budgetary aid and €8.35 billion in military aid have been paid out.
"In terms of longevity, that is what is foreseen: that this €90 billion loan should be disbursed (over) the two years," Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, said on Tuesday in response to a Euronews question.
"It's important to remember that these disbursements are also linked to the reforms that are being introduced in Ukraine, and this is, of course, a critical aspect," she added.
"We are focused now on what is already a very ambitious disbursement plan, and for the moment that's where our focus lies."
Russia's escalation, however, is rapidly adding to the bill.
Moscow has launched a new tactic of non-stop drone attacks aimed at disrupting daily economic activity and sowing terror among civilians. At the same time, it is ramping up strikes of ballistic missiles on critical infrastructure ahead of the winter season.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has asked allies to plug a €23 billion gap in the Ministry of Defence to pay for weapons and remain "competitive" in deep strikes.
"We need more money, much more," Zelenskyy said last week.
As a solution, Zelenskyy suggested the EU front-load a share of the €45 billion earmarked for next year, which would mean having less money available in 2027.
The Commission has not yet received a formal request from Kyiv in that regard.
Member states discussed the matter on Tuesday during an informal ministerial meeting in Ireland, where support for Ukraine topped the agenda.
At the end of the talks, Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said there was "consensus across the room" to "bring forward funding" under the ongoing loan. But she admitted the question required further deliberations in Brussels.
Back to the assets?
In the meantime, Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland have revived the idea of tapping into the immbolised assets of the Russian Central Bank to provide additional support for Ukraine, warning the €90 billion loan "will not be enough".
The EU holds €210 billion of these assets, sanctioned since February 2022.
"What we see is that Ukraine needs more support and, to be honest, we're not providing enough support bilaterally and through the EU, and then what is left is the frozen assets," Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard told Euronews.
"This is what is fair to Ukraine, it's what is fair to taxpayers," she added.
The Commission is treading carefully on the divisive issue.
Last year, the executive threw its weight fully behind an inventive proposal to turn the Russian assets into a financial lifeline for Ukraine. But the plan soon met fierce opposition from Belgium, which holds the majority of the €210 billion.
It eventually fell apart at a make-or-break summit in December, when leaders opted instead for joint debt to finance a €90 billion loan.
Officials in the Commission have never abandoned the idea of tapping the Russian assets but are mindful of tabling a new proposal without a guarantee of success. Capitals are already ensnared in fraught negotiations over the next EU budget.
Instead, Brussels is turning up the pressure on Western allies, who are expected to complement the loan by covering one-third of Ukraine's needs.
"There is one-third which cannot be covered by the EU and where we have been urging our partners to come in and step in," Pinho, the spokesperson, said.
Last month, Norway, a major non-EU donor, pledged 85 billion krone (€7.86 billion) for Ukraine in 2027, matching the amount allocated this year.

Alexander Dobrindt arrives for the first day of a two-day retreat of the federal government coalition cabinet at Schloss Neuhardenberg on Aug. 25, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — Berlin squarely placed the blame for an incursion of explosive-laden drones last month on the Kremlin and announced a raft of retaliatory diplomatic measures.
The incident and Germany’s response mark a new chapter in Europe’s fraught relationship with Russia, with EU leaders lining up to support Berlin.
“Russia’s leadership is treating our country with open hostility,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in Berlin on Tuesday. “With the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership has, in fact, deliberately chosen to further and significantly damage our already severely strained bilateral relationship.”
Standing alongside Wadephul, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the German government determined Russia is responsible even as investigations remain ongoing.
“The attack involved tools such as the drone configuration, various components, explosives and cyber technology that we recognize from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine,” Dobrindt said.
Wadephul announced a series of domestic countermeasures, including the closure of Russia’s Bonn consulate on September 18, stricter entry controls for Russian nationals and the termination of the agreement governing the Russian House in central Berlin — a cultural institution suspected of serving as a hub for espionage operations and whose Russian operator is under EU sanctions.
Germany will also propose new EU sanctions targeting Russian individuals connected to hybrid attacks, while pushing to increase measures targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, Wadephul said. A senior German government official also said Berlin would advocate that the EU reduce the number of 90-day tourist visas issued to Russian citizens and restrict the freedom of movement of Russian diplomats.
The announcement comes as EU foreign ministers are set to meet in Ireland on Tuesday night and Wednesday. “The matter, including additional sanctions, will be prepared by Foreign Ministers at their upcoming meeting,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media after the German announcement.
Advertisement
Given the significance of the announcement, it was not immediately clear why German Chancellor Friedrich Merz didn’t make it himself. But the ratcheting up of tensions with Moscow comes at a sensitive political moment ahead of a state election on Sunday in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) is far ahead in polls.
Dobrindt said the attack was carried out by low-level agents, adding that the technology found at the scene indicated “a high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort in the planning and execution of the attack.”
He also suggested German officials expect more such attacks to follow.
“We assume that Germany is the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia. It can also be assumed that there is a willingness to cause even greater damage through hybrid attacks,” he said. “Thankfully, in Leipzig, this did not happen as had apparently been planned.”
European leaders on Tuesday expressed support for Germany’s retaliatory measures.
Advertisement
“If the gravity of the events is confirmed”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters earlier on Tuesday morning, “there will inevitably be consequences, particularly regarding the sanctions that might be imposed on Russia.”
“NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig,” the alliance’s secretary-general Mark Rutte said on X. “I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response,” he added.
This article has been updated. Hans von der Burchard contributed to this report.

Netanyahu's son sparks British backlash after backing Argentina's Falklands claim: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:53:43 UTC
00:53:43 KST

Mohammad Sio
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Yair Netanyahu, son of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has sparked a backlash from British far-right figures after backing Argentina's claim to sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, Israeli daily Haaretz reported Monday.
Yair Netanyahu wrote on the US social media company X in Spanish that the Falkland Islands belong to Argentina, calling them the “Islas Malvinas,” the name preferred by Argentina. He described the islands as “a bunch of rocks” located thousands of miles from Britain.
His comments came as he criticized the UK Labour government over what he described as “hypocrisy and hostility towards Israel,” which he also called “antisemitic.”
Rupert Lowe, leader of Britain's far-right Restore Britain party, responded by calling on Israel to clarify whether Yair Netanyahu's position reflected the position of the Israeli government.
“Following the intervention of Netanyahu's son, where he states that the Falkland Islands belong to Argentina, it is entirely legitimate to ask what the official Israeli Government position is on the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands,” Lowe said on X.
Lowe also shared Yair’s post and said, “You have enough problems to be focusing on in Israel, Netanyahu. The Falkland Islands are British, and will remain that way. A Restore Britain Government will go to war if necessary to ensure it.”
Former Conservative MP and minister Conor Burns also criticized Yair in an expletive-laden post on X, writing: “Dear Nepoyahu, Piss off. Yours sincerely, Israel’s many friends in the UK (Stronger sentiment available from British subjects in the Falkland Islands).”
Argentine President Javier Milei reposted several of Yair’s posts on X. Netanyahu subsequently said his comments appeared to have “contributed to Israel-Argentina relations ... contrary to the left's propaganda.”
Nile Gardiner, a former aide to British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who led Britain during the 1982 Falklands War, said Yair did not represent the official position of the Israeli government.
“Thankfully this is not the official position of the Israeli government. The courageous Falkland Islanders have exactly the same right to sovereignty, self-determination and freedom as the immensely brave people of Israel. The Falklands will always be British,” Gardiner wrote on X, reposting Yair’s statement.
Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, which it calls the Malvinas Islands, citing succession from the Spanish Crown and historical decrees, while Britain has maintained control and administration of the archipelago since 1833.
In the early 1980s, Argentina and Britain fought what became known as the Falklands War over the disputed archipelago.
The Falkland Islands consist of two main islands, East Falkland and West Falkland, along with more than 700 smaller islands. The archipelago covers about 12,200 square kilometers and lies roughly 480 kilometers off Argentina's southern coast, with an estimated coastline of about 1,300 kilometers.

The German government on Sept. 1 officially accused a Russian intelligence service of attempting to carry out a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August, marking the first time Berlin has directly blamed Moscow for the incident.
"We have clear indications from our intelligence services and partner agencies, as well as from investigations in Germany and in our European partner countries, of Russian involvement," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said during a press conference.
The attempted attack had previously been linked to Russia through media investigations and U.S. intelligence assessments. A drone was reportedly equipped with explosives and intended to strike a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane that is also used to transport military equipment.
The drone's configuration, parts, explosives, and fuel found at the site match those used by Russia in other hybrid operations and in its war against Ukraine, Dobrindt added.
"The German government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," he said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Germany would close Russia's consulate in Bonn and the Russian House of Culture in Berlin in response to the attack.
Berlin will also push for tougher sanctions on Russia, stricter entry controls for Russian citizens, and increased pressure on Russia's so-called shadow fleet.
"We will not allow Russia's attacks to divide us or intimidate us," Wadephul said.
The German government's accusation comes amid growing concerns among Western officials over Moscow-backed hybrid operations across Europe, including arson attacks, infrastructure sabotage, and suspicious drone activity near critical facilities.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte posted on X that the alliance "stands in full solidarity with Germany," following the press conference.
"Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail," he wrote.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she had spoken with Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz that morning, and assured him of EU solidarity.
"The German government has taken strong measures. And the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response."
A succession of other European national leaders followed suit, including the leaders of Sweden, Estonia, Hungary, and Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who praised Germany "for following Poland's example."

Kallas: Tough summer for Putin, EU to further increase support for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:52:08 EEST
00:52:08 KST

EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia had suffered significant economic and personnel losses over the summer, while EU member states were preparing tougher sanctions against Moscow and planned to further increase support for Ukraine.
Kallas made the remarks in Wicklow, Ireland, on Tuesday following an informal meeting of EU defence ministers, which was also attended by Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara.
She said the EU would increase support for Ukraine while continuing to invest in its own defence, describing this as the most effective way to stop Russian President Vladimir Putin. Kallas added that the EU was also preparing its most far-reaching sanctions against Russia.
According to her, Ukraine was increasing military pressure on Russia, with Ukrainian drones disrupting Russian logistics and striking oil refineries deep inside the country, contributing to what she described as Russia's worst fuel crisis in a decade. She also said Russia was losing more than 30,000 troops a month and concluded that the summer had been difficult for Putin.
Kallas said Khmara had stressed during the meeting that air defence remained Ukraine's top priority. She noted, however, that interceptor missiles were in short supply across Europe. She thanked EU member states for reviewing their stockpiles again and said Patriot missiles nearing the end of their service life should, in particular, be transferred or sold to Ukraine.
She added that member states were also considering reallocating existing orders and approaching partners for additional supplies. Kallas stressed that every interceptor provided to Ukraine reduced the risk of a Russian missile hitting a Ukrainian school, home or hospital, while every form of assistance to Ukraine also strengthened European security.
Turning to financial support, Kallas said bilateral assistance to Ukraine needed to continue. She noted that, in addition to equipment, Ukraine required modernised training facilities. Kallas recalled that earlier in the year she had proposed funding the modernisation of training grounds in Ukraine and thanked member states, including Ireland, for providing additional funding for this purpose.
She also said ministers had discussed the future of the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM), including the creation of a coordination group in Kyiv aimed at better incorporating battlefield experience and strengthening military education.
Kallas further noted that cooperation between Ukraine and the EU in the defence industry was expanding. She said there were now more than 120 industrial partnerships between Ukrainian and European companies and described Ukraine as a global leader in battlefield innovation. According to her, deeper integration between Ukrainian and European defence companies was in the mutual interest of both sides.
