Share & more
Ashok Shrestha was doing what he routinely did on his journeys – eating near a riverside – when a raging wall of ice-cold water, slush, and rocks came crashing down a narrow Himalayan mountain valley and swept him away like a leaf caught in a storm.
He had driven his 12-wheel truck up from Barabise, in Nepal’s mountainous Sindhupalchok district, to collect a load from the customs point at the border with China, a trip he had been making for years.
"It swept me away and carried me downhill," he told The New Humanitarian from his hospital bed, his body marked with injuries. Shrestha swam until he reached the riverbank. A friend and another man nearby never made it out of the torrent alive.
According to preliminary geological assessments, the disaster was triggered when a vast section of glacier and surrounding bedrock, about 600 metres wide, collapsed at an elevation of about 5,200 metres, high above the Lhende Khola river on the Tibetan side of the border.
Satellite imagery suggests the mass plunged 1,200 metres to the valley floor, sending a huge cascade of ice, rock, and debris into the Lhende Khola and generating a catastrophic flood that travelled nearly 100 kilometres downstream through the Bhotekoshi river system, destroying buildings, roads, homes, and other infrastructure in its path.
The death toll from the disaster has risen above 1,000 across Nepal and Tibet, with almost 4,500 people listed as missing. Nepalese authorities have reported 987 deaths and 3,916 missing, while Chinese authorities have reported a further 16 deaths and 546 missing. The figures remain provisional as rescue and recovery operations continue in some of the worst-hit areas, which are remote and difficult to access.
Among those missing are dozens of Hindu pilgrims who had been travelling to Kailash Mansarovar, a sacred site in Tibet, many of whom were last reported at the Gyirong Port border checkpoint between China and Nepal.
Nine hydropower projects, nine bank branches, 19 road bridges and 40 kilometres of highway were destroyed or carried away, along with the Gyirong Port complex — Nepal’s principal overland gateway for trade with China. More than 300 vehicles waiting at the checkpoint were lost.
The disaster is already among the deadliest in Nepal’s modern history, with its confirmed death toll approaching that of the devastating 1993 floods, which killed 1,336 people.
The victims were largely people who lived and worked in the corridor by necessity, not choice: border and customs staff, hydropower and bank workers, and truck drivers moving goods through the Gyirong crossing, which suffered catastrophic destruction.
In several areas, bulldozers were being used to recover human and animal remains as a strong stench hung over the scene.
This wasn’t simply some freak occurrence. The same area has suffered repeated flooding and glacial disasters over the past decade, including two significant floods in July 2025, just 13 months before the latest catastrophe.
In July 2016, a moraine-dammed lake called Gongbatongsha, in Tibet’s Poiqu basin, burst after a slope failure and sent a flood into the Bhotekoshi basin, damaging the Arniko Highway and the Upper Bhotekoshi hydropower plant. Researchers found that the flood intensified dramatically as it picked up debris downstream – a process strikingly similar to the way the latest disaster gathered force.
Then, on 8 July 2025, the sudden drainage of a supraglacial lake in Tibet sent a flood down the Lhende Khola, sweeping away the Friendship Bridge at Rasuwagadhi and killing at least nine people. Just three weeks later, on 30 July, the Bhotekoshi flooded again, damaging roads and infrastructure in the same corridor.
Each event may have had its own trigger, but together they point to a region exposed to recurring and well-documented hazards. The question is not simply whether the latest disaster could have been predicted, but whether enough had been learned from the previous ones to warn people in time.
A failed cross-border warning system
The disaster exposed a weakness on both sides of Nepal’s warning system: It had no real-time information about the hazard developing in Tibet, while the monitoring equipment it had installed inside Nepal was destroyed before it could send an alert.
Automatic flood-monitoring stations have been installed along the upper Bhotekoshi river to detect rising water levels and send alerts before floods reach populated areas downstream. But on 26 August, the surge came so quickly that the stations were destroyed, apparently before they could transmit any warning.
“None of the stations was able to send us an alert,” Binod Parajuli, a senior divisional hydrologist at Nepal’s Flood Forecasting Division, told the Kathmandu Post.
His division learned of the flood only at 8:56am, when Rasuwa’s district administration and the national disaster authority relayed reports from people on the ground – about half an hour after the water hit Timure, a settlement near the Nepal-China border. The division issued its own warning downstream within four minutes. By then, however, the flood had already swallowed large parts of Rasuwa.
“We failed,” Parajuli said.
He believes the warning still saved lives further downstream, but said the failure exposed a deeper flaw: Nepal’s sensors could not outrun a flood originating across an international border. A warning system that monitors only what happens inside Nepal, he argued, can never be enough for a hazard that begins somewhere else.
Nepal and China laid the groundwork for closer disaster cooperation in 2019, when their governments signed a memorandum of understanding covering disaster risk reduction, emergency response, information sharing, and the exchange of hydrological data. But in practice, those warning systems have failed to cross the border.
“It is up to the government to keep responding with relief and rescue after each disaster, or to start working to prevent the loss of life in the first place.”
Similar failures have happened before, with floods originating on the Chinese side reaching Nepal without advance warning. They were not taken seriously enough, Anil Pokhrel, former chief executive of Nepal’s disaster authority, told the Kathmandu Post.
“This problem will continue … It is up to the government to keep responding with relief and rescue after each disaster, or to start working to prevent the loss of life in the first place,” he said. Nepal, he added, needs a functioning cross-border system through which warnings about floods, landslides, and other hazards originating in China can reach its disaster authorities in time to act.
There are signs that officials recognise the gap. After the latest disaster, Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology and the China Meteorological Administration held a virtual meeting at which China agreed to notify Nepal as soon as water levels begin rising on its side of the border – restating a commitment made in 2019.
But experts say a reliable warning system needs to go beyond water levels. It must also monitor unstable ice and rock, share information across borders, and give communities enough time to evacuate.
Vulnerable Himalayas
Jeffrey Kargel, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute, a US space research organisation, has spent recent days comparing the Nepal disaster with an earlier Himalayan catastrophe in Chamoli, India, where a chunk of glacier broke away from a steep mountainside, mixed with rock, and became a debris flow that destroyed two hydropower projects and killed more than 200 people.
"The process going on throughout the whole thing is really almost identical, but this one was a bigger event – two to three times larger by volume, with a correspondingly higher death toll,” he told The New Humanitarian.
What worries Kargel is not one disaster, but the pattern behind them. Rock-ice avalanches, in which rock and glacier ice collapse together and turn into fast-moving debris, were until recently considered rare.
Scientists were not systematically looking for this kind of hazard across the Himalayas, where steep, unstable terrain and rapidly changing glaciers create heightened risk. Chamoli changed that. The latest disaster, Kargel said, is yet another warning that the threat needs to be taken seriously.
“We need a new look at risk, and bring the hydropower people into the same room and ask, do they really want to just build hydropower like crazy, without even thinking about the hazards?”
“It changes the risk landscape dramatically,” Kargel said, outlining how that risk could be better understood and mitigated. “Most hazard and risk mappers would look at risk due to landslides individually – slope, geology, proximity to earthquake fault zones, and so on – and calculate hazard maps and risk maps that way. Let’s look at where the glacial lakes are, what are the chances of an outburst? Then let’s do a risk map for monsoon rainfall floods, or snowmelt floods – one process at a time.”
The other challenge is working out which parts of the Himalayas – one of the world’s youngest mountain ranges, still rising today – are most vulnerable. Its steep slopes are full of fractured rock and hanging ice, but scientists still lack a reliable way to identify where a rock-ice avalanche might occur.
“So far, nobody... has really figured out how to handle the problem of rock-ice avalanches,” Kargel said.
That uncertainty raises difficult questions for a region rapidly expanding hydropower as it shifts towards cleaner energy. Hundreds of hydropower projects are reportedly underway or planned across India, China, Pakistan, Nepal and Bhutan, many in valleys exposed to landslides, floods, and other hazards.
Environmentalists and climate activists have long warned that rapid construction in this ecologically sensitive region can amplify the damage caused by floods, landslides, and other natural hazards.
“Hydropower is a way to decarbonise the economy, [but] risk mappers need to start asking if there are some valleys with such a bad history that we should just stop developing them, and withdraw?” Kargel said.
“We need a new look at risk, and bring the hydropower people – the financial backers, political backers, engineers, geologists, electrical engineers and suppliers, the economic planners – into the same room and ask, do they really want to just build hydropower like crazy, without even thinking about the hazards?”
Those decisions are being made in a corridor where people have to live and work, often because there are few alternatives.
Mina Tamang has been frantically searching for her husband Jairam Tamang. The 33-year-old had been driving trucks between the customs point and the Chinese border for over six years.
He called Mina at around 7am on Wednesday while she was having her morning tea. He told her his truck would leave the next day, that his friends were coming, and asked her to collect some chocolates that he was sending her. They spoke for half an hour until he left for the customs office. She has not heard from him since.
“I have registered his name at the hospital and with the police,” she said. “But more than 1,000 people have reportedly registered the names of their missing relatives here. I don’t know how we are going to find him.”
Mir Wafa Rasheeq provided additional reporting from New Delhi. Edited by Andrew Gully.

Elbit Systems, based in Haifa, Israel, employs more than 21,000 people across dozens of countries on five continents. The company reported $2.29 billion in revenue for the three months ended June 30, 2026, and an order backlog of $32 billion as of that date.

UN cuts occupied West Bank food aid by half as funds run short and food insecurity soars amid Israeli violence
The World Food Programme said on Tuesday that funding shortages are forcing it to cut in half its food assistance in the occupied West Bank at a time when it says escalating settler violence and Israeli military operations are driving needs higher.
The UN agency has been providing food, vouchers and cash to 400,000 in the occupied West Bank, mostly in rural areas and the south, such as villages like Hebron, but this will be scaled back to 200,000 people from this month, it said in a statement.
"Severe movement restrictions, demolitions, and widespread displacement in the West Bank have eroded Palestinian livelihoods and contributed to increased food insecurity," Shaun Hughes, WFP Country Director for Palestine, told a Geneva press briefing. "Right now, we should be scaling up our assistance in the West Bank, not cutting these vital lifelines."
Foreign aid contributions by major Western donors, including the United States, have fallen sharply across the board since last year as they prioritise domestic spending and defence.
Violence and land and water seizures by militant Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank have risen during the past three years.
UN bodies and most countries deem Israeli settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations.
Hughes said that humanitarians did not use to consider the West Bank a food crisis, but more a human rights crisis, but that was now changing due to mounting pressures.
“They now find themselves in a chokehold, unable to move freely to access land or jobs, and so unable to afford food for their families. They face incredible injustice and hardship," he said.
Other international aid groups like the UN Palestinian refugee agency also provide assistance to Palestinians in the occupied West Bank but it was not immediately clear if they would step in. That agency also faces major financial constraints.
WFP also said funding shortfalls are affecting its operations in Gaza where it supports 1.5 million people. "Further cuts will be unavoidable unless additional funding is secured," it said.

France, Germany back call for faster, more efficient EU decisions in foreign and security policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:20:09 UTC
22:20:09 KST

Paris and Berlin have thrown their weight behind a call to make EU decision-making on foreign policy and security more efficient, according to a letter seen by POLITICO.
In the letter, addressed to High Representative Kaja Kallas and signed by 11 EU states including France and Germany, the signatories spell out five ways to boost the speed and efficiency of decision-making in common foreign and security policy (CFSP), including potentially increasing the use of qualified majority voting.
Under EU rules, decisions that fall under a CFSP heading must be approved unanimously by all 27 EU countries — a rule that caused major bottlenecks when former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán repeatedly used his veto to block decisions backed by all 26 other capitals.
Advertisement
Germany, in particular, has led calls to move from unanimity voting on CFSP to so-called qualified majority voting (QMV), but France, among other states, has traditionally opposed such a change. The letter opens the door to greater use of QMV without explicitly endorsing any wholesale change in voting methods.
"We continue to strive for consensus wherever possible," reads the letter signed by the foreign ministers of Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain in addition to France and Germany. " But we must also ensure that this culture of consensus fosters common action rather than preventing it — otherwise we will have legitimacy but no strength."
The steps outlined in the letter are:
Emphasizing the principle of "sincere cooperation" between EU states — meaning that countries must honor commitments they have made to one another, even if they are not strictly legally binding.
Using "constructive abstentions" rather than outright vetoes, "so as not to prevent the Union from acting."
Banning linkage of "unrelated matters" to an issue being debated — or cracking down on the practice of holding collective decisions hostage by threatening a veto unless the others agree to a separate national demand.
Encouraging the EU's chief diplomat, currently Kaja Kallas, to explore treaty-based options to improve decision-making. The treaty-based option most commonly invoked is the so-called Passerelle clause, which allows the EU to change decision-making rules without changing any treaties — for example, to allow QMV voting on specific foreign and security policy matters.
Emphasizing the need to spell out the reasons why a country invokes its veto rights for "vital and stated reasons of national policy," namely when a decision is taken by qualified majority.
The letter is due to be discussed this week as foreign ministers gather in Wicklow, Ireland for informal talks in the Gymnich format.
Those talks will also explore options for reforming the European External Action Service, the EU diplomatic branch headed by High Representative Kallas.
According to a Franco-German letter seen by POLITICO, options for reforming the EEAS include making Kallas an executive vice president of the European Commission with "de facto" oversight of external-facing policy units as regards trade, development aid and defense; and embedding much of the EEAS's staff inside the Commission in a new department for external relations.
Staff focused on security and defense policy would remain in the EEAS, and the ratio of one-third of EEAS staff being seconded diplomats from EU states would be maintained in this new unit.
The discussion paper also emphasizes the role of EU states in shaping foreign policy, envisaging a formal role for the High Representative to report to EU leaders on foreign policy matters and receive instructions directly from them during European Council gatherings.

How eating habits affect energy levels throughout the day
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:18:55 EEST
22:18:55 KST

How eating habits affect energy levels throughout the day
Kyiv • UNN
How eating habits affect energy levels throughout the day.
Why your energy can suddenly drop after eating
The most noticeable effects on well-being come not from individual foods, but from the regularity and composition of your diet. If a meal consists mainly of fast carbohydrates—sweet pastries, desserts, sugary drinks, or large amounts of white bread—glucose levels may rise quickly and then fall. For some people, this is accompanied by fatigue, hunger, and difficulty concentrating. At the same time, completely eliminating carbohydrates is not a universal solution. Fiber, protein, and fats are important for more stable satiety. That is why porridge with an egg, natural yogurt with nuts, or whole-grain bread with vegetables usually help maintain satiety better than a candy bar or a bun eaten on the go.
What habits help prevent sharp fluctuations
There is no need to create a perfect menu for every day. It is much more helpful to gradually change recurring habits:
-  not skipping main meals if this leads to intense hunger and overeating afterward; 
-  adding vegetables, legumes, grains, or other sources of fiber to meals; 
-  combining carbohydrates with protein-rich foods; 
-  relying less on sweets as a quick way to “recharge”; 
-  drinking enough water throughout the day; 
-  paying attention to portion sizes and your own feeling of satiety. 
Is diet always the cause of fatigue
No. Daytime sleepiness may be related to sleep deprivation, stress, anemia, thyroid disorders, infections, the use of certain medications, and other conditions. That is why a single symptom cannot determine the cause. If weakness persists for several weeks, severe thirst, frequent urination, unexplained changes in weight, or declining work performance appear, it is worth consulting a family doctor. They will assess your symptoms and risk factors and, if necessary, order examinations.
What is important to remember
Energy levels throughout the day depend on many factors: sleep, physical activity, stress, and nutrition. A balanced diet does not guarantee the same well-being every day, but it helps avoid extremes—prolonged fasting, overeating, and an excess of sugary foods. If fatigue becomes persistent, it is better not to mask it with coffee or energy drinks, but to determine the cause together with a doctor.

As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
September 1, 2026
High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall.
The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released.
Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is known as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Blatten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods.
How much is climate change to blame?
The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists.
Levan Tielidze, research fellow in glacial geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, said the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact."
"As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream."
Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucasus Mountains of North Ossetia in Russia. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24 kilometers (15 miles) and killed around 125 people.
"The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," said Tielidze.
Meanwhile, the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability.
Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century.
For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches."
"These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added.
Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s.
The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event. However, the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain.
The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometers, noted Tielidze.
"These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he said, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change.
Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts?
The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blatten resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse.
But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, said Tielidze.
"In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said. "We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings."
For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added.
Chapagain said the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems.
However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal."
"What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group cocoordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement.
A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures.
"We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt."

Quickparts scales up production for defense programs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:17:13 UTC
22:17:13 KST

- Quickparts announced a nearly $6 million investment adding 12 Stratasys NEO 3D printing systems across facilities in the U.S., France, Italy and the U.K.
- The company said the expansion increases large-format 3D printing throughput by 40 percent to support national security space and defense programs.
Manufacturing company Quickparts announced a nearly $6 million investment in its Seattle Aerospace & Defense Center of Excellence, adding 12 Stratasys NEO 3D printing systems across its facilities in the United States, France, Italy and the United Kingdom, the company said Tuesday.
The deployment is the company’s second major capacity investment in 18 months, following a November 2025 expansion in Seattle and the February 2026 launch of two proprietary materials, DuraKor and ThermaKor. Quickparts said the new equipment increases the company’s large-format 3D printing throughput by 40 percent and replaces earlier-generation machines across its U.S. and European sites.
Quickparts said the investment is aimed at national security space programs and defense manufacturing, sectors where a supplier’s ability to deliver parts on a fixed schedule matters as much as cost.
“Reshoring and industrial resilience are usually discussed as policy. We’re treating them as a balance-sheet decision,” said Avi Reichental, CEO of Quickparts. “Anyone can buy the same machine we just bought. What they can’t buy quickly is a qualified capability delivering to the same standard across four countries, at a scale that took us years to build.”
“Quickparts’ investment reflects the growing role large-format additive manufacturing now plays in critical applications across aerospace, defense, and space,” said Dr. Yoav Zeif, CEO of Stratasys. “We’re proud to partner with them as they scale their ability to support the world’s most demanding programs with proven industry-leading additive manufacturing technologies, materials, software, and services.”
Quickparts produces parts through both its own facilities and a certified network of manufacturing partners across North America, Europe and Asia. The company said standardizing equipment across its Seattle, French, Italian and British sites allows a part qualified in one location to be manufactured to the same standard in another, which it said gives customers flexibility if tariffs, export control changes or regional disruptions affect a specific facility.
Quickparts said its manufacturing work also supports specialty and performance programs in Europe, including motorsport aerodynamics and high-end vehicle production, alongside its space and defense work.

UN cuts West Bank food aid by half as funds run short

Unknown Publisher

22:15:43 KST

UN cuts West Bank food aid by half as funds run short
GENEVA, Sept 1 - The World Food Programme said on Tuesday that funding shortages are forcing it to cut in half its food assistance in the occupied West Bank at a time when it says escalating settler violence and Israeli military operations are driving needs higher.
The U.N. agency has been providing food, vouchers and cash to 400,000 in the West Bank, mostly in rural areas and the south, such as villages like Hebron, but this will be scaled back to 200,000 people from this month, it said in a statement.
"Severe movement restrictions, demolitions, and widespread displacement in the West Bank have eroded Palestinian livelihoods and contributed to increased food insecurity," Shaun Hughes, WFP Country Director for Palestine, told a Geneva press briefing.
"Right now, we should be scaling up our assistance in the West Bank, not cutting these vital lifelines."
The Israeli military agency that coordinates aid in the West Bank, COGAT, referred a Reuters request for comment to the Israeli military, which did not immediately respond.
Foreign aid contributions by major Western donors, including the United States, have fallen sharply across the board since last year as they prioritise domestic spending and defence.
Violence and land and water seizures by militant Jewish settlers in the West Bank have risen during the nearly three years since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks on Israel.
U.N. bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the area as disputed rather than occupied.
Hughes said that humanitarians did not use to consider the West Bank a food crisis, but more a human rights crisis, but that was now changing due to mounting pressures.
“They now find themselves in a chokehold, unable to move freely to access land or jobs, and so unable to afford food for their families. They face incredible injustice and hardship," he said.
Other international aid groups like the U.N. Palestinian refugee agency also provide assistance to Palestinians in the West Bank but it was not immediately clear if they would step in. That agency also faces major financial constraints.
WFP also said funding shortfalls are affecting its operations in Gaza where it supports 1.5 million people. "Further cuts will be unavoidable unless additional funding is secured," it said. REUTERS

PM Narendra Modi at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit.

With Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif in attendance, Modi said countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy, and provide shelter and support to terrorists, must be sent a strong message that terrorism can never be a strategic asset for anyone.The remarks by PM on this occasion are significant also because of the timing. Pakistan assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO from Kyrgyzstan on Tuesday and will host the heads of state summit next year, for which it will invite Modi along with all other leaders.Modi made the remarks while expanding on India’s SCO vision - Security, Connectivity and Opportunity - that he articulated in Tianjin last year. With Chinese President Xi Jinping also present, the PM reiterated India's position that all connectivity initiatives must respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of all States as this is also the "fundamental spirit" of the SCO Charter.Modi said that terrorism continued to pose a serious challenge to humanity and it’s important to not remain confined to an action-reaction approach in the fight against the menace.
“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorist financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens. Therefore, India has consistently called for all tensions and conflicts to be resolved not on the battlefield, but through dialogue and diplomacy,” he said.While underlining the importance India attaches to SCO, Modi said that at a time the world is passing through uncertainty and instability, the Organisation must transform the shared geography into shared opportunities and bring about positive change in the lives of the people. Describing SCO as a confluence of great civilisations, cultures, and ideas, he said that over the next 25 years, people-to-people ties should remain at the heart of cooperation among the member-states.“The true measure of our success should be how many new opportunities our efforts create for young people, how many new markets open up for our entrepreneurs, how much our farmers benefit from technology, and how much better the lives of our citizens become,” said the PM.
According to an Indian readout of Modi’s participation in the summit, Modi stated that strong and trusted connectivity initiatives were important for the group’s shared progress and prosperity.“Underlining that India supports connectivity efforts that link markets, enhance trade and open new opportunities for development, he reiterated that such efforts should respect sovereignty and territorial integrity of nations. He further elaborated that technology, entrepreneurship, innovation, start-ups and people-to-people initiatives open immense opportunities for people in the SCO countries,” said the Indian readout.

In a statement, the army said Maj. Gen. Ismail al-Tayeb, commander of the 4th Infantry Division, received the joint forces, which arrived to take part in military operations against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Blue Nile state in southeastern Sudan.

School year begins in 412 Kyiv schools, nearly 94% of first-graders attend – KCSA
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:14:06 EEST
22:14:06 KST

The school year began on Tuesday, Sept 1, at 412 educational institutions in Kyiv. Of the 16,629 children enrolled in first grade, nearly 94% attended, matching last year's figure, the Kyiv City State Administration (KCSA) said.
"Today Kyiv schoolchildren began a new school year. At the same time, another vocational education institution was damaged in a Russian attack overnight. This once again shows the conditions our education system is working under today. Despite this, it was important for us to ensure in-person learning wherever security conditions and a given institution's capacity allow it. This year, the format of instruction may change depending on the military threat. So schools, as in previous years, are ready to operate in various formats — in-person, blended, or fully remote. What matters most is that children can continue their education, while their safety and the safety of staff remain the priority," Deputy Mayor Valentyn Mondryivsky said.
Of the 412 schools that began operating, 401, or 97%, are working in-person or in a blended format, while 11 schools are fully remote, he said. Some institutions have organized classes in two shifts.
Most elementary school students are attending in person today, according to Mondryivsky. Some schools held celebratory events in gyms and assembly halls so children and staff could reach shelters more quickly in the event of an air raid alert. There were no air raid alerts in the capital at the start of classes, allowing schools to hold planned ceremonies with parents present and begin the school year.
All children who attended school today received free meals.
Attendance at preschools also rose. While 32-35% of enrolled children attended kindergartens over the past week, 45% — nearly half of all enrolled children — attended today.
The new school year also began at the capital's vocational education institutions, with most first-year students attending in person. As of Sept 1, 11,177 people are enrolled in vocational education institutions.
This week, instruction is organized in a blended format, with nearly 60% of students attending in person and the rest in a blended format — for example, theoretical classes may be held remotely while practical classes take place at the institution itself.
"During this exhausting war, it's important for children to feel that life goes on — they're returning to their classrooms, seeing their teachers and friends, starting a new stage. Thank you to the teachers, parents and everyone who made this day possible. May our children have as many ordinary school days as possible — with learning, socializing, friends and the chance to grow," Mondryivsky said.

Alleged Charlie Kirk killer faces ruling on standing trial and death penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:13:38 UTC
22:13:38 KST

A Utah judge ruled Tuesday that the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk must stand trial for aggravated murder, a felony charge that makes him eligible for the death penalty if convicted.
After several hours of closing arguments in Provo, Utah, judge Tony Graf ruled there is sufficient evidence to try Tyler Robinson, 23, who has been charged with the murder of one of the US right’s most prominent figures.
Robinson pleaded not guilty after Graf’s ruling. A trial date has yet to be set.
A key factor in charging aggravated murder is whether the shooter knowingly created a risk of death to anyone else as he carried out the killing.
Judge Graf said: “These circumstances support a reasonable inference that defendant was aware that other individuals were positioned near Mr Kirk when he fired.”
Robinson’s attorneys had argued the shooting should not be a capital offense, as the shooter hit the “intended target” and did not put anyone else’s life at risk. Graf had the option to send the case to trial on a lesser charge of murder, which carries a minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life in prison, said Steve Burton, director of the Utah Defense Attorney Association.
Kirk was fatally shot while speaking during an event at Utah Valley University nearly a year ago.
The proceedings began Tuesday morning with Graf moving to allow cameras in the courtroom during the hearing, despite objections from the defense, and ruling on how the prosecution’s exhibits will be displayed.
The judge also warned the audience of people attending the hearing not to make comments or visible reactions while court was in session.
Prosecutors have accused the former electrical apprentice of firing the single shot that killed Kirk, 31, as he debated with students at the Utah Valley University campus in Orem on 10 September 2025. On Tuesday, the prosecution argued there is a “mountain of evidence that proves [Robinson] is the shooter” and showed video of Robinson on campus the day of the shooting.
Tuesday’s proceedings follow a week-long preliminary hearing in July that was attended by Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk. She attended Tuesday’s session.
During the preliminary hearing, prosecutors presented what they called “overwhelming” evidence, including test results that allegedly show Robinson’s DNA on the murder weapon. Robinson’s lawyers questioned the prosecution’s DNA testing and said police failed to investigate evidence someone else might have carried out the killing.
Prosecutors also allege Robinson, who was in a relationship with roommate Lance Twiggs, targeted Kirk for his political views against gay marriage and transgender rights. That argument could bolster the prosecution as it pursues the death penalty.
Defense lawyers have said there is no evidence Robinson disagreed with Kirk’s political views. Kirk, the co-founder of Turning Point USA, helped build support for Donald Trump among young voters and aided Republican voter turnout efforts.
At a memorial following Kirk’s shooting, Erika Kirk, who became CEO and board chair of Turning Point USA after her husband’s death, said she forgave the alleged shooter.
She has not commented on the death penalty charge.

Joost Niemöller is stepping down as editor-in-chief of far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON), weeks after he said on air that Adolf Hitler had put certain things “very well”.
The broadcaster said the immediate reason was a “difference of view about the editorial direction and recent programming”, according to director-general Peter Vlemmix. Its statement, reported by NOS, runs to two sentences and does not mention the item that set off weeks of criticism.
In the late-July broadcast, Niemöller said there were “certain things of Hitler’s” he agreed with, aside from the Nazi leader’s antisemitism.
Co-presenter Raisa Blommestijn also backed a statement, put to the pair after a clip of a Hitler speech referring to Jewish people, that a cosmopolitan elite was inherently hostile to ordinary people. Both said they did not share all of Hitler’s ideology.
Media minister Rianne Letschert called the broadcast “terrible, distasteful, hurtful and unnecessary”, and the ombudsman for the public broadcasters logged dozens of complaints. The cabinet is examining whether ON can be forced out of the public broadcasting system, and Letschert has said a decision will come “very soon”.
Ongehoord Nederland joined the public broadcasting system in 2022 and has been reprimanded and sanctioned several times for breaching journalistic rules. Niemöller became editor-in-chief about 18 months ago.

UN report reveals most Afghan war victims left 'without justice'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:13:00 UTC
22:13:00 KST

Most civilian victims of Afghanistan's 2001-2021 war have been left "without justice, reparation or even acknowledgement" of their suffering, the United Nations said Tuesday, with one man in Kabul telling AFP "the world has forgotten us".
The U.S. launched a "military intervention" in Afghanistan following the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, ushering in two decades of conflict in which civilians suffered widespread violence and abuses.
More than 40,000 civilians were killed and 77,000 wounded in attacks by Taliban insurgents, the Daesh terrorist group and also during operations by the armed forces of the Afghan Republic or the international coalition led by the United States, the U.N. mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said.
The U.N. mission has documented civilian casualties since 2009 in one of the most exhaustive studies on victims of the 2001-2021 war.
From memory loss to depression and suicidal thoughts, 95% of the nearly 200 victims interviewed by UNAMA "experienced psychological harm".
Most of the victims interviewed who attempted to obtain justice "were unsuccessful", UNAMA said.
An action plan for "Peace, Reconciliation and Justice" was launched in 2006 but "never fully implemented," the U.N. recalled.
The 2020 U.S.-Taliban peace deal provided for intra-Afghan talks but, "did not include any specific provisions for victims' rights, justice or accountability", it added.
After returning to power, the Taliban authorities passed an amnesty law and have shown no public intent to prosecute wartime violations of humanitarian law, UNAMA said.
"Domestic and international efforts to hold perpetrators accountable have been limited and faced numerous barriers," it concluded.

Switzerland hosts Kongsberg’s Protector weapons event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:12:09 UTC
22:12:09 KST

- Twenty-three of 31 Protector user nations gathered in Switzerland in June for Kongsberg's 16th annual Protector Users Working Group.
- Switzerland has fielded more than 750 Protector systems over 15 years, primarily on armored wheeled vehicles.
Twenty-three of Kongsberg’s 31 nations operating the Protector remote weapon system gathered in Switzerland in June for the company’s 16th annual Protector Users Working Group, the company said.
More than 300 users, industry partners and Kongsberg representatives attended the three-day event, hosted at the Wichlen shooting range in the Swiss mountains and co-hosted by armasuisse, Switzerland’s defense procurement agency. Attendees observed live demonstrations of weapon systems engaging both ground and aerial targets, several of which were equipped with Kongsberg’s Integrated Combat Solution and Protector counter-UAS capabilities.
“The demonstration brings together almost the entire portfolio, from our smallest weapon stations to the MCT-30 turret,” said Scott Hall, business development team manager for Land Systems at Kongsberg. “And our Integrated Combat Solution is the brain behind it all. It networks the systems together, allowing vehicles to share information, share targeting data and collaborate in ways that weren’t possible before.”
The demonstrated configurations included a Hybrid Eagle 4×4 fitted with a CROWS weapon station, an Autonomous Eagle 4×4 with the Protector RS4, a Swiss Armed Forces Pionier Panzer equipped with the RS4, an Eagle 6×6 mounting the RS6, and a Piranha IV fitted with the Protector MCT-30 turret. All demonstrated platforms were integrated on GDELS-Mowag chassis.
Kongsberg’s counter-UAS configurations shown at the event included the MCT-30 turret paired with a 30x173mm cannon and Echoshield radar, the RS6 fitted with a Northrop Grumman XM914 cannon and Echoshield radar, and the RS4 mounted with an M134 minigun and a Kongsberg DR100 radar.
Switzerland has operated Protector systems for more than 15 years, fielding more than 750 units across its armed forces, primarily on armored wheeled vehicles.
“Our cooperation with Kongsberg is long-standing and built on a strong partnership. We have been using these systems for more than two decades, particularly on armoured wheeled vehicles,” said Lt. Gen. Benedikt Roos, chief of the Swiss Armed Forces. “Counter-drone defence and interoperability are key priorities for us. Modern conflicts require networked solutions and close cooperation across systems and national borders.”
Conference sessions also drew on operational experience from Ukraine, with discussions focused on system reliability and consistent performance under demanding conditions.
“The primary purpose of Protector has always been to protect the soldier,” said Jørgen Bull, senior vice president of Land Systems at Kongsberg. “Fifteen years ago, much of the focus was on threats such as improvised explosive devices. Today, drone threats are evolving at an extraordinary pace, and we have to evolve with them.”
Attendees could also test Kongsberg’s Protector CORE training system, built around a digital recreation of the Wichlen training area, allowing operators to practice procedures and coordination using real controls in a virtual environment before entering a live training range.
Protector originated in the late 1990s through a partnership between Kongsberg and the Norwegian Armed Forces. The system is now in service with 31 nations across wheeled, tracked and naval platforms.
Kongsberg said next year’s Protector Users Working Group will be held in Norway.

The EU gave Iceland the silence treatment. It didn't work, again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:12:07 UTC
22:12:07 KST

Brussels stayed mostly silent during Iceland's referendum campaign, which ended with 52.8% voting against resuming EU accession talks, echoing its muted response to Brexit a decade earlier.
10 years after Brexit, European leaders once again stayed silent through a landmark referendum on EU membership, showing how little Brussels has learned from its own mistakes.
On Sunday, EU officials absorbed the news that Icelanders had voted against resuming EU membership negotiations, in a knife-edge referendum that split 52.8% to 47.2%. Their response was muted at best.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made no public statement, leaving an anonymous spokesperson to say only that Brussels had taken "note" of the results.
European Council President António Costa was one of the few to break the silence, saying through his spokesperson that "the EU fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic people in today's referendum. Iceland remains one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners."
This reticence was consistent with how the Commission kept a low profile throughout the campaign, raising the question of whether the EU's institutional instinct for neutrality is politically self-defeating when the vote concerns the EU itself.
"We had a very harsh campaign. A lot of money. You could almost hear the echoes of Brexit, and the whole Brexit playbook was part of it," Dagur Eggertsson, MP and former Mayor of Reykjavík, told Europe Today.
Keeping a low profile
The Icelandic government asked Brussels not to interfere.
In a response to a parliamentary question in June, Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir stressed that "this is a domestic matter, this is domestic politics, and it is the domestic decision of Icelanders to start these talks or not, and of course we do not want unreasonable interference."
At the same time, Frostadóttir noted that if people had questions about the EU, it would not be unusual for Brussels to answer them. That effort to keep the temperature down was consistent with the wider pro-EU camp's strategy.
Hulda Þórisdóttir, a professor at the University of Iceland, told Euronews that the Eurosceptic campaign managed to raise the stakes, framing the referendum as a straight choice on EU membership, while the pro-European camp tried to downplay that stake, emphasising it was just about resuming negotiations.
"This is not an election about membership and not about adaptation, as there will be another referendum on an accession agreement if the result is yes," Frostadóttir told the Washington Post ahead of the vote.
Senior EU officials followed a similar script. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos gave several interviews to Icelandic media outlets, including public broadcaster RÚV, focusing on the enlargement process and what the negotiations would entail in practice.
"The Icelandic vote is a warning for Europe. Fears about fishing and emotional arguments, sometimes false, have defeated the reasons for the 'Yes'. We respect the vote, but the message is clear: the EU must change," said MEP Sandro Gozi (France/Renew).
Sovereignty in question
The campaign on both sides focused on economic issues. The 'Yes' camp argued that joining the EU would lower interest rates on debt and reduce currency instability, opening the way to euro adoption.
The 'No' campaign, in turn, warned that EU membership would mean changing how the country runs its fisheries and farming industries — vital interests in the rural regions where the Eurosceptic vote triumphed.
"It wasn't only about economic interests. It was deeper than that. The arguments of the 'No' campaign resonated much more because they were closer to the Icelandic identity," Þórisdóttir said.
For the 'No' camp, in other words, the vote touched on something existential: having won hard-fought independence from Denmark in 1944, Iceland was determined not to cede sovereignty to another, larger power.
"The referendum on August 29th is not just about the European Union. It is about whether we believe the Icelandic people themselves are best placed to determine their future," Björn Bjarnason, a former minister from the Eurosceptic Independence Party, wrote in a blog post.
The underlying message of the successful 'No' campaign was that the EU is not a shield against larger powers, but one of the powers Iceland needs to stay independent from if it wants to remain a fully sovereign member of the international community.
At the same time, Brussels declined to expose itself politically in the campaign, in what some see as a parallel with the Brexit campaign, which shows the EU has not learned the relevant lessons.
Reminiscent of Brexit
Just as Reykjavik has done now, UK Prime Minister David Cameron previously urged the EU institutions not to intervene. In both cases, Brussels respected the request.
"I understand the political principle of non-interference in a constitutional referendum of a member state," Charles Tannock, a former MEP for the UK Conservatives who campaigned for Remain, told Euronews.
"But I do think it was a mistake, though, not to correct lies and misinformation."
Brussels' silence during the Brexit referendum was particularly striking given allegations that a foreign power was providing financial support to the Leave campaign, Tannock said — though he noted no definitive evidence was ever found.
In Iceland, the 'No' campaign was significantly better financed than the 'Yes.'
"It was a mistake not to intervene and not to interfere because we would have been the only ones to destroy the lies which were circulated," European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker told the press in 2019. "I was wrong to be silent at an important moment."
Of course, it is always easier with hindsight to say what should have been done differently — and it's debatable whether senior EU officials speaking out would have helped the European integration cause, given how carefully they would have had to walk that tightrope to avoid a backlash.
Still, on both occasions the EU managed to alienate voters by seeming to threaten their say over their own affairs, while at the same time refusing to play the prominent political role its detractors accused it of wanting.
"The EU has this reputation, rightly or wrongly, of being very top-down, and not really being sensitive about these sorts of arguments regarding protecting national identity and sovereignty," Tannock said.
"The EU could have done much more to say it is a project based on member states, and that Iceland would still be Iceland 100%," he added.

Eesti 200 MP: Remote gambling tax cut not to blame for revenue drop
Eesti 200 Riigikogu member Tanel Tein has defended a controversial online gambling tax cut, arguing it is too early to reverse the policy
A shortfall in projected tax revenues since the break came into effect at the end of last year is not solely due to that break, Tein said.
Tein's comments come after Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu said the tax break would cost the state €31 million in lost revenues, while Cultural Endowment (Kultuurikapital) head Margus Allikmaa called the tax cut an "unjustifiable" move which had left the culture sector with less funding.
The tax cut, introduced last December, was aimed at attracting more online casinos to register in Estonia, with the rate set to drop from six percent to four percent over two years. While gambling tax revenue fell by 9.7 percent in the first seven months of 2026, Tein said the decline was not caused by the remote gambling tax cut alone.
"A 9.7 percent decline in total gambling tax receipts is not the 'loss' caused by the remote gambling tax cut. The legislative amendment changed the remote gambling tax rate. But total gambling tax also includes [state lottery] Eesti Loto and traditional gambling, whose tax rates were not reduced by this reform," Tein said.
He pointed to the two‑month legislative error at the start of the year and noted that the Cultural Endowment's shortfall from remote gambling stood at around €956,000 — a fraction of the total gap.
Tein also rejected Reinsalu's €31 million figure, calling it a forecast and not a guaranteed loss, and warned that hiking the rate from 5 percent to 7 percent would translate into a 40 percent higher tax burden on businesses.
"The €31 million mentioned in today's report is also a forecast. Reinsalu himself told ERR that, according to the Finance Ministry's forecast, this is a figure calculated through 2029 compared with the previous assumption. That calculation assumes, among other things, how the tax base will behave in the future. It is precisely this assumption for which I want to see an impact assessment," Tein said.
The MP also noted that six companies that had not previously operated in Estonia have received operating permits in 2026 — already more than in all of 2025. "It would be equally mistaken to claim that the eight new operators that entered the market in 2024 came because the tax was raised from 5 percent to 6 percent," he said, adding that there is a long lag between a company's decision, obtaining a licence, and actual tax revenue.
Tein said the 2026 tax year is also a transitional period, with operators moving to stricter security and anti‑money laundering requirements. He warned that raising the tax rate now could undermine the long‑term goal of attracting larger international operators.
"The Cultural Endowment's interest should not be to have the highest possible tax rate. It should be to have the largest possible sustainable amount of actual tax revenue reaching culture and sport," Tein said.
"My position is therefore simple: let's give the agreed strategy time. If someone wants to reverse it now, I would first like to see an impact assessment showing that a higher tax rate will provide Estonia and the Cultural Endowment with more tax revenue that is actually collected three or five years from now," he concluded.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) has said the government will hold a debate on the issue in the coming weeks, adding that culture must not lose out and that if the tax cut does not bring additional revenue, there will be no further reduction.

British warship currently defending airspace over Ireland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
14:11:43 BST
22:11:43 KST

A Royal Navy warship and a Merlin anti-submarine helicopter are operating off the Irish coast today, providing air defence for the meeting of EU defence ministers in County Wicklow, with the ship required to remain outside Irish territorial waters, according to The Irish Times.
Conor Gallagher, the paper’s crime and security correspondent, reports that the ship was requested by Irish authorities to provide air defence during the event at Druids Glen, part of Ireland’s hosting of the EU presidency, and that the Irish Defence Forces lack the capability to conduct long-range air defence themselves.
The vessel has its transponder switched off and is not visible on open source marine tracking. The helicopter operating from it was trackable for around two hours on Monday morning, using the callsign Renegade, and The Irish Times reports that it appeared to briefly inspect a Portuguese cargo ship, which an Irish Air Corps aircraft later inspected as well.
The Merlin is the Royal Navy’s principal anti-submarine helicopter, carrying dipping sonar, sonobuoys and a search radar, and is equally capable of building a surface picture, which is the role it appears to be performing here.
The constitutional limit
As we reported last week, the requirement for the ship to stay offshore stems from legal advice to the Irish Government that deploying foreign military forces on active operations within Irish territory would likely be unconstitutional even where their presence had been formally requested. The advice cites Article 15 of the constitution, under which only the Oireachtas may raise a military force on Irish territory.
Irish territorial waters extend 12 nautical miles, or around 22 kilometres, from the coast.
When we asked about the tasking last week, a Royal Navy spokesperson told us: “The UK and Ireland regularly cooperate on shared security challenges. We do not speculate on potential operational tasking of Royal Navy vessels.”
The Irish Government has so far declined to confirm officially that it requested assistance from foreign forces during the presidency, according to the paper.
Criticism at Westminster
The arrangement has drawn objection from at least one British MP. As we reported, John Cooper, the Conservative member for Dumfries and Galloway, wrote to Defence Secretary Wes Streeting on 28 August saying he was aghast at reports that any vessel involved must stay outside the territorial limit.
He wrote: “This insistence that foreign warships remain outside Irish limits hampers their effectiveness. The Royal Navy is being asked to do a bad job. To add insult to injury, British taxpayers are footing the bill for this bodge.”
Cooper accused Ireland of freeloading on defence, argued that its policy of military neutrality has not been matched by investment in its own capability, and noted that while the Irish Defence Forces had spotted uncrewed aircraft in previous incidents they had no ability to interdict them, lacking meaningful air-to-air or surface-to-air capability beyond a small number of short-range missiles.
Not the first time
This is the second occasion on which a foreign navy has provided air defence for Irish EU presidency events. The French air defence frigate Aquitaine was stationed off Dublin on 1 July, outside territorial waters, during events opening the presidency, and did the same off the coast of County Cork the following day during a meeting of EU commissioners, with an Irish naval officer embarked.
Irish forces are running their own operation alongside the foreign contribution. Operation Fianna is directed by a joint task force based at McKee Barracks in Dublin, coordinating ground, sea and air units including anti-drone teams at major events. The Irish Times reports that the Naval Service ship LÉ Samuel Beckett was operating closer inshore off Wicklow on Monday, with a C295 maritime patrol aircraft and helicopters flying patrols.

Nepal deaths cross 1,000 as rescuers continue search for hundreds trapped in tunnels
Rescue teams in Nepal continue to search water-logged hydropower tunnels in the country’s north, where hundreds of workers remain unaccounted for seven days after a flash flood devastated areas near the border with China.
The death toll has risen to 1,003, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said on Tuesday afternoon.
Nearly 4,000 people remain unaccounted for, the country’s Foreign Ministry said, adding about 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries are among them. Some 11,800 have been rescued. 
As the authorities try to bring relief and supplies to survivors , rescue teams are racing to locate the hundreds believed trapped in the 12-13 tunnels of the many hydroelectric projects dotting the Trishuli river corridor. 
The NDRRMA has listed 639 people associated with the hydropower projects as missing. But the authorities have not been able to establish how many of those could be inside the tunnels or may have been swept away.
At the Upper Trishuli-3A Hydropower Project, where rescue teams had located and drilled into the tunnel’s head on Monday, they were still pumping in air and draining water to enable entry. Excavators and rock breakers are clearing access routes to the 4 km-long tunnel, where between 30 and 40 people are believed to be in the underground powerhouse, the Kathmandu Post reported.

Risking their own lives without hesitation, Nepal Army personnel are tirelessly working on the front lines to rescue people affected by this devastating disaster.
Their courage, sacrifice, and unwavering dedication to saving… pic.twitter.com/e7d0lYFeOq
Since Monday, Nepali Army teams working with specialists from other countries have advanced further into several tunnels. The Foreign Ministry said 24 Indian and nine Chinese tunnel-rescue specialists are deployed at the affected sites, while a South Korean team has also arrived in Nepal.
A joint team reached 200 meters into the 9.5 km-long Upper Trishuli-1 tunnel. Rescuers also reached about 50 meters into the Chilime tunnel, and around 150 meters into Langtang – both about 3 km in length.
The Nepalese Army said 279 people had been rescued alive from hydropower projects immediately after the floods, including 221 from Upper Trishuli-3A and 33 from Upper Trishuli-1. More than 21,000 Nepalese security personnel are involved in the search, evacuation, and relief work. The NDRRMA said 37 trucks and 37 utility vehicles carrying food and relief materials had been dispatched to affected areas, with supplies also delivered on nine helicopter flights.
Nepal has requested equipment including LiDAR, temporary bridge units, freezers, DNA testing kits, and high-capacity drones to support rescue and relief operations.
The Foreign Ministry said it is helping families of missing foreign nationals obtain information about their loved ones and, where needed, assist with identification and repatriation, while acknowledging “the pain and uncertainty” of families still waiting for their missing family members.

China-Asean trade passed US$1 trillion mark last year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:10:16 UTC
22:10:16 KST

China's trade with Asean member countries exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time last year, Vice Minister of Commerce Yan Dong said on Tuesday.
The value of bilateral trade reached US$1.05 trillion, up 7.4 percent.
China has remained Asean's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, while the region has been China's biggest trading partner for six successive years, Yan noted.
In the first seven months of 2026, total trade between China and Asean reached US$744.41 billion, an increase of 24.7 percent, accounting for 21.8 percent of China's total foreign trade.
Bilateral investment cooperation between the two sides has continued to climb.
As of July, both the cumulative two-way investment between China and Asean and the cumulative turnover of Chinese enterprises' contracted projects in Asean have exceeded US$515 billion, Yan said.
He was speaking at a press conference on the 23rd China-Asean Expo. Scheduled from September 17 to 21, the expo will take place in Nanning, the capital of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.
The expo features more than 2,200 Chinese enterprises and nearly 1,000 Asean firms.
For the first time, a dedicated exhibition area will showcase the technological and application needs of Asean countries, enabling Chinese enterprises to engage in targeted business matching based on these displayed demands.
This year's expo will upgrade the artificial intelligence exhibition area that was first launched last year.
The area will showcase cutting-edge AI technologies and applications across consumer, enterprise, government, and international dimensions.
A new "AI marketplace" will also make its debut, featuring more than 400 product models available for on-site trial and direct purchase.
Looking ahead, Beijing will actively promote the early entry into force and implementation of the China-Asean Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, signed in October 2025, and facilitate the delivery of cooperation in key areas such as digital economy and green development, Ministry of Commerce official Wang Liping said at the conference.
The nation will also expand imports of quality Asean goods to boost bilateral trade volumes, and explore new space for cooperation in emerging fields, with a strong push for trade in services, as well as digital and green trade, said Wang. (Xinhua)

French Muslim Council decries 'dangerous' political rhetoric on headscarves

13:09:24 UTC
22:09:24 KST

France’s top Muslim representative body has condemned what it called “irresponsible” political statements targeting Muslim women who wear headscarves, warning that such rhetoric could put them at greater risk of hostility and attacks.
The French Council of Muslim Faith (CFCM) said on Tuesday it strongly rejected attempts to associate women wearing headscarves with extremist ideology, arguing that such comments contribute to publicly stigmatising women who freely choose to wear the religious garment.
“Those who participate in this escalation bear political and moral responsibility,” the council said, warning that the rhetoric could expose Muslim women to “insults, threats, intimidation and attacks.”
Council defends freedom of religious choice
The CFCM rejected claims that the headscarf is merely a product of contemporary extremist ideology, noting that forms of head covering appear in the foundational traditions of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
While acknowledging that extremist movements have sought to instrumentalize the headscarf, the council said this does not change its religious or personal nature or justify banning it for women who freely choose to wear it.
“A woman who chooses to wear the headscarf, like one who chooses not to wear it, must be protected and her free choice respected,” the council said.
The group also argued that a public headscarf ban would conflict with constitutionally protected principles, including freedom of conscience, individual liberty and secularism.
CFCM warns against election-driven division
The council criticised what it described as a growing focus on controlling women’s clothing ahead of major electoral deadlines, questioning whether deploying law enforcement to police clothing should be considered a political priority.
It pointed instead to other challenges facing France, including terrorism, crime, drug trafficking, violence and insecurity.
The CFCM warned that using electoral debates to promote “fear, stigmatisation and division” risks deepening social tensions while distracting from the country’s wider challenges.
It called on political leaders to exercise “responsibility and restraint” and urged citizens committed to “freedom, equality and fraternity” to engage in public debate and civic action.
“Let us not make millions of French people hostages to electoral strategies. Let us not put targets on the backs of Muslim women,” the council said.

Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
14:09:14 BST
22:09:14 KST

Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say
- Published
Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave at the end of July.
That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.
She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.
Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.
There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents.
Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security council in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.
Rojas said the influx had led to an exponential increase in sexual assault, and many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta".
The Spanish Society of Epidemiology said the border crisis had highlighted the difficulty in detecting and tackling violence against migrant women and girls.
One 24-year-old woman from Morocco told the BBC she had "put her life in danger" by travelling to Ceuta, and described being sexually assaulted while sleeping among a group of men and women. "I was shocked… If I had known this, I wouldn't have come."
Emergency doctor Susana Ascaso said last month her department at Ceuta University Hospital had treated several sexual assault victims, including one who was just 10 years old.
Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.
The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.
The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".
Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave.
"We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."
The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave.
Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.
In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007.
He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold.
Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.
- Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues 
  - Published4 days ago
Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.
Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe".
He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".
Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.
A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.
Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.
The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.
Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.
