Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
September 1, 2026
The death of Ratko Mladic should have closed one of the darkest chapters in European history.
Instead, it has reopened old wounds, proving that both the Dayton Accords that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian war and the three decades of international engagement that followed never came close to addressing the causes that led to the conflict.
When Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, died on August 27, 2026 in a prison hospital in The Hague, his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo — had been final for nearly a decade.
What was never settled, however — and what, it seems, was never even seriously attempted — is the question of how a society lives with a man who remains a convicted criminal in the eyes of an international court but is viewed by some as a hero and symbol of the Serbian people.
For this reason, the reactions that followed Mladic's death came as no surprise.
Mladic openly mourned in Republika Srpska
In Serbia and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska, one of the two semi-autonomous entities created within Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, Mladic's death was mourned as the loss of a national hero, not the end of an era of crimes — a narrative that stands in direct contradiction to the facts established by international courts.
Senior officials in Republika Srpska, which covers around 49% of the territory of the former Yugoslav republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, called on citizens to gather in squares and light candles "for the salvation of the general's soul."
Milorad Dodik, still the most powerful political figure in Republika Srpska despite stepping down as its president last year after a six-year ban on holding public office imposed by Bosnia's constitutional court, called Mladic's death a "murder," suggesting it was "an organized approach that was meant to lead to a fatal outcome."
In Banja Luka, the de facto capital of Republika Srpska, Mayor Drasko Stanivukovic expressed his condolences to Mladic's family and confirmed that Mladic is not perceived as a man convicted of genocide but as a symbol of "a time and a struggle."
Institutional support in Belgrade
In the Serbian capital, Belgrade, this stance received institutional backing.
Serbia's justice minister announced a funeral with the highest state and military honors.
President Aleksandar Vucic accused the tribunal in The Hague of "uncivilized behavior" for not allowing Mladic to spend his final days outside his prison cell.
Former Interior Minister Aleksandar Vulin spoke of Mladic in the same breath as other Serbian national heroes, invoking a narrative linking World War I to the 1990s, saying, "From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed tied up."
A very different response elsewhere in Bosnia
In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the other main entity in Bosnia, where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, news of Mladic's death was met with unanimous condemnation of the deceased, given that Mladic was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, a town in eastern Bosnia where around 8,000 men and boys were killed in July 1995.
Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, framed the official Serbian response as Serbia's conscious choice. "No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero, nor to attribute his crimes to it. Serbia is choosing this itself," he said.
Representatives of victims and survivors pointed out that any public glorification is a direct insult to the families of those killed.
The European Commission, responding to questions about the announced state funeral, said that "glorifying convicted war criminals is contrary to the most basic European values" and that such practices have no place in either member states or candidate countries.
The European Movement in Serbia warned that a state funeral would amount to "institutional glorification" and a "serious moral, legal and political attack on Serbia." It urged the Serbian government to abandon the plan.
How can this happen?
But how is it possible that a man who has been finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica is still honored as a military commander?
The answer is not simply that he is viewed by some as a national hero. It is structural, and it begins with the Dayton peace agreement itself.
The 1995 Dayton Accords ended the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina by turning existing front lines and territorial control into the constitutional architecture of a new state.
One of the fundamental elements of the agreement was Republika Srpska, which is recognized by all signatories and embedded in the constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina.
That division was not an administrative technicality; it reflected the political reality on the ground at the time negotiations were held, including territories under the control of forces commanded by Mladic.
The compromise was necessary to stop the bloodshed. The problem is that since 1995, it has never been accompanied by a mechanism for dealing with the past that would match the political compromise.
Dayton created a complex constitutional architecture — a state divided into two entities and the Brcko District with a total 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — for a country of just 3 million people.
It is a system built to prevent war, not a system built to produce common citizenship, and was described by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as long ago as 2005 as "neither rational nor efficient."
In such a system, where ethnic identity is built into the very logic of power, denial or relativization of crimes is not a marginal phenomenon, it is a political resource.
In other words, each side sees itself as a victim, which makes joint recognition of committed evil as a precondition for reconciliation impossible.
Price of missed responsibility
Bosnia-Herzegovina has state-level legislation that criminalizes the public denial, gross minimization or justification of genocide and the glorification of persons convicted of such acts.
In reality, however, enforcement of this legislation remains uneven.
Serbia has no such law, and its public authorities, instead of distancing themselves from Mladic's legacy, openly embrace it.
This is not just a symbolic difference, it is the difference between treating the wartime legacy as something shameful to be overcome or as a resource to be politically exploited.
Dayton Accords helped maintain status quo
The international community, which stopped the war in 1995 through force and diplomacy, has subsequently retreated into the role of administrator of the status quo.
The Office of the High Representative, the international envoy empowered to impose laws and remove obstructive politicians under the Dayton Accords, did indeed impose laws and remove obstructive politicians for decades. But in doing so it only stabilized the system without dismantling its causes.
The result is twofold: a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 30 years since the end of the war, and the fact that an ideology that gave rise to that war is still very much alive.

(China Economic Roundtable) China leverages innovation hubs to boost new quality productive forces
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:08:30 CST
22:08:30 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China is leveraging its three major innovation centers to drive industrial upgrading and foster new quality productive forces by tapping their respective strengths, said the guests on the latest episode of China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency.
China has designated Beijing, Shanghai and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area as three major international sci-tech innovation centers. Last year, the country moved to broaden their reach, extending the Beijing center across the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region and the Shanghai center across the Yangtze River Delta.
Chen Baoming, director of the Institute of Scientific and Technical Information of China under the Ministry of Science and Technology, said that the three international sci-tech innovation centers have made solid progress in recent years, with their respective strengths becoming increasingly prominent.
He noted that Beijing's R&D intensity has remained around 6 percent, and the city tops the world in the number of highly cited scientists. Shanghai has produced leading original achievements in physics, chemistry and life sciences. The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area leads the country in the number of high-tech enterprises and Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) patent applications.
Yi Tong, director of the Institute for Innovation Development Strategy at Beijing Academy of Science and Technology, noted that Beijing has been accelerating the commercialization of research outcomes, and optimizing the industrial ecosystem by building a range of innovation platforms.
Zha Hao, chairman and CEO of Shanghai Smartlogic Technology Ltd., has seen firsthand how Shanghai's policies to foster innovation-driven industries can benefit companies like his. As a firm specializing in scientific computing and AI for science, Smartlogic has benefited from initiatives that connect companies with real-world applications and help speed commercialization across the value chain.
For his part, Zhang Zhengang, a professor at South China University of Technology, said that the high-end manufacturing sector in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area has shifted from "scale expansion" to "structural upgrading."
The area is exploring a distinctive model of moving innovation from universities to industry, with "research and development in Hong Kong and Macao, commercialization on the mainland," according to the professor. So far, five Hong Kong universities have established technology commercialization platforms in Qianhai in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, incubating more than 150 sci-tech projects.
Looking ahead, the professor called for greater focus on three areas to strengthen the centers' role as sources of original innovation: basic research, major scientific facilities and the commercialization of research outcomes, providing core technologies to drive new quality productive forces.
China has vowed to improve regional innovation systems during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The systems bring together government, businesses, universities and research institutes, allowing different regions to better leverage their respective strengths and helping move research findings from laboratories toward commercial applications. ■

Why China will not comply with US sanctions on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:08:14 UTC
22:08:14 KST

Why China will not comply with US sanctions on Iran
Beijing will not comply with US measures because it can and because it’s in its interest not to.
On August 31, the leaders of China, Russia and India met in Bishkek for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was also in attendance.
The final declaration of the summit issued on September 1 called for the creation of a new development bank, which in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s words would have “maximum independence from the financial systems of the states which weaponize economic tools in order to obtain unilateral advantages in international affairs”
The summit was held just a week after the United States announced the latest package of sanctions against Iran, which instead of isolation, enjoyed a warm welcome in Bishkek.
As the SCO gathering demonstrated, Washington is already facing major difficulties in ensuring international compliance with its sanctions.
Perhaps its biggest challenger is China. Beijing is once again standing by Iran – not out of moral or ideological motivations, but because it can and because it is in its interest.
Toothless sanctions
By purchasing 90 percent of Iranian oil exports, China has single-handedly kept the Iranian economy afloat – all while evading the US sanctions through a sophisticated network of “dark fleets” (ships used to obfuscate the Iranian origin of their cargo) and “teapot” refineries (private refineries so dubbed for their relatively modest size).
In response to Washington’s “with us or against us” ultimatum on the sanctions, the Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said that “China will do everything necessary to firmly safeguard its rights and interests”. Having fought several trade wars with the US to a standstill, China has developed a high tolerance for US-inflicted economic pain – and an equally low tolerance for being pushed around.
For Beijing, foreign interference in bilateral trade relations with a third country is not acceptable. More importantly, it views Washington’s threat as toothless – and for good reason.
China is well insulated from the US’ Iran-related secondary sanctions. Chinese banks and companies that do business with Iran often do so exclusively, settling transactions in renminbi or through barter – making them effectively immune to US extraterritorial jurisdiction.
Meanwhile, the handful of Chinese companies that still settle transactions in US dollars are hidden beneath layers of shell companies that can be discarded at little to no cost. This forces Washington into an endless game of regulatory whack-a-mole, in which each entity successfully eliminated is quickly replaced by another.
Washington could, of course, sanction major Chinese banks and companies that have no ties with Iran – using them as a bargaining chip to pressure Beijing to rein in those that do. Doing so, however, would invite Beijing to retaliate in kind. With the US economy already strained by the war with Iran and the midterms just around the corner, picking a fight with China is the last thing the US needs.
Iran must not lose
Toothless US sanctions aside, China has another motive for standing by Iran’s side: its defeat could be costly for Chinese geopolitical and economic interests.
From Beijing’s perspective, should Iran lose, the entire Middle East would gravitate back into the US orbit. Regional countries currently exploring alternative security partners would have little choice but to seek refuge once more under the US security umbrella.
Such a shift would not only deal a heavy blow to China’s growing influence in the region but also complicate future cooperation on advanced technologies, including 5G, artificial intelligence, and defence.
Worse still, China’s energy interests could be threatened. The country sources 40 percent of its oil imports from the Gulf, with Iran accounting for 10 percent. With such a significant chunk of oil imports originating from countries under US influence, China’s economic lifeline would effectively lie in US hands.
A victory in Iran would also embolden Washington to continue its pursuit of regime-change in other countries that have close ties with Beijing.
This would make it increasingly difficult for China to protect its interests overseas, as was the case when Panama seized two Chinese-operated ports under US pressure.
China’s caution
That said, China does not see itself in a tight alliance with Iran – hence its reluctance to ramp up support.
It is worried that a total victory for Iran would enable its regional hegemony, driving yet another wedge in the already strained relationship with the Gulf states, and further undermining years of Chinese diplomatic efforts aimed at bridging that divide.
Therefore, Beijing is maintaining a calibrated distance from Tehran – not too hot, not too cold, but just right. The fact that Pezeshkian is yet to be invited to Beijing makes it clear the Chinese authorities are not eager for a tight embrace.
This was apparent at the SCO summit as well. The Chinese leader met with his Russian and Indian counterparts, but did not have a formal meeting with Pezeshkian. There were formal consultations at the level of foreign ministers.
The message is subtle yet unmistakable: Though Beijing values the relationship, it is keeping its distance.
Balance with Washington
When considering the China-Iran relationship, it’s important to remember that relations with the US, although often fraught by rivalry, are very important for Beijing.
Resetting of China-US relations takes priority, which is why two high-level summits are taking place this year: The first one was US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, and the second is Xi’s trip to Washington later this month.
During Trump’s visit to China this May, he and Xi announced that the two countries had agreed on building a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability” – one where cooperation takes centre stage, competition is kept within bounds and never descends into zero-sum games, and war is to be avoided at all cost.
In this context, providing too much support to Iran would be counterproductive – which is why Beijing has stayed out of the war and has pledged not to arm Iran. This is clearly appreciated in Washington. In June, Trump thanked China publicly for remaining “totally neutral”.
At the same time the Trump administration is well aware of China’s economic interest in Iran and was likely not surprised to hear its position on the new sanctions.
The only way out of this self-inflicted predicament is for Washington to shed its hegemonic mindset and return to the negotiating table – anything less will only prolong the misery – both for itself, and for the world at large.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Chinese AI gaining popularity in Kenya for affordability, performance, customization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:08:10 CST
22:08:10 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models are gaining ground among Kenyan developers and technology companies, as their lower costs, competitive performance and open-source nature offer an attractive option for a market seeking affordable and customizable AI solutions.
A recent analysis by The New York Times showed that Chinese AI models accounted for roughly half of AI use on OpenRouter, a platform offering about 400 AI models, up from less than 25 percent a year earlier.
On Hugging Face, another major AI model platform, Chinese AI models accounted for 19 of the 25 most-downloaded open-source systems.
In Kenya, developers and technology companies are increasingly turning to Chinese AI models such as DeepSeek and Qwen for applications ranging from legal technology and business intelligence to document processing and coding.
Michael Michie, founder and chief executive officer of EverseTech, an AI startup focused on local GPU infrastructure and enterprise AI applications, said Chinese models have become the most widely used models in many of the company's projects.
"Most of my clients choose the Chinese one," said Michie, who was recently appointed the responsible AI governor for Kenya, citing cost and computing efficiency as major factors.
Kenya has a limited supply of GPUs, making models that require fewer computing resources easier to deploy on local infrastructure, he said.
"They perform just as well, sometimes even better," Michie said. "In the past, Chinese models were maybe six months or a year behind in terms of capabilities, but now they do the same complex tasks that frontier models would do."
He noted that Chinese models also consume fewer tokens for some tasks, further reducing the computing resources required.
Michie's view is echoed by Mbugua Njihia, a Kenyan technology expert, who said the cost advantage matters especially in Africa, where AI developers face a much more complex linguistic environment than in many other markets.
Against this backdrop, the availability of open-weight models gives African developers greater scope to adapt AI to local needs, Njihia added.
By downloading and retraining the models with relatively small datasets, developers can customize them for local languages, specific industries and other Africa-specific applications without building a model from scratch, Njihia said.
The practical value of such flexibility can be seen in JibuDocs, a document-processing tool developed by entrepreneurs Sentai Simons and Daniele Pisani using a Chinese AI model.
With a Chinese AI model, the tool can process large volumes of documents, extract and organize information, and generate summaries, helping users find specific information without having to manually read through every document, according to Pisani.
For Simons, one of the most important advantages of open-weight models is the ability to use a company's own data to further train and fine-tune a model for specific tasks.
Simons, whose team uses both DeepSeek and Qwen, said Chinese AI models "are very good and can be a very good starting point," he said, adding that, more importantly, it allows users to customize it and continue training it.
That combination of performance and openness is also attracting Kenyan technology company Qhala, which began experimenting with DeepSeek in the second half of 2024 and put more production systems into operation in early 2025 following the release of DeepSeek R1.
Shikoh Gitau, Qhala's chief executive, said DeepSeek's technical research has also influenced how its team approaches AI research and development.
Its research papers on areas such as mixture-of-experts architecture and reinforcement learning have helped the team understand advanced model development and rethink assumptions about the resources needed to build capable AI systems, according to Gitau.
The company is also looking at ways to use DeepSeek to help develop cost-efficient models optimized for African languages and content, Gitau added.
Kenya was one of the 29 founding members of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which was established in July at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai.
Michie said he hoped Kenya could strengthen partnerships with China to expand its computing capacity and establish exchanges that would enable Kenyan developers to learn from Chinese experts in building world-class AI models.
Njihia said Chinese AI models could also be useful in sectors where Africa faces shortages of specialized expertise and infrastructure.
Healthcare triage and diagnostic-support tools trained on local disease patterns and language data could help extend limited clinical expertise to rural communities, provided that data governance remains local, he said.
Disaster prevention is another area where such technology could have practical value, with flood and drought modeling combined with early-warning systems in local languages, Njihia added. ■

China Focus: China issues guideline to regulate automakers' overseas competitive practices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:08:10 CST
22:08:10 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China issued a guideline on Tuesday to regulate Chinese automakers' overseas competitive practices and strengthen corporate compliance, aiming to promote the sound and orderly global expansion of the country's auto industry.
The 20-article guideline provides general guidance for Chinese automotive companies engaged in international operations, with a focus on practices that include overseas marketing, according to a circular released by China's Ministry of Commerce and two other government departments.
It also provides guidance on compliance for automakers in areas such as overseas production safety, quality management, labor protection and data security.
To regulate overseas competitive practices, the guideline encourages automakers to adopt cost-based pricing strategies guided by international market supply and demand, and urges them not to disrupt market competition in pursuit of unfair advantages.
When setting suggested retail prices for vehicles in overseas markets, companies should follow local laws and regulations, market principles and business practices of host countries and regions, establish clear price tiers for different vehicle configurations, and avoid frequent or substantial price fluctuations that could harm consumer interests, according to the guideline.
The guideline also calls on automakers to respect local dealers' and agents' pricing autonomy and conduct promotional activities in line with local laws and customs.
An official with the Ministry of Commerce said the guideline emphasizes legal compliance, fair competition, mutual benefit and win-win cooperation in automakers' overseas practices.
"It will help Chinese automotive companies to fulfill their social responsibilities overseas and better integrate into the economic and social development of host countries," the official said, adding that it will also promote deeper integration and common development of global automotive industrial and supply chains.
Beyond regulating market competition, the guideline also aims to strengthen automakers' localized compliance capabilities. It calls on companies to tailor their operations to local conditions and maintain compliance throughout all business processes.
Automakers should also strengthen quality management and after-sales services in overseas markets, ensure legal compliance in processing data related to connected vehicles and autonomous driving, and protect consumers' personal information.
Industry experts said the auto-sector guideline complements two earlier guidelines issued by the Ministry of Commerce in 2025 on anti-corruption compliance and corporate social responsibility for companies operating overseas. Together, the documents help put China's broader support system for companies operating overseas into practice and tailor it to key industries, experts noted.
Customs data showed that China exported 8.32 million vehicles to more than 200 countries and regions in 2025.
Chinese companies have so far invested in automotive manufacturing in over 80 countries and regions. In July, Chinese automaker Geely Auto and U.S. automaker Ford announced a new cooperation agreement in Spain, marking another step in Chinese automakers' shift toward localized production in Europe.
Commenting on the guideline, Shi Yonghong, vice president of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, said building factories and operating locally demand more complex compliance requirements for Chinese automakers in areas such as environmental protection, taxation, employment and data localization.
"The guideline will support the coordinated overseas expansion of vehicle production, component supply and service networks by covering the entire business lifecycle," Shi was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying. ■

Full text of Chinese President Xi Jinping's speech at SCO Plus meeting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:08:03 CST
22:08:03 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers an important speech during the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhai Jianlan)
BISHKEK, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday delivered a speech at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus Meeting in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan.
The following is the full text of the speech:
Jointly Advocating an Equal and Orderly Multipolar World and Making Global Governance More Just and Equitable
Statement by H.E. Xi Jinping
President of the People's Republic of China
At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Plus Meeting
Bishkek, September 1, 2026
Your Excellency President Sadyr Zhaparov,
Colleagues,
It gives me great pleasure to join fellow members and partners of the SCO family in celebrating the 25th anniversary of our organization. I wish to thank President Zhaparov for his kind invitation and the thoughtful arrangements by the government of Kyrgyzstan.
The meeting today focuses on strengthening the role of the United Nations and building a multipolar world, and it demonstrates SCO's commitment to reforming and improving global governance as required by our times.
Currently, major changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the globe. Hegemonism, unilateralism and protectionism are resurging against historical trends. Nevertheless, the overwhelming majority of the world do not condone power politics, conflict and confrontation, or isolation and backwardness. What they want instead is to hold a place on the world stage through national development and international cooperation. In recent years, the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power. The trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible.
What kind of multipolarity does the world need? How are countries going to take part in and promote it? The international community should build consensus and make the right choice that can stand the test of practice and history. As a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world.
Sovereign equality and mutual respect are fundamental principles. The history of the world is written by all nations. Multipolarity, independent choice of development paths, and greater democracy in international relations are the right way forward. We should ensure equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all countries, regardless of their size, strength and wealth. As an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs.
Balance, order and the rule of law are inherent requirements. The purposes and principles of the UN Charter set the basic norms of international relations, and serve as the bedrock of the postwar international order. We should promote the common values of humanity, reject double standards, exceptionalism, foreign interference, bullying and the law of the jungle, and advance the rule of law in international relations. Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law, and work together to tackle global challenges.
Multilateralism, dialogue and consultation are essential pathways. The domination of international affairs by a few is an injustice left over from history, and global governance dictated by one, a few or a bloc of countries is not true multilateralism. World affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all. The authority and vitality of the UN need to be restored. Multilateral mechanisms, global and regional, should enhance their coordination and improve their efficiency.
Mutual benefit, win-win, and inclusiveness are the way forward for development. Countries are not isolated islands, but partners with intertwined interests and a shared future. Protectionism, decoupling and supply-chain disruption will lead nowhere. We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations.
Colleagues,
After a 25-year journey, the SCO has successfully set a stellar example in conducting relations among big countries, among neighbors, and among countries of different sizes. It has successfully brought together half of the world's population and a quarter of the global economy, generating strong driving forces for development. A more united and vibrant SCO is fully capable of making greater contributions to an equal and orderly multipolar world.
First, we should advance common prosperity in the vast continent straddling Asia and Europe with the SCO Strength. Cooperation within the SCO has been fruitful in political, security, economic, trade, people-to-people and cultural domains, and our organization is now a key platform for Eurasian countries to jointly pursue development and tackle challenges. We should continue to leverage our strengths, unlock our potential, and connect the multiple growth poles across the continent through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. We should empower each other, help each other succeed, and work together to create new opportunities and promote shared prosperity.
Second, we should promote the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom. The organization takes root in the Global South, its heart beats with the Global South, and it is an important pillar of South-South cooperation. We should carry forward the Shanghai Spirit, strengthen and expand the SCO Plus partnerships, and jointly speak up for peace, foster synergy for development, build bridges for cooperation, and pave the way for win-win outcomes.
Third, we should guide the reform and improvement of global governance through the SCO Action. Our organization takes it as its mission and responsibility to make the global governance system more just and equitable. We should stay committed to building partnerships rather than alliances, and engaging in dialogue rather than confrontation. We should adhere to the principle of "planning together, building together and benefiting together" to encourage equal participation in global governance by all countries and ensure all will benefit from it.
Colleagues,
In global governance, stagnation is regression. It is important that SCO member states and partners ride the trend of history and shoulder the responsibility of our times. Let us take the people-centered and action-oriented approach, jointly advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world, make global governance more just and equitable, and build a community with a shared future for humanity.
Thank you. ■

Egyptian-Chinese archaeological team announces new discoveries at ancient Memphis site
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:07:52 CST
22:07:52 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- A joint Egyptian-Chinese archaeological mission has uncovered cultural relics and archaeological remains at the Temple of Sekhmet site in Mit Rahina, Giza Province, west of the Egyptian capital Cairo, Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities has said.
The discoveries provide new evidence of how the area surrounding the temple was used and inhabited across successive periods of ancient Egyptian history, the ministry said on Sunday.
The mission is jointly conducted by Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities and the Shanghai Museum in east China, and is co-led by Reham Zaki of Supreme Council of Antiquities and Chen Jie, deputy director of the Shanghai Museum.
The mission found a residential complex near the temple, along with stone blocks and fragments of statues. Archaeologists also uncovered a limestone structure believed to have been used for wine production.
Other finds include stone blocks, statue fragments and pottery. Some of the stone artifacts date to the New Kingdom period (1550 BC-1069 BC).
Egyptian Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy praised the fruitful archaeological cooperation between Egypt and China, describing the two countries as home to two ancient civilizations with rich cultural heritages.
The latest discoveries demonstrate the close and growing cooperation between the two countries in archaeology, following a number of joint archaeological projects in recent years, according to Fathy.
Chen told Xinhua that the two sides had already begun in-depth cooperation as early as during the exhibition "On Top of the Pyramid: the Civilization of Ancient Egypt," jointly held by the Shanghai Museum and Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities.
Chen said the joint archaeological mission will continue to conduct surface surveys and archaeological excavations of the Temple of Sekhmet and its surrounding areas over the coming quarters, with the aim of further determining and reconstructing the architectural layout, construction process, history of use, landscape changes and evolution of civilization of the temple and even the Memphis area.
The Shanghai Museum will work with Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities to establish a long-term cooperation system covering archaeological excavation, research, conservation, exhibition and utilization, and further promote academic exchanges and mutual learning between the two countries in the field of archaeology, Chen added.
The Sekhmet Temple, discovered by chance in 1959, formed part of the Great Temple of Ptah, the main religious complex of ancient Memphis. The ancient city of Memphis, founded around 3100 BC, served as the capital of Egypt during the Old Kingdom period and remained an important religious and cultural center for centuries. ■

Murmansk Region's oldest nickel mine to host museum exposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:07:48 UTC
22:07:48 KST

MURMANSK, September 1. /TASS/. One of the oldest mines in the Murmansk Region, Kaula-Kotselvaara, decommissioned in 2023, will become a museum, where expositions will be organized inside a real mine, Deputy Director of the Pechenga District's Second School Center for Social Projects Marina Kosheleva told TASS after the Gastro Industry Fest business program.
"It was only a year ago that nobody could believe we would go into the mine, would go there and make a museum out of it," she said. "Now we have builders and specialists who have been implementing the design project. We are working on the first stage - the museum, the office building, and the mine."
The Second School Center, she continued, together with counterparts, has been turning Nickel's industrial heritage into a point of attraction and growth. On Metallurgov Square, where the Gastro Industry Fest was held, there are 42 pieces of equipment that have been lifted from the mine. "You can read on the signs that this, for example, is not just a trolley - it is a trolley that transported a certain number of tons of ore, which then were turned into nickel, and the latter used to be in our everyday objects," she explained.
A strategic session, dubbed From Industrial Boom to Creative Miracle, was part of the festival's business program. The discussion participants - from federal producers to local architects of change - have proved that the future of Arctic single-industry towns is based not on denying the industrial past, but on re-viewing it. "We do realize that the Pechenga District's industry is our past, present and future. Therefore, we decided to view the industry from a different angle, in terms of tourism, to package it into a new product," she continued. She voiced certain tourist sites, including the Kola Superdeep Borehole, the Shpil (Spire) 555 ecology-industrial route, audio tours, and festivals. She also announced plans to create joint tourist routes with the Kirovsky ski resort.
About the mine and the festival
The Nickel town is located in the Murmansk Region's Pechenga District, seven km from the border with Norway and about 200 km northwest of Murmansk. In 2020, the Norilsk Nickel Company, having assets in the district, stopped the smelter in Nickel - it had been the company's oldest production facility. The Kaula-Kotselvaara mine's mothballing began in 2023 due to depleted ore reserves and unprofitable further production. The present plan is to transform the mine into a modern industrial tourism facility.
The Gastro Industry Fest has been held in the town of Nickel in summer since 2021. It is a merger of industrial landscapes and entertainment, of gastronomic experiments of Arctic cuisine and the harsh northern flavor. Every year about 10,000 people attend the event. The festival's organizers are the Second School Center for Social Projects, supported by the Norilsk Nickel Company and the Pechenga Municipal District's administration.

Feature: Power, fuel and water shortages compound Libya's woes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:07:47 CST
22:07:47 KST

This photo taken with a mobile phone shows a man filling the fuel tank of an electric generator in Tripoli, Libya, on July 24, 2026. (Photo by Hazem Turkia/Xinhua)
by Abdelrahman Mohammed Elbakoush
TRIPOLI, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- After owning his truck for seven years, 49-year-old Ahmed Al-Sharif is considering selling it.
Al-Sharif relies on the truck as his only source of income, using it to transport furniture to support his family of six. But these days, keeping it running has become increasingly difficult for him and other drivers in Libya as diesel becomes harder to obtain amid the country's intertwined power and fuel crises, which have lasted more than six weeks.
With the temperature nearing 40 degrees Celsius, he stood beside his truck in a long queue outside a fuel station in the Libyan capital city of Tripoli, waiting for his turn to get diesel.
He told Xinhua that the wait could last two or three days, while power cuts could add more hours as stations stop operating. "If there is a total blackout, we will remain waiting for an unknown period," he said.
The problem is compounded by the high cost of diesel on the black market, where a liter of diesel costs about 8 Libyan dinars (about 1.26 U.S. dollars), more than 50 times the official subsidized price.
"If I buy diesel on the black market, I will not be able to make ends meet with what I earn from daily work after paying for it," he said.
With the new school year approaching and prices rising, Al-Sharif is considering borrowing money to cover his family's needs. He is also looking for another job.
The crisis has not been limited to drivers, as power cuts have also affected businesses.
At a food market in eastern Tripoli, 32-year-old Khaled Ibrahim, a supermarket owner, said power cuts lasting more than 10 hours had caused refrigeration equipment to stop, leaving chilled water unavailable and causing some frozen goods to spoil.
"This is the worst season for me, and I have not been able to continue under these circumstances," said Ibrahim.
The crisis has also spread to the water system, with supplies cut off in large parts of the capital due to disruptions affecting the Great Man-Made River, a major network of pipelines and aqueducts that supplies fresh water to parts of Libya.
In central Tripoli, Rafaa Zaid, the owner of a cafe, was forced to close his business because of the water shortage.
Zaid said power cuts could be temporarily managed with a generator, but the lack of water makes it impossible to operate the cafe, even as he continues to pay rent.
"Every day that passes without opening the cafe means another loss, but what can I do? I cannot work without water," he said.
For Al-Sharif, Ibrahim and Zaid, the shortages are not separate problems. A power cut can shut down a fuel station, making it harder for drivers to get diesel. A shortage of diesel, in turn, raises the cost of running generators, while disruptions to the Great Man-Made River system can leave businesses without water even when they have electricity.
The impact of the power crisis has also been felt beyond homes and businesses.
According to the Libya Herald in late August, the extensive and frequent power cuts and blackouts have led to violent demonstrations in the country, with road blockades involving the setting of fires to rubbish and tires, and the barricading of state buildings with rubble.
Bashir Al-Marash, the chairman of the state-owned General Electricity Company of Libya, assured that Libya's current electricity crisis will end within the next two weeks, the report said.
Although Libya holds the largest proven crude oil reserves in Africa, it heavily imports refined petroleum products such as gasoline and diesel due to domestic processing limitations and infrastructure challenges.
Brega Petroleum Marketing Company is a state-owned Libyan enterprise headquartered in Tripoli that manages the domestic storage, marketing, and distribution of petroleum and refined oil products.
Ahmed Al-Masallati, director of media and communications and official spokesperson for the company, said on Sunday that the global crisis, and specifically the shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the repercussions of global energy crises, have delayed the arrival of some fuel shipments to Libya.
On a local level, he said that reduced production at the Zawia refinery due to power outages and security conditions contributed to a temporary drop in the quantities available for distribution.
Tariq Al-Tarhouni, an energy expert and head of the Department of Renewable and Sustainable Energy Engineering at Libya's Omar Al-Mukhtar University, said the problem goes deeper than a shortage in electricity generation.
"Libya's electricity crisis is not merely a power generation crisis, but a crisis in the management of the entire energy system," he said.
He added that a sustainable solution requires rebuilding Libya's energy system around efficiency, reliability, diversity and decentralization, while rehabilitating conventional generation, strengthening the grid and improving demand management. ■
This photo taken with a mobile phone shows vehicles lining up at a filling station in Tripoli, Libya, on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Hazem Turkia/Xinhua)

Across China: Geologists diagnose hazardous cliffs in central China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
21:07:35 CST
22:07:35 KST

WUHAN, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- During the flood season this summer, orange farmers in the mountain villages of central China's Hubei Province have welcomed teams of geologists who come to assess the hazardous cliffs along the roads their harvest depends on.
It is an innovative disaster-prevention initiative by the Wuhan Center of China Geological Survey, which has dispatched geological experts to conduct on-site inspections of dangerous rock masses in the mountainous areas.
Deep in the mountains of western Hubei, a narrow five-to-six-meter road snakes upward on the slopes. It is the only route for some 700 villagers of Tuzhumiao Village in Zigui County, and the lifeline for transporting navel oranges, the area's pillar produce.
Not long ago, a special team of "doctors" arrived at the site where a landslide had taken place along the road. Wearing safety helmets, they bent down to carefully inspect rock crevices and monitor slope changes - conducting a "physical examination" of the mountain.
"The dangerous rock mass consists of medium-thick bedded siltstone with mudstone inside. Like a sandwich cookie, its middle layer has poor stability. Even worse, the rock mass easily absorbs rainwater, prone to deformation and destabilization," said Xu Yong, a professor-level senior engineer at the Wuhan center.
On the opposite mountainside, a 3D laser scanner tracked every subtle shift in the rock face. Overhead, a drone equipped with survey equipment maneuvered above the site, capturing images from multiple angles. Together, these operations delivered a full "CT scan" of the dangerous rock mass, allowing experts to examine the mountain's overall risks.
"Under the combined effects of rainfall erosion and gravitational unloading, there is a risk of further collapse and deformation here," Xu said. He recommended that local authorities designate warning zones, erect warning signs, and assign dedicated personnel for routine monitoring of the collapsed area.
"Any signs of rock mass deformation should be reported immediately upon detection, while efforts to implement engineering treatment measures should be accelerated," Xu added.
This kind of cliffside "diagnosis" exemplifies Hubei's innovative approach to geological disaster prevention. By sending experts to reach "every village," the province is working to prevent and mitigate geological risks, especially during the summer flood season.
Hubei's vast mountainous terrain and complex geological conditions leave hazard spots scattered across villages. Hidden dangers in mountain gullies and behind houses are easily missed by grassroots teams. Professional inspections are essential in disaster prevention, according to the provincial department of natural resources.
Since the flood season began, dozens of experts from the center have been sent to villages across high-risk geological disaster areas in western and eastern Hubei, conducting on-site inspections and providing tech-support in organizing evacuations and handling hazard risks.
As experts ventured into the mountains, public education on geological hazards advanced as well, with villagers learning to recognize the early warning signs of landslides and collapses. In addition to improving their ability to identify geological risks and take self-rescue measures, many villagers are now becoming "geological disaster observers."
From July 10 when the initiative was launched to Aug. 28, Hubei screened 34,283 geological hazard risks and identified 1,528 new dangerous sites. Nine successful evacuations were organized after inspectors spotted abnormal mountain deformations, with 34 people from 10 households relocated to safety.
Zhao Xinwen, deputy chief engineer of the center, said sudden and clustered geological disasters have in recent years become more frequent due to human engineering activities and extreme rainfall, requiring more systematic, long-term prevention mechanisms.
A joint geological disaster prevention workstation has been established in Enshi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture in collaboration with the center and provincial departments. More such workstations will be set up to strengthen risk prevention and control capabilities, the center said. ■

U.S. Space Force taps Leonardo DRS for sensor technology
Unknown

- Leonardo DRS won an Other Transaction Agreement from the U.S. Space Force to develop sensor technology for space superiority missions.
- The program focuses on detecting and tracking fast-moving threats while improving manufacturing affordability and supply chain resilience.
Leonardo DRS has won an Other Transaction Agreement contract from the U.S. Space Force to further develop sensor technology intended to support space superiority and space control missions, the company said Tuesday.
Under the award, Leonardo DRS will continue developing sensor technology designed to detect, identify, track and target fast-moving threats in challenging conditions. The company did not disclose the contract’s value or a completion timeline.
A central focus of the program is affordability and manufacturability, according to Leonardo DRS. The company said the work builds on advances in sensing and processing technology, aiming toward designs that can be manufactured more efficiently, scaled to meet demand, and supported by a resilient supply chain.
“This award recognizes our innovative best-in-class sensor technology, proven experience and continued investment in space-based capabilities for critical national security programs,” said John Baylouny, President and CEO of Leonardo DRS. “These investments allow our company to push the boundaries of advanced sensing and targeting and implement scaled manufacturing to support national security priorities.”
“We are incredibly proud to support this vital space-based mission,” said Jerry Hathaway, senior vice president and general manager of Leonardo DRS Electro-Optical and Infrared Systems. “This award builds upon our current and next-generation affordable sensing technologies developed by our innovative space and sensor engineering teams and leverages our proven performance and expertise in sensor design and manufacturing.”
Leonardo DRS builds infrared sensing systems used by the U.S. government and allied nations across ground, sea, air and space missions. The company’s broader sensing, secure communications and laser technology portfolio also supports counter-drone systems, autonomous maritime fleet protection, and mounted and dismounted ground combat systems, according to the company.

Gold falls 2% as rising Treasury yields dampen demand

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Gold prices fell around 2% on Tuesday as elevated US Treasury yields increased the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets.
Spot gold declined to around $4,357 per ounce as of 1240GMT, its lowest level since Aug. 19, extending losses after dropping below $4,400 earlier in the session.
Silver suffered a steeper decline, falling 2.8% to $64.65 per ounce. Platinum and palladium also traded lower.
The selloff in precious metals came as US Treasury yields climbed to their highest levels since January 2025 amid mounting concerns that rising energy prices and tensions in the Middle East could fuel inflation.
Higher bond yields tend to weigh on gold and silver because the metals do not provide interest income, making yield-bearing assets relatively more attractive.
Expectations of tighter monetary policy were also bolstered by Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s remarks at the Jackson Hole symposium last week.
Warsh said the central bank would “have work to do” if policymakers were not confident that inflation was returning sustainably to the Fed’s 2% target.
Money markets are pricing in a 66% probability that the Fed will raise interest rates at its meeting later this month, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.
Investors are now awaiting a series of US labor-market indicators for further clues about the strength of the economy and the central bank’s policy path.
The ADP private employment report is due Wednesday, while the closely watched nonfarm payrolls report will be released Friday.
Stronger-than-expected employment figures could reinforce expectations of a rate increase and place additional pressure on precious metals, while signs of labor-market weakness could reduce tightening bets.

Massachusetts progressive Markey, a longtime Israel critic, expected to rout centrist challenger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:06:10 UTC
22:06:10 KST

Massachusetts incumbent and Israel critic Sen. Ed Markey, 80, is expected to handily fend off the more moderate 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton on Tuesday, in the state’s Democratic Senate primary.
Although polls project that Markey, a progressive stalwart, will retain his seat, this race began as a neck-and-neck battle between the old and new guard. Yet in contrast to many recent primaries, the junior candidate in this case is the more centrist of the two.
If current numbers hold, Markey could go from leading Moulton by just single digits two months ago, to trouncing him by 30 percentage points. The incumbent recently “opened a large lead,” with the University of New Hampshire’s Bay State Poll projecting a 63% to 28% victory. That’s a dramatic shift from June, when the survey estimated a 41% to 35% margin. Since then, according to Bay State, Moulton lost moderate support while Markey consolidated socialist and progressive backing.
The University of Massachusetts Amherst offered similar predictions, placing Markey far ahead of his competitor, 60% to 32%. Emerson College Polling, meanwhile, showed a comparable lead for Markey, with the incumbent at 60% and Moulton at 33%.
“At the end of the day, one of the reasons for Moulton’s flame-out is that he had no case to make other than ‘I’m younger than Ed Markey,’” Jeff Robbins, a Boston-based attorney and former Senate investigative counsel, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
“He wasn’t able to obscure that very well,” added Robbins, who also served as delegate to the United Nations Human Rights Commission under President Bill Clinton. He also began organizing rallies in support of Israel in 2012, during his time serving as chairman of the New England Board of the Anti-Defamation League.
Markey's long tenure in Congress
Markey began serving in the US House of Representatives 50 years ago, staying in that role until he was elected to the Senate in 2013. During his time in the House, he was a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, and in the Senate, he has voted for multiple resolutions aimed at cutting military aid and munitions sales to Israel.
Moulton, meanwhile, was born two years after Markey arrived on Capitol Hill. He has been serving in the US House since 2015 and has been critical of both the Democratic socialist agenda and the aging establishment, instead calling for “new energy, new ideas and leaders willing to put people over politics.”
He established the Serve America PAC in 2017 to support the campaigns of “military veterans, other service-driven candidates and next generation leaders” in the 2020 election cycle. The Boston Globe recently threw its support behind Moulton, calling for “new vision and vigor” in “an aging, ailing and deeply unpopular Democratic Party.”
Yet a recent New York Times piece described Moulton as a “rebel without a cause,” who has “tried to drift where he thinks the political winds are blowing.” One such drift relates to his breakup with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee last October, when he announced that he would be “returning AIPAC donations and refusing to accept any donations or support from them.”
“In recent years AIPAC has aligned itself too closely with Prime Minister Netanyahu’s government,” Moulton said. “I’m a friend of Israel, but not of its current government.”
Track AIPAC, a group that documents political spending by pro-Israel lobbies, declared in response that “returning AIPAC’s blood money is better late than never.” The group demanded that Moulton call the war in Gaza a genocide and “stop writing blank checks” to Israel’s “tyrannical regime.”
Citing Federal Election Commission records, Track AIPAC found that pro-Israel PACs have spent about $101,500 on Moulton over his career — a relatively modest amount for a six-term congressman..
“It is clearly the safe thing to do, if you are running for a nomination in the Democratic Party, to aggressively distance yourself from Israel,” said Robbins.
He described the situation as “reflective of the reality that we have seen play out in spades over the last year,” in which Democratic candidates are “running for the hills about AIPAC and treating it as a boogeyman.”
Not only was Moulton’s decision insufficient to recruit AIPAC detractors to his campaign, but it also rattled many members of the Jewish community.
Distancing from the organized Jewish community is a political asset
Political scientist Samuel Abrams at the time described the decision as “the moment when an ambitious, mainstream Democrat concluded that distancing himself from the organized Jewish community is a political asset, not a liability.”
“In today’s Democratic ecosystem, the act of rejecting traditional Jewish institutions has become a badge of progressive credibility,” wrote Abrams, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right public policy think tank.
David Frum, a writer for The Atlantic and former speechwriter for President George W. Bush, suggested that Moulton was “opening the door *just a little* to anti-Jewish feeling,” In other words, Moulton would seek to win his primary by borrowing some “Mamdani energy,” Frum added, referring to the popular progressive mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani.
“If you want to have a prayer of being elected in a Democratic primary in this country, you had better be able to say, ‘I don’t take money from AIPAC. In fact, I never heard of it before,’” Robbins said.
But he stressed Moulton’s 30-point lag in the polls has nothing to do with Israel and everything to do with his opponent’s political shrewdness and refusal to allow anyone “to run to the left of him.”
Markey is not new to staving off a younger, center-left candidate. In 2020, at 74, he defeated the then-39-year-old Rep. Joe Kennedy III — marking the first loss for a Kennedy in a Massachusetts election, according to the Cook Political Report.
If the current polls prove accurate, Tuesday’s race could “mirror Markey’s successful ‘peak-late’ approach to winning in 2020,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said in a statement. “Younger voters appear more likely than older voters to support Markey, suggesting the campaign did not create the generational divide Moulton may have anticipated.”
As for Moulton’s relationship toward American Jews, he has historically denounced hate crimes and voted for resolutions on antisemitism. He also condemned Claudine Gay, former president of his alma mater, Harvard University, when she refused to say that calling for the genocide of Jews would violate the institution’s code of conduct.
Prior to his rejection of AIPAC money, Moulton’s stance on Israel was fairly balanced, with consistent messages on Israel’s right to defend itself, alongside criticisms of the country’s military operations in Gaza and calls for expansions of humanitarian aid.
Moulton’s objections have paled in comparison to Markey’s stance, which has ranged from demanding an end to arms sales to accusing the country of committing war crimes.
Markey did condemn Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel as terrorism, continuing to deplore the “dark day” as “heinous” in a statement two years later. But in that same statement, he also stressed that “more than 65,000 Palestinians have lost their lives in the brutality of the war in Gaza” and called “to stop the bloodshed.”
Markey's position switch on Israel
However, the senator didn’t always disapprove of Israel.
“For a long time he was right there with the Jewish community,” Barry Shrage, a professor of practice at Brandeis University and the longtime former president of the Combined Jewish Philanthropies of Greater Boston, told JTA.
In fact, Shrage and Robbins recalled in a recent Boston Herald column that during a November 2012 Hamas-Israel conflict, Markey asked them to help him organize a pro-Israel rally. The event, they wrote, was “full of appreciation for the fundamental fact that Israel is surrounded by non-state and state actors committed to annihilating it.”
But less than two years later, the tides had turned. After winning a 2013 special election to serve out the remainder of John Kerry’s Senate term, Markey then faced a general election in 2014 for a full Senate term. That summer, Hamas rockets rained down on Israel again, and the military responded to the attacks, as it did in November 2012.
Robbins said that when he and his colleagues decided to organize another rally in support of Israel at the time, he reached out to Markey.
“He ducks. He dodges. He doesn’t return the phone calls. He doesn’t return the emails,” Robbins recalled. “He had calculated correctly that it was not in his interest to have anything to do with Israel anymore.”
Shrage echoed these sentiments, observing that “it turned out to be at least from a political standpoint, if not from a moral standpoint, the right path.”
“It’s not a surprise that Markey is separating himself from Israel in every way that he can,” he added.
Looking toward the future, Shrage said that he had some hope for a turnaround on Israel in the Democratic party if, perhaps, a recent progressive primary winner lost against a Republican in the general election. Some possible examples could include Senate candidates Angie Nixon in Florida or Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.
While Robbins agreed that a loss for El-Sayed could give a slight bump to Democratic supporters of Israel, he was pessimistic about the long-term ability to reverse the party’s increasing hostility toward the Jewish state.
“The only conceivable trigger for a walking back of this trend would be some massacre of Israelis so terrible that even the left would have to concede that Israel had the right to do what it did,” Robbins said.
“The problem with that is, it’s already occurred,” he added.

Israel Election 2026: What do Yousef Jabareen’s Joint Arab List and Mansour Abbas’ Ra’am stand for?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:05:59 UTC
22:05:59 KST

The reduced Joint Arab List and Ra’am are two of many parties vying for citizens’ votes in the election for the 26th Knesset, to be held on October 27.
The current Joint List, composed of Yousef Jabareen’s Hadash, Ahmad Tibi’s Ta’al, and Sami Abu Shehadeh’s Balad, was re-established in a reduced format recently after months of negotiations over whether and how the four main Arab parties would run. Polling has generally shown that the Arab parties would earn more seats in a joint run together.
Despite the four parties initially agreeing to work toward a complete Arab Joint List earlier this year, Ra’am chairperson Mansour Abbas has held off on joining the Arab alliance, hoping his party could be invited to the next coalition independently.
Although the reduced Joint List has left the door open for Ra'am to join it, there has been no indication that Mansour will do so ahead of next week's deadline to submit final party lists.
In an unprecedented move, Ra'am recently added former police official and MK Yoav Segalovitz to its list, after Segalovitz announced his departure from the Zionist, centerist Yesh Atid party.
Segalovitz will be the first Jewish candidate for the Islamist-conservative political party and is expected to receive the second slot on its slate.
The addition of a Jewish candidate to the Arab party’s list has been widely seen as a way for Ra’am to be viewed as a more viable coalition partner.
Abbas has appeared to pursue a more pragmatic approach to Israeli politics and coalition-building than the other major Arab parties, a strategy that could potentially make him a kingmaker if neither major Jewish political bloc can reach 61 seats on its own.
In the 25th Knesset, Ra’am and the Hadash-Ta'al alliance each held five seats. Currently, Ra’am is polling at about five seats, while the reduced Joint List is looking at approximately eight.
Additionally, Ra'am is the only Arab party that has ever joined a coalition, during the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021. Although Ra’am seeks to be part of the coalition again, most opposition parties in the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have rejected the possibility of forming a government with any of the Arab parties.
The three parties making up the Joint List are not ideologically identical.
Broadly speaking, Hadash can be defined as socialist-communist, Ta'al as occupying a position between Hadash and Balad, and Balad as the most explicitly Arab-nationalist of the three.
Hadash
Hadash, the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, is the successor to Israel's Arab-Jewish Communist Party and has historically emphasized Jewish-Arab partnership. The party traditionally reserves a slot for a Jewish candidate, currently MK Ofer Cassif, who is one of the party’s most outspoken voices and has publicly denounced Israel’s war in Gaza and has voiced support for South Africa's ICJ genocide case against Israel.
Ta'al
Ta'al, founded by Ahmad Tibi, occupies a more pragmatic position and is described as a party concerned with balancing participation in Israeli political institutions with protecting the Palestinian cause.
Balad
Balad is the most explicitly Arab-nationalist of the three reduced Joint List parties. Its longtime political demand has been for Israel to become a "state of all its citizens", rather than a state defined as Jewish. Current Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh said the concept was intended to cancel what he described as Jewish supremacy in legislation and the state's political structure.
Ra'am
Ra'am is rooted in the Southern Branch of the Islamic Movement and has taken the most institutionally integrationist approach of the four Arab parties. Rather than rejecting participation in Israeli political institutions, Abbas has argued that Arab citizens can use political participation and coalition negotiations to improve their communities.
Ra'am's primary political philosophy is more focused on practical integration and extracting benefits from government participation. Abbas has previously argued that Arab political participation should be used to address crime, housing, economic development and other problems facing Arab society.
The Joint List has not committed to a particular Jewish-led coalition. Jabareen previously told The Jerusalem Post that the party would seek progress toward a Palestinian state, equality for Arab citizens, action against organized crime and increased budgets for Arab society and local authorities.
Jabareen has also made clear that removing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich from power was a central electoral objective.
He also told the Post that the reduced Joint List's future support for an alternative government would depend on negotiations over the party’s key demands.
Abbas has, meanwhile, historically refused to commit himself to either the political Left or the Right, saying he would not rule out potential coalition partners, making Ra'am potentially more flexible in coalition negotiations than the reduced Joint List.
The Arab faction has been vocal in its support of a two-state solution, end to Israeli-Palestinian conflict
All four of the Arab parties support the establishment of a Palestinian state. Balad has historically opposed the idea of maintaining Israel's current political structure as a Jewish state and has instead advocated a state based on equal citizenship.
Jabareen has stated that the Joint List would push for renewed negotiations with Palestinian leadership to advance the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel.
Ra'am's Abbas has meanwhile pursued a more pragmatic political strategy, emphasizing Arab citizens' interests within Israel while also calling for Palestinian statehood and an end to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
What a vote for these parties is likely to produce
A vote for the Hadash-Ta'al-Balad Joint List is most likely to produce a larger Arab parliamentary bloc focused on Palestinian statehood, equality for Arab citizens, combating crime and increasing state resources for Arab communities.
A vote for Ra’am, by contrast, appears to be a vote for potentially integrating an Arab party into Israel’s next government.
The result is that neither Arab electoral option necessarily translates into a predetermined coalition. The Joint List is positioning itself as an opposition force seeking to replace the current government while using its seats to demand political concessions. Ra'am is leaving itself greater room to negotiate with potential coalition builders.
Keshet Neev contributed to this report.

Police officers also seized three vehicles believed to have been used by the suspects during their alleged arson and assault incidents.

Police condemned the "cases of violence, damage to property and religious symbols," and stated that additional arrests are expected.
The IDF also condemned the incident, saying that "attacks on religious institutions harm the residents of the region and security stability, and divert the attention of the security forces from counter-terrorism and defense activities."
"This mosque is 'only' the 11th mosque to be set on fire since mid-June, but the Israeli government continues to sell us the illusion that it is a 'handful of criminals.' It is clear that hundreds of terrorists, rabbis, ministers, and MKs like [Religious Zionist Party MK] Zvi Sukkot are just another completely accidental 'handful,'" Tag Meir stated in a condemnation of the suspected arsonists.
Tag Meir describes itself as an organization that "resolves to connect different groups in Israeli society in the battle to eradicate racism and violence in Israel," particularly aiming to denounce "price tag" attacks on West Bank Arabs by extremist settlers.
Israel Police requested an extension of their detention, and the investigation is ongoing.

Reporter's Notebook: Pro-Palestinian groups attacked an Israeli architect, he chose to create more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:05:44 UTC
22:05:44 KST

For two days now, I have been walking alongside Yehiel Tsuberi through the picturesque alleyways overlooking Lake Como, and it feels as though I am walking with an unofficial mayor. We are in the heart of what is known as the "Golden Triangle" - the point where the three main towns of Varenna, Bellagio, and Menaggio meet the inverted Y-shaped expansion of the lake. The view is breathtaking, but what fascinates me more than any ancient stone or reflection of mountains in the water is the way the Italians receive Yehiel.
Every few meters, someone stops us. A warm hug, a pat on the back, a wide smile, a flowing conversation in rich, emotion-filled Italian. They laugh with him, dance with him in spontaneous encounters, invite him for local wine. I asked him if these were distant acquaintances or colleagues, and he answered simply: "These are my friends. This is how I live, and this is how I work." We sat together at a table, shared simple, exquisite Italian food, and paused the recorder for a moment just to breathe in the silence and this rare human connection.
Yet beneath this pastoral tranquility and overwhelming local warmth, I was exposed to a jarring, almost unbelievable drama - a story of blind hatred that pursued Yehiel all the way here, and the surprising way he chose to confront it.
The October 7 Massacre and the fire that reached Como
Yehiel is no stranger to Italy. He completed both his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture at the renowned Politecnico di Milano, integrated into leading firms, and obtained Italian citizenship. He knows the local culture, language, and philosophy inside out.
When war broke out on October 7, Yehiel, his wife, and their three children were at the end of a trip to New Zealand, just moments before their planned return to Israel. Airspace closed, utter confusion reigned, and they landed temporarily in Italy. Italian friends opened their doors and hearts, helping them settle in. Yet the moment an opportunity opened - just four days later - Yehiel and his family boarded a flight straight back to Israel. The exact opposite of what many would expect from someone holding a European passport and a home abroad.
However, the war and hostility did not stay within the borders of the Middle East. Recently, Yehiel found himself at the center of an orchestrated, violent, and ugly campaign by pro-Palestinian groups in Italy. It began with an article addressing environmental aspects of his project in the leading newspaper Corriere della Sera, but quickly spiraled into a personal, venomous campaign against him due to his Israeli and Jewish identity: flyers, online videos, hate messages, and protests that reached into the heart of this pastoral region.
Three consecutive articles were published in the Italian press. The local mayor and numerous residents openly stood by his side, appalled that an individual was being boycotted and attacked solely for his nationality, in total contradiction to Italian law and spirit.
The personal confession and the secret kept from his mother
When I asked Yehiel how it feels when such hatred confronts all the goodwill and friendship he invests in Italy, I saw vulnerability alongside strength in his eyes. He shared an intimate, chilling moment: "It's terrifying. These groups are dangerous, and they have painted a target on my back. Until this article is published, my mother had no idea. She doesn’t know what I'm going through here. I kept it from her to spare her the worry. Now, feeling strong and secure in my path, it’s time to tell the story."
Faced with this threat, Yehiel refused to surrender to the natural fight-or-flight response. He chose what he calls the "Third Way" - pro-positivity.
"I will not run away, and I will not waste energy on wars of hatred," he told me as we stood facing the water. "Throughout the generations, whenever the Jewish people were persecuted, their response was always to do more: create more art, write more, build more, contribute more to the world. This attack didn't weaken me; it drove me to act with an intensity I hadn't known before. I delve deeper into my roots, write texts I haven't written in twenty years, and bring Israeli identity and mutual responsibility right into the heart of Italy."
The Jerusalem Continuum: Breathing life into the ancient village
This mission comes to life in the unique project Yehiel is currently building alongside his partner - his former university lecturer and employer, a respected Italian architect. The project is located in Bolognina, an ancient hamlet within the municipality of Perledo, just minutes from the lake's shores.
The structure is designed in organic terraces offering an unobstructed, 100% open view of central Lake Como. Within two months, it will be fully covered with soil and green vegetation, blending entirely into the wild landscape. Yet for Yehiel, the engineering framework is merely an outer shell. The true essence is what he calls the "Jerusalem Continuum."
"In architecture, there is the Athenian, rationalist continuum, which begins with geometric form," he explains. "And there is the Jerusalem continuum, the emotional one, which begins with the person and the human experience. I don't ask how many square meters I can sell; I ask what this village needs to come alive again. These villages are too quiet. My dream is to hear laughter and the sounds of children playing in the central piazza again; to bring tourists who buy cheese and wine directly from locals; to enable weddings from around the world, across all religions and genders, in the church and town hall of Perledo. To turn this project into a heart that pumps fresh life into this place."
Creator-entrepreneur: Calling on Italy to rediscover itself
Yehiel defines himself as a "creator-entrepreneur" - a concept that restores the architect to their Renaissance-era standing, when thinkers were also doers: artists, philosophers, and bridges between different worlds. He avoids aggressive, traditional marketing methods, relying instead on genuine human connection, shared passions, and a love for food, nature, and architecture.
As our tour neared its end, with the sun dipping behind the peaks of Como and painting the water in deep gold, Yehiel summarized the philosophy driving him:
"All of Western civilization rests on two historical pillars - Athens and Jerusalem, Rome and Jerusalem. The great Renaissance humanists, like Pico della Mirandola, learned Hebrew to understand Jewish scriptures, blending Jerusalem emotion with Western logic. You cannot sever one leg and expect the culture to stand. My message to Italians and Israelis alike is to believe in themselves, never surrender their identity, and not be afraid. We don’t need to fight the darkness - our task is simply to kindle more and more light."
