The Altalena’s enduring lesson: Israel must choose unity over division - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:05:43 UTC
22:05:43 KST

In a week that shook the nation, the rediscovery of the Altalena made headlines across Israel.
Seventy-eight years ago, as the Altalena went up in flames on the Tel Aviv beachfront, the Jewish people stood on the precipice of civil war. In today’s divided times, with another election on the horizon, the echoes of the Altalena serve as a stark reminder of the perils of internal strife and the urgent need for unity.
The Altalena affair marked a tumultuous chapter in the birth of the new nation of Israel. In the early days of the War of Independence, the fledgling state mourned the loss of 1,176 soldiers, while the invading Arab armies also suffered heavy casualties. The UN-brokered truce provided a crucial respite for both sides to regroup and strategize.
On June 20, 1948, amidst the ceasefire, the Altalena, chartered by Menachem Begin’s Irgun, arrived off the shores of Israel, laden with immigrants and arms. The conflicting accounts of the ship’s destruction – Begin’s claim of delivering arms to his fighters and David Ben-Gurion’s accusation of a coup attempt – underscored the deep divisions within the Jewish community.
The tense standoff at Kfar Vitkin escalated into violence, leading to casualties on both sides. As the Altalena made its way to Tel Aviv, the clash of ideologies and loyalties reached a boiling point. Ben-Gurion’s firm stance on maintaining government sovereignty and order set the stage for a tragic confrontation on the Tel Aviv beach.
The intense gunfire and mutual animosity that erupted on the beach reflected the deep-seated divisions and animosities that threatened to tear the young nation apart. The aftermath of the Altalena’s destruction left a scar on the collective memory of Israel, a wound that refused to heal.
Contrast between Ben-Gurion, Begin
Ben-Gurion’s controversial statement, “Blessed is the cannon that blew up the arms ship,” contrasted sharply with Begin’s call for unity and restraint, “There will never be a civil war.” Despite the loss of additional Irgun soldiers, Begin’s plea for brotherhood and unity resonated with a message of peace and reconciliation.
As we reflect on the lessons of the Altalena Affair in 2026, we must heed the call for unity and common purpose. In a time of political uncertainty and social discord, we must prioritize the well-being of our nation above all else. Regardless of our political affiliations, we must strive to bridge our differences with love and understanding.
As we approach the upcoming elections, let us remember the legacy of the Altalena and the importance of unity in times of crisis. Just as civil war was averted in the face of intense division, so too must we work towards healing our society and fostering a spirit of brotherhood and compassion.
In these challenging times, let us be guided by the light of unity and common purpose, ensuring that the lessons of the Altalena resonate in our hearts and minds for generations to come.
The writer is currently serving on reserve duty. He is the author of Heroes of Palmar: How one IDF Unit Revolutionized Combat Medicine in Gaza and a respected public speaker, licensed tour guide, and Jewish educator. For more information, visit www.booktuvia.com.

Trump Defends Hosting Russia at G20 as Europeans Voice Disapproval
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:04:14 UTC
22:04:14 KST

President Donald Trump has defended having Russia at the G20 finance meeting amid backlash from European officials who disapproved of the move.
“We’re going to see what happens, but we like getting along with everybody. One of the reasons that I’m so successful, I get along with everybody,” Trump told reporters when asked about the matter.
The U.S. hosted Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at the meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, on Monday where finance officials, central bank governors, and other international figureheads from 20 major economies gathered.
Russia has remained a member of the G20, but the country’s Finance Minister had been physically absent from the G20 summits since the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. European officials remain committed to isolating Moscow over the war.
This time, however, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with his Russian counterpart on the sidelines of the event in Asheville. Russia's Finance Ministry said the pair discussed Russia-U.S. cooperation on financial matters and interaction within the G20 framework.
A Treasury spokesperson told Axios that Bessent and Siluanov spoke about Trump’s Ukraine peace plan and economic growth. A source familiar with the matter is quoted as telling the publication that Bessent ruled out economic relief for Moscow as long as the war in Ukraine continues.
TIME has reached out to the U.S. Treasury and White House for comment.
The U.S. had not publicly announced Russia’s planned attendance ahead of the meeting.
European leaders were irked by the move, with some reportedly refusing to participate in a group photograph if Siluanov was included. Instead, Bessent posed for a photo alongside Siluanov on the sidelines of the summit.
European leaders, U.S. lawmakers voice disapproval over Russia’s inclusion
A spokesperson for Germany's Finance Ministry pointed TIME to remarks Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil shared with reporters at the summit, during which he said he “would have wished that the Russian Finance Minister is not received here at the G20 in the USA as a normal guest.”
Klingbeil added: “Every day, people die due to the Russian attacks. One cannot simply return to normality under those circumstances.” Klingbeil also expressed he had made clear to his fellow European officials he would not pose alongside Russia’s finance minister for the G20 group photo.
The final so-called “family photo” notably did not include Siluanov alongside the ministers and senior officials from other countries.
Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told Reuters he was unhappy to see Russia represented, although he recognized the right of G20 hosts to invite guests.
"We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them,” he said. "So for me it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia.”
Russia’s attendance also drew ire from lawmakers in the U.S.
Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said: “As Russia kills civilians in Ukraine, the White House hosts Putin's sanctioned Finance Minister on U.S. soil. The Trump Admin needs to pressure Putin and his cronies, not offer them a platform. With the House back in D.C., it’s time to pass Russia sanctions.”
A package of tougher sanctions on Russia—pushed by late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham—is making its way through Congress after it was approved by the U.S. Senate early August.
Democratic leaders on Monday jointly urged the White House not to wait to restart stalled Russia sanctions.
“Donald Trump already has ample authority to impose sanctions on the companies, individuals, and vessels propping up a Russian war machine that continues its deadly attacks on Ukraine. Congress does not need to greenlight new tariff authority for the President to impose those sanctions on Russia today,” Representatives Don Beyer of Virginia, Gregory Meeks of New York, Richard Neal of Massachusetts, said in a joint statement, alongside Senators Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Ron Wyden of Oregon.
U.S. officials have previously objected to Russia attending G20 meetings
In the past, U.S. officials have strongly opposed Russia’s participation in G20 meetings.
Asked in March 2022, whether Russia should be removed from the G20, Biden answered: “On the latter point, my answer is yes. That depends on the G20.” If members could not agree to remove Russia, Biden said Ukraine should be invited to attend and observe G20 meetings.
During a finance meeting with global senior finance officials in April 2022 in Washington for the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Spring meetings, former U.S. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and officials representing Britain, Canada, and the European Central Bank walked out when Siluanov began addressing the gathering virtually.
“My decision to work with others to leave when the Russian Finance Minister began to speak was intended to make clear Russia’s behavior so violates, is so offensive to international norms, we’re not willing to allow Russia to participate or to listen to what the Russians have to say,” said Yellen during a subsequent press conference.
The Administration underscored their opposition to Russia’s inclusion in international forums during another meeting with G20 finance ministers in Indonesia in July 2022.
“Russia’s actions are not the actions of a government that upholds international norms and laws. Representatives of the Putin regime have no place at this forum,” said Yellen.

Greenland’s Ice Sheet retreat sends grim message, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:01:35 UTC
22:01:35 KST

STOCKHOLM, September 1. /TASS/. Greenland’s vast ice sheet, which covers about 80% of its territory, is shrinking for the 30th consecutive year, according to the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland (GEUS).
Researchers describe these three decades of negative total mass balance as a "climate signal." The total mass balance last increased in the 1995/96 melting season, and it has been negative every year ever since.
According to the latest calculations from GEUS, during the 2025/26 melting season, the Greenland Ice Sheet lost approximately 173 billion tons of ice, and in 2024/25 the mass loss amounted to 130 billion tons. However, an even larger loss of 458 billion tons was recorded in 2012.
"A single year can be heavily influenced by the weather and therefore does not tell us much about long-term climate trends. That is why we researchers typically look at a 30-year period when we need to say something about the climate. The Greenland Ice Sheet has now experienced 30 consecutive years of overall shrinkage, and this strongly underlines the grim message: global warming is accelerating the melt and causing the Greenland Ice Sheet to shrink over time," Signe Hillerup Larsen, a researcher in the Department of Glaciology and Climate at GEUS, explained.

12 Israeli prison officers charged in death of Palestinian inmate, assaulting 8 others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:01:16 UTC
22:01:16 KST

Israeli prosecutors have filed an indictment against 12 Israel Prison Service personnel over the death of Palestinian security prisoner Thaer Abu Asab and the alleged assault of eight other inmates at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel.
The indictment, filed with the Be'er Sheva District Court by attorney Tal Cohen Adir of the Southern District Prosecutor’s Office, charges all 12 defendants with reckless homicide, aggravated serious bodily harm and multiple counts of aggravated assault causing actual bodily harm.
According to the indictment, one of the defendants was serving as the shift commander in the prison wing where the inmates were being held in November 2023 and was responsible for conducting prisoner counts. The other defendants served as prison guards, members of the Israel Prison Service’s Keter unit and a dog handler.
Prosecutors said that on the afternoon of November 18, 2023, Abu Asab asked the shift sergeant whether there was a “hudna,” or truce, in the war. His remark was relayed to the shift commander.
Before the evening prisoner count, the shift commander allegedly briefed the force about Abu Asab’s question and instructed the defendants to enter the cell during the count, an unusual move that prosecutors said was intended to demonstrate to the prisoners that there was no ceasefire.
According to the indictment, the commander told the officers that he would take responsibility for whatever happened. He also allegedly warned female prison officers who were present at the briefing not to enter the cell so that they would not be harmed.
The commander then led the force to the cell where Abu Asab and eight other inmates were being held. After beginning the prisoner count, he allegedly ordered the defendants to enter.
Prosecutors accuse the officers of acting together to beat and injure the inmates, using punches and kicks, with some also striking them with batons. The shift commander allegedly directed the assault and personally struck one or more prisoners.
After several minutes, the commander ordered the force to stop, according to the indictment. The officers then left the cell without reporting the alleged assault or any unusual incident during the prisoner count.
Abu Asab collapsed shortly afterward and lost consciousness. He was taken first to the prison clinic and later to Soroka Medical Center in Be'er Sheva, where he was pronounced dead.
According to prosecutors, Abu Asab died as a result of the blows he sustained, which caused severe injuries to his heart and respiratory system. The eight other inmates suffered significant injuries.
A separate count charges the shift commander and shift sergeant with obstruction of an investigation.
Prosecutors allege that after police opened an investigation, the shift sergeant instructed one of the guards to lie during questioning about the use of batons.
The shift commander is accused of using another guard, after he had already been questioned, to ask a female prison officer who had not yet been interviewed to coordinate her account with those of the defendants.
According to the indictment, the officer initially gave investigators a false account but later admitted that she had lied and provided her version of what happened.
All 12 defendants are charged with reckless homicide, aggravated serious bodily harm and multiple aggravated assault offenses. The shift commander and shift sergeant additionally face charges of obstruction of an investigation.

Gaps in NHS end-of-life care ‘denying ill children chance to die at home’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:00:58 UTC
22:00:58 KST

Seriously ill children are being denied the chance to die at home because the NHS in many parts of England is flouting its legal duty to provide the care needed to make that happen, critics say.
The widespread failure to provide at-home end-of-life care is forcing children who want to die at home to instead do so in hospital. Campaigners have described it as “cruel”.
The postcode lottery in palliative care means some of the almost 89,000 under-19s in England who have a life-limiting condition may not get their wish to die at home. Medical advances mean their numbers have almost trebled since 2003-04, and the complexities of their illnesses have increased. About 1,600 die each year.
Nick Carroll, the chief executive of the charity Together for Short Lives, said: “It is shocking that children with serious illnesses are waiting to leave hospital because the health and care system is not taking responsibility for their community care. To deny families the chance to spend precious moments together at home before their child dies is simply cruel.”
He accused the NHS of neglect for not ensuring that all children who want to can die at home with specialist teams including doctors, nurses and therapists on hand during their final days. “Families have every right to be upset as they continue to be overlooked,” Carroll said.
The NHS’s 42 integrated care boards (ICBs) are legally obliged under the Health and Care Act 2022 to ensure such care is provided around the clock at home when a child is dying. But 15 (36%) of them do not commission such services, freedom of information requests by Together for Short Lives show.
Only 13 (31%) were able to show they were doing so. Ten (24%) were providing some but not all of the care they should, and three (7%) said they were still organising such care.
The lack of provision means very sick children are ending up having to seek help at A&E or be admitted to hospital, some of whom then die there rather than at home.
Carroll said: “Our research shows that many families, simply because they live in a certain area, may be denied the chance to have their child die in the safety and comfort of their own home because ministers and the NHS have failed to put the right care in place. That should shame us all.”
He blamed the situation on ICBs’ precarious finances and on their “widespread assumption that palliative care is primarily for older adults, despite thousands of children across England living with life-shortening and life-threatening conditions”.
He said while an early draft of the government’s forthcoming “modern service framework” for palliative care specifically mentioned babies, children and young people, that reference was not included in the most recent version.
Sarah Buchan Cooke said it made a huge difference to the whole family when her son Dylan was able to die at home in January 2023, just before he turned four, after a long spell in hospital. He had Sandhoff disease, a rare neurodegenerative condition that left him needing 24/7 care.
Great Ormond Street children’s hospital and Haven House, a children’s hospice, both in London, supported the family in Dylan’s final days.
“At the end of his life it was a beautiful thing to have him at home. I can’t really imagine it any other way. I’m very aware of how fortunate we were,” Buchan Cooke said.
“It breaks my heart to think of other families in our situation not being able to have that same level of care and support. You’re the one who knows your child best. That ability to choose [between home and hospital] means everything.”
In March, Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England, highlighted that some children, including with life-limiting illnesses, were spending months and sometimes years in hospital because of a lack of “safe or appropriate” alternatives elsewhere.
Delays in arranging packages of care, a shortage of children’s social care placements and housing issues were “leaving children and their families in impossible situations”, de Souza said. Such children are disproportionately from poor backgrounds or ethnic minorities, data shows.
The NHS Alliance, which represents ICBs, did not respond directly to the findings. It agreed with the charity that access to end-of-life care for children should be universal but emphasised that commissioning such services could be “complex”.
Ian Perrin, the alliance’s assistant director of integrated care, said: “Every child with a life-limiting condition, and every family supporting them, should be able to access high-quality, compassionate palliative and end-of-life care, regardless of where they live.
“ICBs recognise the vital role that children’s hospices, community services, specialist teams and voluntary sector partners play in supporting children and their families. As the services are delivered through a range of organisations and arrangements vary across the country, this can make commissioning complex and difficult to compare consistently.
“However, ICBs remain committed to working with families, providers, charities and national partners to reduce unwarranted variation, improve access to care and ensure more people can receive care closer to home.”

Raytheon has completed a $50 million expansion of its manufacturing facility in Forest, Mississippi, increasing production capacity for electronic warfare and radar systems including the Next Generation Jammer Mid-Band programme, according to the company.
The 17,000-square-foot expansion is also expected to create 100 skilled jobs by 2028 and takes the total manufacturing space at the site to 445,000 square feet.
Raytheon announced completion of the project on 27 August, saying the new area will serve as a production, test and integration hub for Next Generation Jammer Mid-Band pods for the U.S. Navy and Australian government, alongside work on other airborne radar programmes. The company said the latest project forms part of a longer series of investments at Forest, where it has spent a combined $280 million on three expansions over the past decade.
Barbara Borgonovi, president of Naval Power at Raytheon, said: “Completing this expansion underscores our long-term commitment to Forest and the state of Mississippi. Together with state and local partners, we’re building the workforce, infrastructure and capabilities needed to boost production in support of critical national defense programs.” Raytheon said the Forest plant is now one of the largest defence manufacturing facilities in Mississippi, following previous additions including a 20,000-square-foot expansion in 2013 and a 50,000-square-foot radar production and testing facility completed in 2020.
The latest expansion will concentrate partly on the Next Generation Jammer Mid-Band, an airborne electronic warfare system developed for the U.S. Navy’s EA-18G Growler. Raytheon is responsible for the mid-band element of the wider jammer programme, with the pods intended to provide airborne electronic attack against radar and communications systems. Australia, which also operates the EA-18G, is included among the customers supported by production at the Mississippi site. Raytheon said the expanded facility will also support other airborne radar programmes, although it did not identify them individually in the announcement.
Mississippi Governor Tate Reeves said: “Raytheon’s expansion is not only a great economic development win for Mississippi but also an important investment in America’s national security. I’m incredibly proud of the role Mississippi plays in defending our nation and supporting the men and women who protect our freedoms. This project will build on our state’s proud legacy while bringing 100 high-skill jobs to Forest. It’s another big win for Scott County and Mississippi.”
U.S. Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said: “Rebuilding the American Arsenal creates more opportunities and more jobs right here at home. Today, our partners at Raytheon are expanding their manufacturing capacity and bringing 100 new jobs to Forest, Mississippi. These are critical jobs modernizing our military and supporting our troops – work Mississippi families can be proud of.”

New study sheds light on how DMT alters brain waves to induce the loss of self
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:00:36 UTC
22:00:36 KST

A recent study published in The Journal of Neuroscience found that the psychedelic drug DMT pushes brain activity away from its usual balanced state and toward a more random, less structured pattern. This shift in brain dynamics directly corresponds to the intense feeling of losing one’s sense of self, an experience often reported during psychedelic trips. The results provide a new biological lens through which to view the way human consciousness is constructed and maintained.
To understand the research, it helps to look at a concept from physics called criticality. A system at criticality sits right on the boundary between complete order and total chaos. The human brain normally operates very close to this critical point. Remaining near this boundary allows brain regions to communicate efficiently across both short and long distances.
This state produces a rich variety of brain wave patterns that scientists consider essential for healthy mental function and conscious awareness. When the brain functions near criticality, its electrical activity exhibits what researchers call long-range temporal correlations. This means that past electrical activity in the brain continues to influence future activity over extended periods. Rather than fading out quickly, the echoes of past brain waves linger.
This long-lasting echo effect provides a form of short-term biological memory. It helps humans maintain a coherent stream of thought and a stable sense of identity over time. Classic psychedelics like DMT profoundly alter human perception and brain function by disrupting these normal rhythms. People who take high doses often report a complete breakdown of their normal identity, a phenomenon known as ego dissolution.
During this experience, the boundary between the internal self and the external world appears to vanish. Researchers wanted to know exactly how a powerful psychedelic changes the physical behavior of brain waves to produce this sensation. The research was conducted by a team of scientists including lead authors Mona Irrmischer and Marco Aqil, who are affiliated with the Academic Center for Trauma and Personality in the Netherlands and Imperial College London, respectively. They aimed to see if changes in brain criticality could explain the intense subjective effects of psychedelics.
The research team combined data from two separate studies involving a total of 27 healthy adult participants. In both experiments, participants received an intravenous dose of DMT on one day and a placebo of saline solution on a different day. The researchers recorded the electrical activity of the participants’ brains using electroencephalography, or EEG. This technique involves placing small sensors across the scalp to detect the electrical impulses produced by neurons.
The brain recordings were taken before the injection and continued for twenty minutes afterward. Once the drug’s effects wore off, participants filled out questionnaires rating their subjective experiences. The researchers specifically focused on a question asking participants to rate the statement, “I experienced a disintegration of my usual sense of ‘self’ or ‘ego.'”
To analyze the brain wave data, the team measured the presence of long-range temporal correlations. They used a mathematical tool called detrended fluctuation analysis. This analysis produces a numerical value indicating how close the brain is to a critical state. A value near one suggests a highly structured, complex system near criticality, similar to what scientists call pink noise.
A value near one half indicates a highly random, structureless system far from criticality, comparable to the static of white noise. The researchers found that DMT caused a widespread drop in these numerical values across multiple frequency bands of brain activity. Specifically, the drug shifted the theta, alpha, and beta brain waves away from their normal critical state. Alpha waves typically relate to wakeful relaxation, theta waves are involved in memory, and beta waves are associated with active thinking.
Under the influence of DMT, the brain signals in these frequencies became less complex and more random, resembling the static of white noise. The team then took their analysis a step further to determine the exact nature of this shift. They applied a newly developed mathematical metric that measures the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory brain activity. Brain networks rely on a delicate balance between neurons that stimulate activity and neurons that suppress it.
The coordination of these two forces dictates how information flows through the brain. This measurement helps scientists distinguish whether a brain has shifted into an overactive, supercritical state or an underactive, subcritical state. The results showed that DMT pushed alpha and beta brain waves into a subcritical regime. In this context, the brain networks shifted toward a state dominated by inhibitory signals.
This subcritical state features high randomness but low complexity. The brain’s electrical signals lose their intricate, long-lasting structure and become more uniformly chaotic. Finally, the researchers compared these physical brain measurements with the subjective ratings provided by the participants. They discovered a direct mathematical relationship between the drop in criticality and the intensity of the reported ego dissolution.
The further the alpha and theta brain waves shifted away from criticality, the more intensely the participants felt their sense of self disintegrate. The researchers noted that the shifts away from criticality seen with DMT share similarities with brain states observed during general anesthesia and deep meditation. While anesthesia involves a loss of consciousness and psychedelics involve intense emotional experiences, they both feature a breakdown of the normal, self-reflective stream of thought. This suggests that a subcritical shift in alpha brain waves might be a biological marker for the loss of the conscious self.
The findings add a new layer of detail to the entropic brain hypothesis, a popular theory suggesting that psychedelics increase the overall randomness of the brain. The new data align with the idea that randomness increases under DMT. Yet they provide a new perspective by showing that this randomness corresponds to a drop in mathematical complexity. Rather than moving toward a highly organized but hyperactive state, the brain waves simply lose their intricate architecture.
The specific definitions of complexity and randomness used in this physical analysis warrant precise distinction. In some scientific contexts, a higher degree of randomness implies that a system is more complex. However, in this mathematical framework, the subcritical state induced by DMT is less statistically complex than normal waking consciousness. The brain’s electrical patterns become less predictable, but they also lose the rich structural variety that defines normal cognition.
The study measured brain activity using EEG sensors on the scalp, which primarily capture slower brain waves. It remains possible that faster brain oscillations, which are harder to measure with scalp sensors, behave differently. These high-frequency waves might shift into an overactive, supercritical state under the influence of DMT. Such an overactive state might account for the vivid hallucinations and rich emotional content of the psychedelic trip.
Future research could explore how these high-frequency brain waves respond to psychedelics. Scientists might also expand the analysis to specific moments during the psychedelic experience. Tying specific bursts of visual imagery to real-time changes in brain criticality could provide a more detailed map of how human consciousness temporarily unravels.
The study, “DMT-induced shifts in criticality correlate with self-dissolution,” was authored by Mona Irrmischer, Marco Aqil, Lisa Luan, Tongyu Wang, Hessel Engelbregt, Robin Carhart-Harris, Klaus Linkenkaer-Hansen, and Christopher Timmermann.

Kazakhstan enters a new political era after historic parliamentary reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:00:30 UTC
22:00:30 KST

Kazakhstan implemented a major parliamentary reform, replacing the former bicameral Parliament with a new unicameral legislature, the Kurultai. The new Parliament consists of 145 seats, with five parties securing representation.
Kazakhstan held its first parliamentary election on 23 August, electing 145 deputies to the country’s new Parliament, the Kurultai. The election followed a nationwide referendum in March, which approved a new Constitution that replaced Kazakhstan’s bicameral Parliament with the Kurultai. The new Constitution came into force on 1 July.
The name of the new Parliament also had historical significance.
“Kurultai is a concept and a name that is characteristic of the steppe culture and Turkic civilisation. It reflects our national identity and shows respect for history,” said Nurgazy Anuarbekov, Expert at the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development.
Under the new electoral system, voters cast their ballots only for political parties, which nominated candidates for the Kurultai.
Independent candidates could run for local Maslikhats, Kazakhstan’s equivalent of city and regional councils, but could not stand for the Kurultai.
According to the Kazakh Central Election Commission, five parties secured seats in the new legislature after crossing the 5% threshold.
The Adilet party won 71.17% of the vote and took 110 seats. Auyl received 6.26% and secured 10 seats, while Respublica won 5.56% and nine seats. Aq Zhol received 5.21% and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party 5.11%, with each securing eight seats.
All members of the Kurultai were elected for five-year terms.
“Over 127,000 people were added to the number of voters, meaning those who had reached voting age. This younger generation is also reflected in changing values and dynamics,” said Indira Aubakirova, Doctor of Law, Associate Professor at Maqsut Narikbayev University.
“We should not forget that Kazakhstan is located next to major powers such as Russia and China, as well as the Islamic world,” she added.
What happened at the first sessions of the Kurultai
Kazakhstan’s newly elected Kurultai held its first sessions on 28 and 31 August, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev appointed the country’s first vice president and nominated a new Speaker of Kurultai.
During the first session, Tokayev nominated Aibek Dadebai as Speaker of the Kurultai.
On 31 August, during the second session of the Kurultai, Tokayev appointed Erlan Karin as Kazakhstan’s vice president.
Karin, a former State Adviser and Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration, was one of two candidates proposed for the post.
The second candidate was Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, who retained his position as Head of Government.
The vice presidency had returned to Kazakhstan’s political system following the constitutional changes that introduced the new post.
Tokayev also announced that the Kazakhstan People’s Council would be formed in the second half of September.
“Already in the second half of September, the Kazakhstan People’s Council will be established. This will be the first higher consultative body in the history of Kazakhstan to embody the ethnic, regional, social and socio-political diversity of our country,” the President said.

From the mythical walls of Troy to the ancient vineyards of Bozcaada, Çanakkale's history stretches back thousands of years and still shapes daily life in this corner of Türkiye today.

Grown from native Çavuş, Vasilaki and Kuntra grapes, the island's wine is proof that here, history is still something you can taste.

Starship could create more debris than an anti-satellite test if it explodes in orbit
As SpaceX prepares for a test of the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, experts note the risk of an in-flight incident
5-MIN READ5-MIN
2
 Listen
As Starship, the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, gears up for an attempt to finally reach Earth’s orbit, experts say the risk of an in-flight catastrophe – and a cloud of debris – “needs to be of concern”.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX is expected to launch the Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy booster for the launch system’s 14th test flight and first orbital test flight later this month.
According to one aerospace expert, if the Starship’s upper stage explodes in orbit it could produce debris on a scale larger than previous in-orbit incidents, including an anti-satellite missile test.
During that test, in November 2021, Russia intentionally blew up a defunct Soviet intelligence satellite called Cosmos-1408.
Moriba Jah, a professor of aerospace engineering at The University of Texas at Austin, said the Russian test had detrimental consequences for the operation of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation.
He said if Starship were to explode in orbit, it could create a lot of debris that could become hazards to other objects as well as humans.
“If something like that happened in low-Earth orbit, it would be like the Russian anti-satellite test, but probably a few scales larger in terms of the amount of debris it would generate,” Jah said.

The dog was also diagnosed with heartworm, which typically takes at least six months to develop after a dog is bitten by an infected mosquito.

From Earth to table: following Uzbekistan's seasonal harvests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

Vineyards, melon fields, orchards and almond farms highlight how each season brings different harvests, local traditions and rural experiences for visitors exploring Uzbekistan.
Harvest seasons change the landscape throughout the year. Grapes ripen in the foothills near Tashkent, melon fields fill the plains of Jizzakh region during the hottest weeks of summer, while the warmer climate of Surkhandarya brings some of the country's earliest fruit harvests. For many visitors, following the agricultural calendar offers another way to experience rural life and the people who work the land.
Agriculture remains one of Uzbekistan's most important sectors, supplying domestic markets while exporting fresh fruit and vegetables to neighbouring countries and beyond. At the same time, more farms are opening their gates to visitors, combining traditional farming with agritourism and allowing travellers to experience seasonal harvests firsthand.
Vineyards beneath the foothills of Parkent
Just outside Tashkent, vineyards cover the gentle slopes of Parkent district, an area long associated with grape growing. Benefiting from mountain moisture and favourable climatic conditions, the region produces both table grapes and varieties destined for export.
Among them is the family-run vineyard, established in 2006 on what had previously been pastureland. Today, visitors can walk through the vineyards, learn about grape cultivation and observe harvesting as the season begins in mid-August.
Farm owner Iskandar Urmonov says the farm is gradually moving towards organic production.
“We want to turn our vineyards into organic vineyards. By applying different natural fertilisers, we want to make them organic. If we establish organic vineyards, the door to Europe will be open.”
Unlike many vineyards, these vines rely largely on natural moisture rather than irrigation.
“We grow grapes naturally, on rain-fed land, without irrigation,” Urmonov explains. “The moisture comes from snow and rain.”
Several grape varieties ripen one after another until late autumn. While Tayfi is mainly exported, Rizamat remains popular on the domestic market, and Kishmish can also be dried into raisins, extending the value of the harvest beyond the picking season.
Summer harvest in Jizzakh
Several hours to the south-west, the fields of Jizzakh enter one of their busiest periods of the year. During summer, melons and watermelons reach maturity under long days of intense sunshine, making harvest season one of the region's defining agricultural events.
Planting begins as early as March, with young plants protected beneath plastic covers before the summer heat arrives. By July and August, harvesting is underway and fresh produce is transported to markets and export destinations.
Farmer Bobomurod Mirsaliddinov says the region's climate gives local melons their distinctive flavour.
“The main advantage is that we have the 'Mirzachul Melon' brand. It is recognised because of its unique taste and flavour.”
He says producers are also testing new varieties while introducing more efficient farming methods.
“We want to move to the 'one field-one product' system, so buyers can easily find the crop they are looking for.”
Many harvests are exported to neighbouring countries, while others remain on sale throughout local markets.
Traditional knowledge also continues to guide buyers choosing ripe fruit.
“There is a saying passed down from our ancestors: 'Choose the light watermelon and the heavy melon,'” says local resident Alisher Azimov.
He also advises looking at the stem.
“If the stem is still fresh, the watermelon has just been harvested.”
Earlier harvests in Surkhandarya
The journey then continues south to Surkhandarya, where warmer temperatures allow fruit to ripen earlier than in many other parts of Uzbekistan.
Farmer Yusuf Meliboyev manages a ten-hectare orchard where apples, peaches, plums and grapes are grown together. Different apple varieties mature between June and October, extending the harvest over several months.
“The greatest demand is for Gala apples and then Fuji apples,” he says.
“Because the weather in Surkhandarya is very hot, our apples become especially sweet.”
The orchards use drip irrigation together with canal water when needed, while beehives are placed among the trees during flowering season to improve pollination.
Elsewhere in the region, almond cultivation has expanded rapidly in recent years. Large orchards now cover thousands of hectares, supported by water-saving irrigation systems designed for the dry climate.
Operations manager Suhrob Akabirov says efficient water use is essential.
“Every single tree has its own drip irrigation system.”
After harvesting, almonds are processed, dried and prepared for export. Around 70% of production is sold abroad, while the remainder supplies the domestic market.
Although each region follows its own agricultural calendar, the pattern remains closely linked to climate, water and local knowledge. Visiting during harvest season offers an opportunity to experience working farms, taste produce at its freshest and better understand the agricultural traditions that continue to support rural communities today.

Ukrainian serviceman Danyil "Surfer" Smyrnov killed in action weeks before he would have become a dad

Source: Danyil's wife, servicewoman Yeva "Yunha" Smyrnova
Quote from Yeva: "My Dania 'Surfer' has been killed. His continuation, our son, little Smyrnov, is due to be born in a few weeks. After that, I will take revenge."
Details: Danyil previously commanded an assault group in the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade. He took part in battles in Donetsk Oblast, including on the Avdiivka front. He was wounded in one of the battles and underwent rehabilitation.
After recovering, Smyrnov continued his service in the International Legion, part of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
Danyil's funeral will take place in Kyiv on 3 September. A memorial service will be held at St Michael's Golden-Domed Cathedral (8 Triokhsviatytelska Street). He will be buried at Lisove Cemetery.
What is known about Surfer?
In an interview with the Rada TV channel, Danyil said that he was only 16 when Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Many of the men in his family joined the Territorial Defence Forces, while he helped the military at a checkpoint near his home.
Later, the young man went to Lithuania to study. According to Danyil, his parents insisted that he get an education and learn English. But Danyil chose a different path for himself.
"After that, my uncle suffered a very serious injury in Bakhmut, and that's when I decided that I had to return from Lithuania immediately and help my uncle bring our victory closer. Because no one is going to do it for us," the serviceman said.
Danyil's alias was chosen for a reason – he had been a professional surfer and competed in surfing competitions.
Danyil's wife, Yeva, is an FPV drone operator with a combat unit in the Rubizh Brigade, where she goes by the alias Yunha. She also joined the armed forces at the age of 18.
Yeva said in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda: "I celebrated my 18th birthday in Vienna, bought a ticket to Kyiv, and from there, almost a week or two later, I signed a contract as soon as I had the opportunity. But in fact I had made the decision long before that. I had wanted to do it from the very beginning and understood that this was something I could handle."
Danyil and Yeva met during the war. Their son is due to be born in a few weeks.
"I understand that through my own efforts, I can at least contribute in some way to making sure that one day my children can live in a beautiful, peaceful country," Yeva said.

21:59:00 KST

In Japan, books written about Abe Shinzo, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, have become an industry unto themselves. However, most of them tend to reflect a partisan bias – perhaps fitting for such a controversial political figure, who once described himself as a “fighting politician.” At worst, his detractors have portrayed him as a would-be dictator, while his devotees have cast him as a messianic figure. More analytical assessments, meanwhile, have earned his foreign policy a strong reputation as pragmatic and realistic.
Yet, until recently, no full-length biography of Abe had been published, partly for the obvious reason that his death came so suddenly. The closest thing to a biographical study was Tobias Harris’ “The Iconoclast,” published in 2020. That has now changed. A more comprehensive biography on Abe by Hattori Ryuji, professor of Chuo University, was just released by Chuo Koron Shinsha.
Hattori’s short but detailed biography of Abe Shinzo could be regarded as a revisionist work in its own right, challenging the conventional wisdom – one that has also gained international currency – that Abe can be strictly characterized as a realist foreign policy thinker. Written by a diplomatic historian, the book focuses extensively on the foreign policy decisions made during Abe’s tenure as prime minister, drawing on newly declassified diplomatic documents that the author was able to access. Hattori’s conclusion is that, while Abe possessed a “remarkable strategic vision,” he was ultimately “an imperfect realist.”
Abe’s visionary thinking was an outlier in a country whose postwar prime ministers – almost all of them from the Liberal Democratic Party – were generally known for their conciliatory approach and skill in building intraparty coalitions. They were politicians more accustomed to working behind the scenes than articulating bold visions in public.
Among Abe’s many foreign policy conceptions, the most famous was the “Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” a strategic vision that not only articulated Japan’s broader interests in the world but also encouraged other governments to adapt to a new century in which the influence and potential of the Indo-Pacific region had become greater than ever before.
One of the clearest examples of the practical implementation of this vision was Abe’s promotion of free trade. His administration played a crucial role in bringing the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) to fruition after the United States withdrew from the original TPP, while also advancing the Japan-EU Economic Partnership Agreement and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) negotiations.
However, while Abe’s vision of maintaining a liberal international order fostered a strong affinity with the West, his misconceptions and even biases may have constrained his ability to pursue constructive diplomacy in East Asia. This, in turn, highlights the imperfect side of Abe’s realism. According to Hattori’s account, Abe’s eagerness to reach deals with Russia and China may have led him to surrender valuable leverage – and, perhaps more importantly, some of the legitimacy underpinning Japan’s position on the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China claims as the Diaoyu. In negotiations with Beijing, this resulted in a memorandum that could be interpreted as acknowledging that a territorial dispute existed, even though Japan’s official position has long been that no such dispute exists.
Abe also failed to achieve a breakthrough in his foreign policy toward the Korean Peninsula. He built a reputation as a champion of the Japanese citizens who had been abducted by North Korea. Yet he was ultimately unable to translate his hardline stance into a successful diplomatic strategy, nor was he willing to resort to inducements – the road not taken.
Also, vis-à-vis South Korea, Abe never developed a genuine rapport with any of his counterparts, unlike some of his successors. His determination not to give an inch on historical controversies constrained his ability to compromise, plunging bilateral relations into their worst state since the normalization of diplomatic ties. Nevertheless, when Abe did in fact cede ground – as in the agreement with South Korea that acknowledged Japan’s remorse over the “comfort women” while framing the settlement of the issue as “final and irreversible” – his failure to follow through on the resulting rapprochement allowed the issue to resurface once there was a change in government in Seoul.
The apparent failure of Abe’s East Asian diplomacy is all the more remarkable given the influence of his grandfather, Kishi Nobusuke. Kishi instilled in his grandson a mission to right the wrongs of the U.S. occupation – most notably, by revising the pacifist Constitution – as well as a commitment to a strong alliance with the United States, which Kishi himself helped lay the foundation for by revising the security treaty on more equal terms.
Although Kishi was said to have been influenced by Pan-Asianism and understood the importance of maintaining good relations with Japan’s neighboring countries, the premium he placed on Asian diplomacy was not inherited by his grandson. In fact, Abe seemed emotionally incapable of identifying Japan with the East rather than the West. This sentiment was manifested in a book he co-authored in 1996, when he was still a rising young conservative. The book warned: “Such an excessive attachment to the idea that ‘we are a part of Asia’ can become a dangerous spark that, from a policy perspective, risks triggering fatal mistakes.”
To understand the limits of Abe’s realism, it is necessary to identify the factors that prevented him from fully realizing the realist ideal. These included his historical perceptions, his strong concern with his political legacy, and his sense of duty and personal sentiment. Taken together, these characteristics suggest that Abe may be better understood as an idealist in the broader sense: a political actor who sought to translate deeply held beliefs and principles into political reality, regardless of the distance between his ideals and the circumstances he faced.
Hattori himself does not characterize Abe as an idealist. Nevertheless, his contribution in questioning the realist label so often attached to Abe as a foreign policy strategist represents a meaningful starting point for a more clear-eyed and constructive discussion of a politician who continues to evoke considerable passion and controversy.
More pages will be written about Abe, both domestically and abroad, in the years ahead. And with every page turned, the present will see how much of a mark he left on Japan.

Russia’s Starlink Rival Suffers Major Satellite Launch Failure

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:58:55 UTC
21:58:55 KST

Russia’s attempt to rapidly develop an alternative to Starlink has suffered another setback after all 16 Rassvet satellites launched in July failed to reach their intended operational altitude, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
None of the satellites in the second batch, launched on July 19, had reached the anticipated altitude of 550 kilometers (342 miles) as of Aug. 31, according to satellite-tracking data cited by ISW.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Many remained between 300 and 400 kilometers (186-249 miles), while some were experiencing orbital decay. At least two were reportedly heading toward reentry into Earth’s atmosphere.
ISW noted that these satellites were also well below the reported intended operational altitude of 870 kilometers (541 miles) for the Rassvet system.
Why lower orbits pose a problem
Satellites in lower orbits have shorter operational lifespans because of increased atmospheric drag and greater fuel consumption, ISW said.
It remains unclear how long the lower-altitude satellites will stay in orbit, but they are unlikely to operate for as long as Russia had projected.
Of the first batch of 16 Rassvet satellites launched on March 24, only 12 had reached the anticipated altitude of 550 kilometers as of July 31 and remained there as of Aug. 31.
Those 12 satellites provided Russian forces with two daily connectivity windows over Ukraine, lasting up to 90 minutes each.
Moscow rushing to replace lost Starlink access
ISW assessed that Russia is likely rushing to deploy Rassvet satellites after losing access to Starlink communications over Ukraine on Feb. 1.
Graham’s ‘Sanctions Bill From Hell’ Against Russia Hits House Roadblock
The shutdown forced Moscow to rely more heavily on Rassvet and likely accelerated its planned timeline for creating a fully operational Starlink alternative.
The apparent failure of the entire second batch to reach the required altitude suggests Russia was unprepared to accelerate deployment at this pace and will probably face further delays, ISW said.
Even a partially functioning Rassvet constellation could still threaten Ukraine. Limited satellite communications may allow Russian forces to conduct more precise attacks using remotely controlled unmanned systems and improve battlefield connectivity during available coverage windows.
Russia would need hundreds of satellites
Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, which is developing Rassvet, has said Russia plans “dozens” of additional launches to deploy “hundreds” of satellites.
Ukrainian presidential adviser on defense technologies Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov estimated in May that Russia would need at least 200-300 operational satellites to establish stable, around-the-clock connectivity over Ukraine.
ISW said Russia is unlikely to achieve that goal soon because it depends on the costly and scarce Soyuz-2.1b medium-lift launch vehicle.
Russia has reportedly conducted only six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches across all state and commercial missions since 2022. At that rate, Russia could launch no more than 128 Rassvet satellites over four years, with no guarantee that all, or even a minimum effective quantity, would become operational.
Only 37.5-percent of the Rassvet satellites that had launched as of August 2026 had reached sustainable operational altitudes, ISW said.
Ukrainian attacks would cause further delays
Ukrainian assaults against Russian satellite production and launch infrastructure would further disrupt the program.
Ukraine targeted the Progress Space Rocket Center overnight on Aug. 14-15, a facility that manufactures Soyuz launch vehicles, according to ISW.
Ukrainian forces also attempted to attack the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on Aug. 23. Russia reportedly launched both Rassvet batches from the site.
ISW said Ukraine’s ability to threaten both launch-vehicle production and scarce launch infrastructure could further delay Russia’s effort to build its own Starlink alternative for military use in Ukraine.

Mindfulness may lower blood pressure in just 8 weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:58:41 UTC
21:58:41 KST

Mindfulness may lower blood pressure in just 8 weeks
- Date:
- September 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
- Summary:
- Mindfulness, gratitude, and optimism training may improve blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart-health measures within just eight to 12 weeks. The strongest programs paired daily practice with regular reinforcement, suggesting that improving psychological well-being could become another tool for protecting cardiovascular health.
- Share:
Simple practices such as mindfulness, gratitude journaling, and optimism training may improve several markers of cardiovascular health within a matter of weeks. A recent study found that these positive psychology interventions were consistently associated with improvements in blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart disease risk factors. Because some of the benefits appeared to be connected with healthier behaviors, including better eating habits and increased physical activity, the researchers said continued reinforcement may be necessary to maintain progress over time.
Rosalba (Rose) Hernandez, a professor of social work at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, led the research team. The group reviewed results from 18 randomized controlled trials that tested positive psychology and mindfulness interventions designed to improve mental or physical health.
How the Heart Health Programs Worked
The programs varied widely in how they were delivered. Some relied on structured phone sessions, journaling paired with brief check-ins, or digital tools such as apps and text messages. Others involved interactive in-person group meetings or hybrid approaches that combined face-to-face activities with online tools and virtual sessions.
Most programs included weekly sessions along with activities participants completed at home to reinforce what they had learned. The majority lasted between six and 12 weeks.
The studies generally enrolled groups of 50-200 adults who already had elevated cardiovascular risk, including uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure, or other health conditions. Participants were usually in their late 50s to mid-60s. Among studies that reported gender, women made up 35-55% of the participants.
"In hypertension and postacute coronary syndrome cohorts, mindfulness-based programs delivered over an eight-week period reduced systolic blood pressure and lowered inflammatory markers such as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and fibrinogen," said Hernandez, who is a Fellow of the American Heart Association. "A 12-week spirituality-based digital intervention achieved one of the largest reductions -- reducing systolic blood pressure measured with a standard cuff by 7.6 points, and central systolic pressure -- which is measured in the aorta as it leaves the heart -- by 4.1 points."
Finding the Right "Dose" of Positivity
Previous research on positive psychology often did not clearly establish how frequently people needed to practice these techniques, or for how long, to gain health benefits, Hernandez said. Her team wanted to determine what level of participation was most consistently associated with improvements in cardiovascular health.
The review showed that programs with more frequent participant contact tended to produce the most reliable physiological benefits. Hernandez said this finding highlights the potential value of incorporating positive psychology strategies into long-term cardiovascular treatment and prevention.
The strongest behavioral changes came from an eight-week WhatsApp-based program that paired weekly sessions with daily microtasks. Participants were encouraged to become more physically active, improve their diets, and take their medications as prescribed.
Another program that incorporated motivational interviewing increased cardiac patients' activity by 1,800 steps per day while also improving medication adherence. By comparison, the mindfulness programs improved physical activity and diet, but did not produce the same medication adherence benefit, according to the study.
"The therapeutic dose that was most consistently linked with improvements in blood pressure, inflammation and endothelial function was daily practice reinforced by weekly sessions over eight to 12-week periods," Hernandez said. "Therapeutic dosing typically involved high-frequency dosing over this time period to obtain short-term physiologic benefits, while ongoing less-intensive contact may be needed to sustain behavioral change."
Mental Health as Part of Heart Care
The study was published in the journal Cardiology Clinics. Co-authors included University of South Florida social work professor Soonhyung Kwon; Alyssa M. Vela, a professor of surgery and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine; and Katharine S. Edwards, a professor of cardiovascular medicine and of psychiatry and behavioral medicine at Stanford Medicine.
"The findings of this study further point to the importance of attending to mental and behavioral health for cardiovascular disease prevention and cardiovascular health optimization," Vela said. "This speaks to the need for routine screening and integration of cardiac behavioral medicine to allow for access to important interventions."
The findings contribute to a growing body of evidence connecting psychological well-being with cardiovascular protection. Traits and experiences such as optimism, positive affect, and gratitude have increasingly been associated with healthier hearts.
Earlier Research Linked Optimism to Healthier Hearts
The new work builds on a prior study led by Hernandez, which found that people with the highest levels of optimism tended to have healthier hearts. That research was published in the journal Health Behavior and Policy Review.
That earlier study was funded by the National Institutes of Health and the National Center for Research Resources. It was co-written with preventive medicine professors Kiarri N. Kershaw, Juned Siddique and Hongyan Ning, all of Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine; preventive medicine and epidemiology professor Donald M. Lloyd-Jones of Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine; psychology professor Julia K. Boehm of Chapman University; social and behavioral sciences professor Laura D. Kubzansky of Harvard University School of Public Health; and Distinguished Professor of Epidemiology Dr. Ana Diez Roux of Drexel University.

Materials provided by University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Original written by Sharita Forrest. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

Oil rose in price amid a new escalation in the Middle East
Kyiv • UNN
Brent rose to $92.14, while WTI rose to $87.92 per barrel. Markets reacted to the resumption of hostilities between the United States and Iran.
Oil prices rose by approximately 2% on Tuesday, as the resumption of hostilities between the United States and Iran in the Middle East renewed concerns about supply disruptions from the oil-producing region, UNN writes, citing Reuters.
Details
Brent crude oil futures rose by $1.65, or 1.82%, to $92.14 per barrel by 12:01 GMT (15:01 Kyiv time), while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose by $2.16, or 2.52%, to $87.92.
At this level, oil contracts recouped most of the losses incurred last week amid the renewed escalation of the conflict in the Middle East.
On Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened further strikes on Iran after the first exchange of direct attacks between the countries since late July, raising tensions in a conflict that recently developed into an economic confrontation.
"The exchange of 'tit-for-tat' missile strikes between the U.S. and Iran confirms the view of those who believe that even if this is not an 'eternal war,' this conflict will continue and continue," said PVM analyst John Evans.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Tuesday that his country would immediately reciprocate if the United States returned to its commitments under a temporary peace agreement signed in June.
The efforts of mediators, including Qatar and Oman, to reach an agreement on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, through which about one-fifth of the world's oil and LNG supplies were transported before the war began in late February, have so far proved unsuccessful.
"The renewed military action between the U.S. and Iran has raised concerns about prolonged disruptions to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz," said Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen, adding that the absence of further buying suggests that the market is betting that supplies will not be disrupted more than they already have been.
Two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by unidentified projectiles within several minutes of each other on Monday while transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
The number of visible commercial vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday was approximately five per day, according to Kpler data. None of the five vessels was a crude oil tanker.
"The hopes that emerged last week for the future resumption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have suffered a serious blow. The question is also whether, if the escalation resumes, the unofficial movement of vessels through the strait can continue unhindered," Commerzbank analysts wrote.
Analysts surveyed by Reuters in August expected oil prices to remain above $80 per barrel in 2026, as shipping disruptions continued.

Leonardo DRS adapts counter-drone system for use at sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:57:14 UTC
21:57:14 KST

- Leonardo DRS announced the Maritime-Mission Equipment Package, adapting its ground-based counter-drone technology for use on ships.
- The system combines radar, electro-optical sensors, electronic warfare and optional kinetic weapons, and is rated Technology Readiness Level 9.
Leonardo DRS has adapted its ground-based counter-drone technology for use at sea, packaging it into a system called the Maritime-Mission Equipment Package, or M-MEP, the company said in a social media announcement.
The M-MEP is built to detect, identify, track and defeat drones threatening ships, using a modular design intended to work across a range of vessel sizes. Leonardo DRS said the system can be deployed on manned or unmanned surface vessels starting at 14 feet in length and larger.
“As unmanned aerial threats continue to grow in range, autonomy, and scale, maritime operators need protection that is both agile and mission ready,” Leonardo DRS said. “The Maritime-Mission Equipment Package (M-MEP) from Leonardo DRS is designed to bring advanced Counter-UAS protection to the maritime environment through a platform-agnostic, rapidly integrated solution.”
The system combines active and passive radar with electro-optical and infrared sensors to detect single or multiple incoming drones, according to the company. For jamming, the M-MEP uses GPS and 4G/5G electronic warfare systems designed to disrupt drone guidance signals once a threat has been confirmed.
Leonardo DRS said the M-MEP can also carry kinetic weapons to physically intercept drones when configured to do so, an option the company said reduces reliance on more expensive missile systems against small, low-cost drone threats. The company rates the system’s detection and engagement technology at Technology Readiness Level 9, the U.S. government’s designation for a system proven through successful operational use.
The M-MEP is built on Leonardo DRS’s broader Mission Equipment Package product line, which the company has developed for uncrewed surface vessels used in naval operations. The maritime variant is adapted from ground-based counter-drone systems the company has fielded for the U.S. military.

Explosive devices damage power lines near German coal plant
At least one device detonated, but others failed to go off. No one was hurt and there was no major blackout in the area
Improvised explosive devices were used on Tuesday in a sabotage attack near a coal-fired power plant in Germany, with several electricity lines damaged and supply briefly interrupted, officials said.
Several makeshift bombs were found around 8am local time at the Preilack substation, which distributes power from the nearby Jaenschwalde plant that runs on lignite and also burns rubbish, a police spokeswoman said.
At least one of the devices detonated but others failed to go off, she said, adding that no one was hurt and there was no major blackout in the area, about 100km (60 miles) southeast of Berlin.
Power plant operator LEAG said in a statement that “an attack was carried out on the Preilack substation, through which the electricity generated at the Jaenschwalde power plant is fed” into the grid.
LEAG said there was a “technical failure” in a unit at the power plant, and a possible connection with the incident was being investigated.
Grid operator 50 Hertz claimed that unidentified perpetrators damaged several lines in its grid.

Blockade succeeds where sanctions failed as Iran oil exports stall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Blockade succeeds where sanctions failed as Iran oil exports stall
LONDON, Sept 1 - For the first time on record, Iran has gone about seven weeks without shipping meaningful crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz, as a U.S. naval blockade succeeds where years of sanctions failed by cutting off one of Tehran's main sources of foreign-currency earnings.
Unlike previous sanctions campaigns, when Iranian crude continued reaching buyers despite restrictions, the current blockade has stopped fresh crude cargoes reaching China, Tehran's only major remaining oil customer, increasing pressure on government finances and foreign-currency reserves.
Since the U.S. reinstated its blockade on Iran on July 14 as part of their six-month conflict, no Iranian crude cargoes have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz to China, according to Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers.com.
As a result, Iran can only sell crude to China from floating storage in Asia, which it cannot replenish as crude accumulates aboard tankers inside the strait.
"Even at the height of maximum-pressure sanctions in 2019-20, some Iranian crude cleared Hormuz every single month; at no point did outbound flows fall to near-zero for a sustained stretch as they have since mid-July," Vortexa analyst Claire Jungman said.
Iran loaded about 220,000 to 255,000 barrels per day of crude oil and condensate in August, according to Vortexa and Kpler estimates, down from roughly 740,000 bpd in July and about 2 million bpd in March.
The collapse in exports is draining one of Iran's main sources of foreign-currency income and could force Tehran to finance spending by printing money, risking even higher inflation, Kpler analyst Homayoun Falakshahi said.
The International Monetary Fund estimates Iran's inflation rate at nearly 70% this year, the world's third-highest after Venezuela and Sudan.
Last week, Washington sought to increase the pressure by threatening countries that continue trading with Tehran, while stopping short of immediately imposing penalties.

THE BLOCKADE AND BEYOND
Iran currently has 29 tankers inside the strait carrying 36.11 million barrels of crude, TankerTrackers.com co-founder Samir Madani said.
The U.S. blockade does not extend along Iran's entire coastline. It sits farther south, between the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, where U.S. Navy vessels vet ships departing from and approaching Iranian ports.
Beyond the blockade zone, dozens of Iran-linked shadow-fleet tankers remain active, with 51 vessels operating in the Gulf of Oman and another 81 making deliveries in Asia or waiting off Malaysia, according to David Tannenbaum of Blackstone Compliance Services.
Reuters could not independently verify those figures.
IRANIAN CRUDE STILL FOR SALE, BUT FOR HOW LONG?
Iranian crude remains openly available, with cargoes for September and October delivery to China being offered, traders said.
They said available volumes are lower than for July and August because floating storage outside the Gulf is shrinking as no fresh supply arrives.
Iranian crude in floating storage west of the blockade line rose to 41.7 million barrels by August 26 from 35.5 million at the end of July, while total Iranian crude afloat fell to 107 million barrels from 135 million, according to Vortexa data.
"China can grab whatever's floating around in their neck of the woods, but that's about it for now, really," TankerTrackers co-founder Samir Madani said.
Once sold, empty tankers cannot return to Iranian ports because of the blockade, leaving vessels idle offshore.
Vortexa's Jungman said 27 sanctioned tankers linked to Iran's oil trade are currently waiting off Sri Lanka in ballast, unable to return to Iran. REUTERS

Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said in an interview aired on 31 August that Russia remains "more than a strategic partner" because existing treaties make the two countries allies, adding that the change in the government program's wording should not be interpreted as an end to that relationship.
Mirzoyan was responding to Armenia's new 2026–2031 government program, which replaces the "strategic ally" and "strategic partnership" language used in the previous five-year plan with a commitment to "transform and deepen" relations with Russia. The previous program referred to an "Armenian-Russian strategic alliance" and pledged to strengthen "allied relations and strategic partnership" with Moscow.
Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan explained on 27 August that keeping the strategic-partnership language would raise questions about why Russia and the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization had failed to fulfill their security obligations to Armenia in 2022.
Armenia has removed the language of alliance from its government program without ending the treaties, CSTO membership, or energy ties that still bind it to Moscow.
Azerbaijan attacked Armenian territory near Jermuk in September 2022, striking positions inside sovereign Armenia rather than the disputed Nagorno-Karabakh region. Yerevan invoked Article 4 of the Collective Security Treaty, the clause treating an attack on one member as an attack on all, and requested assistance. The alliance sent a fact-finding mission but no troops. requested military assistance. Armenia froze its participation in the CSTO at all levels in 2024, stopped financing it, and has boycotted its summits and military exercises.
Why the alliance frayed
Armenian trust in Moscow had deteriorated further by September 2023, when Azerbaijan retook Nagorno-Karabakh after a brief offensive and Russian peacekeepers deployed to the region did not intervene. Armenian officials accused them of failing to protect the enclave's population.
Yerevan has since moved closer to the European Union. In March 2025, Armenia's parliament passed a law to launch the accession process, though Pashinyan has said any actual membership would require a referendum, and Armenia has not applied to join.
What still ties Armenia to Russia
Even so, Armenia remains heavily dependent on Russia for energy. Russia supplied the bulk of Armenia's natural gas in 2021, and Armenia imports all of its nuclear fuel from Russia, leaving it effectively reliant on imported fuel for nearly 70% of its electricity, according to the International Energy Agency. The country remains a member of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union.
Mirzoyan acknowledged that strains had emerged in recent years, citing statements by Russian officials, coverage in Russian media, and Moscow's restrictions on imports of Armenian goods. He called for relations to be made "healthier" and returned to a course of "mutual respect," and said Yerevan did not want a "war of words" with Moscow. Pashinyan said on 1 September that he expected to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin later that day in Bishkek.

Summer favorite Saaremaa drew more tourists this season
While the tourism sector still has room for improvement, Saaremaa businesses and officials say the Western Estonian island has seen more visitors this summer.

Eva and Thomas, two Polish cyclists, began their trek in Tallinn two days ago.
"Yesterday we were in Hiiumaa, and we're going to Latvia and Lithuania," said Eva. "And we are going to finish in Suwalki."
Veiko, an Estonian who also traveled from Tallinn, said he takes a similar cycling trip each summer, typically riding more than 100 kilometers in both Hiiumaa and Saaremaa.
"I rode 30 yesterday, today will be 60, and we'll see from there," he said.

"We were already seeing a nice flow of people at the beginning of May," Kuuse recalled. "This season has been very different from the previous two — it started early and there have been a lot of foreign tourists."

Three Dutch nationals remain missing after deadly Nepal floods
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Rescue workers in Nepal are still trying to trace three Dutch nationals among more than 4,000 people reported missing since the devastating floods that swept through the border region with Tibet last week.
They include two tourists, 29-year-old Christiaan Berghuis from Nijkerk and 51-year-old Maaike Moolhuijsen from Haarlem, who were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred Tibetan mountain, when the disaster struck.
Their names were confirmed by the family support organisation Names de Familie. The third missing person is a Dutch woman who emigrated to Nepal, the foreign affairs ministry said.
The two visitors were part of a group of 80 people who were travelling from Kathmandu to Mount Kailash when a glacier in the Himalaya collapsed on Wednesday morning, causing the Bhote Koshi river to burst its banks and flood a large area with water and mud.
A spokesman for the Isha Foundation, which organised the trip, told RTL Nieuws the immigration office where the travellers were waiting at the time appeared to have been inundated.
Death toll passes 1,000
“At the moment nothing is known about the conditions of the people who were in the immigration office,” the spokesman said. “We are in constant contact with their families and are supporting them in every way possible.
“The last contact we had with our volunteer who was in charge of the group was around nine minutes before the flood happened.”
The Isha foundation was set up in 1992 by Jaggi Vasudev, an Indian yoga teacher better known by the name of Sandhguru.
A spokesman for the foreign affairs ministry said: “Their families in the Netherlands have been unable to contact them. The fear is that they were in the affected area at the moment of the flood.”
The death toll from the floods passed 1,000 on Tuesday as rescue workers continued to pull bodies from the water further downstream.
Altogether nearly 4,000 people are still unaccounted for in Nepal, as well as 546 in Tibet. They include around 900 hydropower workers who have been trapped in flooded tunnels for nearly a week.
