Press review: US-Iran war resumes as EU readies to fund Ukrainian conflict beyond 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 1. /TASS/. The US and Iran resumed hostilities after a one-month lull; the EU is preparing to fund Ukraine beyond 2028; and the recap of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s first day in Bishkek at the SCO summit. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: US-Iran war resumes after month of lull in hostilities
The US has blocked all attempts by the Persian Gulf states to resolve the conflict with Iran. In the early morning hours of August 31, the two sides clashed once again: the Americans attempted to destroy missile launchers on Larak Island, prompting the Iranian army to target US military bases in Jordan and the UAE. Washington justified its actions by claiming that the Iranians were allegedly preparing to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, the US is intensifying economic pressure on Tehran and its partners. The US Treasury Department stated that it would impose secondary sanctions every week for financial transactions with Iran.
Washington’s attack has effectively undermined the efforts of mediators from Oman, Qatar, and Pakistan to achieve a regional settlement, international relations expert Yelena Suponina told Izvestia. The reason for such steps lies in US President Donald Trump’s lack of a long-term strategy, Konstantin Blokhin, a leading researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Center for Security Studies, noted. According to him, the US leader "flits" from one foreign policy agenda to another just to be remembered as one of the greatest presidents in US history. As a result, the Americans are unable to focus solely on the Middle East, creating chaos with their actions.
The White House’s economic pressure could prove more dangerous than direct military clashes, for which Tehran has historically been prepared, Suponina added. In turn, Blokhin emphasized that Washington will certainly not succeed in alienating China, the main importer of Iranian oil and, at the same time, a partner in BRICS and the SCO. Trump has already imposed restrictions on Chinese banks. The international community is still far from reaching a consensus in this standoff: Tehran will continue to receive the necessary goods, services, and political support through third countries anyway, the expert concluded.
This latest escalation in the Middle East highlights the failure of diplomatic efforts and Washington’s return to a force-based approach. While this strategy is unlikely to force Iran to capitulate, it will undoubtedly destabilize global energy markets and intensify the pre-election struggle within the US.
Media: EU readies to fund Ukrainian conflict beyond 2028
Brussels hopes to integrate Ukraine’s defense-industrial complex into the European defense industry in the long term. The EU intends to continue bringing the defense sectors closer together and expanding joint projects with Ukraine. The two parties are already harmonizing standards, developing joint production, and preparing the groundwork for continued support for Kiev beyond 2028. However, the Russian Foreign Ministry views these plans as an attempt to extend the conflict. Meanwhile, following CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent visit to Moscow, Kiev has once again begun discussing potential contacts on peace as early as September.
The policy of integrating the defense sectors of the EU and Ukraine has been established in the bloc’s documents for years, but Brussels has recently accelerated the process. In the roadmap for defense readiness through 2030, Kiev is considered part of the European defense industrial base. "The European Commission is actively working to deepen Ukraine’s integration into the European defense technology and industrial base, as well as expand practical cooperation between Ukrainian and European defense industries," a spokesperson told Izvestia.
Meanwhile, the Russian Foreign Ministry is highlighting Brussels’ longer-term plans, in particular, the Ukraine Reserve financial mechanism totaling approximately 100 billion euros in the draft EU budget for 2028-2034. "We view this move as yet another deliberate attempt to prolong the conflict in Ukraine," Russian Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Department Director Vladislav Maslennikov noted.
At the same time, a diplomatic settlement to the conflict remains stalled. The EU is still not directly involved in the negotiation process, although discussions on the need for its own contacts with Moscow have been underway within the bloc since the beginning of the year. "It's clear that the EU's negotiations aim to give the Ukrainian armed forces a respite from combat operations, to save the Zelensky regime by any means necessary, to preserve Ukraine as a springboard for ‘containing’ Russia, and, in essence, to create constant threats to our security," Maslennikov stressed.
Meanwhile, the US goal is to secure concessions from Russia so that Moscow will agree to the terms sought by the European war party and Kiev, Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti. He explained that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will resume their mediation efforts between Russia and Ukraine once the US administration acknowledges the reality of the situation: Moscow is winning on the battlefield. Moreover, according to him, Washington has so far been unable to pressure either Kiev or Europe.
Vedomosti: Recap of first day of President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Bishkek for SCO summit
Vladimir Putin’s agenda in Bishkek, where the Russian president arrived on August 31 to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit, began with bilateral meetings with world leaders. The summit itself is being held on September 1. Following the SCO and SCO Plus meetings, Putin will resume his bilateral meetings. The Russian leader will then fly to Vladivostok to participate in the Eastern Economic Forum.
Putin’s first meeting on the sidelines of the SCO summit was with Chinese President Xi Jinping. This is the second meeting between the leaders this year. Chinese official documents explicitly emphasize the importance of "top-level diplomacy," so the meeting between the leaders of Russia and China plays a significantly greater role in the development of bilateral relations, Alexander Lomanov, head of the Center for Asia-Pacific Studies under the Russian Academy of Sciences’ World Economy and International Relations Institute, told Vedomosti. According to Beijing, the strongest strategic relationships are built precisely through meetings between leaders, and constant contact between Putin and Xi contributes to "the development of mutual political trust." Lomanov noted that the practice of regular meetings between the leaders of Russia and China is already a "long-standing tradition," which is undoubtedly advantageous for both Moscow and Beijing.
After meeting with Xi, Putin held a bilateral meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Putin held another bilateral meeting later in the day, with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. Bilateral meetings between leaders are routine at any multilateral event, and it would be strange if they did not take place, Valdai Club expert Andrey Kortunov emphasized. According to him, the Russian president has many topics to discuss with Modi and Xi as it is important for Russia, India, and China to compare their positions within a broad international context and understand how the parties are responding to new crises and whether they can form a constructive stance. As for Tokayev, Putin’s meeting with him is also quite understandable: Russia and Kazakhstan cooperate closely, and Astana has emerged as a supplier of petroleum products to Russia. The expert also suggested that Putin and Tokayev discussed other issues related to Central Asia’s development, and that the Kazakh president briefed his Russian counterpart on recent constitutional changes and the country’s development in general.
Following the SCO and SCO Plus meetings, Putin will continue to hold bilateral meetings: with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Tajik leader Emomali Rahmon, Turkish head of state Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Izvestia: Nepal risks facing economic disaster
Nepal faces economic paralysis. Experts predict that the risk of another devastating flood is high. Landslides have blocked the gorges through which two major rivers flow, and the situation is further complicated by monsoon rains and the rapid melting of Himalayan glaciers. As a result, a natural dam could burst and unleash millions of cubic meters of water onto the population. The current damage from the destruction has already reached nearly 10% of the country’s GDP. The death toll has exceeded 900, and more than 2,000 people are missing. There have also been casualties in Tibet. India also sees a threat of new devastating floods in its border regions. In Nepal, dissatisfaction with the authorities’ actions could trigger mass protests and lead to a deep political crisis.
The risk of another disaster is extremely high and is driven by a whole range of natural factors, Elsa Shirgazina, a research fellow at the Center for the Indian Ocean Region under the Russian Academy of Sciences’ World Economy and International Relations Institute, told Izvestia. The monsoon season continues in the region, and weather forecasts indicate that torrential rains will not cease in the near future. Heavy precipitation is exacerbated by the rapid melting of Himalayan glaciers, which raises the flow of water into blocked gorges.
India is also concerned about the situation's further impact on the region. "The current situation in Nepal is assessed by Indian authorities and analysts as a large-scale humanitarian and environmental disaster that directly affects Indian interests. As of late August 2026, the threat of new devastating floods in India’s border regions remains high due to the risk of newly formed landslide-dammed lakes bursting and forecasts of prolonged rainfall," a source close to official circles told Izvestia.
The natural disaster struck the heart of the local economy. The hydropower sector was critically affected. The destruction and flooding of the cascade of hydroelectric power plants have led to a significant decline in power generation. This affects not only household consumption, but also disrupts the operations of small industrial enterprises across the country, Shirgazina emphasized.
At the same time, the Nepalese government will have to shift its resources from development to rebuilding homes and infrastructure and paying compensation. Without large external loans, the country will not be able to cope, and this will inevitably add to the national debt, the expert noted.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Impact of Venezuela giving some of its oil to US on global market
US President Donald Trump announced the conclusion of "the biggest oil deal in world history." The Americans will gain control over 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan oil reserves for 25 years. On average, US companies will be able to raise their daily production by 7.12 million barrels over the next quarter-century. Given that the US currently produces just under 14 million barrels of oil per day and consumes 20.6 million barrels, the country could eliminate the need to import crude oil with these Venezuelan reserves.
According to Valery Andrianov, an associate professor at the Russian Financial University, US Secretary of State Mark Rubio estimates that Washington will need to invest $100 billion in Venezuela’s oil industry. If this investment is for developing 25 blocks (17 of which have already been approved, and eight of which are considered promising) and increasing the country's production level to 1.5 million barrels per day, then that figure is quite reasonable, he told Rossiyskaya Gazeta.
However, oil production at new fields in Venezuela will require billions of dollars in investment and will not begin to turn a profit for at least five to seven years, Maxim Malkov, a Kept partner and head of the firm’s oil and gas practice, emphasized. Fields currently under development will also require investment in enhanced oil recovery methods and equipment upgrades in the coming years. The expert noted that US companies currently take virtually all the oil produced in Venezuela and sell it at high global prices, reaping the profits. However, no investment decisions involving US companies in Venezuelan oil production projects have been made yet.
In turn, Andrianov revealed that the US is working to push Russian companies out of Venezuela. Licenses issued by the US in the first half of the year to conduct operations in Venezuela’s oil sector contain strict restrictions.
They categorically prohibit any transactions, investments, or technological cooperation involving companies from Russia, China, Iran, Cuba, and North Korea. Moreover, revenues from the sale of Venezuelan oil are now deposited in foreign escrow accounts controlled by US banks. Therefore, transactions with Russian or Chinese companies and payments for their participation in oil and gas projects in Venezuela are technically impossible.
At the same time, the economic benefits of Venezuelan projects for the US are not as clear-cut as they may appear at first glance. Andrianov stressed that the US government's strategic goals take precedence over commercial considerations for specific companies. While the commercial appeal of projects in Venezuela is relative, they allow the US to bolster its strategic position in the global market and become a regulator on the supply side.

Bulgaria vs North Macedonia: Iva Mihaylova Case May Reach Strasbourg

====================================================================================================

More nothing now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
18 minute listen
Our kids were playing Settlers of Catan over the holidays. Or rather, they weren’t. They’d rearranged the strategy game’s hexagonal tiles into an archipelago of islands that no rulebook recognises, imagined ‘bridges’ built from wood, brick and stone, and invented a purpose for the game about network connectivity that had nothing to do with earning points. They were not playing Catan. They were playing in Catan, using its materials as components to make a world the designers never imagined.
My first instinct was to reach for the rulebook and teach them how the game actually works. My next was to figure out how I could win. It took me a while to realise what I really needed to do: build up the courage to ask if I could sit in and build with them. That was the moment something shifted – not for the kids, who were already there, but for me: a 48-year-old professor sitting on the carpet, making islands and building bridges without a point in sight.
You can play a game or you can play in a game. When you follow the official rules, pursue the stated objective, and measure yourself against opponents or a scoring system, that’s competition: playing a game. The Greeks had a word for this kind of play: agôn, from the god who personified conflict, struggle and contest. But when my kids disassembled the board and turned it into a world, they were doing something older and stranger. They were engaged in what the French sociologist Roger Caillois, in his taxonomy Man, Play and Games (1958), called paidia: free, spontaneous, unstructured play. The kind with no winner, no score, and no optimisation. The kind of play that has almost no place in adult life and, arguably, the kind we need the most, especially now, when even our leisure comes with leaderboards.
The entire architecture of digital life – with its algorithmic feeds, frictionless production and the ambient expectation that we should be consuming or optimising at all times – nudges us towards chasing outputs rather than generating meaning. We track our sleep and score our calm. Fitness apps turn the morning run into a contest; meditation apps gamify stillness with streak counters; language apps award achievement badges for what used to be called curiosity. Even journaling apps nudge users toward consistency scores. The gamification of leisure has turned into work everything that used to exist as its counterpoint. Leisure has become a third shift with its own metrics, its own guilt, and its own sense of falling behind.
The philosopher C Thi Nguyen calls this ‘value capture’: the process by which a game’s simplified, legible values start to colonise the real-world activity the game was supposed to serve. Their power arises from the fact that games don’t just create worlds, but new visions of the good, telling players what to care about by virtue of what the game rewards through scores. When you’re doing Duolingo to maintain your streak, or when your place on the running app’s leaderboard replaces the reason you started running, that’s value capture. The metric ate the meaning.
The Dutch historian and cultural critic Johan Huizinga saw this coming almost a century ago. In Homo Ludens (1938), he argued that play is not marginal to civilisation but, rather, generative of it. For Huizinga, law, philosophy, poetry and war all emerge from play’s ‘magic circle’: the bounded space where ordinary rules are suspended and something else becomes possible. Huizinga worried that the play element had been declining in Western civilisation since the end of the 18th century, eroded by industrialisation and professionalisation. What he feared has now been fulfilled. It’s not that we killed play; we captured it and harnessed it to a productivity framework. Then we packaged and sold it for passive consumption. The magic circle was instrumentalised into a dopamine hit.
What’s missing is neither ‘fun’ nor ‘competition’. We have plenty of those and, to be clear, I’m a huge fan of both. I grew up playing soccer and skiing. In my teens and 20s, I was a serious rock climber. Later I evolved into a competitive ultramarathon runner and now have 50-plus races under my belt, thousands of miles on trails in my legs, and two age-group national titles to my name. Agôn is what I do on weekends. But it’s not where I find meaning, build community, or figure out who I am.
A large part of the trouble is that we’ve eliminated the conditions in which free play arises. Watch the subway car on any morning commute. Every head is bowed to a screen. Not working, not thinking, just filling the time. Candy Crush in the checkout line. Instagram between floors in the elevator. Mere seconds of unstructured time trigger panic, and our fingers reach unconsciously for our phones. But boredom isn’t a problem; rather, it’s the condition in which the mind, left alone, begins to play by itself, to wander, associate, drift toward the transitional space where unexpected connections assemble unbidden. Every moment that we fill with a screen forecloses the free play of the mind. We don’t just need different games. We need more nothing.
Minecraft (owned by Microsoft) and Lego are corporately branded IP ecosystems framed as toys for children
Caillois saw the full spectrum of play: from agôn (competition) and alea (chance), to mimicry (role-playing) and ilinx (vertigo and disorientation). All four types sit on a continuum between paidia (complete improvisation) and ludus (structured rules). However, contemporary game culture tends to collapse this entire spectrum into one narrow band: competition plus structure. We have no category (not in the App Store and not in our cultural vocabulary) for paidia without agôn: our culture has no home for free, exploratory, contemplative play that refuses to compete.
Of course, paidia still erupts wherever people stop keeping score: kids on a playground invent rules then abandon them mid-sentence, Minecraft’s creative mode hosts millions of players building dreamworlds for the sake of building; Lego, at its best, is a pure paidia portal – recombinatory, autotelic, improvisational. But these exceptions clarify the problem: Minecraft (owned by Microsoft) and Lego are corporately branded IP ecosystems framed as toys for children. It’s not that free play has vanished, it just exists under constant threat of value capture. We do it in spite of our platforms, not because of them.
Moreover, the kinds of play that refuse to compete or optimise, or produce a measurable outcome, lack cultural prestige and social infrastructure. The British psychoanalyst and paediatrician Donald W Winnicott would have recognised this absence as a clinical emergency. In Playing and Reality (1971), Winnicott argued that play is not what children do on the way to becoming productive adults; it is a crucial part of how human beings maintain their worlds. Through play we become present to our own experience, capable of surprise, alive to the difference between going through the motions and actually being there.
Winnicott’s key concept is transitional space, though ‘space’ is misleading here because he has in mind not a location but a condition. Think of a conversation so engrossing that you forget you’re speaking and say something you didn’t know you thought until you heard it leave your mouth. You’re not entirely inside your own head (fantasy) and you’re not entirely performing for an audience (compliance). You are in between. That in-between zone – neither fully private nor fully public, neither pure inner life nor pure external task – is what Winnicott called transitional space. It’s where creativity, art and what he called ‘imaginative living’ originate.
His most radical claim still hits like an urgent diagnosis: ‘It is creative apperception more than anything else that makes the individual feel that life is worth living.’ He contrasts this with compliance, a relationship to external reality that ‘carries with it a sense of futility’. It is worth pausing to unpack this fully. Winnicott is arguing that what makes life meaningful is ultimately not achieving goals, having a family or even making art. It’s about how we see the world. ‘Apperception’ names a mode of encounter in which perception is not passive reception but active engagement. The difference is subtle but decisive: in ordinary perception, the world is simply there and the self adjusts to it; in creative apperception, we co-create the world, forging something between self and environment in the zone of play.
Compliance, by contrast, is life lived on someone else’s terms, following scripts, bowing before scores and metrics: moving through a world already defined in advance. Nothing new is risked, nothing genuinely one’s own is made. Most people, Winnicott believed, experience just enough creativity to recognise its absence, sensing that they are mostly ‘living uncreatively, as if caught up in the creativity of someone else, or of a machine.’
That last sentence, written in 1971, strikes me as the most prescient insight from 20th-century psychology for our time. Long before the personal computer, before the algorithm, and before we voluntarily installed surveillance engines in our pockets and called them phones, Winnicott worried about being caught up in the creativity of a machine. He also had a solution: play. For Winnicott, play is the condition of feeling real on a daily basis.
Friedrich Schiller, writing almost two centuries before Winnicott, made the same case from the other direction. In On the Aesthetic Education of Man (1795), he argued that human beings are torn between the pull of raw sensation and the push toward abstract order, and that only what he called the ‘play drive’ integrates both. It’s a bold claim. Schiller wrote that ‘man only plays when he is in the fullest sense of the word a human being, and he is only fully a human being when he plays.’ Winnicott tells you what play does psychologically: it makes life feel real. Schiller tells you what it does metaphysically: it makes you whole.
Simply put: adults need play as desperately as children do – a zone where inner life meets outer materiality and something unpredictable emerges. The Greeks, of course, had a term for this. Aristotle’s medieval fanboy Thomas Aquinas identified eutrapelia, the habit of knowing when and how to play well, as a genuine and discrete virtue. A person who never plays is as disordered as one who never works. I’m not talking about ‘work-life balance’, an exhausted metaphor that still treats play as recovery time for the next productive thing. To practise the virtue of eutrapelia means that a good life requires play. You don’t earn it. You practise it, daily.
The question, then, isn’t whether to play. It is where does the practice live, and how can we regain it in our daily lives, and valorise it in our culture.
For years, I’ve commuted on foot from Grand Central Station to 14th Street, 30 blocks, give or take. I told myself it was exercise, or that I was saving the subway fare, or that I liked the air. But the truth is I was thinking. Or rather, I was letting thinking happen. The lecture I couldn’t outline at my desk would assemble itself somewhere around 34th Street, the important points falling into sequence with my footfalls, the argument clarifying as if the motion itself were doing the editing. I wasn’t working on the lecture. I was walking in it, the way my kids were playing in Catan.
Walking increased the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems by 60 per cent
The experience is ancient and well-documented. Friedrich Nietzsche reputedly walked six to eight hours every day, and insisted in his Twilight of the Idols (1889) that ‘Only thoughts that come by walking have any value.’ Aristotle’s Lyceum was called the peripatetic school for its walkways (peripatoi). Jean-Jacques Rousseau claimed that he could compose only while walking. Albert Einstein walked from his home at Princeton, New Jersey to the Institute for Advanced Study and back each day, and supposedly told colleagues that the walk was where the real thinking happened; the office was where he wrote it down.
Contemporary research confirms these intuitions, this idea that walking is a form of play for the mind as well as the feet. In 2014, Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz at Stanford University found that walking increased divergent thinking – the capacity to generate multiple solutions to open-ended problems – by roughly 60 per cent. Curiously, a treadmill facing a blank wall worked nearly as well as wandering Stanford’s campus, suggesting that it’s the exercise, not the scenery, producing the results. Metronomic motion allows the thinking to arrive.
Push the body further and something stranger happens. Caillois’s taxonomy includes a category almost nobody talks about: ilinx, the play of vertigo and disorientation. Spinning until you’re dizzy. Or running past the point where the split times stop mattering and the self loosens its grip. I know this territory from the inside. The first question at the start of a 100-mile race isn’t whether your legs are ready. It’s whether your mind is: wanting to win might get you to the start-line of your local 5K, but agôn won’t get you to the finish of an ultra-marathon. And it’s a love of trails that makes those miles magical. Nguyen would call this striving play. The goal exists to make the experience of striving possible, not the other way around. The finish line is just the means; the journey is the destination.
Our son does something similar in our basement, though his materials are metal, wood and stone rather than miles of trail. He crafts with scraps of found steel, fixes electric motors, carves wooden animals, shapes copper into jewellery and stone into rings. Nobody assigned this. No tutorial dictates the sequence. The material teaches the craft: copper tells you what it wants to become; stone suggests a shape and you listen or it breaks. At the workbench, inner vision meets the friction of the physical world and something neither planned nor accidental emerges.
Wherever adults build or stumble into transitional space, play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score
My son doesn’t sell what he makes. He gives it away: the knife to a friend, the carved animal to a teacher. Play pursued for its own sake, with no metric and no market, overflows into generosity precisely because nothing was extracted. When something beautiful emerges from a process that asked for nothing, the most natural thing in the world is to give it away. What he makes enters the world not as commodity but as gift.
I see the same dynamic at my day job, though, again, the materials are different. I’m a professor of literary studies, and the best sessions in my seminars have nothing to do with instruction. They obey the logic of improv: ‘yes, and’. A student notices something strange in a passage (a word that doesn’t fit, a silence where speech should be) and someone else picks it up, turns it over, connects it to something from three weeks ago, and suddenly the room is thinking a thought nobody walked in with. The seminar, at its best, builds transitional space inside an institution that mostly rewards compliance. It opens up the zone between private thought and public evaluation, where a student says something she didn’t know she believed until she heard it leave her mouth.
The same dynamic lives in a jazz combo finding a groove nobody charted, a graphic designer noodling with shapes until one surprises her, a group of friends kicking a ball around with no teams and no score. It lives in my son’s basement workshop and on the trail at mile eight, and in the 30-block walk where the lecture writes itself. Wherever adults build or stumble into transitional space – where inner life meets outer material and something unpredictable emerges – play is doing its work even if we’re not keeping score.
Aristotle thought that contemplation (theoria) was the highest human activity because it was done purely for its own sake, absorbing the entire human person. For centuries, and across domains of religion, the academy and the law, that hierarchy held, ranking the contemplative life above the active life, thinking above doing. But maybe the question itself is misleading. The question ‘What is the highest human activity?’ is itself a competition, an agôn. Play doesn’t enter that contest. Play dissolves it. Play is autotelic and relational, solitary and shared, serious and free; it refuses the binary.
Schiller, Huizinga and Winnicott were not wrong; play does makes life worth living. The capacity for play – the willingness to stop optimising, to sit on the floor, to walk without a destination, to make something and give it away – embraces a virtue with an old name: eutrapelia. It is the habit of playing well. The ordinary magic of being real.

Russia kills at least 12 on sixth night of drone attacks on Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:59:40 UTC
18:59:40 KST

At least 12 people have been killed in and around Kyiv overnight as Ukraine’s capital endured a sixth consecutive night of Russian drone and missile attacks aimed at shattering infrastructure and lowering the morale of the city.
Eight of the dead were reported killed in Kyiv, including seven at a railway depot on the city’s left bank, and four were killed in Boryspil, to the east of the city, in a wave of strikes at about 2.30am after hours of air alerts.
A further four people were killed in other parts of Ukraine, regional officials said, in 28 waves of attacks that included a strike on a border crossing point with Romania on the Danube at Orlivka.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, said “a significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack” and that Russia was taking advantage of a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors.
In a morning post on social media, Zelenskyy said: “Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient.”
Kyiv and the surrounding towns and villages have come under sustained attack in the past few days. Thirty-eight people were killed after a Russian drone struck an ammunition store in Myla, 15 miles west of Kyiv, on Thursday, the hit causing hours of secondary explosions and damaging nearby homes.
Ukraine’s air force said Russia had attacked 28 locations, focusing on the cities of Kyiv and Odesa and their surroundings. Air defences shot down five Iskander ballistic missiles, two Banderol and five Kalibr cruise missiles and 187 out of 218 drones. Officials no longer reveal the total numbers of missiles fired.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, the chief executive of Ukrainian Railways, said six of the seven people killed in and around the depot were employees of the network. Another rail worker was hospitalised, he added.
Kyiv has been chronically short of air defence systems since the supply of Patriot interceptors dried up. The Patriots are the only weapon that can effectively stop high-speed Russian ballistic missiles, made at the rate of about 60 a month.
Lockheed Martin, the US company that makes the most capable Pac-3 interceptors, produces about 600 a year, but US military supplies have been depleted during the US war with Iran. Ukraine is trying to secure a stockpile of about 300 for the winter, paid for by European allies, in a supply deal agreed with the US.
Moscow appears to be trying to take advantage of an absence of air defence capability before winter, in an escalation of a conflict nearly deadlocked on the frontline. Ukraine has been responding by attacking oil refineries, warehouses and other military facilities deep inside Russia, aiming to hurt the country’s economy.
Ukraine’s GUR military intelligence said it had attacked an oil refinery at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, about 550 miles (885km) from its border. Russian officials said a civilian was killed in the border Belgorod region in an attack.
Russia captured 35 square miles (56 sq km) of Ukraine’s territory during August, analysis by the AFP news agency concluded. It was Moscow’s largest advance since February but still much lower than the 150 square mile a month average of 2025.
There remains little serious diplomatic effort to end the war, although on Monday India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, urged Vladimir Putin to end the war in public remarks at a bilateral meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
“Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, while every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace. We need to move from endless war to an end to the war,” Modi said.
Putin appeared impatient, tapping his feet as he listened. “Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path,” he replied.

President of Somaliland expected to make first visit to the US in the coming days, in a push for state recognition

President of Somaliland expected to make first visit to US in the coming days, in a push for state recognition
Somaliland is of strategic interest to the United States due to its location near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the main shipping lanes of the Red Sea
The President of Somaliland, Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, is scheduled to travel to Washington in the coming days for his first visit to the United States since taking office. This trip comes a few months after Israel’s decision to officially recognize Somaliland as an independent state, a first by a UN member country.
The visit represents a new and important step in Somaliland's efforts to obtain broader international recognition. The territory, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991, has since functioned as an autonomous entity with its own institutions, but is still not recognized by the majority of the international community.
Israel had officially recognized Somaliland in December 2025, paving the way for swift rapprochement between the two countries. In June, President Abdullahi made a historic visit to Israel, during which he was notably received by President Isaac Herzog and Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
Somaliland had also inaugurated an embassy in Jerusalem.
The question of possible American recognition remains open, however. After the Israeli decision, Donald Trump indicated that he was not yet ready to take this step and that he wanted to study the matter first. The visit of the Somaliland president to Washington could now allow Hargeisa to present its arguments directly to the American administration.
Somaliland presents a particular strategic interest due to its location on the Horn of Africa, near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the main maritime routes of the Red Sea. Israel and Somaliland have already expressed their willingness to develop their cooperation in several areas, including security, agriculture, water, health, and the economy.

Former Ukrainian president has made offer to Zelenskyy amid Russia’s new type of war on Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:58:37 UTC
18:58:37 KST

Former Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko, leader of the opposition European Solidarity party, has offered to unite with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a new type of government. He has explained his initiative as necessary to save the country and adopt crisis-response measures amid a new phase of the war.
Russia's strike campaign has become a governance problem as much as a military one. Each attack on Kyiv costs the city about $12 million, and they now arrive almost twice a week. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on 28 August that, roughly speaking, 90% of retail chains' food logistics had been destroyed in the latest attacks, which included jet-powered drones that trigger an air alert in Kyiv every hour.
"We are the opposition, but we are ready to cooperate with the authorities in the legislative provision of all necessary decisions, up to the creation of a coalition and a government of national unity," he said.
Speaking in a video address on 31 August, he set out five issues to solve for the parliamentary session.
One: keep the capital running
The current barrage has forced Kyiv to a near-standstill, with alerts sounding through the working day. If they are permanent, Poroshenko argued, the rules for how the city runs must change, and the government, military, transport operators, and business must agree on a single published procedure. When the capital is shut down for hours, much of the economy stops with it, and the lost billions never reach the army, he added.
"Let us say honestly what Putin is doing. He wants to switch Kyiv off. To make people finally say: it is impossible to live here," Poroshenko said.
Two: give parents a school plan
The school year opens on 1 September under a rule allowing in-person classes only where a school has a shelter with room for everyone. Kyiv's administration told UNN that 94% of city schools have basic shelters, but capacity limits set the ceiling, forcing shifts or blended formats when a shelter cannot hold every child at once.
"Tomorrow is 1 September. Thousands of parents still do not understand how their children will study, especially where there are no proper shelters," Poroshenko said.
Three: return Kyiv's money
Kyiv has lost revenue to the central budget even as its defense costs climb, a dispute with the government that predates the barrage. Poroshenko demanded the return of about $180 million to the budget, along with the personal income tax paid by combat brigades.
"This week Kyiv is forced to carry out a budget sequester for the first time," he explained, cutting spending on doctors, teachers, and the socially vulnerable to fund the city's own defense.
Four: scale up war-risk insurance
Russia's strikes have hit businesses faster than any recovery system can answer, with warehouses and logistics hubs among the targets this month. Business needs war-risk insurance, money for rapid recovery after strikes, new logistics, and the ability to invest in its own protection, including private air defense, Poroshenko said.
Five: fund energy resilience now
Putin has named energy as his main target, the former president pointed out, and the coming winter is the pressure point. Kyiv's small, maneuverable generation, cogeneration, and backup power for hospitals, water utilities, and communications must be installed now, he added.

war are continuing to push up Italian inflation, which was 3.3%
in August, Istat said Tuesday.
                                    
                                       
				According to preliminary estimates, in August 2026, the national
consumer price index (NIC), excluding tobacco, will increase by
+0.5% month-on-month and +3.3% year-on-year (from +2.9% the
previous month).
                                    
                                       
				"In August 2026, inflation will rise to +3.3% (from +2.9% in
July), supported by the trend in energy prices (from +11.6% to
+17.0%), which are still affected by international tensions,"
explains the national statistics institute.
                                    
                                       
				The 'acquired' inflation for 2026 (i.e., the inflation that
would occur in the year assuming that the index itself remains
at the same level as the latest available monthly data for the
remainder of the year) is equal to +2.9% for the general index
and +1.9% for the core component, Istat said.
                                    
                                       
				Finally, the stats agency said that In August, the annual rate
of change in prices for the so-called "shopping basket" (food,
household goods, and personal care products) remained stable (at
+1.0%), while the rate of change for frequently purchased
products increased (from +3.4% to +4.3%).

FBI court filing says Nigerian president was subject of US criminal investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:56:30 UTC
18:56:30 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
 
A sworn declaration filed by the FBI in a US federal court has reaffirmed that Nigerian President Bola Ahmed Tinubu was a subject of a criminal investigation involving the agency and the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in the early 1990s.
The declaration, filed Aug. 28 before the US District Court for the District of Columbia, forms part of an ongoing Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lawsuit seeking access to US law enforcement records relating to Tinubu.
The FBI said the records sought in the case were “compiled in furtherance” of its investigation of multiple individuals for drug-trafficking crimes, according to excerpts of the declaration published by Washington-based lobbying firm Von Batten-Montague-York.
The firm, which has been retained by former Nigerian Vice President Atiku Abubakar, said it obtained a large volume of records from the FBI and was reviewing and redacting some of the material before publication.
The latest filing follows an April 2025 ruling by US District Judge Beryl Howell, who found that public filings by the US Justice Department had already officially acknowledged that Tinubu was one subject of a criminal investigation involving, among other agencies, the FBI and DEA.
The judge consequently ordered the FBI and DEA to search for and process non-exempt records sought under FOIA.
The case was brought by Aaron Greenspan, who requested FBI records relating to Tinubu, including his entire FBI file and interview records from 1992 and 1993.
The records relate to a broader investigation into a Chicago-based heroin trafficking and money-laundering operation in the early 1990s.
The court’s 2025 ruling, however, did not find that Tinubu committed a drug-trafficking offense, nor did it amount to a criminal charge or conviction against him.
The FBI has continued to withhold or redact portions of the records, citing exemptions under US freedom-of-information law covering personal privacy, confidential sources, law enforcement methods and information that could endanger individuals.
Tinubu’s legal team has also challenged further disclosure of records in the case, according to recent court filings.
The renewed disclosure comes as Nigeria’s political parties prepare for the 2027 presidential election, with Atiku among opposition politicians seeking to challenge Tinubu’s administration.

Air conditioners save thousands of lives every year in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:56:18 UTC
18:56:18 KST

Household air conditioning prevents over 5,000 heat-related deaths every year in the United States alone, a new study found.
As rising temperatures take a toll on human health, air conditioning at home is about more than comfort. A recent study published on Monday in Nature Health found that it also saves thousands of lives.
Over 5,260 heat-related deaths are prevented every year in the US, reducing heat-attributable mortality by more than half, according to a new study by Yale School of Public Health and the Yale School of the Environment.
“Everyone agrees that air conditioning works, but knowing that it works for one person is not the same as knowing how much death it prevents across an entire population,” Kai Chen, senior author of the study and an associate professor of epidemiology at Yale School of Public Health, said in a press release.
But turning the air conditioning up to maximum does not necessarily save more lives, the study found. Maximum cooling offered no additional health benefits compared with average use, highlighting the need to balance the health benefits of air conditioning against the environmental costs of excessive use, including higher energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions.
Lower-income and heat
The researchers analysed nearly 30 million death records from 2010 to 2020, matching each death with the daily temperature in the county where it occurred. They then compared those patterns with estimates of household electricity consumption for cooling in each county.
The researchers focused on actual cooling use rather than air-conditioning ownership. Knowing whether a household has an air conditioner says little about whether residents can afford to run it, or how often they do so, Chen said.
The findings shed light on how lower-income households cope with extreme heat, said Narasimha Rao, a study co-author and professor of energy systems at the Yale School of the Environment.
“While some choose to turn on their ACs, others make the uncomfortable choice of bearing the heat to save money for food,” Rao said.
Furthermore, the findings could also have implications for housing policy, said Robert Dubrow, a study co-author and founding faculty director of the Yale Center on Climate Change and Health.
“Landlords in the United States are required to provide heating in the winter, and our study contributes to a compelling body of literature that indicates they also should be required to provide cooling in the summer,” Dubrow said.
The study comes as, across the Atlantic, in Europe, the question of air conditioning has become a political battle. French politicians have drawn ideological battle lines over air conditioning as Europe struggled with record-breaking temperatures, reaching over 40°C.
Meanwhile, the European Commission advocates a "holistic" approach that combines passive and efficient cooling technologies. Rather than encouraging mass installation of air-conditioning units, Brussels wants Europe to prioritise cooler buildings and cities through design, insulation and passive measures, using efficient air conditioning where it is genuinely needed.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:55:00 UTC
18:55:00 KST

Iran will immediately reciprocate if the United States honors its commitments under an interim deal signed in June, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tuesday.
He made the comments at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek after the first exchange of direct attacks in the U.S.-Iran conflict since late July, with the U.S. striking Larak Island and Iran then launching attacks on two U.S. air bases in Jordan.
"I am stating clearly that if the U.S. returns to its commitments under the Memorandum of Understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate," Pezeshkian was quoted as saying by state media.
He was referring to an interim deal signed in June between Tehran and Washington in efforts to end the war, which started with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. The deal quickly unraveled amid disagreements over its implementation.
Tehran has repeatedly said it will allow free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global oil supplies, only if Washington implements the terms of the agreement.
Pezeshkian said in Bishkek Monday that war was in no one's interest and that Tehran was still open to a negotiated solution in its conflict with Washington.
"We continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region," he said, adding "the solution to the existing problems is dialogue and cooperation."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also urged the US to "return to its commitments and to what their president signed."
"In that case, everything can be put back on the right track," he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump, however, told Fox News "there will be a response" to the Iranian attacks but told reporters in the Oval Office Monday that the renewed strikes did not signal a return to full-scale war.
After six months of conflict, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping Hormuz closed and the U.S. persisting with a naval counterblockade of Iran.
"We're going to hit them hard," Trump said, according to a Fox News reporter who spoke to him briefly. "There will be a response."
Earlier Trump had called Iran "a Failed Nation," saying on social media that its military was decimated, its finances were crumbling "and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country."
Despite traffic remaining throttled six months on, Trump has claimed the U.S. navy has "total control" of the strait and has even called it U.S. territory, with Washington last week announcing it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.
Iran, however, insists it is in charge of the sea lane. The Revolutionary Guards said Monday a "rogue" oil tanker caught fire near the strait after it hit two mines while attempting to transit an "illegal route."
The U.S. military called the claim "disinformation," saying: "No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz."
Mediators, meanwhile, have tried for months to broker an end to the war, but an earlier truce and memorandum of understanding fell apart.
Sporadic attacks resumed, but ultimately tapered off, with the US last striking Iran on July 29, after having attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights earlier that month.
With diplomacy stalled, Iran's foreign minister Monday accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of tricking Washington into going to war.
"In Hebrew, Netanyahu openly crows that he suckered the US administration into a war on Iran on behalf of Israel," Abbas Araghchi wrote on X. "In English, he praises POTUS' leadership. Serpent."

New Zealand to make cervical screening free for all eligible women
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:53:19 CST
18:53:19 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Cervical screening will be free for all eligible women aged 25 to 69 in New Zealand from March 1, 2027, the government said Tuesday.
Health Minister Simeon Brown said in a statement that an estimated 786,000 additional women would become eligible for free cervical screening under the policy.
Currently, about 55 percent of women eligible for cervical screening have to pay for an appointment, which can cost between 35 and more than 100 NZ dollars (about 21 to more than 59 U.S. dollars), the government said.
Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers, the statement said, noting that almost every case is caused by HPV, a common virus, which the screening test detects long before any cancer develops.
When cervical cancer is found early, about 91 percent of women survive, but survival falls to around 19 percent once the disease has spread, it said.
Minister for Women Nicola Grigg also released the New Zealand Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan 2026-2040, which aims to reduce cervical cancer to fewer than four cases per 100,000 women a year across all population groups by 2040.
The plan sets targets for 80 percent of women to be up to date with screening by 2030 and for 90 percent of young people to have received their first HPV vaccine dose by age 15 by 2035. ■

====================================================================================================

Major copper-gold discovery made in east China's Anhui
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:53:02 CST
18:53:02 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China has made a major breakthrough in copper and gold exploration in the eastern province of Anhui, discovering a deposit that could become a large-scale resource base and bolster the country's capacity to secure key mineral supplies.
The Chating copper-gold deposit, located in Xuancheng City, sits in the Nanling-Xuancheng copper-gold district within the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River metallogenic belt, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Tuesday.
Located in the heart of the Yangtze River Delta, the Chating copper-gold deposit is a recently discovered concealed porphyry deposit beneath volcanic cover, with the potential to reach super-large scale, according to the ministry.
The main ore body measures about 1.2 kilometers in length and 1.1 kilometers in width, with the maximum apparent thickness encountered in a single borehole reaching 1,371 meters.
Preliminary estimates suggest the deposit's potential copper resources exceed the scale of several large copper mines, while its gold resources could surpass the equivalent of more than 10 large gold mines.
Drilling has yet to fully penetrate the deeper sections of the ore body, leaving considerable room for upward revision of resource estimates. Associated silver and sulfur resources could also be recovered and utilized.
If developed, the deposit is expected to become a super-large copper-gold production base in east China, the ministry said.
Anhui's natural resources authorities began funding and organizing general surveys of the Chating area in 2008, with a survey report submitted in 2018.
In September 2025, the exploration right for the Chating copper polymetallic prospect was offered through a public listing. Tibet Yulong Copper Co., Ltd. secured the right the following month for 8.6 billion yuan (about 1.27 billion U.S. dollars). The company then stepped up exploration investment and completed nearly 100,000 meters of drilling within four months, the ministry said.
The Chating discovery is part of a broader upswing in mineral exploration across China. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), the country identified 398 new large and medium-sized strategic mineral deposits, including oil and gas fields, with historic breakthroughs in bulk minerals such as copper, gold and potash, the ministry added.
China is also stepping up efforts to expand its domestic copper resource base. Under an implementation plan for high-quality development of the copper industry for 2025-2027, the country aims to increase its copper ore reserves by 5 percent to 10 percent by 2027.
The plan calls for intensified exploration in key copper metallogenic belts, the addition of more copper reserves available for development, the development of copper resource bases in key regions, and the construction of a number of new large and medium-sized copper mines.
Similar efforts are moving forward in the gold sector. Under an implementation plan for high-quality development of the gold industry for 2025-2027, China's gold resources are expected to increase by 5 percent to 10 percent during the period, while gold and silver output will grow by more than 5 percent.
The plan also calls for stepped-up geological exploration in key western areas and in the deep and peripheral zones of existing large and medium-sized mines. The copper-gold polymetallic resource area along the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River is listed among the plan's key exploration regions. ■

Feature: Braving chest-deep mud, Chinese rescue team races to find survivors in mudslide-hit Nepal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:52:50 CST
18:52:50 KST

KATHMANDU, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The mud was knee-deep at first. Then it rose to the rescuers' chests.
About 1.8 kilometers into a tunnel in Bidur, Nuwakot District, Nepal, Zhao Bo, deputy commander of the Chongqing-based national tunnel emergency rescue team, which is run by the China Communications Construction Company, said they could no longer walk. Their legs sank into sediment and could barely be pulled free. "We had to crawl our way forward."
Zhao is one of the Chinese rescue experts now racing against time to search for possible survivors in areas hit by the deadly mudslide in Nepal, where roads have been cut off and tunnels have been buried under thick layers of mud and sediment.
The team eventually reached about 2.3 km from the tunnel entrance. They shouted into the darkness, knocked repeatedly and blew whistles, waiting for any response.
For nearly 20 minutes, there was none.
Zhao said that the team had traveled about 2.5 km into the tunnel, but the passage farther ahead was almost entirely buried in mud. To conserve their strength, they eventually turned back.
The search is not over. It is only the beginning of a rescue operation constrained by mud, water, blocked roads, limited helicopters and difficult mountain weather.
On Sunday morning, two Chinese Y-20 transport aircraft carrying rescue supplies arrived at Kathmandu International Airport, bringing four Chinese tunnel rescue experts. Five other Chinese tunnel rescue experts had arrived a day earlier to assist with the search and rescue operation in Nepal.
At a Nepalese rescue command center in Bidur, helicopters take off and land almost continuously as rescue operations proceed at a tense and urgent pace.
But the number of helicopters available is limited, while demand for aerial rescue and transportation is enormous. Chinese experts have to coordinate with the Nepalese side to use the available aircraft.
Time is another major constraint.
For safety reasons, each tunnel exploration mission could last no more than two hours. Meanwhile, Nepal's rugged mountainous terrain and complicated weather conditions sharply limit the daily time helicopters can operate safely.
The difficulties are even more severe inside the tunnels.
On Sunday afternoon, two Chinese rescue experts returned from a search mission in a tunnel.
Exhausted from the operation, they nevertheless sat down and immediately began reviewing video footage recorded inside the tunnel with their colleagues, assessing the conditions and discussing the next rescue plan.
Li Yingping, an expert from the Kunming-based national tunnel emergency rescue team run by the China Railway No. 2 Engineering Group Co., Ltd., described the tunnel as being filled with sediment.
"The mud has become like porridge," Li said.
The mud, about 2 meters deep, could not support a person's weight and was also unsuitable for a small rescue boat, he said.
Pan Jiangyuan, another tunnel rescue expert who also participated in the Sunday afternoon operation, said insufficient transport capacity was another major obstacle facing the rescue effort.
Pan said that the only available means of transport at present are helicopter air drops and manual carrying, making it difficult to get certain rescue equipment and instruments to the site.
Despite these obstacles, the rescue teams have continued to move toward areas that ordinary rescue vehicles cannot reach.
To speed up rescue efforts, every Chinese search mission is conducted jointly with Nepali military personnel and local project engineers. Nagendra Bahadur Bhandari, a Nepali military rescuer who worked with Pan, said that they cooperate very well with each other.
On Monday, eight Chinese rescue experts flew to the disaster zone in two groups for another round of operations.
Near their target area, they spotted three Nepalese people waiting to be rescued.
The Chinese team immediately guided them toward a safe platform where a rescue helicopter could land. The three people were subsequently rescued by the Nepalese military.
Nepalese authorities said Tuesday that the death toll from massive mudslides had risen to 1,010, with 4,599 people still missing.
"The Chinese rescue team stands ready to explore every last corner, no matter how tough the situation gets," Zhao said. ■

Indonesia develops groundwater monitoring system to reduce peatland fire risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:52:39 CST
18:52:39 KST

JAKARTA, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Indonesia's National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) is developing a groundwater monitoring system aimed at reducing the risk of forest and land fires, particularly in peatland areas.
Albertus Sulaiman, head of BRIN's Climate and Atmospheric Research Center, said the system is designed to monitor groundwater conditions in peatlands, detect changes that could indicate increased fire risks, and track carbon emissions from these areas.
"Groundwater level data can serve as an early warning system to identify when land begins to become vulnerable to fires, as declining groundwater levels cause peatlands to become drier," Sulaiman said Tuesday.
Recent BRIN research showed that peat swamp forests play an important role in regulating local rainfall, storing large amounts of carbon and maintaining water balance, making them crucial to climate resilience.
Sulaiman added that peatland management for cultivation can involve the construction of canals to regulate water levels. However, excessively low groundwater levels can dry out peatlands and increase the risk of fires. ■

Thailand's manufacturing sector maintains growth in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:52:39 CST
18:52:39 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's manufacturing sector remained in an expansion territory in August, driven by strong increases in output and new orders, while business optimism reached its highest level since January, a survey showed on Tuesday.
The Southeast Asian country's manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) came in at 53.8 in August, marginally down from 54.2 in July, signaling a further solid improvement in overall operating conditions, according to S&P Global.
A PMI reading above 50 indicates growth in the goods-producing sector, while a reading below 50 reflects contraction.
The upturn resulted from a sharp rise in manufacturing output, marking the second-fastest growth rate so far in 2026, thanks to improved demand and new customer acquisitions, S&P Global said in a statement.
Meanwhile, new business inflows climbed notably in August, extending the sequence of growth to 16 consecutive months.
Despite that, the latest survey recorded a fractional drop in employment numbers across the manufacturing sector, which contributed to capacity pressures as evidenced by another moderate accumulation of unfinished work.
The PMI reading pointed to a sustained improvement in business conditions since May 2025, with strong rates of output and new business expansion illustrating faster growth than average in the first half of the year, said Tim Moore, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Moore said improved demand conditions, stabilizing supply chains, and modest inflationary pressures all helped to boost business optimism in August.
Sentiment in the year-ahead outlook for manufacturing production soared to a peak not seen since early this year, significantly outperforming the long-term average, he noted. ■

OCBC foresees rise in ASEAN FDI as AI, supply-chain shifts fuel inflows
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:52:28 CST
18:52:28 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows into ASEAN remained resilient through 2025 and early 2026, supported by continued investment in manufacturing, financial services and artificial intelligence (AI)-related sectors, OCBC Group Research said on Tuesday.
FDI into the region is expected to remain on an upward trajectory over the medium term, underpinned by supply-chain diversification, expanding AI and data center investments, and continued policy reforms, the research house said in a note.
However, authorities are increasingly shifting their focus from the quantity of investment to its quality, seeking greater domestic value creation, employment generation and sustainable resource utilization.
Against a backdrop of narrowing basic balances, volatile portfolio flows and potentially tighter global monetary conditions, maintaining a steady pipeline of long-term FDI will be critical to supporting external stability and sustaining regional growth, it said.
Total FDI inflows into ASEAN rose to 245.7 billion U.S. dollars in 2025 from 223.1 billion dollars in 2024. Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines accounted for 236.7 billion dollars of the total in 2025, with Singapore alone attracting 151 billion dollars.
Early indicators for 2026 also remained encouraging. Combined FDI inflows into the six economies rose 5.5 percent year-on-year to 60.9 billion dollars in the first quarter, from 57.8 billion dollars a year earlier.
The trend, however, was uneven, with inflows declining in Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand, while Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam recorded increases, according to OCBC. ■

Groningen University launches Frisian language degree
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:52:25 UTC
18:52:25 KST

Groningen University launches Frisian language degree
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Groningen University has launched a bachelor’s degree programme in the Frisian language, the first standalone course in the country’s second official language for 15 years.
Three students began the course this week, which covers linguistics, history and Frisian culture. Frisian was taught as a degree in its own right until 2012, when it was absorbed into a broader programme on Europe’s minority languages, Minorities & Multilingualism.
That programme drew too few students to survive and the university said it would phase it out from the 2025/26 academic year, leaving the academic study of Frisian at risk of vanishing altogether.
A rescue from The Hague
 The course was saved after the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW) recommended, in a report on the future of Frisian studies, that the state pay for a dedicated bachelor. The government agreed to put in €340,000 a year, with further provincial money.
For legal reasons the new degree sits as a Frisian track within the university’s Dutch Languages and Cultures programme, though the focus is now entirely on Frisian.
Professor of Frisian Arjen Versloot said he was happy with the intake, even though a course usually needs around 20 students to break even. “There are often only five students in French and German too, so as a small language we can’t complain,” he told regional broadcaster Omrop Fryslân.
Teachers in demand
 The degree is also meant to supply qualified teachers. Since August, schools in Friesland have been required to use more Frisian in the classroom under new curriculum rules, and Versloot expects strong demand for teachers able to deliver it at the highest level.
Frisian is spoken by around 470,000 people in Friesland and is the closest living relative of English.
Reading and writing proficiency in Frisian has risen sharply over the past two decades, despite fewer people speaking the language at home, according to a recent survey.
Around 58% of residents in Friesland now say they can read Frisian well or very well, up from 46% in 2007. Self-reported writing proficiency nearly doubled over the same period, from 9.6% to 18.9%.

Explosion at police station in Rivne claims life of deputy head of department; ammunition may have detonated - SBI

18:51:52 KST

Explosion at police station in Rivne claims life of deputy head of department; ammunition may have detonated - SBI
Kyiv • UNN
An explosion at a district police station in Rivne claimed the life of the deputy head of the department, while three other law enforcement officers sustained serious injuries. The SBI is investigating the possibility that ammunition detonated due to violations of storage regulations.
The State Bureau of Investigation is investigating the circumstances of an explosion at one of the district police departments in Rivne and indicated who was injured — the deputy head of the department was killed, while the head of one of the departments, another deputy, and an inspector of one of the divisions sustained serious injuries, UNN writes.
Employees of the SBI have launched an investigation into an explosion at one of the police stations in Rivne, which killed one law enforcement officer and injured three others
As noted by the SBI, "the explosion occurred on August 31, 2026, at approximately 3:30 p.m. in the courtyard of Police Department No. 1 of the Rivne District Police Department."
As a result of the detonation, the deputy head of the department was killed. The head of one of the departments, another deputy, and an inspector of one of the divisions also sustained serious injuries. They have now been hospitalized
It is reported that "according to preliminary information, one of the munitions may have detonated on the premises of the institution due to a violation of the rules for the safe storage of explosive substances."
According to the bureau, SBI employees immediately began urgent investigative actions after the incident. The scene examination has now been completed, fragments and official documentation have been seized, witnesses are being questioned, and a series of expert examinations has been ordered to establish the circumstances and causes of the explosion.
Preliminary legal classification of the offense: negligent storage of firearms or ammunition (Article 264 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

Russia Reportedly Strikes Odesa With KAB Guided Bombs for First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:51:22 UTC
18:51:22 KST

Russia has reportedly attacked Odesa with guided aerial bombs (KABs) for the first time, according to local reports, marking a potentially significant expansion in Moscow’s use of the powerful weapons against Ukraine’s southern port city.
No Ukrainian official source had confirmed the use of a guided aerial bomb against Odesa city as of publication. However, residents reported hearing the characteristic explosions during the Aug. 31 attack, while local and humanitarian channels reported that a KAB had been launched toward the city.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Odesa came under a combined Russian attack late Monday, Aug. 31, with Moscow launching Shahed attack drones, Banderol loitering munitions and guided aerial bombs.
While Russian KABs have previously reached parts of Odesa region, local sources said the Aug. 31 attack was the first time a guided bomb was recorded striking Odesa itself.
KABs are conventional aerial bombs fitted with guidance and glide kits, allowing Russian aircraft to release them from a distance and hit targets without flying directly over the area being attacked.
Russia has increasingly modified older Soviet-era bombs with guidance systems and wings, turning them into relatively cheap but highly destructive stand-off weapons.
The bombs pose a particular danger because of their large warheads and the difficulty of intercepting them. Depending on the model, Russian glide bombs can carry hundreds of kilograms to several tonnes of explosives, while newer versions have reportedly reached ranges of more than 100 kilometers.
Ukraine’s War Chest Shrinks as Europe Mulls Gamble with Russia Billions
That combination – heavy explosive payloads, increasing range and the ability to be launched from aircraft operating outside the immediate target area – allows Russia to threaten cities farther from the front line while reducing the exposure of its aircraft to Ukrainian air defenses.
The reported use of KABs against the city could signal that Russia is expanding the operational range of the weapons, which have been used extensively against Ukrainian cities and frontline positions.
Local Telegram channels reported that Russian drones approached Odesa from the direction of the Black Sea as Ukrainian air defenses engaged the incoming targets. Russian Su-34 and Su-35 fighter jets were also reportedly active during the attack.
At least one drone was reported shot down over the city.
The attack also caused power outages in several parts of Odesa, with residents reporting that electricity disappeared shortly after a series of explosions. The strikes reportedly damaged energy infrastructure, although the extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
Fires also broke out in the city, including fires involving trucks, according to preliminary reports.
Ukrainian authorities had yet to provide a full assessment of the damage and casualties as of the initial reports.
The reported first-ever KAB strike on Odesa is notable because the city lies significantly farther from the front line than many Ukrainian locations routinely targeted by Russia’s glide bombs.

Estonia to raise pension age to 65 years, 4 months in 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:51:00 UTC
18:51:00 KST

Estonia to raise pension age to 65 years, 4 months in 2029
The Ministry of Social Affairs has proposed setting the old‑age pension age at 65 years and four months from 2029 — a rise of four months on the current benchmark.
Under a new system taking effect from next year, the pension age will be set annually based on life expectancy, rather than a person's year of birth.
Estonian law requires the legal retirement age for each year to be established by regulation two years in advance. The old‑age pension age is calculated on the basis of a five‑year average of life expectancy at 65 in Estonia — for 2029, this is based on the years 2021–2025.
The 2029 pension age applies to people born between October 1963 and August 1964. For those born from September 1964 onwards, the pension age will depend on the pension age established for 2030.
The Ministry says regularly hiking the legal retirement age is a widely used EU measure to ease demographic pressure on state pension systems. Nearly half of EU member states link rises in the retirement age to increases in life expectancy. In Denmark, for example, the old‑age pension age is 67 now and is set to rise to 70 by 2040.
As of January 1, 2026, there were 331,000 pensioners in Estonia, including 315,000 old‑age pensioners. According to a Ministry of Finance forecast, the number of pensioners will increase to around 340,000 by 2060.
