====================================================================================================

Ukraine’s War Chest Shrinks as Europe Mulls Gamble with Russia Billions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:30:43 UTC
18:30:43 KST

Europe’s grand €90 billion answer to Ukraine’s funding crisis survived for just eight months before Volodymyr Zelenskyy began proposing that part of next year’s allocation should be paid early.
Ukraine says it has already raided money earmarked for the second half of 2026 and is now staring down a €23.1 billion hole in its defense budget.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
That is why a letter from the foreign ministers of Sweden, Poland, Spain and the Netherlands has dragged Europe’s Russian-frozen-assets fight back onto the table. The four governments say the €90 billion package will be insufficient and want Commission experts to explore new uses for Russia’s immobilized assets.
Bringing some of the 2027 money forward could fill part of this year’s hole. It would also obviously leave Ukraine with less money next year. That is the approaching financial cliff: Ukraine could run short again during 2027, while the EU’s next seven-year budget only begins in 2028. European governments would have to improvise another financial bridge in the meantime.
The letter therefore returns to the €210 billion in frozen Russian assets, presenting them as the rope that could pull Ukraine back from the financial cliff edge. What’s new in the letter is that it acknowledges that a way must be found to share the responsibility and liability of using the money, so that Belgium is not left carrying the risk alone, the obstacle that stalled the plan in December.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, August 30, 2026
Until now, the Russian principal has largely been reserved for Ukraine’s eventual reconstruction. Sikorski argues that “it is better to use it to stop the aggression … rather than wait until the end of Russia’s aggression to spend it on reconstruction”.
There is a clear logic here. Money spent defending Ukraine today can preserve its cities, factories and power stations, leaving less for Europe to rebuild later.
Next year is arriving early
Ukraine says its defense ministry faces a $27 billion, or €23.1 billion, funding gap this year. The shortfall includes around €6 billion in advance payments for equipment due in early 2027.
Zelenskyy has suggested advancing part of the EU money scheduled for 2027, although the Commission says it has yet to receive a formal request.
What is interesting here is that front-loading fits a pattern. If you look across Europe’s funding mechanisms, each one finds a different way to turn tomorrow’s resources into weapons or budget support today.
In simple terms, each plan reaches into a different part of the future. The G7 loan brings forward the profits that Russia’s assets will generate over many years. The €90 billion package places the EU budget behind money borrowed from financial markets while waiting for Russian reparations. The proposed reparations loan would use the underlying Russian cash, leaving Euroclear with an EU promise to replace it. That final step explains why collective guarantees are important as Europe may have to provide the money if it ever has to be returned to Moscow.
The instruments are distinct, and the same euro has not literally been spent several times. Even so, Europe has addressed successive immediate crises by placing claims on future profits, budgets and reparations.
There’s nothing crazy about it. Governments borrow all the time because urgent bills can’t always wait for tomorrow’s tax money. But clever financial tricks don’t make the political gamble vanish; they simply push the costs down the road. And sooner or later, someone will have to shoulder the risk if the promised reparations or government funds fail to cover the bill.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Belgium holds the vault and the risk
That responsibility leads to Belgium. Around €210 billion of Russian central-bank assets are immobilized in the EU, with roughly €185 billion held by Euroclear in Brussels.
Belgium slammed the brakes on the earlier reparations-loan plan, fearing a legal nightmare: Russian lawsuits, massive damages claims or a sudden order to hand the money back. The plan effectively asked Belgian to carry the risk for Europe’s geopolitical experiment, but Brussels insisted that any potential liability had to be shared across the continent.
The previous Commission proposal already went some way to recognizing that problem. It envisaged national guarantees divided according to each country’s share of EU gross national income, with coverage eventually moving to the EU budget.
The catch was that governments still had to sign up voluntarily, raising fears that chunks of the plan could be left without cover. Belgium demanded ironclad protection against every legal and financial threat so that it wouldn’t be stuck picking up the tab.
The letter puts the issue back on the table but stops well short of a deal. It offers no figure for the loan, no clear guarantee plan and no fix for Belgium’s objections. The four governments can force the issue back onto the agenda, but turning it into a workable plan will still require the backing of Europe’s biggest economies.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Survival comes before reconstruction
Poland’s Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski makes a strong case for taking the gamble. “Russia will not get this money back until it pays reparations to Ukraine, so it is better to use it to stop the aggression, that is, to defend Ukraine, rather than wait until the end of Russia’s aggression to spend it on reconstruction,” he said.
The logic is to spend the money now on air defenses, ammunition and Ukrainian weapons factories, and Ukraine may save its cities, power stations, factories and territory from destruction. Every building and piece of infrastructure left standing could mean a smaller reconstruction bill later. A stronger Ukraine could also have a better hand when peace talks eventually begin.
Of course, nobody can put an exact price tag on the calculation. One euro spent on defense will not automatically wipe a fixed amount off the reconstruction bill. Ukraine will still need vast sums after the war, while the frozen Russian assets are limited. But the order matters. There can be no meaningful reconstruction if Ukraine does not survive as a sovereign, functioning country.

Subdivided-flat registration rate at 42.5% as ‘early bird’ phase deadline passes
Industry observers say ownership complications and low awareness have slowed landlords’ applications under new housing regulations
Property-ownership complications and low public awareness have slowed landlords’ registration of Hong Kong subdivided flats under new housing regulations, industry observers have said, after the government received only 42.5 per cent of the applications expected in the first phase.
Monday marked the deadline for the initial six-month “early bird” registration phase under the Basic Housing Unit Ordinance. Landlords who applied during this period were eligible for a waiver of HK$3,000 (US$382) in certification fees per subdivided flat for each of the first three years.
The legislation came into force in March to phase out substandard subdivided flats. The government estimates that about 80,000 flats across the city could be accredited, but only about 34,000 units were registered during the first six months.
Scott Leung Man-kwong, deputy chairman of the Legislative Council’s housing panel, described the 42.5 per cent application rate as acceptable but said the HK$3,000 discount was not a significant incentive for landlords to apply early.
“For inherited properties, sometimes the verification of legal ownership could delay the application,” he told a radio show on Tuesday.
“We’ve seen cases where a son inherited a flat from his father that is already subdivided. The tenants continued to pay rent and they did not process the legal transfer of the property. But now, with the application for basic housing units, they will have to do so.”

America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:30:14 UTC
18:30:14 KST

America has the power to defeat Iran. Why can’t it use it?
The war against Iran, launched by the United States and Israel six months ago, was conceived as a lightning campaign against a weakened and already battered enemy.
As far as is currently known, the immediate trigger was the unrest that swept Iran in January, which appears to have convinced the Israeli and American leadership that the government in Tehran was teetering on the brink of collapse and required only a final push.
At the beginning of the campaign, Donald Trump confidently predicted that the war would last a month or six weeks, and sometimes suggested it could be over even sooner. Instead, it’s become one of the defining events of the 21st century and its long-term consequences may ultimately prove comparable to those of the September 11 attacks or Russia’s military operation in Ukraine, and perhaps even surpass them.
Among the most important consequences is the damage inflicted on the United States’ position as the principal guarantor of security for the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, a role Washington gradually assumed after the Second World War, initially alongside Britain and later largely on its own.
The war has exposed two fundamental weaknesses in that first, the United States has proved unable to protect the oil infrastructure and essential services of the Gulf monarchies from devastating attacks by a middle-ranking power such as Iran, and second, it has failed to guarantee freedom of commercial navigation in strategically important waters against attacks by Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen.
This is important far beyond the military sphere where America’s role as the Gulf’s security guarantor, spectacularly demonstrated during Operation Desert Storm in 1990-91, became one of the foundations of the post-Cold War international order. It influenced not only the foreign policies of the Arab monarchies but their financial decisions, as they invested enormous sums in the United States partly because their relationship with Washington provided them with security.
The scale of the American commitment in 1990 illustrates how much has changed.
To defend Saudi Arabia and defeat Iraq, the United States concentrated about 540,000 troops in the region, roughly a quarter of the active-duty strength of the US armed forces at the time. Seven of the Army’s 18 active divisions and two of the Marine Corps’ three divisions participated, while six of America’s 15 aircraft carriers were deployed, along with approximately 1,600 of its 6,500 combat aircraft.
Desert Storm was ultimately an overwhelming American victory achieved at remarkably low human cost, but American planners didn’t know beforehand that casualties would be so limited. Pre-war estimates envisaged as many as 20,000 casualties, including 6,000 to 7,000 dead, but despite those projections and substantial opposition in Congress, President George H.W. Bush and his administration went ahead.
The contrast with today is amazing as the United States is no longer capable of assembling anything resembling its 1990 force in the Middle East. Around 50,000 American personnel have been deployed for the current operation against Iran, supported by approximately 300 aircraft and just over 20 warships, including two aircraft carriers.
Nor has Washington managed to mobilize its allies on anything approaching the same scale, while Britain alone contributed about 35,000 personnel to the campaign against Iraq in 1990, no American ally from outside the Middle East has made a comparable contribution to the present war.
There has therefore been a radical decline in the resources the leading Western power can mobilize to defend what it regards as vital global interests, as well as in its ability to draw upon allied military power.
Curiously, this has happened without a comparable decline in America’s share of global military expenditure, given the United States accounted for roughly 35-37% of world military spending in 1990 and around 33% in 2025. This discrepancy should encourage greater skepticism about attempts to measure military power simply by comparing defense budgets.
Yet resources are only part of the explanation as more important is Washington’s apparent inability to use effectively the formidable capabilities it still possesses.
The United States undoubtedly retains the technical capacity to inflict a crushing military defeat on Iran and overthrow its government through a sufficiently large joint military operation, even with substantially fewer forces than it deployed against Iraq in 1990, but the obstacle is the price.
Any decisive operation involving a substantial ground component would probably produce many thousands of American casualties, including hundreds, and more likely thousands, of deaths. The political system that accepted such risks in 1990 appears unwilling to accept them today.
The extraordinary effort mounted on April 5, 2026, to rescue the pilot of an F-15 shot down by Iran illustrates the problem, as the United States reportedly committed 176 aircraft to the rescue and lost three manned aircraft and two or three helicopters, representing some $300 million worth of equipment.
The determination to save individual servicemen is understandable, but a military cannot expend resources on that scale to prevent individual casualties while simultaneously fighting a major war intended to achieve decisive strategic objectives.
The same caution is visible elsewhere, seeing as American troops have been kept away from the most dangerous areas, while US warships have operated at considerable distances from the Iranian coast, reducing their effectiveness. Washington has also sought to minimize public attention to its casualties, despite their relatively small number, in marked contrast with its approach during the much more dangerous operations of the early 1990s.
Then there is the financial constraint. The 1990-91 Gulf campaign cost the US budget about $64 billion, or around $120 billion when indirect costs are included. Adjusted for inflation, that would exceed $300 billion today. By mid-July, the current operation against Iran had already cost approximately $37 billion. The total is now likely between $40 billion and $50 billion, even though the campaign has failed to produce the decisive result originally envisaged.
The lesson is therefore more complicated than the simple claim that American military power has disappeared because the United States retains enormous military and financial resources. What’s changed is its ability to concentrate those resources, mobilize allies, and accept the human and financial costs required to achieve decisive political objectives.
Desert Storm demonstrated what American military supremacy looked like at its height, but the war against Iran is revealing something very different, a superpower that can still inflict enormous damage, but increasingly struggles to convert its military superiority into the political outcomes it seeks.
This article was first published by the magazine Profile and was translated and edited by the RT team.

As Chinese chipmakers snap up local gear, self-sufficiency drive faces commercial test

As Chinese chipmakers snap up local gear, self-sufficiency drive faces commercial test
Industry leaders caution that the semiconductor equipment sector must now transition from technical viability to commercial reliability
Chinese chipmakers are setting increasingly aggressive targets to source production equipment locally, adding pressure on domestic toolmakers to come up with machines that are reliable in the exacting environment of high-volume wafer production.
Several new wafer fabrication plants, or fabs, in the country were setting explicit localisation targets, according to Jie Chen, chairman of Britech Semiconductor Equipment (Shanghai) Corp, who spoke at an industry conference in eastern China’s Wuxi on Monday.
“One large customer here in Wuxi is aiming for 80 per cent localisation of equipment at its new fab,” Chen said.
However, industry leaders caution that the equipment sector must now transition from technical viability to commercial reliability, a shift Chen described as moving from a “zero-to-one” phase into a “2.0 era”.
“Making one machine is easy, but can five machines be the same as the first? What about 10, 50 or 100?” Chen said, noting that fabs required absolute consistency across multiple chambers and machines. He added that the industry’s “final exam” would come when Chinese toolmakers could win top overseas clients without home-turf advantage.

Dyson’s Next Act Is an Electric Toothbrush With a Camera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Whenever Dyson enters a new product category, a ripple effect usually follows, with the buzz growing so loud that competitors are forced to react. The company did this with stick vacuums and premium hair dryers. Now it's aspiring to upend the oral care business.
On Tuesday, Dyson announced the CameraJet, a two-in-one electric toothbrush and flosser, to help you clean those pearly whites. It's not the company's first hybrid experiment (that would be the short-lived Dyson Zone air-purifying headphones), but as a pairing of two technologies, this makes far more practical sense—even if the word camera isn’t one you’d typically expect in the name of an oral device.
The CameraJet is an electric toothbrush with an embedded flosser that shoots liquid into the gaps between your teeth as you brush. How does the device know when the brush head is right above a gap that needs blasting? A built-in endoscope camera analyzes 28 images per second, shooting bursts of rinse as you move the device over your teeth.
Dyson calls this the Gap Optical Targeting system. The company says it’s powered by a macro-lens camera and a machine learning algorithm trained on 470,000 dental images that Dyson collected during the six years it spent developing the product. Dyson says the magic happens within 100 milliseconds—the camera sees the gap and flushes it with a mouth rinse, all while you brush normally.
The fluid jet itself has some interesting engineering. Dyson notes that it's a conical jet, which the company claims removes plaque more effectively than the “needle-type jets” used by competing stand-alone water flossers. Dyson says its cone-shaped jet of fluid can remove plaque over a wider area using less pressure, making the brush gentler on gums and enamel.
For testing this, Dyson created its own proxy plaque in collaboration with the National University of Singapore's Faculty of Dentistry. This allowed the designers to iterate and test the brush’s plaque-removing prowess in the lab without running a clinical trial after every minor change.
Right below the brush is a tank where the gadget stores 12.5 milliliters of alcohol-free mouth rinse. A diaphragm pump and pressure chamber ensure the jets shoot out no matter how you hold the brush, which Dyson claims gives the CameraJet an edge over its peers, which it says lose performance when tilted. A docking station refills the toothbrush with mouth rinse in three seconds with the touch of a button. It also recharges the CameraJet and gives it a nice resting place on your sink. There's a travel case for packing the whole thing up.
Finally, we get to the bristle brush head. Dyson says it's contoured precisely to reach a “greater proportion of the tooth's surface,” with firmer inner bristles and softer outer bristles. A radio-frequency identification (RFID) tag inside measures how many cleans it has completed, so you'll know exactly when to replace the brush head. There's also a softer version of the brush head for people with sensitive teeth and gums.
Don't forget the sonic oscillation! That's a normal part of an electric toothbrush, where it vibrates side to side to clean your teeth. Dyson's CameraJet uses variable sonic oscillation, which varies the angle of oscillation as you brush. The company says this design prevents the bristles from stalling under pressure.
All of this brings us to the CameraJet's biggest claim: that it “removes up to 69 percent more plaque than market-leading premium electric toothbrushes in hard-to-reach areas.” (Dyson's small print says this is based on laboratory tests in the brush-only variable mode in hard-to-reach areas.)
The CameraJet connects to your phone over Bluetooth (there's also Wi-Fi support), where it will show up in the MyDyson app. You don't need to open the MyDyson app to use the toothbrush. But if you do use the app, you can look through the brush’s camera in real time and watch the device shoot liquid into your tooth gaps. If you're worried about putting a camera in your bathroom, Dyson says not to worry; the camera is active only when you open the live view through the MyDyson app or when the brush is automatically scanning your teeth to find the places to shoot those rinsing jets. The company says it does not record or store images locally on the CameraJet or in the cloud.
If you decide to use the app, you can get personalized feedback, coverage mapping to make sure you're cleaning all your teeth, and even a guided cleaning mode. Also, if you don't want the CameraJet to shoot its jets automatically, you can use the manual jetting mode.
There are two more things you should consider before bringing this tech into your bathroom.
Dyson products command high prices, and the CameraJet will unsurprisingly cost you a pretty penny: $499. It comes in blue and pink, and each CameraJet comes with a refill dock, two regular brush heads, and a charging cable.
The final catch is that you cannot use any old toothpaste and mouth rinse. Dyson has a proprietary “non-foaming” toothpaste coming soon, which is crucial, because foam will block the camera. The “low-foaming” rinse is also specifically designed to work with the entire system. You'll be able to sign up for a Dyson subscription to get toothpaste, rinse, and replacement brush heads on a recurring basis. However, you can use any third-party rinses and toothpaste if they are sodium lauryl sulfate–free, as that substance causes foaming.
Around one in three adults in the US reports flossing daily, and multiple studies show that people often spend less than a minute brushing instead of the two minutes recommended by the American Dental Association. By combining brushing and flossing, Dyson is pitching that its product condenses two steps into one, though we'll have to see if its camera-equipped brush can successfully blast those jets into just the right spots.

Man cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A man has been cleared of plotting to kidnap princesses Amalia and Alexia, the eldest daughters of king Willem-Alexander and queen Máxima, after a court ruled he was suffering from a psychosis at the time.
Anne Romke van der H., 33, believed he was in a relationship with Amalia, 22, and fantasised about marrying her before living in the wilds in Poland with her and her 21-year-old sister.
He bought items from a hardware store designed to use as a survival kit, including knives, cooking equipment and two hatchets, one of which he inscribed with Alexia’s name.
The prosecution service said he intended to abduct or attack the two princesses if they were unwilling to go along with his plans.
But a court in The Hague ruled there was no evidence that van der H., from Groningen, was preparing an actual attack on Amalia and Alexia or intended to threaten them.
A psychiatric assessment found he was schizophrenic and had become obsessed with the royal family, particularly the two princesses.
He was found guilty of insulting six police officers and smashing a window, but the court did not impose a fine or punishment because he was in psychosis at the time.
The court said the offences were not severe enough to justify a compulsory treatment regime (tbs), but Van der H. told the judges at an earlier hearing that he was willing to undergo voluntary treatment.

Ukrainian Parliament will work in shelter during air-raid warnings – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:27:00 EEST
18:27:00 KST

Ukrainian Parliament will work in shelter during air-raid warnings – photos
Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian Parliament) sessions are planned to continue in a shelter during air-raid warnings. Workstations for members of parliament have been set up in the basement, in the parliamentary conference hall and adjacent corridors.
Source: a statement by Ukrainian Parliament Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk at a meeting with journalists, attended by an Ukrainska Pravda correspondent
Details: The Rada's administrative office has been developing a voting system outside the session hall since the beginning of the full-scale war, but there had been no need to use it until now, Stefanchuk noted. Given the increase in Russian attacks, MPs will be offered the option of continuing to work in the shelter.
Quote: "I want to immediately dispel some myths. People say that MPs will vote from unknown locations using unclear methods. The Rada's rules of procedure provide for two types of voting: using the electronic system and by show of hands. Voting by hand is not an option, because consideration of each document would take an indefinite amount of time. Therefore, we have developed an alternative electronic voting mechanism to preserve all procedural rules."
Details: Stefanchuk recalled the main provisions of the parliamentary rules of procedure. First, sessions must be held exclusively in the Rada building. Second, MPs may vote only in person.
The speaker stressed that "everything possible" has been done to ensure that every parliamentarian can vote in person in the shelter using the electronic system.
Currently, 368 workstations for MPs have been set up in the conference hall and adjacent corridors. As of 1 September, there are 392 MPs in the Rada. "We based our planning on maximum attendance during recent sessions. But we will find a way to accommodate the full composition of parliament in the shelter if necessary," Stefanchuk clarified.
After an air-raid warning is issued, MPs will have approximately 10 minutes to descend to the shelter and continue voting. After the all-clear is given, parliamentarians will return to work in the session hall. An online broadcast of the session from the shelter will be provided.
Viacheslav Shtuchnyi, head of the Rada's administrative office, explained that electronic voting will be carried out using QR codes placed on MPs' personal voting cards.
"For voting in the shelter, each MP's voting card will have a QR code that can be used to access the network. This is a closed network defined by the perimeter. If an MP leaves these boundaries, the connection will be lost and it will be impossible to continue voting. Since the card is personal, no one else will be able to access the system using that code," Shtuchnyi explained.
MPs will be able to vote using either their personal phones or work tablets.
The parliament speaker stressed that parliamentarians will test the new system over the coming week. A draft resolution will subsequently be adopted to formalise the mechanism.

U.S. Army boosts funding for new Kentucky TNT plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:26:37 UTC
18:26:37 KST

- The U.S. Army modified its TNT production facility contract with Paligen Aerospace & Defense, bringing the total value to $435 million.
- The Kentucky facility will be the first domestic TNT production site in the United States since the 1980s, targeted for completion around 2027.
The U.S. Army has ordered $30.8 million in additional work under a contract to build a domestic factory to manufacture TNT in Kentucky, bringing the deal’s total value to $435 million.
The modification, awarded to Paligen Aerospace & Defense LLC, based in Tampa, Florida, covers design, construction and commissioning work on the facility. Army Contracting Command in Rock Island, Illinois, is managing the contract, which is expected to run through February 15, 2029.
TNT is the primary explosive used to fill 155mm artillery shells, along with a range of other munitions from artillery rounds to aircraft bombs. The Army has described the facility as the first domestic TNT production site in the United States since the 1980s, when the Radford Army Ammunition Plant in Virginia halted TNT manufacturing. The Army originally awarded the $435 million contract in November 2024 to Paligen’s predecessor company, then known as REPKON USA, without competitive bidding.
The facility is being built at a commercial site in Graham, Kentucky. According to Paligen, the plant is designed to use automation, digitization and a new waste neutralization process, with construction and full operation targeted within 36 months of the original award, putting completion around early 2027. The award was funded in part through the 2024 Ukraine Supplemental appropriation.
Paligen Technologies, the parent company formed when REPKON USA rebranded in March 2026, has expanded significantly since the TNT contract was first awarded. The company acquired a 38-acre manufacturing facility in Garland, Texas, from General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems in March 2025, along with defense engineering firm McCormick Stevenson Corporation. Paligen now employs more than 400 people across facilities in Florida, Kentucky and Texas.
The push to rebuild domestic TNT capacity has gained added urgency since October 2025, when an explosion destroyed an Accurate Energetic Systems facility in Humphreys County, Tennessee, which had been supplying TNT to the Pentagon. The loss of that plant left the Army without any operating domestic TNT source while the Kentucky facility remains under construction.
The Army’s investment in domestic TNT production has come as the service has separately struggled to rebuild its broader artillery shell manufacturing base. ProPublica reported that General Dynamics failed to get two 155mm shell production lines in Mesquite, Texas, operating as planned before the Army shut the effort down, even as the company continued receiving other Army contracts totaling $2.5 billion since that shutdown.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC’s 3DFabric platform can increase AI computing density and memory bandwidth while improving power delivery and cooling, TSMC Advanced Packaging R&D Director Chen Yen-ming (陳燕銘) said Tuesday.
Speaking at the Heterogeneous Integration Summit ahead of SEMICON Taiwan, Chen said AI is pushing chipmakers to find new ways to fit more computing power into smaller spaces, per CNA. He said better chip design alone is not enough, and companies also need to improve how chips are connected, powered, and cooled.
Chen said AI computing performance is improving fivefold each year, while AI models are also processing several times more tokens, or units of data. He said TSMC’s 3DFabric platform brings together several technologies, including CoWoS advanced packaging, to fit more computing power and memory into AI systems while improving data transfer and cooling.
For System on Integrated Chips, Chen said TSMC plans to reduce the connection spacing between parts of its A14 chips to 4.5 micrometers by 2029. TSMC is also applying its technology to high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI systems, with HBM4 base dies made using its N12 process expected to cut power consumption by more than 45% and increase bandwidth 2.5 times, CNA reported.
Chen said TSMC is also developing its Compact Universal Photonic Engine (COUPE), which connects electronic and optical components to move data more efficiently. TSMC plans to move COUPE closer to the main chip by placing it on an interposer, which Chen said can further improve power efficiency and reduce delays.
CoWoS packaging will also allow TSMC to fit more components into a single package as package sizes grow, Chen said. He said TSMC expects a CoWoS package that can support 24 HBM stacks and exceed 14 times the size of a standard reticle by 2029, while the number of AI computing transistors in a single package is projected to grow more than 48-fold from 2024 to 2029 and HBM bandwidth to increase 34-fold.

Iran, Kyrgyzstan review proposal for joint oil refinery construction
TEHRAN – In a significant move toward deepening energy and economic ties, Iran and Kyrgyzstan have agreed to jointly review a proposal for the construction of an oil refinery in Kyrgyzstan. The announcement came on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and Shanghai-Plus summit held in Kyrgyzstan on Monday.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who met with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov on the summit's margins, confirmed that Tehran has reviewed the proposal positively and agreed to its principle. "Kyrgyzstan's proposal for the joint construction of a refinery in this country has been reviewed positively, and Iran agrees with the principle of this proposal," Pezeshkian stated.
Under the proposed framework, Iran would supply the crude oil required for the refinery, while the resulting petroleum products would be divided between the two nations. The Iranian president described this model of cooperation as a timely opportunity to elevate the level of economic and energy collaboration between the two countries.
The proposal comes at a critical juncture, as energy cooperation has been a central pillar of bilateral relations in recent years. Kyrgyzstan, which currently depends heavily on imports to meet its domestic oil and petroleum product needs, stands to benefit significantly from domestic refining capacity. If finalized, the partnership could expand beyond simple oil and product trade into joint investment, refining operations, technical and engineering services, and the marketing of petroleum products.
President Japarov welcomed the expansion of economic and energy cooperation with Iran and extended an invitation to capable Iranian companies active in oil exploration to bring their expertise to Kyrgyzstan. This invitation is expected to pave the way for a greater Iranian corporate presence in Kyrgyzstan's oil projects and the utilization of Iranian technical and engineering capabilities across various sectors of the Central Asian nation's petroleum industry.
Expanding bilateral economic ties
The refinery proposal is part of a broader push to strengthen economic relations between the two countries. In early August, Iran's Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, met with Kyrgyzstan's Minister of Economy and Commerce, Sydykov Bakyt Tolomushevich. During that meeting, both sides emphasized the development of trade exchanges, joint investment, and the expansion of cooperation in industry, mining, energy, transport, and free zones.
The two ministers underscored the vast capacities for economic cooperation and stressed the importance of advancing trade and investment within the framework of regional agreements, including the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. They also discussed joint production for export to third-country markets, increased collaboration in the export of knowledge-based products, pharmaceuticals, and medical equipment, as well as expanded cooperation between free zones.
Mining, energy, and transit cooperation
In the mining and energy sector, Kyrgyzstan's mineral wealth was a key topic. Iran announced its readiness to cooperate in exploration, extraction, processing, provision of technical and engineering services, modernization of mining industries, and the transfer of technical knowledge.
On the transport and transit front, the two sides emphasized the activation of the Bandar Abbas–Osh railway route, the establishment of direct flights, the reduction of transit costs, and the completion of regional corridors. They also highlighted the importance of participating in China's "Belt and Road" initiative and utilizing Iran's strategic transit position to connect Kyrgyzstan to regional and international markets.
Banking and financial infrastructure
To facilitate this expanding economic partnership, both countries agreed on the development of banking, logistics, and transport infrastructure. Other key agreements included holding a joint banking committee, utilizing national currencies in bilateral transactions, establishing joint investment funds, and employing modern financing methods.
As Iran and Kyrgyzstan continue to build on their growing partnership, the proposed joint oil refinery stands as a potential flagship project—one that could redefine the contours of their economic and energy cooperation for years to come.

More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire came into force in October 2025, according to Gaza health officials. The Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed in militant attacks during the same period. REUTERS

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday urged countries with air defence interceptors nearing expiration to provide them to Ukraine, saying the country lacks the systems needed to protect civilians.

“Diplomatic efforts are still ongoing, but no results at the moment,” she said, adding that it was important that there be “no tolls, no fees” for routes that had previously been open.
The ministers were also set to discuss the protection of critical undersea infrastructure and what more could be done jointly.
Kallas said they would also discuss a possible European mission to support the Lebanese armed forces.

Taipei’s Zhinan Temple begins rebuilding after fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:25:28 UTC
18:25:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei’s Zhinan Temple has begun planning the restoration of its Lingxiao Hall after a fire severely damaged the 60-year-old building on Aug. 24.
More than 100 firefighters were deployed, and no one was injured. The blaze damaged about 1,500 square meters of the building, destroying the first floor and damaging about one-third of the second floor.
Zhinan Temple Chair Kao Chao-wen (高超文) said the rebuilding project is expected to take at least three years and cost more than NT$100 million (US$3.16 million). Kao said the temple has begun cataloging the damage, filing insurance claims, and raising funds for the restoration, per CNA.
Kao said a fire investigation determined that faulty electrical wiring caused the blaze. The fire spread rapidly after reaching wooden decorative panels in the upper part of the hall, he said. The temple will carefully assess damaged religious artifacts and decorations before deciding what can be restored and what must be replaced.
Undamaged bronze statues blackened by smoke will be cleaned, while damaged statues will be repaired by craftspeople. Items that were destroyed will be recreated, Kao said. The temple will also assess damage to carved decorations, paintings, and roof tiles.
“We will strive to present the original appearance and preserve the ancient style,” Kao said, adding that the goal is for the restored hall to retain the appearance familiar to generations of worshippers. Because the project involves traditional sculpture and other specialized craftsmanship, architects and skilled artisans will be consulted on the design and restoration, he said.
Kao said structural engineers have inspected the building and determined that its main structure remains suitable for restoration, with reinforcement to be carried out where necessary. The temple plans to install fire-resistant materials and establish an upgraded fire protection system as part of the reconstruction.
The Taipei City Government has said it will establish a cross-departmental task force to assist with restoration, involving the Department of Civil Affairs, Fire Department, Department of Cultural Affairs, and other agencies. Although Lingxiao Hall is not designated a historic site, both central government and municipal officials have expressed concern over the damage.
The hall was constructed from 1963 to 1966, according to Zhinan Temple records. The temple describes it as a six-story reinforced-concrete structure featuring elaborate dragon and phoenix decorations and a combination of southern and northern Chinese architectural styles.
Kao said the temple has announced a fundraising account through its official Facebook page and hopes public support will allow reconstruction to begin as quickly as possible. He said any surplus funds remaining after restoration will be used to support firefighters by helping improve firefighting equipment and training.
Kao also expressed concern for the firefighters who responded to the blaze and said he hopes to cooperate with the Taipei City Fire Department to support firefighters injured or killed in the line of duty. Kao said he deeply understands the hardships and risks involved in their work, per CNA.
Zhinan Temple, located in Taipei’s Wenshan District, is one of the city’s best-known Taoist religious centers. The temple complex is also a popular destination for visitors because of its mountain setting, proximity to the Maokong Gondola, and views of Taipei and surrounding areas.
Kao thanked the public for its concern following the fire and said the temple’s priority is to restore the damaged hall while creating a safer environment for worshippers. “We hope to provide everyone with a safe and secure place in the future,” he said.

Taiwan airlines’ long-haul fuel surcharge to rise to NT$2,670
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:25:13 UTC
18:25:13 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Fuel surcharges on international passenger flights operated by Taiwan-based airlines will rise Sept. 7 as aviation fuel prices increase.
The Civil Aviation Administration said in a press release that the surcharge for short-haul routes will increase to US$32.50 (NT$1,028) per passenger per flight segment, while the long-haul surcharge will rise to US$84.50. This marks the fifth adjustment this year and the second consecutive monthly increase, per Mirror Media.
The agency said state-owned CPC Corp.'s latest international aviation fuel price rose from US$147.57 to US$156.79 per barrel, moving the applicable surcharge level from the 12th to the 13th tier.
The short-haul rate applies to routes in Asia, excluding India and the Middle East, and will increase by about NT$79 per flight segment. The long-haul rate covers Europe, the Americas, Africa, Oceania, Antarctica, India, and the Middle East, and will rise by about NT$206 per segment.
The agency has used a floating fuel surcharge mechanism with Taiwan-based airlines since 2005, based on CPC’s posted international aviation fuel price. No surcharge is imposed when the price is below US$40 per barrel, while rates start at US$5 for short-haul routes and US$13 for long-haul routes when the price is from US$40 to below US$50.
For every additional US$10 increase in the fuel price, the surcharge rises by US$2.50 for short-haul routes and US$6.50 for long-haul routes. The agency said the system adjusts surcharges in line with changes in fuel costs.
To address consumer concerns and protect passenger rights, the agency has instructed airlines to provide information on the share of fuel costs in ticket prices and how surcharges are calculated. Travelers can check the latest surcharge details on individual airlines’ websites before purchasing tickets.
International oil prices have fluctuated sharply this year amid instability in the Middle East, with long-haul fuel surcharges peaking at US$117 in April, Mirror Media reported. They then fell in June and July as oil prices declined, with short-haul and long-haul surcharges dropping to US$27.50 and US$71.50, respectively, before rising again in August.

India's GDP growth: BJP hails 'economic resilience'; Congress asks where are the jobs?

Prasad compared India’s performance with growth recorded by several other major economies while Khera argued that a single quarter of strong GDP growth should not be treated as evidence of broad-based economic prosperity.
NEW DELHI: The BJP and Congress on Tuesday traded sharply contrasting assessments of India’s economy after official data showed GDP growth of 7.8 per cent in the April-June 2026 quarter. While the BJP hailed the performance as evidence of resilient economic management, the Opposition questioned whether the growth has translated into jobs, higher incomes and wider prosperity.BJP leader Ravi Shankar Prasad held a press conference where he described the latest growth figures as “particularly significant”. He argued that India had expanded rapidly despite heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty during the quarter, including the Gulf crisis, disruptions to oil supplies and supply-chain pressures.“Today is a very encouraging day. The latest report shows that India’s GDP growth stood at 7.8 per cent in the April-June 2026 quarter. The figure of 7.8 per cent is particularly significant because, during this period, the Gulf crisis had intensified. There were concerns over oil supplies, disruptions in supply chains, and uncertainty across the global economy. Despite all these challenges, India’s economy grew by 7.8 per cent,” Prasad said at a press conference in Delhi.
Prasad also compared India’s performance with growth recorded by several other major economies, saying Canada grew by around 1.5 per cent, Germany by 1 per cent, the UK by 2.1 per cent, Malaysia by about 6 per cent, South Korea by around 3.7 per cent and the US by roughly 2 per cent during the same period.
He attributed India’s performance to what he called effective economic management and praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership.“Today, I would like to congratulate and commend India’s economic management. I also wholeheartedly congratulate the honourable Prime Minister for his vision, wisdom and leadership,” Prasad said.The Congress, however, challenged the BJP’s interpretation of the GDP figures, arguing that headline growth alone does not adequately capture the economic conditions faced by ordinary Indians.Congress leader Pawan Khera questioned how the 7.8 per cent growth figure was benefiting young people and farmers, while also pointing to concerns over employment, manufacturing, education and income distribution.“The Prime Minister comes up with a reel, a video. Ask him: the largest demographic in this country is the youth. How does this GDP growth affect the youth? How does it address the issues that young people face? The largest occupation in this country is agriculture. How does this GDP growth affect the agricultural sector? If it doesn’t benefit these two sectors, how does it affect the dwindling manufacturing sector? Look at the manufacturing data. So, what is he even talking about? A handful of people contribute to the growth of this country, but where is the redistribution of income? Where is the distribution of income? So, let’s talk about these fundamental issues. 80 per cent of this country depends on free ration. Is that what good GDP growth does for the country? That’s our question.”
Khera had earlier taken his criticism to X, arguing that a single quarter of strong GDP growth should not be treated as evidence of broad-based economic prosperity.“One quarter of 7.8% growth is not an economic spring. If India has truly "bloomed," why do rampant unemployment, leaked exam papers, and a crumbling education system define the ground reality? Why is the republic's prosperity not translating into the prosperity of its public? GDP measures national output - not jobs, not wages, not opportunity. If it measured any of those, the future of India's youth would not look so bleak. Modi can manage his headlines. For India's youth, the question remains the same as ever: Where are the jobs?”
At his press conference, Khera also questioned whether the strong GDP reading had resulted in tangible improvements in the cost of living and employment conditions.“On one hand, they say, "Look at the GDP of a single quarter and applaud." On the other, they say, "Don't buy gold, don't host lavish weddings." They themselves sit abroad while telling the country's citizens not to travel overseas and to save money. 80% of the population relies on free rations, but keep applauding... Regarding this 7.8% figure—what benefit is the country's largest sector, agriculture, deriving from it? The youth constitute the country's largest demographic; what benefit are they getting? Have their issues been resolved? Have milk prices dropped? Is there no longer a need for free rations? Have you rectified the employment situation to reverse the 45-year record low? Is manufacturing back on track? What happened to the MSME sector? What happened to the unorganized sector? If you have answers showing a positive outcome, then we, too, will applaud.
The competing responses underline the political divide over how India's economic performance should be assessed. While the BJP has used the 7.8 per cent quarterly expansion to highlight India's relative resilience amid global disruptions, the Congress has focused on whether headline GDP growth is being reflected in employment, household incomes and opportunities for India's young population.

In Verkhnekamyanka, Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces hit an area where Russian military equipment was concentrated.
In Borisovka, Russian Belgorod Region, Ukrainian forces destroyed a fuel and lubricants depot used to supply Russian military equipment.

Recyclable airplanes developed by Swiss researchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:24:00 UTC
18:24:00 KST

Recyclable airplanes developed by Swiss researchers
Scientists in Switzerland are working to make airplanes recyclable. A newly developed composite material is intended to ensure that lightweight and robust components no longer inevitably end up in landfill or incinerators.
Materials used in the construction of planes or trains must be lightweight, robust and flame-retardant. Until now, however, such composite materials have not been recyclable. Researchers have now developed a material designed to combine these properties, the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology (EMPA) announced on Tuesday.
The material developed is a multi-layered composite. A core made of a heat-resistant aramid honeycomb structure is sandwiched between layers of glass or carbon fibres. Epoxy resin is used as the binder. Such resins cannot normally be melted down or dissolved. As a result, composite materials of this kind often end up in landfill sites or are incinerated.
The EMPA researchers added a phosphorus-containing molecule to the epoxy resin. This additive not only makes the material flame-retardant but also enables it to be recycled. Once cured, the resin can be softened again under certain conditions and reshaped.
More
Making synthetic fuels: a Swiss scientist’s bid to decarbonise cars and planes
Recovering all components
The main aim of the project was the complete recycling of the composite material. Using a solvent and heat, the composite can be broken down into its constituent parts. This allows the aramid honeycomb structure and the glass or carbon fibres to be recovered.
According to the researchers, the new material meets current fire safety requirements and achieves almost the same mechanical properties as conventional epoxy resin.
The next step is to scale up the manufacturing and recycling processes. The EMPA research team is also investigating further potential applications for the plastic, such as in the energy sector and the construction industry.
The project was carried out in collaboration with the industrial partner Elantas and supported by Innosuisse.

India’s anti-terror agency to question jailed Ukrainian mercenary
India’s federal anti-terror agency will interrogate a Ukrainian and an American who were arrested in March for allegedly entering the country’s restricted areas without permits, and crossing over into neighboring Myanmar to provide training to armed groups.
A Delhi court on Monday allowed the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to interrogate Ukrainian Viktor Kaminskyi and American Matthew VanDyke on September 2 and 3.
Both men are currently in Delhi’s Tihar jail. The two, along with five other Ukrainians – Petro Hurba, Taras Slyviak, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Marian Stefankiv, and Maksim Honcharuk – were arrested from three different cities while trying to fly out of the country.

U.S. Army orders $712.5 million worth of artillery fuzes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:20:54 UTC
18:20:54 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Action Manufacturing Co. a contract worth up to $712.5 million to produce M739A1 artillery fuzes.
- The indefinite-delivery contract runs through August 31, 2031, with only one company submitting a bid.
An artillery shell won’t explode without one small part screwed into its nose or tail: the fuze. The U.S. Army just signed a $712.5 million contract to keep a steady supply of them coming.
Action Manufacturing Co., based in Bristol, Pennsylvania, won the contract to build, inspect, test, package and deliver M739A1 point detonating and delay fuzes. Only one company bid for the job. Army Contracting Command in Newark, New Jersey, is overseeing the deal, which runs through August 31, 2031.
An artillery shell by itself is basically dead weight, a heavy metal tube filled with explosive that does nothing until something triggers it. That trigger is the fuze. Without one, you don’t have a weapon, you have expensive scrap metal.
The M739A1 is a “point detonating/delay” fuze, which means it can be set two different ways depending on the target. Set to detonate on impact, it explodes the instant the shell hits something, useful against troops or equipment out in the open. Set to delay, it lets the shell punch through a roof, a bunker wall or several feet of dirt first, then explodes a fraction of a second later, deep inside whatever it just penetrated. That flexibility is why the Army buys these by the hundreds of thousands rather than relying on a single fixed design.
The contract is structured as an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity deal, which is standard practice for parts like this. Instead of committing to buy a fixed number of fuzes up front, the Army sets a ceiling price, in this case $712.5 million, and orders however many it actually needs over the life of the contract as demand comes up. Work locations and funding get sorted out order by order rather than all at once.
The Army hasn’t said how many fuzes it expects to actually buy under this ceiling, where the manufacturing work will happen beyond Action Manufacturing’s Bristol facility, or how this order fits into the broader push to rebuild American artillery ammunition stockpiles that have been drawn down by years of supporting Ukraine.

Annual global climate-related losses to reach $450 bln — FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:18:59 UTC
18:18:59 KST

LONDON, September 1. /TASS/. Annual global losses from climate change could reach $450 bln in a "typical year" in the coming years and rise even further in catastrophic years, the Financial Times (FT) reported, citing US analytics company Verisk Analytics (VA).
Two years ago, such losses from natural disasters, including damage to expanding infrastructure, totaled $320 bln, according to UN estimates. Meanwhile, new data from risk modeling company VA show that as much as 62% of global losses from natural disasters, averaging around $279 bln, are uninsured.
The rising losses reflect the growing impact of climate change. Against this backdrop, the insurance industry, faced with mounting losses from catastrophic risks, is covering an increasingly smaller share of the total estimated damage. Major insurers have also withdrawn entirely from some regions, declining to renew policies in areas facing growing risks.
The magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck Myanmar in March 2025 caused an estimated $12 bln in damage, of which insurers covered less than $100 mln, according to Verisk Analytics. Losses from the July 2025 floods in Texas, which killed 130 people, were estimated at $1.1 bln, but most of the damage was uninsured.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez linked Russia, Israel, and international far-right networks to a disinformation campaign following a mass migrant arrival in Ceuta in late July, while ruling out any involvement by Moroccan authorities.
Around 5,000 migrants, including 1,200 minors, remain in the enclave. Nine out of ten people who arrived during the initial wave have already been returned to Morocco, according to Cadena SER.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a recent interview with Cadena SER's "Hoy por Hoy," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez stated that executive authorities continue to investigate the causes behind the unprecedented influx of people reaching the autonomous city of Ceuta.
Sánchez explained that the government must base its actions on verified facts and identified the distortion of a Supreme Court ruling regarding swimming migrants as a key factor amplified across social media platforms and criminal networks.
Sánchez specifically identified Russia, Israel, and international far-right groups as sources of fake news aimed at using migration to destabilize Spain and create divisions within Europe. However, he clarified that this activity does not necessarily indicate direct actions by the respective foreign governments and noted that the complete origin of the campaign remains under investigation.

Sánchez denied any contradiction between statements made by Defense Minister Margarita Robles, who noted that CNI shared intelligence regarding boundary crossings, and Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska, who stated there were no warnings of a mass entry of that magnitude.
The Spanish prime minister emphasized that security measures were heightened before the event based on available data, though the full extent could not be anticipated.
The prime minister explicitly ruled out any involvement by the Moroccan government, describing Rabat’s cooperation.
"Not one of the intelligence services with which the Spanish government regularly collaborates raises doubts about the involvement, in one way or another, of the Moroccan authorities," Sánchez stated. A buyer has been found for the former Audi car assembly plant in Vorst (Greater Brussels): the Heylen Group, a company based in the Kempen District is purchasing the site. It plans to develop a large business park, hosting local firms and international players. In the long term, the project is expected to create 3,000 jobs, roughly the same number as the jobs lost due to the closure of the Audi car assembly factory. A year and a half ago, the last car rolled off the production line at the Audi factory in Vorst. Since then, the site, covering some 55 hectares, has stood empty.
Heylen Group snaps up Audi site in Vorst: 3,000 new jobs on the way at new business park
For a long time, it was unclear what would become of Brussels’ largest industrial site. Among other possibilities, it was mooted as a potential defence site. That will not be happening after all.
Heylen Group comprises more than 40 companies and is owned by an entrepreneur from Herentals (Antwerp Province). Heylen aims to turn the site into “one of Brussels’ most dynamic economic centres”.
‘Rings Park 21’
The project has been named ‘Rings Park 21’. Dozens of businesses are set to move in, ranging from large to small players. Exactly which companies these will be is not yet clear. Part of the site is also set to be opened to the public. The nearby Vorst-Zuid railway station will also be integrated into the project.
‘Bringing together SMEs and established industrial activities is precisely the model of urban economy that we want to develop in Brussels,’ says Laurent Hublet, the Brussels Employment and Economy Minister (Francophone centrist Les Engagés). ‘This project is in line with that and ensures that the site continues to serve the Brussels economy and the people of Brussels.’
To attract entrepreneurs to the site, the minister has promised incentives, such as tax incentives and fast-track planning permission.
Employment recovery
‘Rings Park 21’ is expected to create at least 3,000 jobs – roughly the same number as the old Audi workforce. Heylen Warehouses aims to create these jobs as quickly as possible.
“We’re getting started straight away, because every day counts when it comes to employment. The urgency is not only financial but also social: the sooner this forward-looking project becomes operational, the sooner Brussels can restore the lost jobs and generate a new dynamic for growth,” says CEO Ralph Caspanni. The company expects it will take just under 10 years to roll out the entire project.
The purchase price has not been disclosed. In March, the group also acquired a large part of the former Caterpillar factory in Gosselies, near Charleroi (Hainault Province). There, 37.5 hectares are being redeveloped into an SME-zone.

Estonia's new expert panel to tackle online risks to youth mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:18:00 UTC
18:18:00 KST

Estonia's new expert panel to tackle online risks to youth mental health
An expert panel convened by the Estonian government is examining online risks to youth mental health in a push for solutions to make digital spaces safer for kids and teens.
The panel will submit recommendations to the government by the end of 2026, covering measures for kids and teens, parents and guardians as well as the state that preserve the benefits of digital technology while reducing potential harms.
"Youths' anxiety and mental health issues are a serious and growing concern," said Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform). "Several countries have introduced or are considering restrictions on youths' social media use in recent years, but more crucial than bans are solutions that actually help our young people."
The panel's leading experts, he added, will work with researchers, youth workers and representatives of youth themselves to find effective ways to reduce the negative effects of social media.
Troubling studies
The move comes amid signs of growing problematic digital use among Estonian kids and teens.
A 2025 University of Tartu study found students were increasingly exposed to disturbing online content, sexually explicit messages and excessive internet use, with harmful content and cyberbullying also linked to poorer mental well-being.
A 2022 National Institute for Health Development (TAI) found symptoms of social media addiction among 8 percent of 11- to 15-year-olds, up from 6 percent in 2018.
The study also linked social media use with lower life satisfaction, less sleep, weaker school performance and more frequent depressive episodes.
The researchers stressed, however, that digital technology itself does not cause mental health issues, with its effects depending on how and why it is used.
Practical solutions, not blanket bans
The newly convened panel brings together experts in media studies, psychology, neuroscience, education, mental health, child protection and youth work, along with a youth representative. University of Tartu media studies professor Andra Siibak was elected panel chair.
"Our common goal is to develop multilevel solutions based on scientific research and international best practices and tailored to Estonia's circumstances and our young people's experiences," said Siibak.
"We will be working with young people to develop and discuss these solutions to ensure our recommendations are not only evidence-based but also genuinely workable for the target group they are meant to serve," she added.
The panel will examine risks associated with both social media and online video game platforms.
Its next meeting is scheduled for September 14.

Euro area annual inflation accelerated to 3.3% in August, its highest level since September 2023, when it stood at 4.3%, according to a flash estimate released by Eurostat on Tuesday.
The rate rose from 2.9% in July, remaining above the European Central Bank’s medium-term target of 2%.
Consumer prices increased 0.4% on a monthly basis in August, the EU’s statistical office said.
Energy was the main driver of the acceleration, with annual energy inflation climbing to 14.3% from 10.3% in July. Energy prices increased 2.9% month on month.
Annual inflation for non-energy industrial goods also rose to 1.2% from 0.9%.
In contrast, services inflation eased to 3% from 3.3%, while inflation for food, alcohol and tobacco remained unchanged at 1.2%.
Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, edged down to 2.4% from 2.5%. Inflation excluding only energy remained stable at 2.2%.
Among euro-area members, Lithuania recorded the highest annual inflation rate at 5.8%, followed by the Greek Cypriot Administration at 5.2% and Bulgaria at 5.1%.
Spain’s annual inflation climbed to 4.5%, while the rate stood at 4.2% in Belgium, 3.2% in Italy, 2.9% in Germany, and 2.7% in France.
The lowest annual rates were recorded in Estonia at 1.3%, Malta at 1.9%, and Finland at 2.4%.

Israeli army forces raided Tuesday the countryside of Daraa province in southern Syria, in the latest violation of the Arab country’s sovereignty, Syrian Alikhbariah TV reported.
An Israeli force made up of 10 military vehicles advanced into Jamlah village in the Daraa countryside and deployed among residential neighborhoods, the broadcaster said.
Earlier Tuesday, the television said Israeli forces stationed at Al-Jazeera barracks in the western Daraa countryside opened fire toward residential homes in Maariya village.
The incidents come amid continued Israeli violations of Syrian sovereignty and incursions into the country’s southern territory.

The violations come despite meetings between Damascus and Tel Aviv aimed at reducing escalation.

On July 26, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa said his country was working with several countries to reach a security agreement with Israel, adding that if the deal succeeds, it could pave the way for comprehensive peace without Syria giving up its right to the occupied Golan Heights.
Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967. After the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in late 2024, Israel declared the 1974 disengagement agreement collapsed and occupied the Syrian buffer zone and other sites, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon (Jabal al-Sheikh).

Cigarettes are on the decline in the EU, but how popular are smoking and vaping still?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:13:26 UTC
18:13:26 KST

Despite the EU's goal of creating a "Tobacco-Free Generation" by 2040, more than 16% of people over 16 smoke and vape every single day. Who are the biggest smokers in the bloc?
It's well-known that smoking is harmful to your health, and the use of cigarettes in Europe is seeing a slow yet steady decline.
In 2025, one in six people aged 16 or older in the EU used tobacco and related products, such as e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, every day, according to Eurostat.
The statistics office said that 20.8% of men smoked every day, compared with 12.6% of women.
However, both shares decreased slightly compared with 2022, when 22.2% of men and 13.1% of women smoked daily.
Tobacco kills 1.1 million people in Europe each year, with 153,000 of those dying from exposure to second-hand smoke, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Furthermore, deaths from lung cancer attributable to tobacco use are 71% for men and 46% for women.
As tobacco is such a prevalent cause of cancer, the EU has brought in measures to stem its use, including a goal to reduce its use to less than 5% of the population by 2040 under its Beating Cancer Plan.
Tobacco use varies by age, although not significantly. People aged between 35 and 49 years old registered the highest share (21.3%) of daily users of tobacco, e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, according to Eurostat.
This was followed by people aged between 25 and 34 at 19.9%, and those aged between 50 and 64 at 19.8%.
Which countries smoke the most?
Among EU countries, Bulgaria (26.3%), Sweden (23.9%) and Croatia (23.6%) recorded the highest shares of the daily use of tobacco and related products.
In contrast, the Netherlands (9.9%), Ireland (11.7%), Belgium (13.6%) and Luxembourg (13.8%) had the lowest shares.
In 17 EU countries, the share of people who used tobacco and related products daily decreased between 2022 and 2025.
The largest decreases were in Spain and Luxembourg, while Croatia and Lithuania recorded the largest increases.
Are citizens aware of the smoking consequences?
Despite years of tobacco-control policies, graphic warnings and public-health campaigns about the dangers of smoking, medical journal BMJ Open found that awareness of its health consequences has barely improved over the past two decades.
More than 90% of respondents knew that smoking can cause lung cancer.
Yet, only about 80% identified heart disease as a consequence of smoking and even fewer knew about the stroke risk as well as second-hand smoke risks.
Researchers found that awareness that smoking causes lung cancer increased significantly in the Netherlands in the same timeframe, but declined in countries such as Germany, France, and Romania.

Xi's visit to Egypt marks Chinese interest in Middle East, Egypt's push to keep growing - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:12:26 UTC
18:12:26 KST

China’s President Xi Jinping is visiting Egypt this week. The three-day visit is important as it showcases China’s continued interest in the Middle East.
It is his first to Egypt since 2016, MBN News noted, and it “coincides with the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries. Egypt was the first Arab and African state to establish relations with the People’s Republic of China in 1956.”
The MBN report adds that “the anniversary offers both governments an opportunity to highlight a partnership that has expanded into infrastructure, trade, telecommunications, space technology, defense, and artificial intelligence. Behind the official celebrations, however, is a more practical question: Why has Egypt become so important to China?”
Why indeed? Egypt is a large country with around 100 million people. It has the Suez Canal, and it is situated at the junction of the Middle East and North Africa. It plays a role in Libya and Sudan and historically was a leader in the Arab world. Egypt was also an important country during the Cold War and has continued to be an anchor of the entire region.
However, instability during the Arab Spring and the rule of Mohammed Morsi left questions about what comes next. In recent years, Egypt has stabilized and also invested heavily in new military-security institutions.
China Daily noted that “in congratulatory messages exchanged on May 30, on the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic ties between the two countries, President Xi Jinping said China-Egypt relations have become a model of amity, solidarity, and cooperation among developing countries, as well as a benchmark for collective cooperation between China and Arab states and between China and Africa.”
China is keen to work with Egypt
The report says that Xi is keen to work with Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi. This can lead to a “push for the growth of China-Egypt relations, featuring greater strategic guidance, stronger synergy for development, and broader international influence.”
China has been seeking greater inroads in the Middle East. It would like to see economic blocs such as BRICS and SCO expand their role in the region. However, it is cautious, as it saw how a 25-year deal with Iran did not pan out. It is wary of the instability caused by the Iranian conflict.
“Egyptian President al-Sisi said Egypt and China have stood shoulder to shoulder through different historical periods, and that bilateral relations have maintained steady growth over the past 70 years. He expressed the hope of working with Xi to advance bilateral ties and jointly build a more stable multipolar world with a greater capacity to address global challenges,” China Daily noted.
The report goes on to note that “China and Egypt signed a memorandum of understanding on jointly building the Belt and Road in January 2016, when Xi made a state visit to Egypt. In 2024, the two countries signed a cooperation plan to further align the Belt and Road Initiative with Egypt’s Vision 2030.”
Chinese companies have played a role in “building the Central Business District in Egypt’s new administrative capital and the 10th of Ramadan light rail transit system.”
Economic and trade initiatives are clear: “Tarek Nosseir, president of the Cairo-based think tank Global Forum for Future Studies, told Xinhua News Agency that Chinese participation in major projects had helped to localize advanced technologies, attract investment, support national development plans, and create tens of thousands of jobs. He also pointed to collaboration in renewable energy, the national power grid, and transportation networks,” China Daily added.
There is a lot of talk about how both countries are ancient civilizations. China feels comfortable placing its bets on a country like Egypt because of this fact, since it has such a long past. Egypt’s Ahram Online also mentioned how the countries have ancient civilizations.
Ahram also noted that the visit coincides with the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries, echoing the same message of discipline being put forth in Cairo and Beijing: “Ambassador Ezzat Saad, executive director of the Egyptian Council for Foreign Affairs (ECFA), said Egypt and China represent two of the oldest civilizations in human history.
“This year also marks 10 years since Xi’s historic visit to Cairo, during which he delivered a major address at the headquarters of the Arab League and presented China’s policy towards the Arab world.”
The Ahram report added that “relations gained considerable momentum following Sisi’s assumption of office in 2014, particularly because of his appreciation of China’s experience in achieving comprehensive and sustainable development. The two countries subsequently elevated their relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership.”
Egypt's relations with the BRICS group
BRICS also came up in the messaging: “Egypt began engaging with BRICS through the BRICS Plus framework in September 2017. China introduced the format during the BRICS summit in Xiamen, which Sisi attended at Xi’s invitation,” Ahram added.
“China has become one of Egypt’s most important economic partners, while Egypt provides Beijing with a strategically located gateway to Arab and African markets through its ports, transport networks, and the Suez Canal. Egypt, in turn, benefits from Chinese investment, expertise, and technology in infrastructure, energy, transport, telecommunications, and industry.”
A few other details are worth noting, based on Egyptian government media coverage.
Among them, that Sisi has made eight trips to China, and that “Egypt’s Investment and Foreign Trade Ministry put bilateral trade at about $19.52 billion in 2025, describing China as one of Egypt’s largest trading partners.”
Additionally, Egypt has sought to increase exports to China, while Chinese investment is believed to exceed $10 billion in Egypt, focusing on “construction, textiles, electronics, energy, transport, and industrial manufacturing.”
Furthermore, “the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone in Ain Sokhna is a central part of the relationship,” Ahram added. “A July 2025 agreement expanded the TEDA industrial zone from seven to about 10 square kilometers. The zone hosted 185 companies when Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited Egypt that month.”
Many projects are continuing, including manufacturing investments.

Kenya aviation workers end 2-day strike after deal with government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:12:19 UTC
18:12:19 KST

Andrew Wasike 
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Kenyan aviation workers on Tuesday called off a two-day strike that disrupted air traffic and caused flight cancellations and delays at major airports across the East African country after reaching a return-to-work agreement with the government and aviation authorities.
The Kenya Aviation Workers Union (KAWU) agreed to immediately end the industrial action after signing the deal with the Transport Ministry, Kenya Airports Authority (KAA), Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) and Kenyan carrier Jambojet.
“The employees shall resume their respective duties and cooperate with management to ensure the immediate restoration and continuity of normal operations,” the agreement said.
Under the deal, agency fees owed to KAWU and held by KAA will be released to the union immediately.
KAWU and KCAA will also resume negotiations on a collective bargaining agreement, with KCAA committing to honor and implement the outcome.
The agreement also states that workers who participated in the strike will not be victimized, intimidated, discriminated against or subjected to disciplinary action over their involvement.
A separate dispute between KAWU and Jambojet over recognition of the union remains before the courts, with both sides agreeing to abide by the eventual ruling.
The strike began Sunday and disrupted operations at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) in Nairobi, as well as airports in Mombasa, Kisumu and Eldoret.
Kenya Airways said some of its flights were canceled, delayed or otherwise disrupted, while RwandAir canceled its WB452 and WB453 services Monday due to air traffic control constraints at JKIA.
It was the second major aviation workers’ strike in Kenya this year.
In February, KAWU members staged another strike that disrupted Kenyan airspace and operations at JKIA for about a day and a half before returning to work following government-mediated talks.
