Britons face ‘risk premium’ for energy as US-Israel war on Iran intensifies
A price cap increase is on the way, the latest blow to people already struggling with rising costs.
London, United Kingdom – Andrew, a 70-year-old retiree from the eastern English city of Norwich, had enrolled months ago in a fixed-rate energy plan for 18 months, learning from earlier price shocks caused by wars.
“I guess I saw this coming,” he told Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4How has life changed for Iranians six months into the war?
- list 2 of 4Who are the economic winners and losers of the US-Israel war on Iran?
- list 3 of 4Petrol prices strain US households as oil giants Chevron, Exxon profits soar
- list 4 of 4Inside the UK’s ‘stressful’ cost of living crisis Burnham hopes to tackle
Days ago, Ofgem, the energy regulator for England, Scotland and Wales, announced a 4 percent increase of the energy price cap from October 1, 2026, a result of the sharp rise in wholesale gas prices due to the United States-Israel war on Iran.
“The situation doesn’t look any clearer … the fog of war is still there, and who knows when it will blow away,” said Andrew, who requested that his surname be withheld for privacy.
The end of his fixed-rate plan is not something he likes to think about.
“I don’t think there’s going to be clarity,” he said. “I can’t see that the current state of geopolitics will allow for any resolution. I’m starting to think, if it’s not one conflict zone, it will be another.”
According to Ofgem, 35 percent of households in England, Scotland and Wales are on similar, fixed-rate energy plans, and will not be immediately affected by the Ofgem price cap increase.
Most, however, will face higher bills in the winter, an added blow to a nation already struggling amid a continued cost-of-living crisis.
A household using a regular level of energy will pay about 60 pounds ($80) a year more.
The UK government, alongside the increase, announced a tax cut on monthly electricity bills as part of a wider effort to shield people from the increasingly stark economic impacts of the Iran war as winter approaches. The tax cut is noted to last until the end of the 2027 financial year, but both experts and everyday people are not so sure that costs will be under control by then.
While the move on tax gives people “room to breathe, it doesn’t fix the fundamentals”, Ahmed Tabaqchali, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera.
“We are not going to see a return to normality as far as the Strait of Hormuz is concerned. One way or the other, whatever end-game with the US and Iran, there is now a change to the status quo,” said Tabaqchali, who has worked in capital markets for more than 25 years.
Volatility is not a temporary concern, he said.
“As long as the United Kingdom relies on energy imports, we are going to be impacted by geopolitics,” said Jack Burt, a PhD candidate at the University of Cambridge, researching novel forms of energy storage.
Before the Iran war, roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through the Strait of Hormuz, the only route connecting the Gulf to the ocean. Iran shut the strategic waterway not long after the initial US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in late February, triggering a global energy crisis.
Shortly after those initial strikes, the UK House of Commons Library released a briefing noting that the Bank of England would likely scrap plans to lower interest rates, while predicting that household gas bills would increase.
“Higher energy costs are likely to result in the UK economic activity weakening,” the report said.
Ofgem’s move is the latest development in the ongoing energy crisis stemming from the war.
Wholesale prices have risen by 11 percent over the past three months, noted Ofgem, with Neil Kenward, the body’s director general for markets, underlining that “high international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK”.
The price cap applies to gas and electricity, while the tax cut applies to electricity bills, meaning households that do not use gas will fare better than those that do.
A ‘risk premium’ for energy supply
While diplomatic efforts in the Gulf region have focused on keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, US attacks on Iran over the weekend – the first in a month – threaten continued destabilisation.
“The consumer is going to be paying a ‘risk premium’ for energy supply,” noted Burt.
Following the 2022 full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, when monthly energy bills hit all-time highs, the UK moved away from gas coming through Russian pipelines “and became much more reliant on other suppliers of liquid natural gas, mostly coming from the Middle East”, he said.
Ozan, 20, a business owner in northeast London, said that “it’s getting more and more difficult to absorb the rises” for small business owners.
“Ultimately, the customer is also suffering, leading to less disposable income, meaning less spending.”
Last week, the Centre for Economics and Business Research forecast that by the end of 2027, the average UK household’s real spending power will be reduced by 2,400 pounds ($3,200), as the prices of everyday goods continue to increase.
Ofgem’s price cap will be reviewed again in January, following a quarterly schedule. But experts are predicting a continued rise in prices, painting a bleak picture for the UK’s energy sector.

Indian consulate in UAE issues warning over biometric fraud targeting nationals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:13:01 UTC
17:13:01 KST

The advisory urged nationals not to share their passports, Emirates IDs, biometric data, including eye, face or fingerprint scans, or personal and financial credentials with unauthorised individuals or agencies under any circumstances.
NEW DELHI: The consulate general of India in Dubai has warned Indian nationals in the UAE, particularly blue-collar workers, against handing over biometric data. The warning advised the workers against unauthorised agents claiming to help with visa regularisation, Emergency Certificates, Exit Permits, Emirates IDs or employment, after reports of fraud involving the misuse of fingerprints and facial scans.In an advisory issued on Monday, the consulate said it had received information about individuals and agents allegedly exploiting Indians seeking assistance with immigration and documentation procedures. The fraudsters reportedly ask victims to provide fingerprints or face scans, which can then be used without their knowledge to conduct financial transactions, open bank accounts or obtain loans and credit cards in their names.The consulate cautioned that such misuse could leave victims liable for financial obligations or transactions they did not authorise. In some cases, those affected could also face multiple fines, travel bans and even imprisonment.The advisory urged nationals not to share their passports, Emirates IDs, biometric data, including eye, face or fingerprint scans, or personal and financial credentials with unauthorised individuals or agencies under any circumstances.
It also clarified that biometric information required for procedures such as exit permits, Emirates IDs or visa regularisation must be provided only at official UAE Government facilities or counters. People were specifically warned against submitting such information through private individuals, agents or third-party service providers claiming to be authorised by UAE authorities.The consulate also sought to dispel a potential source of confusion by stating that biometric information is not required for certain consular services.The advisory said the Consulate General of India in Dubai and the Embassy of India in Abu Dhabi "DO NOT require any fingerprint scan or face/eye scan from applicants for the issuance of a passport or emergency certificate."It warned that any person or agent demanding such information while claiming to represent the Indian Embassy or consulate would be engaging in fraudulent activity and should not be entertained.
Indians approached by unauthorised individuals seeking biometric data or Emirates IDs have been advised to contact the Pravasi Bharatiya Sahayata Kendra through the toll-free number 80046342, WhatsApp or SMS at 00971543090571, or email pbsk.dubai@mea.gov.in to verify credentials or seek assistance.
The consulate urged Indian nationals living in or visiting the UAE to exercise caution, independently verify the credentials of anyone offering immigration or documentation-related services, and report suspicious activity to the Indian consulate and the relevant UAE authorities.

Japan, US agree on need for continued coordination to stabilize yen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:12:27 UTC
17:12:27 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
 Japan and the US agreed that continued coordination is essential to ensuring orderly movements in the yen and maintaining global financial stability, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Monday.
Katayama met US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the sidelines of a two-day Group of 20 finance ministers and central bank governors meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.
“We confirmed that an orderly yen exchange rate is essential for the stability of global financial markets, including those of the United States, and that the continued coordinated efforts of Japan and the United States contribute to achieving this shared objective,” she told reporters after the meeting.
The two officials also reaffirmed the significance of their countries’ recent joint intervention in the foreign exchange market, Katayama said.
The meeting came about a month after Japan and the US conducted their first coordinated yen-buying intervention since the 1998 Asian financial crisis.
The intervention was launched on July 31 after the yen weakened to a 40-year low near 164 against the dollar.
Japan spent a record 15.4 trillion yen ($96 billion) between late July and August to support its currency, according to data released by the Finance Ministry last week.
The move initially strengthened the yen, but the currency subsequently erased those gains and weakened beyond the psychologically important level of 160 against the dollar late last week.
Katayama declined to say whether the yen’s recent movements were orderly but stressed that Tokyo remained prepared to take decisive action against disorderly fluctuations.
The yen’s weakness has largely been driven by the wide interest-rate gap between Japan and the US. Although a weaker currency supports Japanese exporters, it also raises the cost of imported energy, food and raw materials, weighing on household consumption.
Ahead of the meeting, Bessent said he expected the Japanese government and the Bank of Japan to take further steps that would lead to a stronger yen.
A senior Japanese Finance Ministry official, however, said Bessent did not make a specific request during the roughly 30-minute meeting, according to Kyodo news.
Katayama also briefed Bessent on Japan’s efforts to balance economic growth with fiscal sustainability amid concerns over the country’s heavy public debt burden.

Philippine digital service tax collections hit 307 mln USD in H1
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:10:25 CST
17:10:25 KST

MANILA, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Tax collections from foreign digital service providers in the Philippines reached 17.5 billion pesos (about 307 million U.S. dollars) in the first half of 2026, local media reported Monday.
According to the Manila Bulletin on Monday, the amount accounts for three-fourths of the government's full-year target of 23.1 billion pesos, compared to the 6.6 billion pesos collected in the initial six months of the value-added tax (VAT) on digital services program, according to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR).
BIR Commissioner Charlito Martin R. Mendoza said the growth reflects rising digital activity among consumers and businesses.
The 12-percent VAT on digital services took effect in June 2025, which was the only tax reform that generated new revenues, while other measures cut revenues by over 2.6 billion pesos. Total BIR collections reached 1.99 trillion pesos in the first half, up 5.3 percent year on year. ■

Shaun the Sheep hailed on latest list of storm names
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:10:12 UTC
17:10:12 KST

From a five-year-old weather enthusiast to a beloved animated sheep, the inspiration for the list of storm names for this autumn and winter is wide and varied.
Austen, Boelo and Chloe will be the first named storms of this winter, meteorologists have revealed, after more than 40,000 suggestions were submitted by the public.
The UK’s Met Office, in partnership with Ireland’s Met Éireann and the Dutch national weather forecasting service KNMI, released the list for the 2026-27 season on Monday.
People submitted names in honour of a much-loved labrador puppy, meteorological pioneers and Shaun the Sheep, from the animation Wallace and Gromit.
The Met Office said the purpose of naming storms was serious as it helped people take notice, prepare and stay safe in severe weather.
The organisations have been naming storms since 2015, with the list running from early September to the following August. It coincides with the start of meteorological autumn, when the likelihood of low-pressure systems and the potential for storms severe enough to be named increases.
In the last year, four names were used from the list, reaching the letter D with Storm Dave on 1 April, although the UK was also affected by a further three storms named by other European meteorological services: Benjamin, Claudia and Goretti.
The third name in this year’s list, Chloe, was selected by the Met Office after being put forward more than 120 times, including by the mother of a five-year weather enthusiast who is “fascinated by the weather” but can also “create a storm by herself” when she is tired.
The name Finn was suggested for a two-year-old boy described by his family as “wild and a force to be reckoned with”, while Ivy was nominated in honour of a nine-month-old labrador puppy affectionately known as “the absolute destructor”.
Shaun also joins the list after a public vote that was run as part of a collaboration with the British animation studio Aardman, which is behind Wallace and Gromit.
Holly Clements, the Met Office head of warnings and guidance, said: “For more than a decade, storm naming has helped us communicate the risks from severe weather more effectively. A named storm provides a clear focus for forecasts and warnings, helping more people understand the potential impacts and take action to protect themselves, their families and their property.”
Storms are given a name when they are deemed to have the potential to have a medium or high impact in the UK, Ireland or the Netherlands. Wind is the primary focus, although additional issues such as rain or snow are also considered.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tells Russia’s finance minister Russia won’t get economic relief until Ukraine war ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:10:10 UTC
17:10:10 KST

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tells Russia’s finance minister Russia won’t get economic relief until Ukraine war ends
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Russia’s Finance Ministry head Anton Siluanov there would be no “economic relief” for Moscow until the Russia–Ukraine war ends, sources told Politico and Reuters.
The ministers’ meeting centered on US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Ukraine.
According to those sources, Bessent told Siluanov that the United States would withhold economic relief from Russia until the war ends, though it is not specified whether he meant an easing of sanctions. When the Russian minister “tried to discuss areas of interest,” Bessent cut him off, saying “nothing is possible until the war is over.”
Erin Browne, US Treasury undersecretary for international affairs, told Politico the meeting had been “productive,” with the two men discussing “Trump’s plan for peace and economic growth.” Bessent, she said, told Siluanov that “the war needs to end.”
Russia’s Finance Ministry, in a brief statement issued the evening of August 31, stated that the two sides had discussed “issues of Russian–American cooperation on the financial track,” as well as “cooperation issues” within the framework of the G20.
The Bessent-Siluanov meeting took place in Asheville, North Carolina, on the sidelines of a G20 summit of finance ministers and central bank governors. It was the first time Russia’s finance minister had attended a G20 summit since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Anton Siluanov’s visit had not been announced in advance.

Ukrainian Drone Attack Sparks Fire at Ust-Luga Port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:09:52 UTC
17:09:52 KST

A Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at northwestern Russia’s Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major hub for oil exports, local authorities said early Tuesday.
Leningrad region Governor Alexander Drozdenko said air defense units intercepted 52 drones during a four-hour assault over the region.
“Damage and fire were recorded in the Ust-Luga port area as a result of the drone attack,” he wrote on Telegram, adding later that there were no casualties.
By around 9:30 a.m. Moscow time, Drozdenko said the fire was extinguished.
Ust-Luga, Russia’s largest shipping terminal on the Baltic Sea and second-largest nationwide behind Novorossiysk, was previously attacked by Ukrainian drones and caught fire on Aug. 14.
According to Reuters, Ust-Luga handles 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day. Last year, more than 32.8 million metric tons of refined products were exported through the port.
Elsewhere, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said at least 21 drones were intercepted on approach to the capital overnight Tuesday.
In the southwestern Belgorod region, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev reported one death and 16 injuries following shelling and drone strikes over the past 24 hours.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 516 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Monday evening and Tuesday morning.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, Russian attacks killed at least 12 people in Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, local officials said.

Burnham to tell MPs he wants to ‘unlock positivity’ in first Commons statement as PM – UK politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:09:13 UTC
17:09:13 KST

Andy Burnham has declared his government can make “this next decade better than the last” in a confident and relatively non-partisan address to MPs. Speaking in parliament for the first time since becoming PM more than six weeks ago, Burnham gave a wide-ranging opening statement and then took questions from more than three hours. Burnham said:
When I stood outside Downing Street six weeks ago, I said Britain needs a circuit breaker after a decade of turbulence, negativity, point scoring and divisive politics.
This is what I have outlined today.
A clear, coherent, and credible approach to growth that can unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility in every postcode in Britain.
Our job in here is to make it real by taking a place first rather than party first approach.
It starts with reasserting basic standards for Britain, that this is a country where no one sleeps rough and no community is blighted by an illegal waste tip.
And from there, working together to build a new sense of optimism around the country.
We can make this next decade better than the last.
We can lift the prospects of all our people and places.
Burnham repeatedly made a point of stressing his desire to collaborate with opposition parties, as part of his commitment to doing politics in a new way. He was relaxed and good-humoured and, although he faced criticism from some opposition MPs, he was generally given a fair hearing. He did not have any surprise new announcements, and much of what he said repeated arguments had made over the summer. On many issues he indicated that final decisions have yet to be taken. With the statement still running after three hours and 20 minutes, Burnham is still on his feet.
After Burnham had been taking questions for two and a half hour, Jeremy Corbyn told him the session had lasted “longer than the longest World Cup match”. He asked if Burnham would back rent controls.
Burnham said he thought he and Corbyn took part in longer hustings debates during the 2015 Labour leadership contest. On housing, he said “a package of measures to turn the housing market around” was needed.
Julian Lewis (Con) told Burnham he thought the local government reorganisation amounted to “shameless gerrymandering”. Lewis represents New Forest East, and he said his constituency was being “torn apart” with part that looks towards the New Forest being taken over by Southampton.
Burnham said he would ask the community secretary to look at this.
Burnham says he is 'concerned' about plans for Freeview TV to be switched off by 2034
David Mundell (Con) asked Burnham if he would review plans for terrestial Freeview TV to be switched off in 2034. This decision would affect a lot of elderly people in rural areas, he said.
Burnham replied:
I am concerned about those plans. I know some of my constituents in Makerfield rely on Freeview. There is perhaps an opportunity to look at this as part of the BBC’s BBC charter renewal process.
I can’t give [Mundell] a final answer today, but I recognise it’s a genuine issue that he’s raised. I know it will be of concern to his constituents and let me have a proper look at it.
In response to a question from Labour’s Marsha De Cordova about Europe, Burnham said the next UK-EU summit might take place “the month after next” (ie, in November), but this was still being finalised.
In response to a question from Ellie Chowns, the parliamentary leader of the Green party, Burnham said that he was committed to a carbon neutral future and he was willing to work with the Greens on this.
Burnham said Law had “misunderstood” what Burnham was saying. He said he was ruling out a border poll now. He said he was “very aware of every word in the Good Friday agreement”, which says there should be a border poll if there is clear majority support for one, and he said he would “stick to it 100%”.
He also said he cared about Northern Ireland and visited it often.
Burnham suggests Shropshire could also get devolution benefits without being part of combined authority
Helen Morgan, the Lib Dem MP for North Shropshire, said there are no immediate plans for Shropshire to have a combined authority or mayoral authority. People there were worried this would mean they would lose out under Burnham’s devolution plans, she said.
Burnham said he thought devolution deals would only work with unitary local government. He went on:
I don’t think it will work with a two-tier system, but that’s why I said to colleagues in Cornwall, I’m quite happy to see if a deal can be done for a single unitary authority. [See 5.02pm.]
That is what I understand members of parliament for Cornwall want working with the leader of Cornwall council. If that is the settled view, I’m not going to try and impose something else. Let’s work with that.
And the same could be true in Shropshire, but it needs to be effective and functional and be able to stand on its own two feet.
Burnham urges Scottish government to back bringing Glasgow's bus service back under public control
Zubir Ahmed (Lab) asked Burnham if he could do anything to improve the bus service in Glasgow.
Burnham said he had been surprised to learn how expensive bus fares were in Glasgow. He said he thought there were moves to put the buses under public control in the city, but he had been told the Scottish government was not in favour. He said he hoped they would adopt that approach.
He went on:
A great city like Glasgow should have public transport under its own control. And what I see in Scotland, there is something of the same problem as England, where the capital city has a public transport system that is way beyond what anywhere else has.
Burnham says he has 'open mind' about beefing up elections bill with caps on political donations
Labour’s Stella Creasy said Reform UK has raised £9m in donations this year, with £8m coming from just three UK-based donors. She went on:
Chequebooks are already circling the next general election, and if we wish to defend our democracy and make sure that all voices can be heard equally, we need to make sure it’s not money that talks.
She urged Burnham to accept amendments to the representation of the people bill that would put caps on how much individuals and companies can donate to political parties.
Burnham said that bill as drafted (which only caps the amount that can be given by donors living abroad) was just a start. He went on:
I don’t think anyone on the front bench is saying it’s the end of this matter. We do need to go further.
I would encourage [Creasy] to engage with the Defending Democracy taskforce.
And certainly I have an open mind about what those further measures might be.
Burnham says he '100%' backs getting social media companies to remove non-consensual explict content more quickly
Wera Hobhouse (Lib Dem) asked about women secretly being filmed on nights out. She said:
In many towns and cities across the country, women are secretly filmed on a night out and the videos are posted online with vile, degrading, misogynistic contents and comments.
And the women only find out once these videos have been shared 100,000 times and more, and they do not know what to do and we need to change something.
Will the prime minister support the campaign to end this vile practice, including looking at reform to make misogyny a hate crime?
Burnham said, as the father of two daughters, this issue was very much at the forefront of his mind. He said he had recently met Georgia Harrison, who was doing “amazing” campaigning in this area.
He said Harrison wanted social media companies to remove non-consensual explicit content immediately, not just within 48 hours, which is the current deadline. A 48-hour deadline was“totally unsatisfactory”, Burnham said. He said he would support changing that “100%”.
Burnham says E1 settlement on West Bank could kill off prospects for two-state solution for Israel and Palestine
Debbie Abrahams (Lab) asked Burnham would he would do to stop the building of illegal settlements on the West Bank.
Burnham said the plans for the E1 settlement were particularly worrying. They would “lead to decisions being made before the Israeli election which, as I understand it, could imperil, if not end, the two-state solution”.
He went on:
So these matters are urgent. They do need to be confronted. And I believe we will be updating the house soon on those matters. [See 3.04pm.]
Burnham tells Reform UK's Richard Tice he's wrong to think it's either/or with fossil fuels and renewables
Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader, asked when the government would approve the applications for the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields in the North Sea. He repeated his claim about the rush to net zero being “stupid”.
Burnham said Tice needed a better grasp of the facts. He explained:
In Greater Manchester it costs £30 to charge a bus with electric charge, £200 plus to fill a tank of diesel. He really does need to look into the facts a little bit more before he makes statements like that in this house.
Solar panels on people’s homes can bring down the cost of their energy and it.
And, yes, we need to be pragmatic. We will still need to rely on oil and gas for some years to come.
The mistake [Tice] is making is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.

Luxembourg drops approval for Israel bonds issue: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:08:49 UTC
17:08:49 KST

Luxembourg drops approval for Israel Bonds issue: What that means
Israel’s future borrowing in EU markets remains uncertain as Luxembourg moves to let bond prospectus expire.
Luxembourg is not renewing its authorisation for the issue of Israel Bonds since it expired on Monday, leaving Israel with an uncertain future over its ability to borrow via investors in European markets.
Last month, Luxembourg’s Finance Minister Gilles Roth told broadcaster RTL that the financial regulator, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF), had decided in May not to renew approval for the bond prospectus beyond its August 31 expiry date.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Spain requests emergency funding from the EU over Ceuta migrants
- list 2 of 3Why a Christian group is suing the Dutch government for West Bank trade ban
- list 3 of 3Billions flow between EU institutions and Israel, despite Gaza genocide
A bond prospectus is a legal document that gives investors detailed information about a bond and its issuer before it is launched onto the market. It is produced under the supervision of the financial market within which the bonds are issued – in this case, Luxembourg.
Here’s what we know.
What are Israel Bonds?
Israel Bonds, issued through the Development Corporation for Israel (DCI), are debt securities by the State of Israel that represent a loan from an investor to the Israeli government. Investors earn interest on the bonds they have bought.
Capital raised via Israeli bonds is not earmarked for specific purposes but forms part of the Israeli government’s overall financing, which means it can be used to fund defence and military spending.
Following the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel and the subsequent launch of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the Israeli government increased its military financing, and Israel Bonds were marketed worldwide as opportunities to “support Israel at War” in the same year. According to Amnesty International, the country raised $4.5bn on international markets through the sale of these bonds between October 2023 and January 2025.
Israel Bonds issued in the European Union raise about $2.5bn a year, according to Israel’s Ministry of Finance.
Focus on the number of Israeli bonds held by countries in the EU has intensified as Israeli attacks in Lebanon, Gaza and the occupied West Bank continue, and has given rise to what critics say are inconsistencies in countries’ approach to the plight of Palestine.
In the same month that Luxembourg took over the prospectus for Israel’s bonds, for example, it also recognised the state of Palestine.
Why is Luxembourg involved in this?
Because Israel is not an EU country, Luxembourg’s financial regulator acts as a guarantor for EU investors by approving the prospectus – the legal disclosure document that provides potential investors with information about the bonds’ offering and their issuer before they are sold.
Ireland had previously served as the regulatory home for Israeli bonds after the United Kingdom, which had held the position before that, left the EU in 2020.
Following sustained pressure from parliamentary and civil society groups over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Ireland’s Central Bank Governor Gabriel Makhlouf confirmed last September that his country would not renew its approval.
Luxembourg then took over approval of the prospectus.
But CSSF Director General Claude Marx told RTL last month that it would not be approving the prospectus for another year, saying it would “circumvent the European rules” to accept transfers of the prospectus for consecutive years.
However, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) told the Luxembourg Times earlier this month that it does allow consecutive permit transfers.
“Yes, a national competent authority can accept the transfer of the approval in two consecutive years,” a spokesperson said, stressing that they were commenting on the general application of the regulation.
What does this mean for Israel?
With Luxembourg no longer approving the prospectus, Israel will now need to persuade another EU country to take over if it wants to continue issuing bonds in the EU market.
It currently remains unclear which country might be prepared to do so.
In the meantime, Israel still has access to other markets around the world to issue bonds – notably its major ally, the United States. Since 1951, the DCI has raised billions of dollars via bonds in the US financial market – about $2.5bn a year.
What pressure has there been on countries issuing Israel Bonds?
In July, Amnesty International called on Luxembourg, Ireland and all EU member states to stop the sale of Israeli bonds or “risk complicity in Israel’s ongoing genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip”.
In a public statement, Steve Cockburn, the regional director for Europe at Amnesty International, said Israel has become “increasingly reliant on foreign investments to finance its genocide, apartheid and unlawful occupation and bankroll its crimes against Palestinians”.
“Israel Bonds increase the funds available to the government and thereby help finance Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in the occupied Gaza Strip that has wiped out entire families, levelled civilian infrastructure, including hospitals and schools and left 90 percent of the population forcibly displaced with their homes in ruins,” he said.
“Allowing these bonds to be sold in the EU markets comes with an enormous ethical and legal cost. International law is clear: All states have an obligation not to aid or assist in genocide and the obligation to prevent it,” Cockburn added.
Amnesty International added that from 2022 to 2024, the budget for the Israeli army grew from 4.2 percent to 8.3 percent of Israel’s gross domestic product (GDP).

Polish Fighter Jets Intercept Russian Il-20 Reconnaissance Aircraft for Seventh Time in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:07:12 UTC
17:07:12 KST

Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 ELINT surveillance-reconnaissance aircraft near the Polish coast.
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Polish Minister of National Defense, announced this.
Approximately 30 km north of Łeba, the fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft flying over the Baltic Sea.
According to the Polish military, the Russian aircraft did not violate Polish airspace. Polish fighter jets intercepted and escorted it in accordance with established procedures.
The Polish Armed Forces noted that Russia was once again testing the readiness of Poland’s deterrence and air defense systems.
Since the beginning of 2026, Polish fighter jets have intercepted Russian military aircraft over the Baltic Sea at least nine times.
The first recorded incident occurred on March 13, when Polish MiG-29s intercepted and escorted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft.
The number of such incidents increased in April. On April 8, Polish F-16s intercepted a Russian Il-20. The following day, April 9, Polish fighter jets intercepted another Russian Il-20.
On April 24, Polish F-16s intercepted two Russian Su-30 fighter jets over the Baltic Sea.
The next such incident was recorded on May 13, when Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over international waters in the Baltic Sea.
July was particularly active. On July 14, Polish fighter jets intercepted an Il-20 approximately 30 km off the coast of Ustka. On July 15, they intercepted two Russian Su-30SM2 fighter jets that had arrived from the Kaliningrad region.
On July 16, Polish aircraft were scrambled twice to intercept Russian aircraft. First, the fighter jets intercepted two Su-30s, and later that same day, an Il-20.
Thus, in 2026, Polish fighter jets have conducted nine separate interception operations involving Russian military aircraft.
In addition to Poland, multinational forces under NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission also protect the airspace of the Baltic states.
In June 2026, French Rafale fighter jets conducting NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission intercepted six Russian military aircraft in the Baltic region.

Rheinmetall’s LUNA NG drone gets German certification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:06:51 UTC
17:06:51 KST

- Germany's Bundeswehr Aviation Authority granted provisional airworthiness certification to Rheinmetall's LUNA NG drone, designated HUSAR.
- The system has completed about 150 flights and 200 flight hours under civil operating licenses, with an endurance of more than 12 hours.
Germany’s Bundeswehr Aviation Authority has granted provisional airworthiness certification to Rheinmetall’s LUNA NG unmanned reconnaissance system, the company said, clearing the German military to fly the drone independently for training and testing.
The certification marks a step toward full type certification for the aircraft, which the Bundeswehr will field under the designation HUSAR, short for Highly Efficient Unmanned System for Medium-Range Reconnaissance. Rheinmetall said the majority of required certification criteria have already been met.
The LUNA NG is certified to civil aviation safety standards rather than military-only requirements, a distinction Rheinmetall said allows the drone to fly in regular, restricted airspace rather than being confined to dedicated military training areas.
“Certification is carried out according to the same standards as for large aircraft, such as an A320,” said Mike Schmidt, CEO of the Air Unmanned Space business unit at Rheinmetall. “A particular challenge in this case was that critical components, such as the autopilot or safety-critical navigation systems, had to be developed and certified in-house. There are simply no certified systems for tactical unmanned aerial vehicles on the market.”
Rheinmetall said the drone has completed around 150 flights and roughly 200 flight hours under civil operating licenses. The first Bundeswehr pilots and verifiers have already been trained on the system, giving the German military qualified personnel to operate it independently for training and testing purposes under the new provisional certification.
The LUNA NG is designed for sustained airborne reconnaissance, target classification, and real-time detection of objects, with an endurance of more than 12 hours, according to Rheinmetall.

Rheinmetall delivers first Lynx XM30 prototype to U.S. Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:02:52 UTC
17:02:52 KST

- American Rheinmetall delivered the first of eight Lynx XM30 prototypes to the U.S. Army under a $764 million EMD contract.
- The delivery follows General Dynamics' XM30 Wolf prototype delivery last Friday, with both companies competing to replace the Bradley.
American Rheinmetall delivered the first of eight Lynx XM30 prototypes to the U.S. Army, the company said, entering the vehicle into government-led developmental and performance testing under the XM30 program’s Phase 3/4 Engineering and Manufacturing Development contract, valued at approximately $764 million.
The delivery comes days after General Dynamics Land Systems delivered its own XM30 Wolf prototype to the Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, last Friday, putting both companies competing to replace the M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle on a similar testing timeline.
“Delivering our first prototype to the Army is an important step as the XM30 Combat Vehicle program enters a more visible phase,” said Matthew Warnick, CEO of American Rheinmetall. “Team Lynx now has the opportunity to show the Army that we can deliver on the promise of a modern replacement for the Bradley.”
American Rheinmetall said it will deliver the remaining seven prototypes later this year for use in operational unit training. That rollout runs parallel to the technical evaluations already underway, part of the Army’s Transformation in Contact 2.0 initiative, which is intended to rapidly prototype, test and field new technology directly to deployed and training units. Once the vehicles clear initial military safety checks, soldiers will move into active field maneuvers, a training phase the company said culminates in large-scale combat simulations.
“Executing a parallel evaluation timeline requires a level of industrial agility that Team Lynx was built for,” Warnick said. “We are proving that the U.S. Defense Industrial Base can move at the speed of operational relevance, stripping years off traditional development timelines to get the right capability to the Warfighter.”
Production of the Lynx prototypes runs across multiple states. Turret fabrication takes place in Plymouth, Michigan, before subsystems move to Slidell, Louisiana, for hull and chassis integration. Completed vehicles undergo automotive shakeout trials to confirm mechanical readiness, then return to Louisiana for final paint and detailing. The process ends with a joint inspection alongside the Defense Contract Management Agency before the government formally accepts each vehicle.
The Army is expected to select a winning XM30 design in 2027. Additional General Dynamics XM30 Wolf prototypes are separately planned for delivery to Fort Hood, Texas, ahead of testing that could lead to a full-rate production decision for that design.

Red circles represent the sites for prospective canopies relative to the border facility captured in satellite imagery and as seen through its blueprint | Images: Planet Labs, edited by NK News, Rosgranstroy

In late July, a Russian official from the bordering Khasan settlement said the opening would take place some time in early September, possibly to coincide with the Sept. 1-4 Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, with Putin expected to attend.
It is not clear whether Putin’s agenda will include the bridge’s opening ceremony or if the project has even been completed. 
Apart from the delays and ballooning costs, the project has recently faced other headwinds, including a $1.5 million lawsuit filed against its main contractor TonnelYuzhStroi by one of its material suppliers.

Could this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:00:48 UTC
17:00:48 KST

In the polluted waters of Marina Palamós on Spain’s Costa Brava, Manuel Maldonado, a sponge biologist, noticed something unusual last month: red starfish had started settling in the area.
Nearly two years earlier, the Spanish National Research Council scientist and his colleagues had begun transplanting sea sponges into the port to study whether they could survive in its polluted waters.
Only one species, the chicken liver sponge (Chondrosia reniformis, also called the kidney sponge), which is found along the Mediterranean coast but rarely seen in the harbour, managed to survive. Its resilience, and the arrival of the red starfish, suggests sponges could be used to clean up pollution in ports.
Sea sponges are some of the Earth’s oldest ecosystem engineers. Previous research has shown that abundant communities can reshape their surroundings in positive ways. They can filter pollutants from enormous volumes of water, cycling nutrients in the process. They also enhance biodiversity by attracting marine animals that live within and around them, such as worms and crustaceans.
All of this points to their potential as a tool for renaturalising harbours, some of the most disturbed marine environments in the world. The accumulation of pollutants such as rubbish and oil, the introduction of invasive species from ships and persistent noise pollution make it incredibly difficult for marine life to thrive there.
But first, it has to be proved that sponges can survive in harsh environments. “So we tested different Spanish species with the idea of finding some that could survive in a harbour environment,” says Maldonado, who led the research.
The team focused on five sponge species commonly found on the coast, chosen because their abundance suggests they are good survivors. “You also don’t want to use a very sensitive or protected species,” he says. “It has to be something you can handle and transport to the harbour.”
The sponges were collected from a site about 18 miles (30km) south of the harbour where they were transplanted. Maldonado’s student and study co-author, Carlota Escarré, monitored their health using underwater photography and inspection.
Escarré conducted dives every 20 to 64 days over the course of 15 months, braving early hours and cold waters at the harbour.
All the red encrusting sponges (Crambe crambe), leather sponges (Scalarispongia scalaris) and stinker sponges (Ircinia oros) shrank and eventually died during the study. But almost 92% of the chicken liver sponge specimens survived the polluted water.
“It was a surprise for all of us,” says Escarré. Some even managed to reproduce asexually, bringing their numbers up to 40 from 24.
Experts hope the study finally puts sea sponges, long overlooked in favour of the more charismatic coral, on the map.
“This study shows what we in the sea sponge community have known for years,” says Andreu Santín Muriel, a marine biologist at the University of Porto’s Interdisciplinary Centre of Marine and Environmental Research, who was not involved in the work. “Sponges are excellent potential species for bioremediation and habitat recovery.”
He adds: “A lot of effort has been put in the past decades for coral restoration; we understand the importance of corals very well. But sponges provide more ecosystem services, yet they’re not as attractive, so they have received way less money.”
David Amptmeijer, a doctoral researcher at Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon, who was not involved in the research, says it is important to note how localised the study is. It is unclear if these same sponges could survive, for example, in a harbour in Maine.
Though Amptmeijer believes sea sponges have great potential for pollution management, he says a lot more research is needed before scientists can fully understand how they interact with pollutants.
Maldonado suspects the chicken liver sponge – a high-microbial-abundance sponge (hosting diverse communities of symbiotic microorganisms within its tissues) that takes ammonium from seawater and releases nitrate – is able to cope with pollution thanks to its diverse microbiome. “We will start working on this after the summer,” he says.
He and his team will continue monitoring the sponges over several years, but they also hope to study other organisms: he has written a proposal for a project that combines sponges with oysters, which are also powerful filter feeders.
Santín Muriel says sponges have been around for at least 600m years. “They have survived at least five mass extinctions, and they’re still thriving in today’s oceans. That means they’ve most likely already encountered a lot of environmental problems throughout their existence.”
It’s not so strange, then, to think that sea sponges may already have the solutions to many of the problems humans face today.
“We tend to look more to technology to solve environmental pollution,” Santín Muriel says. “But marine organisms most likely have already developed toolkits that could help us clean the oceans.”

Gaza's roadmap to nowhere: Why Israel won't give up control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:00:13 UTC
17:00:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's roadmap to nowhere: Why Israel won't give up control
Israel was caught by surprise when Hamas agreed at the end of July to decommission its weapons in Gaza in lockstep with the Israeli army’s withdrawal from the enclave.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has even referred to the acceptance of the Board of Peace’s roadmap by Palestinian factions as a “diplomatic 7 October”.
For months, Israel has made disarmament in Gaza its sole pretext for its continued genocide in the enclave and systematic violations of the October 2025 ceasefire.
“If only Hamas were to lay down its arms, all of this would be over” has been Israel’s standard talking point to justify killing over 1,200 Palestinians in the past 320 days of supposed calm, as well as restricting aid and movement, banning reconstruction, and advancing the “Yellow line” of ethnically cleansed areas.
Yet, as soon as Hamas and seven other Palestinian factions agreed to Tel Aviv’s demand, the Israeli government went into panic mode. Netanyahu rushed to formally reject the roadmap while his ministers called it “dangerous for Israel” and vowed to continue daily killings and ethnic cleansing.
The Israeli army, meanwhile, has escalated its bombing campaign in Gaza.
Even after the Board of Peace tried to provide ample assurances to Israel that it could continue to bomb Gaza, occupy 70% of Gaza’s territory, and only withdraw after Hamas’s total disarmament, Netanyahu has continued to reject the deal.
“Hamas accepted [the roadmap] to call Netanyahu’s bluff,” a senior Arab mediator told The New Arab. “They knew he would not comply.”
Israel's grip on Gaza
Despite the Board of Peace rewriting the terms of the roadmap to Israel’s satisfaction, Netanyahu’s reluctance to accept it stems from the fact that any progress in Gaza would threaten the far-right coalition that keeps him in power.
The Israeli Prime Minister promised his base ethnic cleansing in the Palestinian territory. Half of his coalition ministers and Knesset members recently marched for rebuilding Jewish-only settlements in Gaza, while Israel’s Defence Minister is campaigning on how he wiped out entire Palestinian cities.
Even if Hamas disarms without any Israeli withdrawal or suspension of airstrikes, the roadmap remains a nonstarter for Israel because it would constrain its ability to control Gaza.
For instance, under the roadmap, Israel would have to allow the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) to enter the enclave along with an International Stabilisation Force (ISF) to collect weapons.
The Israeli government views this as a nightmare scenario, because the presence of international forces on the ground would make it difficult for Israel to retain military operational freedom in Gaza.
That is why Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich warned that a multinational force in Gaza would be “dangerous for Israel” because it “will monitor us, separate us from Hamas and restrict [Israeli military] activity in the Strip”.
Likewise, the roadmap would oblige Israel to fulfil its obligations under Phase One of the Trump 20-point ceasefire plan before or alongside Hamas’s disarmament.
Those obligations include allowing a minimum of 600 trucks of humanitarian aid to cross into Gaza daily as well as 60,000 temporary housing units and 200,000 tents, while allowing the repair of basic infrastructure such as electricity, water, sewage, roads, hospitals, and bakeries.
But this would negate Israel’s policy to keep Gaza "destroyed for generations to come," as put by former Israeli General Giora Eiland.
Even minimal humanitarian measures that would make Gaza less uninhabitable are viewed by Israel as an existential threat. Its war, which has cost more than $140 billion, was explicitly aimed at transforming the enclave into an apocalyptic wasteland, leaving Palestinians with no option but to leave.
The status quo suits Israel
A former senior Israeli official, who had until 2024 worked closely with Netanyahu, told The New Arab that the Israeli premier prefers the current stalemate over making any “big changes.”
“We have all the leverage, we have the upper hand, what’s the incentive for us to engage?” he said.
The former official explained that Israel is comfortable with the current status quo in Gaza because it allows it to retain control of a depopulated 70% of the enclave, while avoiding the cost of feeding and sheltering its displaced population.
Similarly, the façade of the ceasefire means Hamas cannot attack Israeli troops behind the ‘Yellow Line’, so Israel doesn’t need to station a significant number of troops to defend the area.
Two senior officials from mediating Arab countries told The New Arab that the current status quo is ideal for Israel, with no changes in Gaza expected at least until after the October elections.
One official said that their expectation for the Trump plan has from the start been to “reduce the killing, get more food in, and prevent ethnic cleansing”.
The other official told The New Arab that the only way to move forward with the roadmap is to “drag Israel kicking and screaming”, but Trump’s Board of Peace has so far exerted no meaningful pressure on Netanyahu.
Israel's opposition isn't any better
The former Israeli official cautioned against any optimism over the likelihood of Israeli opposition parties winning in the upcoming elections.
“The opposition is attacking Netanyahu from the right, not the left. They are saying he’s about to squander the achievements in Gaza and bow down to Trump,” he told The New Arab. “They are promising to be tougher.”
The veteran Israeli politician Haim Ramon even warned that “people who choose [Naftali] Bennett are actually choosing another Netanyahu - only more extreme”.
He added that Israeli opposition leaders such as Bennett or Avigdor Lieberman “may be trying to present themselves as centre or ‘moderate’ right-wing, but in reality, they are political hawks, advocates of the complete Land of Israel, whose extremist views are identical to those of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich”.
Bennett, for reference, once infamously bragged: “I already killed lots of Arabs in my life, and there is absolutely no problem with that.”
A senior Arab official from a mediating country told The New Arab that if the opposition wins, it could complicate the situation in Gaza even further.
“If [Gadi] Eisenkot becomes prime minister, the international pressure on Israel would disappear, and we’d get told we need to give him time and space to consolidate his regime to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.”
Muhammad Shehada is a Palestinian writer and analyst from Gaza and the EU Affairs Manager at Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor

US-North Korea summit appears to be 'possible at any time,' Seoul spy agency says

2026-09-01
08:00:11 UTC
17:00:11 KST

Trump met Kim three times during his first term, once declaring they were "in love," in high-profile summits aimed at securing a denuclearisation deal, but no tangible progress was made.
A summit between the United States and North Korea appears possible "at any time" as signs have emerged of dialogue between the two sides, a lawmaker citing South Korea's spy agency said on Tuesday.
US President Donald Trump said last month he plans to again meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, but the public response from Pyongyang has been mostly muted and analysts were sceptical of imminent talks.
"Regarding the North Korea-US summit, there was an analysis that it should be viewed as possible at any time," South Korean lawmaker Youn Kun-young told reporters, citing a briefing by the National Intelligence Service.
"It was stated that while no facts regarding concrete contact between the two sides have been presented, there are signs of dialogue," he added.
Trump, eyeing a revived bond he claims to have with Kim, also said in August it was important to "get along" with the North Korean leader, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 "very powerful" nuclear weapons.
The North has since said Kim had "good memories and feelings" about Trump and that the relationship between the two leaders remains "excellent" but did not clearly respond to the US president's overtures.
Trump's comments floating a new meeting were accompanied by Washington scaling back joint US-South Korean military drills in August.
That move alarmed Washington's Asian allies, while sparking speculation that he was seeking a foreign policy win as the Iran war stalls.
Ballistic missiles
Hours after Trump's August remarks that it was important to get along with Kim, North Korea fired more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area.
Then Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, said Trump's decision to scale back the drills with South Korea was Seoul's "comeuppance."
Separate maritime exercises set to begin on 7 September between the United States and allies South Korea and Japan have also drawn an angry response from Pyongyang.
Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies, noted Moscow-backed Pyongyang appears to have little motivation to seek US talks.
"From North Korea's perspective, as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the Russia-Ukraine war and the deepening confrontation with South Korea, the US and Japan on one side and North Korea, China and Russia on the other, there appears to be little incentive for dialogue," he added.
Trump met Kim three times during his first term, once declaring they were "in love," in high-profile summits aimed at securing a denuclearisation deal, but no tangible progress was made.
The US president even bucked decades of US policy by stating North Korea was "sort of a nuclear power" in October 2025.
But Trump's comment at the time, that he was "100 percent" open to meeting Kim again, have gone unanswered.
China, Washington's chief geopolitical rival, has also been a major North Korean trading partner and a key source of diplomatic and economic support for the country, hit by multiple international sanctions.
South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae-myung has pursued engagement with the North since taking office in June 2025, in contrast to his hardline predecessor Yoon Suk-yeol.
But Pyongyang has rejected his overtures, labelling Seoul its "most hostile" enemy and declaring itself an "irreversible" nuclear state.

Per Ardua ad Astra: Air Command redesignated to Air & Space Command
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
09:00:00 BST
17:00:00 KST

Air Command, the headquarters of the Royal Air Force, has been redesignated as Air and Space Command, reflecting the RAF’s role as the Lead Command for Space across Defence.
Air Command was formed in 2007, when Strike Command was merged with Personnel and Training Command into a single command. It has now become Air & Space Command, underscoring how the RAF is responsible for both domains – generating and employing air and space power to defend the nation.
Air & Space Command, led by the Chief of the Air Staff, will continue to be responsible for UK Space Command, which safeguards UK and allied interests in space. Air & Space Command will also continue to lead the RAF Groups, which deliver air power and train RAF personnel.
“Space is essential to defence, security, prosperity, and our modern way of life. But it is also a domain of growing strategic competition. It has fast become an operational domain in its own right, and is vital to our ambition to develop and mature the integrated force. The RAF’s core mission of gaining and maintaining control of the air is fundamentally dependant on our freedom of action in and through the space domain.
It is now more important than ever for space power to be planned and delivered through the highest levels of military leadership, like all other domains. Our new HQ Air & Space Command will lead the delivery of space power with the same dedication that it leads for the air domain.”
Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth
Chief of the Air Staff
Under the Lead Command Model, the military commands of the UK armed forces will take leadership of different activities that are important to all of defence. The RAF’s selection as the Lead Command for space reflects its historic connection to the domain, having established the UK’s ballistic missile early warning system at RAF Fylingdales in 1963 and launched the SKYNET 1A satellite in 1969.
From Lancasters to satellites: RAF High Wycombe’s journey from Bomber Command to Air & Space Command
Bomber Command was formed in 1936, to control the RAF’s growing pre-war bombing force. It was initially based at RAF Uxbridge in West London, but with tensions in Europe rising, the UK government decided to relocate Bomber Command to a safer location – within reach of London, but harder for enemy aircraft to find and attack from the air.
RAF High Wycombe was established in 1938 as the new location for Bomber Command, located in the woods of the Chiltern Hills near the villages of Walter’s Ash and Naphill – just outside High Wycombe. RAF High Wycombe would be home to Bomber Command headquarters for another thirty years.
In 1968, Bomber Command was merged with Fighter Command to form the new Strike Command, based at RAF High Wycombe. This new command controlled the RAF’s combat aircraft, including all its bomber and fighter forces.
RAF High Wycombe was home to Strike Command for nearly 40 years. In 2007, Strike Command merged with Personnel & Training Command to form a single Air Command to act as the headquarters for the entire RAF.
With the growing importance of space to daily lives, as well as military operations around the world, UK Space Command was formed under Air Command in 2021. UK Space Command’s mission is to safeguard the UK’s national and military space interests and enable UK forces to operate globally.
Air Command operated for nearly two decades before its redesignation to Air & Space Command in 2026.
Your journey into space: Space careers in Air & Space Command
The following roles may be of interest if you wish to pursue a space career in the Royal Air Force:
The RAF is the only service with a dedicated Air and Space profession. Currently serving personnel who wish to transfer to the RAF Air and Space Operations (ASO) profession should contact the ASO Professions Advisory Team.
UK Space Command is a joint command with personnel from across the UK armed forces. If you are interested in careers in the space domain with the Royal Navy or the British Army, please visit Royal Navy jobs or British Army jobs. Civil Service roles at UK Space Command are advertised via Civil Service Jobs.

Escapism in Architecture: ArchDaily's September Editorial Focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

At a moment when architects across the globe are revisiting earthen construction, reassessing vernacular technologies, and forging visceral connections between communities and the land beneath their feet, others are sketching habitats for the Moon and designing the built environments of a Martian colony. Architecture firms, engineers, and space agencies are investing serious intellectual effort into structures that would need to be raised from scratch on another world. Two impulses, one returning to the soil, the other reaching for the stars, are unfolding simultaneously within the same discipline. And the tension between them raises an uncomfortable question: what, exactly, are we trying to escape?
This month, ArchDaily explores The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds, a critical exploration of why the architectural imagination has always sought refuge in alternative realities and what those fantasies reveal about the present. From megastructures and underwater cities to sci-fi habitats, digital environments, and cinematic worlds, escapism has long been a powerful driver of design speculation. The question is no longer whether architecture dreams of other worlds, but why — and for whom.
The coverage approaches this theme through several lenses. It traces how cinema, from Studio Ghibli's liminal domestic spaces to Bollywood's imagined Indias, has shaped architectural vision beyond the blueprint. It examines how the colonial logic of the "new world" — the blank-slate fantasy projected onto Latin America centuries ago — resurfaces in the language of space colonization today. It asks what it means to design bunkers and arks as exits from a future we ourselves built, and whether digital environments represent genuine architectural laboratories or merely new forms of retreat. It also looks at how astronomy and futuristic urbanism have inspired built form.
Running through all of these threads is a single ethical fault line: who gets to imagine new worlds, and who is left behind in the ones we abandon? The architecture of escapism is never neutral. It reflects cultural desires, technological optimism, and, more often than not, concentrated wealth.
As this month's coverage unfolds, readers are invited to ask if speculation is a necessary tool for reimagining the future, or a distraction from its most urgent demands. When architecture looks up at the stars or imaginary worlds, who is still looking at the ground?
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Lure of Escapism in Architecture and Alternative Worlds. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

Sudan: Bringing water and healthcare to displaced people in South Kordofan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
07:59:35 UTC
16:59:35 KST

Women queue at water points in the Al-Safa camps in Abu Jubayhah locality, South Kordofan state, Sudan. Jerrycans surround them, waiting to be filled. Until recently, getting water meant walking at least three kilometres.
This daily scene is part of a wider reality in Abu Jubayhah, which has become one of the main areas hosting displaced people in South Kordofan. Some live in camps such as Al-Safa, while many others have settled within the host community.
According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), 57,880 displaced people are living across 62 locations in Abu Jubayhah, making it the second-largest hosting locality in South Kordofan, after Kadugli. Local authorities estimate the true number to be higher.
The scale of displacement may not be immediately visible in Abu Jubayhah town, but the conditions in the camps near the town centre tell a different story.
“When you go to the camps, you see the conditions people are living in,” says Ayşe Bilge Öztürk, MSF project coordinator in Abu Jubayhah.
Families live in temporary and semi-permanent shelters, including fabric tents and straw structures covered with plastic, as well as some concrete structures. Some tents are as small as 10 square metres, leaving little space for daily life. Many of the displaced people are women and children.
“The support available has not kept pace with the number of people who have arrived or the length of time they have been displaced,” says Öztürk.
The support available has not kept pace with the number of people who have arrived or the length of time they have been displaced.
Water: One of the first needs
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) began our response in Abu Jubayhah in June 2026. Providing water in the three Al-Safa camps were among our first priorities.
At first, water was brought to the camps by truck while teams worked to establish a more sustainable water source. This included drilling a borehole, laying a water network and installing a solar-powered water pump. Teams also repaired latrines and provided cleaning materials.
Since we began this activity, MSF has provided more than one million litres of water to the community. Families in the camps depend on this water.
Aisha Ahmed first stayed in a school after being displaced before moving to Al-Safa camps. She remembers water as one of their most urgent needs at the time.
“Sometimes we would go a whole week without water,” Aisha says. “Now, after MSF drilled the borehole and extended the network, water is available 24 hours a day.”
Smiling, Aisha describes how she feels about the change: “I am happy. Now the water is there whenever we need it.”
For Aisha and other displaced people living in the camps, the change was not only about having water available. It also meant no longer having to go so far to collect it. Previously, people had to walk at least three kilometres each day to reach a water source.
Bringing healthcare closer to people
Water is only one of the needs displaced families have.
During one visit to the Al-Safa camps, an MSF team met a mother whose daughter was suffering from severe diarrhoea and needed urgent medical care. The team assessed the child and referred her to Abu Jubayhah hospital. Cases like this show how living conditions and health needs can become closely connected for families in the camps.
As teams identified more health needs, they began testing for and treating malaria in Al-Safa camp. Soon, however, patients were arriving with other health conditions, leading us to broaden our medical activities.
At the reception area for newly displaced people in Abu Jubayhah, MSF teams established a clinic. They screen new arrivals for malaria, malnutrition, and maternal health and general health conditions, and refer those who need immediate medical attention. 
MSF also provided logistical support to a multi-antigen catch-up vaccination campaign led by the Ministry of Health, which included measles, rubella, polio, and yellow fever vaccines, alongside other routine vaccinations. Many displaced people also live within the host community and rely on the same basic services.
At Abu Jubayhah General hospital, MSF is strengthening the emergency department through rehabilitation, equipment, medicines, and other essential supplies, while access to more specialised care remains limited.
Rainy season
The rainy season brings further challenges, as unpaved roads make it harder for people to move around and for teams and supplies to reach some locations.
Despite these challenges, something fundamental has changed in daily life in the Al-Safa camps — water is now closer and more reliably available.

Estonia sends new border guard rotation to Latvia
A new unit of Estonian border guards was sent to Latvia at the start of the week to combat illegal migration and protect the European Union's external border.
The new ESTPOL11 rotation replaced the team who have been working in Latvia for the last two weeks.
The 11-member team will take part in border patrols in areas where migration pressure is highest. Estonia has sent officers, service dogs, drones and other specialised equipment.
Last month, Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the Police and Border Guard Board, said Estonia will continue supporting Latvia because migration pressure in the region remains high.
He said that Latvian authorities have prevented more than 9,000 illegal border-crossing attempts this year.
"Our aim is to prevent a temporary migration route from developing into a permanent one. To this end, we are taking part in border patrols on the Latvian-Belarusian border together with our Latvian colleagues to prevent illegal border crossings, while at the same time working to ensure that people who have entered Estonia illegally are returned and that people smugglers and their accomplices are caught," Kommusaar said.

'Russia considers itself at war with Europe, even if Europe does not see itself at war with Russia,' Ukraine's FM warns

The Bonn consulate – which will now have to close by 18 September – is Russia’s last remaining consular post in Germany, aside from its embassy in Berlin.
It’s the latest escalation in diplomatic relations between the two countries.
In 2023, the German foreign ministry revoked the licences for four other Russian consulates in Frankfurt, Hamburg, Munich and Leipzig, after Moscow moved to cap the number of German officials allowed in Russia and Germany had to shut its own consulates in Kaliningrad, Ekaterinburg, and Novosibirsk.
At the moment, Germany still has two diplomatic outposts in Russia: its main embassy in Moscow and its last remaining consulate in St Petersburg. It also has three honorary consults in Kazan, Saratov and Vladivostok, its website shows.
Following today’s decision, it’s probably not entirely unreasonable to suspect Russia may target that St Petersburg post as part of its response.

Sikorski has a history with closing down Russian consulates in response to what Poland said were Russian-inspired acts of sabotage in Poland.
