2026-09-01
06:32:31 UTC
15:32:31 KST

A senior Palestinian church affairs committee on Tuesday condemned the demolition of a Christian family’s home and the bulldozing of its farmland by Israeli occupation forces in the occupied West Bank.
The Presidential Higher Committee for Church Affairs said in a statement that Israeli forces demolished a home and razed agricultural land belonging to the Christian Abed family in the al-Saqi area of Birzeit, north of Ramallah.
In a separate incident, the Christian family of Bashir Naim Kouna was forced to leave its home in the village of Taybeh, east of Ramallah, following persistent threats and attacks by illegal Israeli settlers, the committee added.
The family had moved into the house only about a week earlier after spending more than $300,000 building and furnishing it over seven years, according to the Al-Baidar Organization for the Defense of Bedouin Rights.
The group said the house had all required municipal permits.
The church affairs committee described the demolition, land razing, and displacement as violations of international law and part of a policy aimed at seizing Palestinian land and imposing illegal settlement expansion by force.
It said attacks on the homes and lands of Palestinian Christians amount to “an attack on the entire Palestinian presence,” stressing that Christians are an integral part of the Palestinian people, history, and identity.
The committee said demolitions, land seizures, and forced displacement continue across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, Masafer Yatta, the Jordan Valley, and the governorates of Nablus, Bethlehem, and Ramallah, as well as in Gaza.
It called on the international community to halt the violations and hold those responsible accountable.
Taybeh is the only remaining Palestinian town whose population is entirely Christian.
On August 11, the committee warned that Israeli attacks on Christian communities are threatening their deeply rooted presence in Palestine.
It said the assaults are “no longer isolated incidents” but part of an ongoing pattern involving settler violence, land confiscation, illegal settlement expansion, and restrictions on freedom of worship.
The committee also warned that Taybeh’s population is falling as growing numbers of Christian families had been forced to leave Palestine since 2023 amid escalating Israeli attacks.
Like other Palestinian towns in the occupied West Bank, Taybeh has faced escalating attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their property, aimed at pressuring them to leave their land, particularly in areas adjacent to illegal settlements and settlement outposts.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,489,640 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:32:28 UTC
15:32:28 KST

Russia has lost around 1,489,640 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 31.
The figure includes 1,440 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,320 tanks, 25,257 armored combat vehicles, 142,332 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,954 artillery systems, 2,079 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,597 air defense systems, 440 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 2,452 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Major developer faces liquidation as funding deadline brought forward

Bathla Group's collapse may be imminent as funding deadline brought forward
In short:
Hopes for an eleventh-hour cash injection into the crumbling Bathla Group are fading fast as some lenders take matters into their own hands.
The administrators have brought forward a deadline to the end of Tuesday to see if the business has any chance of survival.
What's next?
Administrators are preparing to shut down the company imminently if funding cannot be secured.
Hopes for crumbling property developer Bathla Group are deteriorating fast as a crucial deadline was brought forward while some lenders took action into their own hands.
Bathla's administrator, Teneo, has said it is preparing to shut down the company by the end of the day as hopes of securing $20 million in emergency funding fade away.
The realisation came after a meeting with lenders on Monday night failed to secure the commitment needed.
Teneo senior managing director Stephen Longley told Nine's Today Show: "We'll start planning at the end of the day for the wind down of the business," and said the situation was "very dire".
"We're running out of hope for a holistic solution to finish the 45 construction projects," he said.
"We've had intensive discussions with lenders, but I don't think we're going to get enough funding in place."
Mr Longley's latest comments were more pessimistic than yesterday, when he told ABC's The Business that he remained hopeful of securing a last-minute lifeline from lenders.
He also said, at a press conference on Monday, the property firm had "no cash", but could still complete at least 45 construction projects if it received more funding.
Human cost of financial collapse
Some of Bathla's 350 staff have not been paid for eight weeks while the developer has accumulated debts exceeding $3.2 billion.
Bathla's administration has left the fate of 200 building projects across NSW in jeopardy, with about 2,000 homes under construction and another 13,000 in its development pipeline.
Some private credit lenders have taken control of individual worksites and will be responsible for delivering particular projects.
The ABC understands a 312-apartment block development in Pemulwuy in Sydney's west is going ahead after the lender, PAG, made a commitment to continue paying contractors directly.
A manufacturing contractor who provided his first name, Moqvul, said that PAG had told him not to worry and continue working on the Pemulwuy site.
Mustafa, the owner of a kitchen joinery business, told the ABC he had received a written commitment from PAG, but it did not extend to any other Bathla sites.
He was also unsure what it meant for outstanding bills that his business was owed.
"No-one is giving us any clear image of where we are heading," Mustafa said.
"We are stressed. We owe the ATO, we owe the suppliers, we owe the workers."
Another contractor, Charbel, said the situation "didn't look good" and said he had four kids and was owed "a fair bit" of money from Bathla.
Administrators had tried tapping existing lenders for extra funds and late last week asked the New South Wales government for a $20 million lifeline to keep the business afloat.
However, the state government refused to offer any bailout money.
Teneo also said it had borrowed $1 million from its own head office so Bathla Group could afford to pay for vehicle registrations, petrol and "just to keep the lights on".
Its situation has also left questions around how home buyers will be impacted, including deposits.
Mr Longley said on Monday as many as 1,000 deposits could have been paid to the developer, and that some of those may have been used.
"Some of the contracts allow the deposits to be used by the business, deposits have been used as the contracts allow," he said.

‘The mountains are changing’: What the floods tell us about the future of India’s Himalayas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:30:46 UTC
15:30:46 KST

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”
To support relief efforts in Nepal, you can contribute to the prime minister’s Disaster Relief Fund here.
What else we’re reading about
RSS in New York | Last weekend, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed Indian Americans at New York’s Madison Square Garden calling for global unity. The Quint reported that the newly formed group behind the event has RSS links. The visit was opposed by several diaspora groups that reject the RSS’ Hindu nationalist ideology and criticise its record on minority rights.
Books and backlash | A reading session organised in Ahmedabad after a private school was forced to drop books by Malala Yousafzai and Anne Frank was allegedly disrupted by a group affiliated with the rightwing Bajrang Dal. Three people have been arrested.
Indian cinema abroad | Two Indian films have been selected for the Busan International film festival, which begins on 6 October. Birds in the Dark, by Shashank Walia, explores an unexpected human connection while Tamil writer-director Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi is set in the world of home-care workers.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Photographer Aashim Tyagi (@aashim), who once documented Art Deco architecture in Gujarat’s Balasinor, suggests a prehistoric side quest: “I was intrigued by the town’s reputation as the ‘Jurassic Park of India’ and a little digging led me to a dinosaur museum in neighbouring Raiyoli. It’s set amid open fields near one of Asia’s largest fossil beds where Rajasaurus narmadensis and a dozen other species once roamed. Much of the museum and the village’s paleontological preservation is owed to Aaliya Babi of Balasinor’s erstwhile royal family, earning her the nickname ‘Dinosaur Princess’. Balasinor and its dinosaur museum are a worthwhile detour from Ahmedabad or Baroda.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
176
India ranked 176th, second from the bottom, in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index, which evaluates countries on environmental health, climate change and ecosystem vitality. The country recorded negative values on air-quality indicators but showed an improvement on the index’s 10-year change metric. In 2022, when India had been ranked last, the central government had dismissed the EPI’s conclusions, saying it used “unscientific methods”.

Locals raise doubts about explosives factory to be built in western Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Locals raise doubts about explosives factory to be built in western Estonia
The state plans to build an explosives plant in Piirsalu in Lääne County, but residents in the village of Piirsalu feel decisions are being made over their heads.
The state plans to build an explosives plant in Piirsalu that would produce up to 1,200 tonnes of RDX a year and create 75 or more jobs.
The area is already home to a Defense Forces tactical training area and a Defense League shooting range. A Soviet missile base was once located here.
The local Lääne-Nigula government supported the building of the plant.
"The arrival of jobs has some impact in areas with a declining population. Since a sufficient number of better-paying jobs are expected there, that is quite an important argument," said Mayor Janno Randmaa.
Council Chairman Sven Köster, who lives in Piirsalu a couple of kilometres from the site of the planned plant, does not see the explosives plant as a threat.
"It will be a proper chemical plant that meets European standards. During the Soviet era, there were Soviet servicemen there – with their missile forces, they certainly caused more pollution," he said.
Piirsalu is a village away from the main highway, with no shop or school. But salmon live in the river, which is why it is a nature conservation area. Many locals are concerned about how the explosives plant will affect the natural environment and their quality of life.
Village elder Lea Lai asked what would happen if the drilled wells run dry. The village elder recalled a case in Salajõe village in Lääne County, where, after lengthy disputes, a peat producer built a drinking water system.
"It is assumed that the developer or the municipality will then dig us a new well. We know that Salajõe village did not get a well for ten years. They had to prove it, prove it, prove it," Lai said.
The Ministry of Defense said studies show this is not an issue.
"As part of this environmental study, we have also carried out a groundwater study. It shows that there should in fact be no impact on local wells. The plant would draw its water from deeper groundwater layers than the local wells," said Indrek Sirp, special adviser for defence industry development at the Ministry of Defense.
Rein Kruusmaa, a member of the Risti subdistrict council, said residents draw up development plans, but when development actually arrives, it happens over the heads of local people.
"The local government operates on the basis of its development plan. Unfortunately, none of the measures in the development plan are implemented. What gets implemented are the things brought here under pressure from developers. Be it a wind farm, large solar parks, or a defense industry park," he said.
Sirp said that Europe needs explosives for the production of ammunition. In addition, the plant would create the conditions for producing ammunition in Estonia.

Kengo Kuma to Receive the 2027 Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Japanese architect Kengo Kuma has been selected to receive the Andrée Putman Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2027 Créateurs Design Awards (CDA). The award, one of two Legacy Awards presented by the organization, recognizes a career that has influenced architecture and the built environment across generations and geographic contexts. Kuma will receive the honor during the CDA Awards Ceremony, which will take place at the Shangri-La Paris on January 16, 2027.
Born in Yokohama in 1954, Kuma founded Kengo Kuma & Associates in Tokyo in 1990 and opened a Paris office in 2008. Across more than three decades of practice, his work has explored the relationship between architecture and nature, often drawing on Japanese architectural traditions and reinterpreting them through contemporary materials, construction methods, and spatial approaches.
Among Kuma's projects are the V&A Dundee in Scotland, the FRAC Marseille, and the Cité des Arts et de la Culture in Besançon. His practice was also involved in the design of the Japan National Stadium in Tokyo, built for the 2020 Summer Olympics, and the Saint-Denis Pleyel station in Paris, which was completed in 2024. His work has extended across cultural, civic, transportation, and institutional projects in Japan and internationally.
Related Article
Christian de Portzamparc to Receive the 2026 Créateurs Design Awards Lifetime Achievement Award
Alongside his architectural practice, Kuma has maintained an academic and research-oriented career. He has been a professor at the University of Tokyo since 2009 and has previously taught at Keio University, Columbia University, and the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His work has also been accompanied by a number of international recognitions, including the Wood Design Award and Global Award for Sustainable Architecture in 2016, the Japan Art Academy Prize and Imperial Prize in 2024, and the Prix Versailles for Best Museum and the 38th Louis I. Kahn Award in 2025.
 In my design practice, I consider myself a long-distance runner. I believe the most important thing is to keep running over the long term with a single goal in mind: achieving harmony between humans and nature. Writing is also a vital part of this journey; the ideas that come to me while running often take the form of essays and books. – Kengo Kuma
The Lifetime Achievement Award is named after French designer Andrée Putman and is selected by members of the Créateurs Design Association rather than through an open submission process. Previous recipients include Norman Foster, Tadao Ando, and Christian de Portzamparc. According to Yuri Xavier, Co-Founder of the Créateurs Design Awards, the decision recognizes Kuma's continued exploration of the relationship between tradition and contemporary architecture. The announcement of Kuma as the 2027 recipient coincides with the opening of submissions for the 2027 Créateurs Design Awards. Entries will be accepted from September 1 through October 31, 2026, across 15 categories covering architecture, interior design, product design, and art and culture.

UBS scores interim win on capital buffer rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:27:33 UTC
15:27:33 KST

UBS scores interim win on capital buffer rules
UBS bank notched up an interim victory in its multi-year struggle against Switzerland’s push to make it hold billions of extra dollars in capital.
The Zurich-based bank should be able to use convertible debt, known as AT1s, for as much as 50% of the extra requirement, provided that those instruments are reformed, lawmakers from the key Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee of the Senate said on Monday.
+How to tame UBS without making the bank toothless
Since the collapse of Credit Suisse more than three years ago, the Swiss government has been seeking ways to make its lone remaining global bank crisis-proof. A key plank of its reform agenda is a capital requirement hike of around $20 billion, intended to make sure that UBS’s foreign businesses can’t sink its domestic entity.
UBS executives have argued that the measure will make it uncompetitive. The bank has tacitly backed the AT1 measures as a potential compromise.
More
Credit Suisse AT1 bond ‘rip-off’ could cost Swiss taxpayer
The “committee has backed a materially softer approach,” said Joseph Dickerson and Theo Massing, analysts at Jefferies, in a note. “The result would enable UBS to have more flexibility around how it meets the Swiss government’s demand to back foreign subsidiaries.”
Soften impact
The bank didn’t immediately comment on the committee decision. The Swiss Bankers Association, a lobby group, said in a statement that it welcomed the reform proposals for AT1 instruments but rejected the stricter capital requirements.
The committee’s endorsement, if it makes it through a legislative process due to run until at least next year, would soften the impact of the extra capital requirement on the basis that debt funding is generally cheaper than pure equity.
+ Read about the fight between UBS and Swiss regulators
The committee voted 10-2 in favor of the 50% recommendation, with one abstention.
While the upper house committee’s stance will influence the debate ahead, it’s only one step in a lengthy legislative process. Lawmakers in the more left-leaning lower house could reverse some of the concessions to UBS.
The Social Democrats, the second-largest party in parliament, issued a statement on Monday criticising the committee’s stance. That signals a potentially harder fight as the political process continues.
Bonus pool reduced
The next stop is a vote on the upper house’s floor that’s set to take place during the chamber’s autumn session from September 14 to October 2.
AT1s were born in the aftermath of the global financial crisis as a way to increase a bank’s loss-absorbing capacity. UBS is a substantial player in AT1s globally, and the debt that it has issued accounts for about 7% of the $286 billion European market.
Debt investors generally expect lower returns on their capital than equity investors. Using less equity also helps the bank’s profitability metrics and can affect bonuses.
UBS should back all of the value of its foreign units, using the combination of equity and AT1 debt, the committee said. That meets the government’s initial demand – though the finance ministry has criticised the use of AT1s as not reliable as a means of absorbing losses in a crisis.
The lawmakers backed changes to the instruments that would enable them to kick in earlier in stress situations, addressing a key weakness of AT1 debt that emerged during Credit Suisse’s decline.
Under the proposal that lawmakers backed, UBS would face several obligations in case it falls below its minimum requirement for highest-quality equity capital, CET1. According to a draft distributed to journalists, the bank would be barred from paying dividends or making any share buybacks as well as from paying coupons on its AT1 bonds.
At the same time, the bonus pool would be reduced.
Erich Ettlin, the president of the committee, said on Monday that the solution would “serve Switzerland,” and “is no victory for UBS.”
More
Switzerland outlines stricter too-big-to-fail banking rules

Shein shares fall on Hong Kong debut as parcel duties and Iran costs bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:26:17 UTC
15:26:17 KST

Shein has listed in Hong Kong after failed attempts in New York and London, as US tariffs and rising shipping costs squeeze the fast-fashion giant's profits.
Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell as much as 10% on their trading debut on Hong Kong's stock market on Tuesday, before recovering some of their losses, following years of delay to the company's plans to list publicly and regulatory setbacks in Europe and in the US.
Shein's initial public offering opened on 24 August, with the final share price set a week later on 31 August. Trading began the following day, on Tuesday.
The gap reflects standard IPO process, as investors placed their orders over about a week, the banks running the deal then fixed the final price and decided who got shares, and trading opened a few business days later once the exchange gave the final go-ahead.
The listing marks the end of a long search for a stock market willing to take Shein after plans to list in New York and London stalled amid scrutiny over its Chinese supply chains, forcing the company to turn to Hong Kong instead.
New US and EU tariffs on low-cost parcels from China, along with rising shipping costs from the war in Iran, have contributed to Shein's swing from a $395 million (€340mn) profit to a $99 million (€85mn) loss in the first quarter of this year.
Shein raised about $1.7 billion (€1.46bn), pricing shares at HK$48.56 (€5.33) each, in one of the city's biggest share sales this year.
"Shein's Hong Kong listing marks a new starting point," said Leigh Gui, Shein's chief financial officer, in a short speech at its listing ceremony.
But in early trading, the shares fell to below HK$44 (€4.83) before losses narrowed.
Tariffs squeeze profits
Shein has built its appeal to customers on ultra-fast, affordable fashion, delivered from China to the West within days.
However, the end of "de minimis" tariff exemptions in the US and the European Union has raised duties on low-value parcels from China, including Shein's products. Higher logistics costs, driven partly by the war in Iran, have also squeezed the company's low-price business model and profitability.
Tariff costs have forced Shein to raise prices, "cutting into its main advantage," said Jacob Cooke, CEO of WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
Back to its roots
Shein, pronounced "she-in," earlier explored listing its shares in New York and London, and moved its headquarters from China to Singapore in 2021.
But increasingly strict scrutiny by Beijing and by regulators in the US and Europe led it to embrace its Chinese roots and switch to a Hong Kong listing.
Launched in 2012 in China, much of Shein's operations were in the southern province of Guangdong before it moved its corporate headquarters out of the country.
"Guangdong is Shein's roots, and the starting point of our journey," founder Sky Xu said in a speech in February.
Pivoting its focus back to China also highlighted the advantages Shein derives from a supply chain system that "only exists" in Guangdong, said William Ma of GROW Investment Group, referring to its small-batch, fast-response manufacturing model.
Shein has hit other roadblocks in expanding in Europe. In February, the EU launched a probe into the company with a focus on "illegal" products, including alleged child sexual abuse material.
In May, Shein acquired San Francisco-based eco-friendly clothing retailer Everlane, a move some analysts said was not the best fit.
Hong Kong's IPO boost
The company's market value was roughly $27 billion (€23.2bn) as it listed in Hong Kong, a fraction of its peak valuation a few years ago.
"Shein has probably missed its golden listing window due to the shift of momentum toward AI and tariffs, which can affect valuations and profitability," said Gary Ng, a senior economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.
Still, Shein's listing is welcome news for Hong Kong, as the Chinese territory makes increasing efforts to hold onto its role as a global financial hub following a downturn in 2023.
Hong Kong's stock exchange has had a strong year for IPOs, raising more than $40 billion (€34.4bn) so far.
There is also a backlog of companies seeking to list there, said Lorraine Tan at investment research firm Morningstar.

YANGON, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Myanmar's Ministry of Finance and Revenue has extended tax exemptions on imports of high-speed diesel, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fertilizers through Sept. 30, 2026, the state-owned daily The Global New Light of Myanmar reported on Tuesday.

The ministry has also extended a two-percent advance income tax exemption on imported fertilizers to support the continued development of the agricultural sector and reduce production costs for farmers, it said.
For imported LNG, customs duty, commercial tax and advance income tax will remain exempt to support power generation and help reduce electricity costs amid rising global fuel prices, the ministry said. ■

(China Economic Roundtable) China facilitates flow of resources to strengthen regional innovation systems
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
14:23:01 CST
15:23:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- China is stepping up efforts to facilitate the flow of innovation resources and strengthen regional innovation systems, said the guests on the latest episode of China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency.
China has vowed to improve regional innovation systems during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The systems bring together government, businesses, universities and research institutes, allowing different regions to better leverage their respective strengths and helping move research findings from laboratories toward commercial applications.
China's three international sci-tech innovation centers are Beijing (Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei), Shanghai (Yangtze River Delta), and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.
Facilitating the flow of innovation resources, such as talent, capital, and technology, is a central focus in efforts to strengthen regional innovation systems.
Yi Tong, a researcher with the Beijing Academy of Science and Technology, said at the roundtable that Beijing is taking multiple measures to facilitate the flow and allocation of innovation resources.
The capital city has established the country's first leading group for the integrated development of education, science and technology, and talent, and rolled out three-year action to promote the commercialization of scientific and technological achievements, according to Yi.
In Shanghai, the local authorities have launched a special initiative targeting technology companies, which helps smart technology companies connect with application scenarios, accelerate commercialization and drive development across the entire value chain, said Zha Hao, chairman and CEO of Shanghai Smartlogic Technology.
In the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, efforts are also underway to remove barriers to the cross-regional flow of innovation resources, said Zhang Zhengang, a professor at South China University of Technology.
The region is building innovation platforms to pool resources, forming a model in which Hong Kong contributes scientific research, Guangdong supports commercialization and the global market provides broader opportunities for application, Zhang noted. ■

Witnesses have said the ferry, a wide-bodied catamaran, was lurching violently before crashing into the water, the impact tearing open part of its bow.

China’s solar power capacity surpasses coal for first time

People ride bikes on a street in Beijing, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo)
China's installed solar energy capacity has surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time, the national energy body said on Sept. 1, hailing the milestone.
China, the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases that drive climate change, has pledged to peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060.
"As of the end of July this year, China's installed solar power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts," the National Energy Administration (NEA) said.
"For the first time, photovoltaic installed capacity surpassed coal-fired power, becoming the largest power source category in China," it added.
The country's coal-fired power installed capacity, the energy body said, stood at 1.285 billion kilowatts.
Coal has been China's key power generation source for decades and a key driver of its planet-warming emissions.
But the country's coal-fired power generation fell by nearly 2 percent in 2025, despite rising energy demand in the world's largest emitter, data showed in February.
China has seen an explosive growth in its renewable installation, with coal's share in its energy mix edging down in recent years.
The country installed a record 315 gigawatts of solar power and 119 gigawatts of wind power capacity last year, over 80 percent of total newly installed power generation capacity, according to the China Electricity Council.

“The Russian attacks on the Ukrainians are getting harsher and harsher,” an EU official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

But there appears little they can do to massively increase the supply of desperately needed air interceptors to Ukraine -- beyond pressuring European countries that still have stockpiles and urging the likes of Japan and South Korea to share more.
While the Kremlin escalates its air campaign against Ukraine, there have been growing worries that Moscow is also looking to deflect from its battlefield troubles by ramping up operations in Europe.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said his country has increasingly “found itself in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers” after an explosive-laden drone was found in August at Leipzig airport, a crucial military transport hub.

6 Wounded, Including a Child, in Russian Strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Region

- Sanctions, assets, reforms -

But while crises rage around the globe from Ukraine to Iran, the EU ministers will also open a debate on reforming how the bloc runs its diplomacy as it seeks impact in an increasingly hostile world.
While some advocate overhauling the EU’s diplomatic service under foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, others say now is not the time for institutional reshuffling and that the 27 nations need to focus on better coordinating their positions.

====================================================================================================

India-Russia: A Changing Equation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:18:00 UTC
15:18:00 KST

On August 31, in Bishkek, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi did something that New Delhi has increasingly been willing to do in public: he told Vladimir Putin that the war in Ukraine needs to end.
Meeting the Russian president on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, Modi said that every day the war continues is a setback for humanity and called for a move “from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities.” Putin thanked him and said Russia was moving towards peace, while maintaining Moscow’s longstanding position that any settlement must meet Russian conditions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On the surface, this looks like a significant diplomatic intervention. It is also consistent with Modi’s increasingly familiar language on Ukraine: India supports dialogue, diplomacy and a negotiated settlement. But the problem with New Delhi is not what Modi says to Putin. It is what India does with Russia immediately before and after saying it.
Just one week before the Bishkek meeting, India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar was in Moscow for two days of talks. On August 24, as Ukrainians were commemorating their independence day, India and Russia held the 27th session of their Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic and Cultural Cooperation. A week later, Modi and Putin reviewed progress across the full spectrum of the bilateral relationship, including economic ties, defense, energy, space and mobility, agreeing to continue strengthening what India officially calls its “Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership.” Modi also highlighted the importance of the upcoming BRICS summit on Sept. 12-13 in New Delhi, which Putin plans to attend.
Drone Attack Sparks Fire at Russia’s Key Baltic Oil Port of Ust-Luga
The juxtaposition is revealing. India is asking Russia to end the war while simultaneously working to make its partnership with Russia more commercially viable and less vulnerable to the consequences of the same war.
That does not make India’s diplomacy meaningless. Nor does it mean India has chosen Russia over the West. New Delhi is pursuing a familiar oath of “strategic autonomy,” keeping channels open to all major powers. But there is a growing gap between India’s rhetoric about ending the war and the practical direction of its relationship with Moscow.
Three areas make that gap particularly visible: energy, trade and transport connectivity.
Reliable energy trade – a two-way street
Energy remains at the heart of the India-Russia economic partnership. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, India emerged as the second-largest buyer of Russian crude oil after China. Washington’s tariff pressure subsequently placed renewed emphasis on India’s dependence on Russian energy and on the role of Russian oil revenues in financing Moscow’s war effort. The Trump administration sought to use India’s position vis-à-vis Russia as leverage in its broader trade negotiations with New Delhi in order to get concessions.
Indian purchases of Russian crude did temporarily decline, but the trend proved short-lived. The latest Kpler figures, reported by the Financial Times, point to a sharp reversal, with Indian purchases reaching record levels this summer. In June and July 2026, India imported more than 2.6 million barrels of Russian crude per day, accounting for more than half of its crude imports.
Yet, the more interesting development is that the energy relationship is becoming increasingly reciprocal. Faced with domestic fuel shortages following sustained Ukrainian attacks on its refineries, Russia has begun importing refined petroleum products from India. A 68,000-ton gasoline shipment from India recently reached Russia, with further Indian supplies expected.
This marks an important shift. Russia remains a crucial source of crude for India, but India is increasingly becoming a supplier of refined fuel to Russia. The relationship is being shaped not only by longstanding strategic ties, but also by the unintended economic consequences of the war itself. Ukraine’s campaign against Russian refining infrastructure is shaping a new form of interdependence within the India-Russia energy relationship.
Trade imbalance – and the financial settlement problem
Trade presents a different problem. India-Russia merchandise trade reached roughly $68.7 billion in 2024-25, but Indian exports accounted for only $4.88 billion. The imbalance is overwhelmingly driven by Russian exports of crude oil and petroleum products, fertilizers, coal, metals and other commodities.
For New Delhi, the challenge is therefore not simply to increase the volume of bilateral trade, but to change its composition. India wants to expand exports of pharmaceuticals, machinery, chemicals and food products, while encouraging greater Indian investment in Russia.
The trade imbalance also exposes a persistent weakness in the financial architecture of the relationship. Although India and Russia have pursued settlement in national currencies, Russia has accumulated substantial rupee earnings from its exports to India without sufficient Indian imports to recycle those funds. The Reserve Bank of India acknowledged the problem in March, saying it was working on additional ways for Russian counterparts to use accumulated rupees for Indian imports or investment.
The issue is therefore not the complete absence of a local-currency settlement mechanism, but its limited ability to solve a fundamentally unbalanced trade relationship. Without more Indian exports and investment, simply settling trade in rupees does not eliminate the surplus. Reaching the two countries’ declared $100 billion trade target by 2030 will therefore require not just more trade, but more balanced trade – and a more effective way of recycling the financial flows generated by Russian energy sales.
Making transit corridors commercially viable
The third challenge is connectivity. If India and Russia are serious about reaching their $100 billion trade target, they will need transport links that are faster, cheaper and less vulnerable to geopolitical disruption. The challenge is no longer simply to build alternative corridors, but to make them commercially viable.
The International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) remains the most established option, connecting India with Russia through Iran and the Caspian region. It provides an alternative to the Suez route and could reduce both transit times and costs. Its commercial success, however, depends on sufficient cargo volumes, streamlined customs procedures and reliable multimodal logistics.
The Chennai-Vladivostok Eastern Maritime Corridor offers a more direct maritime alternative, potentially reducing transit time from around 40 days to approximately 24. Its real value will depend on whether it can support two-way trade – carrying Russian energy and commodities to India while providing a competitive route for Indian pharmaceuticals, machinery, chemicals and food products to Russia.
The Northern Sea Route is the longer-term bet. It could deepen India’s access to Russia’s Arctic and Far Eastern economies, but remains commercially more challenging, requiring specialized vessels, polar navigation capabilities and supporting infrastructure.
The three corridors therefore face different tests: the INSTC needs scale, Chennai-Vladivostok needs two-way cargo, and the Northern Sea Route needs to prove its commercial viability. Their success will ultimately be measured not by the number of agreements signed, but by whether they can move goods reliably and competitively.
But their significance extends beyond transport economics.
All three are part of a broader effort to build alternatives to routes and financial systems that have become more vulnerable to geopolitical pressure. They are instruments for ensuring that India-Russia commerce can continue even as the international economic environment around Russia becomes more fragmented.
Empty rhetoric
The contradiction exposed in Bishkek is that India continues to talk about ending the war while building a stronger, more durable relationship with Russia designed to survive that exact war.
Modi told Putin that the world must move from “endless war” to “end of war.” Yet, around the same meeting, India was proactively deepening cooperation with Moscow in energy, trade, finance and connectivity – precisely the areas that can help Russia withstand the economic consequences of the war.
India is not responsible for ending a war it did not start. Nor is it wrong to pursue its own interests. But New Delhi is one of the few major powers with both enormous economic ties to Russia and direct access to Putin. It has leverage, and it has chosen not to use it in any meaningful way.
Instead, India is insulating its relationship with Russia from the war while asking Russia to end the war.
That is not pressure. It is accommodation – wrapped in the language of peace.

Flash estimate: Inflation in Estonia up 0.3% in August
Estonia's annual inflation fell to 1.3 percent in August, its lowest level since spring 2021, Statistics Estonia said.
The harmonized index of consumer prices (HICP) rose 0.3 percent between July and August, with housing and transport costs up but food and non‑alcoholic beverage prices falling.
The flash estimate, which includes tourist expenditures, will be refined once more detailed data on August prices are received.
Lauri Veski, Consumer Price Statistics Service Manager at Statistics Estonia, said the year‑on‑year increase has not been this low since the economy was recovering from the coronavirus pandemic.
"Compared with August 2025, the index was primarily influenced by the increase in housing‑related and transport costs, on the one hand, and by the fall in the prices of food and non‑alcoholic beverages, on the other hand," Veski said.
The consumer price index (CPI) uses weights reflecting the average expenditure structure of Estonian residents, while the HICP also takes into account tourist spending, naturally highest in Estonia in the summer months, and is comparable to international indices.
The CPI for August will be published on September 7, and the finalized HICP data on September 16, Statistics Estonia said.
More detailed information is available from Statistics Estonia here and here.

India's prime minister tells Putin to end 'endless war' against Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:17:56 UTC
15:17:56 KST

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged Russian President Vladimir Putin on Aug. 31 to move from "endless war" toward ending Russia's war against Ukraine.
The remarks marked a public appeal from the leader of one of Russia's partners and largest energy customers for Moscow to end the war, even as India continues to deepen its economic ties with Russia.
"Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, whilst every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace," Modi told Putin on the sidelines of the annual Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek.
"We need to move from endless war to an end to the war, to a cessation of hostilities."
Modi also reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward in resolving conflicts, according to the Indian Prime Minister's Office.
At their first in-person meeting this year, the two leaders discussed defense, energy, trade, space, and mobility, as well as the Black Sea region, maritime trade, and the safety of Indian seafarers.
Russian state media reported that Putin briefed Modi on developments in Russia's war against Ukraine.
India remains Russia's second-largest customer of fossil fuels, only behind China. Purchases of Russian oil from the two countries have helped replenish Moscow's budget since 2022.
Putin also met Chinese President Xi Jinping at the two-day SCO summit, though the Kremlin said their talks only "superficially" touched on the war in Ukraine and focused on bilateral ties.
Despite the rare public appeal to end the war, Modi called Putin "my friend" and praised growing economic ties between India and Russia.
In July, Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev also publicly called for Russia's war against Ukraine to be frozen, urging a return to peace negotiations. His remarks marked a rare public call from the leader of one of Russia's close regional partners for Moscow to pursue a negotiated end to the war.
Russia and India will continue strengthening what India describes as their "Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership." Modi said he expects to host Putin in India for the BRICS summit on Sept. 12–13.

Vijay opens Mettur dam, brings Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu delta farmers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:16:32 UTC
15:16:32 KST

(Photo: AM Shudhagar) The Mettur dam is traditionally opened on June 12 every year to facilitate the cultivation of kuruvai in the Cauvery Delta region. The opening was delayed this year as water levels in the Cauvery basin reservoir remained low.
METTUR (SALEM): Chief minister of Tamil Nadu C Joseph Vijay on Tuesday released water from the Mettur Dam to meet the drinking water requirements and support samba cultivation in the Cauvery delta districts, the rice granaries of the state.As of Tuesday morning, the dam’s water level stood at 91.56 feet, with a storage of 54.452 tmc ft and an inflow of 10,857 cusecs. Water Resources Department officials said the release will be continuously monitored and regulated according to irrigation needs.Departments including Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Water Resources, and Revenue and Disaster Management have been directed to coordinate with district administrations to ensure effective utilisation. The government stressed that every cubic foot of water must benefit farmers, warning against illegal pumping, unauthorised extraction, and violations of permitted irrigation schemes.
Joint monitoring teams comprising officials from the Electricity Distribution Corporation, Water Resources Department, Revenue Department, and Police will patrol day and night to prevent misuse.
Reaffirming the state’s legal entitlement to Cauvery water, the chief minister said Tamil Nadu would not compromise on its rights upheld by the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal and the Supreme Court’s 2018 verdict.
The govt continues to pursue legal and administrative measures to secure the state’s share.The government continues to pursue legal and administrative measures to secure the state’s share.Acknowledging the deficit in the southwest monsoon and the impact of El Niño, Vijay said the release was a planned measure to manage limited resources and safeguard samba cultivation. Farmers were urged to adopt medium-duration rice varieties and water-saving methods such as direct seeding.“Let us use water sparingly, ensure it reaches the end user, and make samba cultivation a success,” the chief minister appealed.
V Senthil Kumaran is currently working as the Special Correspondent for The Times of India, focusing on the districts of Salem, Namakkal, Dharmapuri, Krishnagiri, and Erode.
As the sole representative for these five districts in Western Tamil Nadu, Senthil Kumaran covers a wide range of topics, including crime, education, and civic issues. He has exposed numerous scams and held several government officials accountable for their actions.
In addition to his journalism work, he holds an MBA in Human Resources, an M.Sc. in Psychotherapy, and an LLB, along with a BA in English Literature.

Death toll from Nepal-China floods tops 1,000, around 4,500 still missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:16:10 UTC
15:16:10 KST

The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China has surpassed 1,000 as rescue teams work to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
Nepal’s disaster agency said on Tuesday that 987 deaths had been recorded in the country, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths in Tibet in their latest update on Sunday.
The combined death toll now stands at 1,003, while 4,462 people remain missing across the two countries.
In Nepal, the number of missing people fell to 3,916 as rescue efforts entered their seventh day, while 546 people were reported missing in China.
Foreign nationals among missing
The missing in Nepal include 583 foreigners from more than 30 nationalities, according to the disaster authority.
China has reported 261 foreign nationals among those missing, according to state media.
Indians account for one of the largest groups of missing foreigners. New Delhi said 275 Indian citizens and 128 people of Indian origin were missing in Nepal.
The US State Department said on Sunday that 85 US citizens were missing.
Reports citing Nepal’s tourism board and foreign embassies said 62 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 42 Australians and 33 British nationals were also missing.
Glacial collapse triggered floods
The disaster began on Wednesday with a chain of events high in the Himalayas, when a glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appeared to involve the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
In neighbouring India, authorities in Uttar Pradesh said they had recovered 17 bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal that were believed to belong to flood victims.
Indian authorities are working to identify the bodies, which have not been included in the overall death toll.

Washington to press G20 on light-touch AI regulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:16:00 UTC
15:16:00 KST

(AP Photo)
Tech bosses including Elon Musk, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and OpenAI's Sam Altman are participating in a G20 meeting in North Carolina this week amid a global debate on how governments should address the dangers of artificial intelligence.
The meeting in Chapel Hill, home to the University of North Carolina, a leading U.S. research hub, takes place on Sept. 1-2 and will be attended by ministers from the world's leading economies, including Japan, Germany, France, India and South Korea.
The United States holds the rotating G20 presidency this year and is hosting a series of ministerial meetings ahead of a leaders' summit that President Donald Trump will convene on Dec. 14-15 at his Trump National Doral resort in Miami.
Washington has framed its host year around limiting regulatory burdens and promoting new technologies.
The Chapel Hill meeting is organized by White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who will attempt to get attendees to sign on to a commitment to light-touch AI regulation.
The meeting is spread over two days, with Musk joining by video call and Huang and Altman expected in person for fireside chats with Lutnick.
Google DeepMind boss Demis Hassabis will also participate, Kratsios in a post on X said.
According to a report published by Bloomberg and re-posted on social media by Kratsios, the U.S. will push something called the Carolina Principles, a policy where governments commit to avoid creating new regulatory bodies to regulate AI.
The meeting takes place just weeks after OpenAI revealed that testing of its AI models went seriously awry, when so-called AI agents, while operating without human supervision, went onto the internet and broke into the internal systems of Hugging Face, a kind of online library for AI software.
The incident is still causing major ructions in Silicon Valley, with some, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates, calling for the industry and officials to urgently come up with ways to govern the development of the sector.
In the fallout, Google's Hassabis in July called for the United States to create an organization that would test the most powerful AI systems before they can be released to the public.
The new regulatory body would be modeled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), the private watchdog that polices Wall Street brokerage houses under federal oversight.
The Trump administration is largely committed to a hands-off approach that would leave the industry to find ways to self-regulate, even as companies race furiously to stay ahead in AI despite the risks.
In a sign that his administration is loath to create any obstacle for the AI industry, Trump on Aug. 31 attacked opponents of artificial intelligence data centers, saying they would end up "backwards and poor" and were helping rival China.

What does Iceland’s “No” vote mean for the EU’s enlargement policy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
06:15:29 UTC
15:15:29 KST

Iceland won’t reopen EU membership negotiations after 58.2 percent voted against in Saturday’s referendum. Does this challenge whether the EU can still attract stable, wealthy democracies for reasons beyond finances?
On Saturday, Icelanders were called to the polls to vote on whether the country should resume negotiations to join the European Union. 52.8 per cent voted “No” and the government has no official mandate to go back to the negotiation table.
Unlike other candidate countries, where membership depends on deep institutional reforms, Iceland’s case is different. It is a wealthy, stable country that aligns closely with EU democratic values and principles.
“In the previous accession process, 27 of 35 negotiating chapters were opened and 11 were provisionally closed. Moreover, through the EEA and Schengen, Iceland already applies a substantial part of EU legislation and is deeply integrated into the Single Market”, said Christine Leuchtenmüller, Head of Regional Programme Nordic Countries at the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung.
However, according to Leuchtenmüller, Saturday’s outcome “primarily reflect[s] Iceland’s particular political and economic circumstances” and should not “allow for broader conclusions about EU enlargement”.
Iceland's vote also questions the EU’s wider security outlook, especially as the bloc depends more on enlargement to boost its global influence and security. This approach has become more critical following Russia’s war in Ukraine, strained relations with Washington, and conflicts in the Middle East.
Reasons for accession
Accession negotiations with Iceland would have moved quickly as the island already implements much of EU law. “In the previous accession process, 27 of 35 negotiating chapters were opened and 11 were provisionally closed. Through the European Economic Area and Schengen, Iceland already applies a substantial part of EU legislation and is deeply integrated into the Single Market”, said Leuchtenmüller.
For PM Kristrún Frostadóttir’s government, reopening accession talks was a flagship initiative. The intention was to build a better security shield and economic anchor for Iceland. Reasons included economic pressures, such as inflation peaks of 10.2 per cent and interest rates at 9.25 per cent, and urgent security threats from Arctic instability and diplomatic frictions over Greenland. Adopting the euro and entering the EU Customs Union would have lowered living costs and helped its defence and sovereign interests.
“Icelanders did not vote against Europe; they voted against redundancy. When a country already has the single market, Schengen and open borders, the marginal value of a seat must outweigh shared control of its core resource”, said MEP Mika Aaltola from the European People’s Party (EPP) and shadow rapporteur in the European Parliament of the report on the EU’s diplomatic strategy and geopolitical cooperation in the Arctic.
Ukraine and Moldova also mainly consider EU membership a security choice. Russia’s invasion made EU accession key for Ukraine’s future, while Moldova faces Russian interference and pressure of its own. Both became official candidates in 2022, formally opened accession negotiations in 2024, and have since moved through the process in parallel.
Membership would give both countries access to the full EU single market and potentially billions in European funding for modernisation, infrastructure and, particularly for Ukraine, reconstruction.
Meanwhile, Montenegro and Albania are currently the frontrunners. Montenegro has been negotiating since 2012 and already opened all 33 policy areas, while Albania, a candidate since 2014, accelerated its negotiations in recent years. For both, membership promises greater investment and access to EU funding and markets. The accession process is also designed to drive domestic reforms, particularly on corruption, judicial independence and the rule of law.
Candidates Serbia, North Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina also see membership as a route towards greater economic development and political stability, but their paths have been slower. Serbia has been negotiating with Brussels for more than a decade, but its relationship with Kosovo, concerns over democratic standards and its continued ties with Russia complicate progress.
North Macedonia faces obstacles such as disputes with neighbouring EU members, and Bosnia and Herzegovina still needs significant institutional and rule-of-law reforms. For all three, accession means access to a market of around 450 million people, greater investment and a stronger political position within Europe.
The most complicated cases are Georgia and Turkey. Georgia became an official candidate in 2023, but its accession process has stalled amid EU concerns over democratic backsliding and the direction of its government, despite strong historical public support for European integration. Turkey has been a candidate since 1999 and began negotiations in 2005, making it the longest-running candidate, but its talks have been frozen for years because of concerns over democracy, fundamental rights and the rule of law, as well as disputes involving Cyprus.
Does enlargement benefit the EU?
For the EU, enlargement matters most for security and geopolitical influence, particularly since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Bringing neighbouring countries closer to the bloc reduces border instability and limits the influence of powers such as Russia and China in Eastern Europe and the Western Balkans.
Ukraine and Moldova are particularly important to this strategy because of their position on the EU’s eastern flank. Integrating the Western Balkans would bring a region surrounded largely by EU member states more firmly into European political and security structures.
A larger bloc would also represent a bigger market and population and could strengthen Europe’s negotiating power on trade, foreign policy, energy and security at a time of growing competition between the United States, China and Russia.
On the economic side, new members would increase the size of the EU’s single market, creating new opportunities for trade and investment and helping connect European transport, energy and supply networks. The Western Balkans, for example, are important transit routes between different parts of the continent and could play a greater role in European energy and infrastructure networks.
Enlargement is also designed to promote democratic and institutional reforms in countries seeking membership. Candidates must meet EU standards on the rule of law, judicial independence, fundamental rights and the fight against corruption and organised crime before they can join.
This gives Brussels leverage to encourage reforms beyond its current borders and, in turn, can strengthen the EU’s own security by improving cooperation on issues such as migration, border management and cross-border crime.
How can a country join the EU?
EU membership is a merit-driven process that requires countries to align with EU values and legislation. Any country can apply to join the EU, but it must first meet the 1993 Copenhagen criteria. These include stable and democratic institutions; respect for the rule of law and human rights; a functioning market; and the ability to take on the obligations of membership, including implementing the full body of European law. Negotiations formally begin once these conditions are met. Then the EU Commission and the EU Council grant the country candidate status.
The Commission starts with a screening process to determine how well the candidate is prepared. Then it must implement EU law, and where necessary, make reforms across 35 policy areas (called “chapters”) divided into six thematic clusters. These include the fundamentals (such as justice, public administration, economic functioning, and fundamental rights), internal market, competitiveness, green agenda, agriculture and cohesion, and external relations. The last two chapters, "institutions” and "other issues", include matters which come up during the negotiations but are not covered by any other chapter.
Chapters are opened individually and provisionally closed once the Commission and the Council consider that the country has made sufficient progress and implemented enough reforms.
Once all chapters are concluded, the Commission decides whether the country is ready to become a member of the EU, followed by the Parliament and the EU Council’s final green light. Upon a positive decision, the member states and the candidate country sign and ratify the accession treaty.
Negotiations can take years, although the Commission wants to speed up the process, depending on the candidate’s reforms and political stability. They are also lengthy as each step requires unanimous agreement from all member states. Hungary, for example, has blocked Ukraine's progress for years, despite receiving candidate status in 2022.
Out of the seven candidate countries, Montenegro is the frontrunner, with all chapters opened and 18 provisionally closed. Albania has opened all chapters and closed three, followed by Serbia, which opened 22 chapters and closed two. Moldova and Ukraine opened the fundamentals and external relations chapters, while North Macedonia is still in the screening process. Negotiations with Turkey stalled in 2018.
