Poland pivots to home-grown defence production as it builds Europe's biggest army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:20:53 UTC
14:20:53 KST

Poland pivots to home-grown defence production as it builds Europe's biggest army
WARSAW/GDANSK/PRAGUE, Sept 1 - As Poland builds Europe's biggest army, it is pivoting toward domestic and other central European defence companies to reduce reliance on far-flung suppliers unable to quickly ramp up deliveries, government officials and companies say.
Polish spending on defence procurement from domestic companies, including joint ventures with other central European companies, has risen nearly four-fold since 2022 to 30.4 billion zlotys ($8.15 billion) last year, according to Armaments Agency data analysed by Reuters.
While the Ukraine conflict has prompted higher defence spending across Europe, in Poland it's a top priority as the country shares a border with Ukraine and sees Russia as an existential threat, officials say.
"We're building the largest land army in Europe," Deputy State Assets Minister Konrad Golota told Reuters.
"The fact that something is used by our army and the fact that it's manufactured in Poland is becoming increasingly important."
State‑linked Polish defence firms have stepped up capital spending again in the past year, and more than a dozen government officials, companies and experts told Reuters that Warsaw's new push reflects a shift that creates opportunities for defence firms in the region.
This year, Poland is expected to spend around €53 billion ($61.45 billion) on core defence expenditures, the fourth-highest in the EU behind France, Italy and Germany, according to NATO data, up from €44 billion in 2025 and equal to around 4.7% of gross domestic product.
While big-ticket systems such as U.S.-made Patriot missile batteries, Abrams tanks and F-35 fighter jets remain important, Polish officials say expanding domestic and regional production of drones, ammunition and other frequently used equipment has become a priority.
REGIONAL SHIFT
Poland's strategy reflects a broader rethink across Europe as governments seek to rebuild defence industrial capacity after the war in Ukraine exposed how quickly modern conflicts can deplete ammunition stockpiles.
"This is not merely an investment to ensure we have a highly developed defence industry, which serves as a driving force for the Polish economy, but a matter of supply chain independence," Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
"It ensures independent supplies to the front line should the need arise."
Until recently, defence firms in countries such as the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary had a more limited presence in Poland, which relied heavily on state-owned producers such as PGZ and U.S. suppliers.
Now those companies see an opening.
Czech-based CSG, a major supplier of ammunition to Ukraine, signed a series of agreements in recent months to expand production in Poland.
These include a transfer of propellant production technology to PGZ subsidiary MESKO and an agreement with PGZ to expand production of drones, missiles, ammunition and armoured vehicles.
CSG's Polish unit has also acquired defence component maker Domar MS.
In August, CSG signed an agreement worth more than €100 million with PGZ unit Dezamet to supply components for 155 mm artillery ammunition and a separate €150 million contract with Huta Stalowa Wola for fighting vehicle equipment.
"Central Europe is undergoing a broader shift in how defence industrial capacity is built," CSG Polska Chief Executive Wojciech Grzonka told Reuters.
"Poland is a strategic market for CSG and one of the key directions for our long-term development and expansion of production capabilities."
'NEAR-SHORING' PIONEER'
Other defence groups are responding to Warsaw's push.
Polish arms maker Grupa Niewiadow, a Niewiadow PGM unit, is setting up 155 mm ammunition production with KNDS Ammo France, with output expected to reach 180,000 rounds annually from next year.
PGZ said in March it will partner with Estonia's Frankenburg Technologies to manufacture ultra‑short‑range air defence systems in Poland.
Zdenek Rod, a defence expert at CEVRO University in Prague, said Poland was emerging as a pioneer in efforts to "near-shore" military production within Europe.
"For years, supplies from the United States were a priority to ensure NATO interoperability," Rod said. "Now Poland is also trying to ensure resilience against global disruptions by turning more toward regional and European suppliers."
Polish officials also told Reuters they are discussing expanded industrial cooperation with countries including Slovakia and Hungary.
Germany's Rheinmetall said rising demand from Poland was one reason it was establishing production capacity there and developing a regional maintenance and repair hub for land combat systems.
"The demand generated by Poland's defence modernisation programme justifies establishing full-scale production sites there, which can be integrated into European supply chains and contribute to redundancy and resilience in the European defence industrial system," Rheinmetall said.
The Polish Armed Forces surpassed 220,000 personnel this year, one of Europe's biggest, and Poland, along with Estonia, is one of few NATO members that are close to their NATO commitment to spend 5% of GDP on defence by 2035. In another sign of its defence industry ambitions, Warsaw last month offered to jointly produce missiles for the Patriot air defence system with Ukraine and the United States.
"If you want to sell in Poland, you have to invest in Poland, you have to transfer technology, you have to work on joint projects with us," Deputy State Assets Minister Golota told Reuters.
"The more factories and know-how we have on our side, the better our defence is." REUTERS

Türkiye, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia agree first steps for defense alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:20:16 UTC
14:20:16 KST

Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have agreed to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia to oversee work under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
The body will initially be headed by a secretary-general from Pakistan for a three-year term, according to a joint statement issued after the pact’s first Strategic Political and Defense Committee meeting in Istanbul on Aug. 31.
The meeting brought together the foreign and defense ministers and military chiefs of the three countries.
“We formally adopted the first institutional decisions of the Mecca Defense Alliance,” Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said following the talks.
The three countries agreed to take further steps to institutionalize their cooperation, strengthen collective deterrence and support efforts to ease tensions and resolve regional crises peacefully, the statement said.
They will also seek to improve their defense capabilities and military interoperability through defense industry cooperation, joint technology development and joint production.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the agreement in Mecca on Aug. 7.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack against one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all.

Two dead and one still unaccounted for in Grand Canyon flash floods, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:19:45 UTC
14:19:45 KST

Rescue efforts were hampered on Monday by more heavy rains that swept through the region, a natural part of the seasonal monsoon that frequently causes flash floods.
The number of people unaccounted for after a deadly flash flood hit part of the Grand Canyon has fallen to one as US Park Rangers said they had managed to make contact with over a dozen people who had been missing.
A monsoonal downpour that lashed the northern side of the huge canyon sent torrents of water, rock and debris down a popular hiking course on Saturday, washing out campgrounds in Bright Angel Canyon and around the historic Phantom Ranch.
Two men are known to have died in the sudden flood whose bodies were recovered as search and rescue teams moved in, amid fears that many more could have been swept away at one of the most popular and dramatic tourist spots in the United States.
But late on Monday, Dave Black of the National Park Service said nearly all those who were known to be in the canyon had now been found.
"There is one person unaccounted for that we know of right now," he told reporters in Grand Canyon Village, Arizona.
Black said 82 people had been rescued over Saturday and Sunday as a huge operation swung into gear and rangers had been canvassing the park's camping permit system to determine who might have been there when disaster struck.
"They've cross-checked between permits, license plates, any information they have, and talked to family members, made sure that they were out," he said.
Rescue efforts were hampered on Monday by more heavy rains that swept through the region, a natural part of the seasonal monsoon that frequently causes flash floods in the many creeks, gullies and washes that make up the arid landscape.
Black said better weather expected on Tuesday would help in the hunt for the one person still known to be missing, as well as any day hikers who may have been caught up in the flood. Day hikers do not require a permit to be in the canyon.
"We are still actively searching...we are absolutely holding out hope that that person is still alive," Black said.
Water pipeline damaged
The flooding damaged or destroyed 40% of the Transcanyon Waterline, a key water pipeline into Grand Canyon National Park, the park service said on Monday.
It announced water restrictions in its most visited area and a ban on wood and charcoal fires in areas where the lack of water might hamper firefighting efforts.
The 20-kilometre pipeline runs from the Roaring Springs source on the North Rim to the South Rim, providing drinking water and fire suppression, according to the park's website.
The flooding also resulted in "significant impacts to infrastructure," destroying footbridges and blocking hikers from crossing Bright Angel Creek, the park service said.
The Grand Canyon remained open to visitors, despite the tragedy. On Monday, dozens of people, many of them foreign tourists, huddled under umbrellas or wore rain ponchos as they stood on the South Rim snapping selfies and straining to make out the Colorado River far below.
Trails down into the canyon from the South Rim were also passable, but staff were warning of the potential dangers, with sudden squalls possible at any time.
The hike down into the wild belly of the canyon from one popular starting point takes many visitors around four hours, one staff member said, while the return journey would likely add another six.
Flash floods are common in Northern Arizona because the arid, sparsely vegetated environments there have little capacity to absorb rain, the park's website said, urging visitors to be especially cautious from July to mid-September.

The lame duck’s swan song: Why Trump’s final two years in office could be his most chaotic period yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:17:09 UTC
14:17:09 KST

In January, Trump will officially become a “lame duck” — a president serving out the second half of his term without the possibility of seeking reelection. Normally, that means a president’s influence begins to wane — but Trump’s case is different. He has already demonstrated a willingness to bypass Congress, test the limits of judicial constraints, and largely disregard public opinion, relying instead on an exceptionally loyal inner circle while running the federal government through executive orders. After the midterms — particularly if Republicans lose control of the House — Trump may feel even less compelled to heed the word of Congress or abide by established norms, potentially leading to further chaos both at home and abroad.
Thanks to America's system of term limits, the end of Donald Trump's political career is already coming into sight. However, the paradox is that this reality could make him more dangerous as the next two years develop. The less of a political future Trump has, the less incentive he has to safeguard his approval ratings or worry about the consequences of his decisions. In other words, the weaker he is as a politician, the freer he is as president.
A “diluted” Trump vs. the “pure” version
There is a striking contrast between Donald Trump’s first and second presidencies.
His inner circle during his first term consisted largely of technocrats pursuing an institutional approach to government. They saw Trump as a big child and themselves as the wise "adults in the room" who could keep the president under control. Inexperienced as he was, Trump listened to advisers even when they repeatedly blocked or sabotaged his initiatives. However, that did not save him from two impeachments — one over his abuse of power in his dealings with Volodymyr Zelensk, and the other after the events of January 6 (by which point most of his remaining political allies had abandoned him).
After miraculously surviving an assassination attempt in July 2024, Trump came to feel his own mortality while simultaneously claiming to be convinced that he had been spared for a revolutionary mission. “God saved me to make America great again,” he later declared.
During his second term, Trump stopped listening to anyone but himself and assembled his team primarily on the basis of personal political loyalty. In doing so, he sought to eliminate the managerial chaos, leaks, and inefficiency that had plagued his first term.
Today, almost no one can tell Donald Trump “no.” The traditional independence of the intelligence agencies has been eroded almost beyond recognition, and Trump openly demands that the Justice Department investigate his political opponents. Meanwhile, investigations into Trump himself — a regular feature of his first term in the White House — have become virtually unthinkable.
The Republican majority in Congress effectively withdrew from governing the country during the first year of “Trump 2.0.” Congress made permanent the tax cuts that will leave the country with trillions of dollars in additional debt and raised no objections when Trump launched a war with Iran despite his failure to consult the legislative branch. Finally, Trump blocked $400 billion in spending that had been approved by Congress, a clear violation of the Constitutional principle that places the government’s purse entirely in the hands of Congress.
The U.S. Supreme Court, despite its 6-3 majority of Republican appointees, has not always sided with Trump. For example, the court declined to abolish birthright citizenship and struck down most of the tariffs Trump imposed on imports from around the world. Still, even before his second term, the court recognized broad criminal immunity for presidents, sharply reducing the risk that Trump could later face prosecution over decisions and actions taken while in office.
Perhaps most importantly, under Trump 2.0 presidential power has been so openly transformed into personal enrichment that it borders on corruption — from the aircraft gifted to Trump by the Qatari government to the billions earned by his family through opaque deals during just the first year of his second term. There has also been unprecedented interference in private business, as when Trump demanded the resignation of Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan over his alleged ties to Chinese companies (even if, after Tan met with Trump at the White House and explained himself, the threat disappeared). In the end, the administration reached a deal under which the government would acquire nearly 10% of Intel in exchange for financial support.
Presidential power has, for the first time, been so openly transformed into personal enrichment that it borders on corruption
The New York Times editorial board has distilled these developments into a 12-point “autocracy index,” that covers everything from Trump's circumvention of the legislature and pursuit of political opponents to suppression of dissent and the use of power for personal gain. Still, elections have not been abolished, and independent centers of power have survived — precisely where Trump’s vulnerability begins.
The patriarch’s autumn
However weak Congress may appear, Republicans’ once-total submission to Trump has begun to weaken. They fear losing control of one or even both chambers in the midterm elections if they continue to back the president unquestioningly, and they have even dared to vote for a resolution calling for an end to the war with Iran.
As during Trump’s first term, the courts remain the most effective check on executive overreach. In addition to the Supreme Court rulings mentioned above, a series of decisions by lower courts has blocked key elements of Trump’s immigration and tariff policies from being adopted. The judiciary has also prevented Trump from firing a member of the Federal Reserve Board and restricted a number of political appointments at the Justice Department that were made in violation of proper procedures. As a result, Trump has discovered that, although the system of checks and balances has been significantly weakened, the president still cannot act with complete disregard for the will of the other branches of government.
Finally, public opinion has turned sharply against Trump. His already low approval rating continues to slide, with two-thirds of Americans saying they disapproved of his job performance as of mid-August. Democrats, despite being consumed by their own internal problems, have begun to recover in the polls.
The economy has traditionally been a Republican stronghold, with the party positioning itself as the champion of low taxes. But in an August Reuters/Ipsos poll, voters gave Democrats a narrow edge over Republicans on economic issues: 38% to 35%. At the same time, a majority said they trusted neither party to handle the economy.
Under the circumstances, Trump's endorsement is no longer a guarantee of victory in GOP primaries. Even if most of Trump's preferences prevail at the polls, as of August roughly a dozen Trump-backed candidates had lost their races to represent the party in Congressional and gubernatorial elections this November.
Endorsement no longer guarantees victory in Republican primaries
“Trump will naturally begin to lose influence, especially after the midterm elections,” an unnamed White House adviser acknowledged in an interview with Reuters. Meanwhile, presidential historian Douglas Brinkley told the agency that Trump’s leadership style is a “mess” that will not produce results, regardless of which party controls Congress following the mid-terms.
As summer draws to a close, current forecasts fairly confidently predict that Republicans will lose the House of Representatives, while it remains unclear which party will control the Senate. On Aug. 25, the prediction market Kalshi put the odds of Democrats taking the House at 86% while giving Republicans a 53% chance of retaining control of the Senate.
The outcome will play a key role in Trump’s ability to govern going forward. If the Republicans retain control of both chambers, the president will have another two years to pass legislation and confirm judges. Trump is already being called the de facto speaker of the House, and a Republican victory would only strengthen the president’s influence over Congress.
However, if Democrats take the House, they will be able to block most of Trump’s legislative agenda, and the budget will become the subject of constant bargaining. Democrats will also gain the power to investigate the administration, subpoena officials to testify at hearings, and demand documents. A Republican-controlled Senate, however, would allow Trump to continue pushing through appointments and blocking initiatives originating in the House.
If the Republicans lose control of both chambers, legislative gridlock will be compounded by serious difficulties in confirming administration officials and federal judges. Trump’s main tools will be executive orders, the power to veto legislation passed by Congress, and direct control of the federal bureaucracy. At the same time, a Democratic Congress will be able to use the budget, investigations, and legislation to constrain the White House. This is the scenario with the greatest potential for an open confrontation between the branches of government — and for Trump to test the limits of his own powers even further.
No holds barred
A weakening of Trump’s political position will not necessarily constrain him — quite the opposite. There are sound theoretical grounds for that conclusion.
In 2018, political scientist Marc Shehker published a study arguing that term limits create accountability problems for U.S. governors. This followed the 2016 examination by political scientist Philip Potter of the behavior of U.S. presidents in their final terms; he concluded that they were more ambitious than during their first terms, particularly in foreign policy. As Trump becomes a “lame duck,” his support is weakening and Republicans are becoming less afraid of him. Yet he still retains enormous power that he can exercise more or less unilaterally.
With no need to campaign for reelection, Trump may even feel free to ignore public opinion. At the height of his trade war with the wider world, he argued that American children would now have “two dolls instead of 30,” implying that voters had become accustomed to living far beyond their means. Trump was even more explicit when the war with Iran sent gasoline prices soaring and accelerated inflation: he called it “a small price” to pay for security.
With no need to campaign for reelection, Trump may ignore public opinion
A second presidential term creates an inherent imbalance: a president’s incentive to negotiate with Congress and remain responsive to voters can disappear before his ability to act unilaterally does. Trump appears to sense this. In their recently published book, Regime Change, journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan write that the president has grown less interested in the backlash to his policies. According to Swan, Trump “doesn’t care at all” about the outcome of the mid-term elections. Instead, he is focused on his legacy as a historical figure.
Whatever the outcome of the November elections, Trump will enter 2027 at the peak of his presidential power, with little incentive to seek compromise with either allies or opponents. Against a backdrop of economic troubles, an unpopular war with Iran, mass deportations, and new ideological battles at home, political tensions may only intensify.
Trump’s critics have often optimistically suggested that he had reached the limits of his reckless and dangerous behavior. Yet his political career has repeatedly demonstrated otherwise: Trump can still keep raising the stakes, turning his unpredictability into an ever greater threat for the country's stability.

British man deported from Sweden despite living there since childhood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

A 34-year-old British man who has lived in Sweden since he was 10 has been deported in the latest of a series of Brexit-induced catastrophes for UK citizens in the country.
John Sellers was told to leave despite living in Sweden for 24 years, having been educated in the country and newly married to his Swedish partner, Caroline.
“It is time people know how people are being treated here, and it is time to show what Brexit has caused,” he said, as he described his near seven-year struggle to remain in the country.
“Quite frankly, we have been holding our tongues too long. I am very well aware that different countries have different rules on immigration, but none of this would have happened were it not for Brexit,” he said.
His parents moved to Sweden from Essex under the free movement rights that came with the UK’s membership of the EU because they liked the education system and thought it was a “good place to bring up children”.
His father died when he was 16, and his mother moved back to England once he finished a college course to become a teacher.
He was deported in January after three failed attempts to remain in the country and is still fighting to return to Gothenburg, where he was hoping to build a family with his new wife.
“Whenever I come to England, I feel like a tourist. Sweden is my home,” Sellers said.
“It is horrible. Not only do I feel like I’ve let down Caroline, I’ve let down my family, let down myself. I’ve been ripped from the love of my life, my other half.
“The pain is … I wish people wouldn’t have to go through this kind of pain, because you’re not whole. You’re broken.”
Hit with the cost of fighting deportation, and lack of work due to the deportation, he said he does not know how long it will be before he can physically hold his wife in his arms again.
Caroline, who has chronic conditions including fibromyalgia and symptoms of long Covid, including chronic fatigue, is trying to get back on her feet to return to teaching, but the case has caused a huge level of stress and upset.
She said: “It’s just horrible – the feeling of finally having someone to help you with things, someone to lean on and someone who is always there for you and then having to spend so much time, effort and money on fighting the government just to be able to continue that relationship.
“There are so many things we want to do. We just want to spend our lives together, and it’s so hard having to fight for that, especially when I am not well to begin with.”
Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, is poised to respond to Swedish MP Håkan Svenneling’s demand for a review of the approach to British residents in the country post-Brexit.
Svenneling intervened last month after it emerged one of his constituents, 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, was told to leave.
Thomas has until 7 September to leave, but her friends and supporters are pleading with Forssell to freeze removals and review a policy critics have said is not consistent with the Brexit withdrawal agreement.
Another elderly British citizen, George Mason, who is in full-time dementia care, was told to leave the country in August but has won a stay of execution until 28 September while the migration authorities consider the “obstacles to enforcement”, his son said.
The Guardian is aware of another British man detained by police on Tuesday and told he will be deported.
Caroline Sellers said she and John decided to go to the media because it was important for politicians and officials in Brussels to see how Sweden’s interpretation of Brexit was “crushing people, crushing families” rather than protecting them, as politicians promised.
Eurostat data shows that Sweden has the highest number of Brexit-related deportations of Britons of all EU member states. About 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave the country since Brexit, one-third of the entire number of removal orders issued across the 27-member bloc since Brexit in 2021.
The problem centres on the Migration Agency’s apparent refusal to allow late applications from people who were not aware they had to formally apply to remain post-Brexit – a process used in only 12 other EU countries.
Before, Brexit deportation of an EU national to another member state was only permitted in exceptional circumstances involving threats to national security.
But in the post-Brexit scenario in Sweden, deportations of Britons have been ordered even when no crime is involved.
The UK Foreign Office has expressed concern on multiple occasions about Sweden’s approach to late applications. It is understood that senior officials at the European Commission are also watching with interest.
David Milstead, an activist with the Brits in Sweden group, wrote in the Guardian last month that complaints about the Swedish approach had first been made years ago.
Part of the problem, he says, stems from the lack of communication to registered British people living in the country, causing missed deadline applications.
He said the Sellers’ case was “yet another example of systemic failings in Sweden’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement”.
He added: “There are welcome signs that the Swedish government is taking these problems more seriously, although it is too early to know what will follow. Any remedial action needs to come soon, because people are suffering now.”
Sellers was aware that Brexit might affect his right to stay in the country and, without any communication from government authorities, he considered his best option was to apply for Swedish citizenship.
This he did in September 2021, before the Brexit deadline of 31 December that year.
Not only was his citizenship rejected, but two subsequent attempts to remain in the country under family rights in national migration laws via his partner, now his wife, were also turned down.
The latest adjudication, after he appealed against the first decision to refuse him residency on the grounds of a family relationship with Caroline, whom he had yet to marry, was that they had “not lived together abroad for an extended period of time”.
The migration court had noted that other evidence of a durable relationship was “insufficient”.
The Sellers are now appealing for a review of the judgment with fresh evidence.

‘I want to live’: the disabled people unable to go abroad because of care funding refusal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

Disabled people are being blocked from travelling abroad by NHS care boards and local councils that refuse to let them use their care funding outside the UK, the Guardian has learned.
Campaigners warn of a “postcode lottery” in England where the right of a disabled person to travel overseas depends on where they live or the whim of local officials – even when there is no extra cost to the taxpayer.
Disabled care users report having to abandon travel plans at the last minute, or go for years without a break, when authorities refuse to pay for their care abroad, even though they have agreed to meet all the travel expenses.
The Guardian is aware of instances where individuals have had requests for care and support for overseas travel turned down by NHS officials – only to have the decision reversed when they threatened legal action.
Lucy Robinson, 38, told the Guardian she had been prevented from attending international work events and going on a holiday because health officials in Oxfordshire had refused to allow her to use her care package abroad.
Robinson, who is quadriplegic and has a team of 24-hour personal assistants, is often required to travel in her role as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation. She has received NHS support for some trips.
She said the experience had caused huge stress: “Travel is one of the things that defines my life, in terms of most of the work I do, but also because I like travelling. My quality of life is based around that. I want to live, not just to exist.”
The cases have led to calls for national guidance amid concerns there are no clear or consistent NHS or council-wide rules clarifying the right of disabled people to take their carers abroad. Their care packages typically provide them with personal assistants for help with dressing, movement and night support.
Campaigners have emphasised this is not about “holidays on the NHS”. There is no extra cost for the health service or local authorities, which are already paying for the care. In almost all cases, the care recipient is expected to pay for their assistant’s expenses and arrange their insurance.
“Refusing to pay for care and support abroad does not deliver any financial savings for the taxpayer,” said Carol Barraclough, the advocacy and support manager at the Spinal Injuries Association. “We’d like to see national guidance on this that is effective and clear on the rights of all disabled people to take their carers outside the UK.”
Robinson said the Thames Valley NHS integrated care board (ICB) told her in April it had rejected her care request to attend a conference in Germany because “NHS funding responsibilities cease at the UK border”.
As a result, she was forced to abandon planned work events in Norway and Albania. She was able to go to Germany only because her 69-year-old mother stepped in as her 24/7 carer.
The care board made a rapid U-turn in June when Robinson threatened the health board with legal action, arguing it was acting unlawfully. It then agreed to fund her care overseas on condition she dropped plans for a judicial review.
Analysis by the Guardian shows a wide variety of policies across councils and the NHS. Some are explicit that overseas care is possible, while some agree in principle but attach a string of conditions. Others say overseas travel is allowed only at the discretion of their officials.
“There’s a postcode lottery in NHS care and support policy to allow recipients of funding to take their assistants with them outside the UK,” said Barraclough, who added she was aware of several cases where disabled individuals had been turned down for care abroad.
Giselle Hoad, the founder of the Adult Social Care Warriors campaign group, said: “There’s a concern that cultural prejudice about disability – that we don’t have families, partners, or jobs – means the care system sometimes assumes disabled people should be satisfied with opportunities closer to home.”
Disabled people in England can get care funding through two main sources: NHS continuing healthcare, which provides support for daily living for people with the highest needs, and social care paid for by local councils.
 Anne-Marie Irwin, a solicitor at Rook Irwin Sweeney who represented Robinson, said NHS care boards had a legal duty to meet a disabled person’s assessed needs. As long as the care user remains a resident of the ICB’s area this duty does not stop if they temporarily leave the UK.
Thames Valley said it did not comment on individual cases. It added that where a patient requested temporary travel abroad an ICB “may consider if it’s appropriate to continue commissioning care to meet their assessed health needs while they are outside the country”.
It said its decisions were informed by considerations of patient safety, practical care delivery factors and risk assessment and insurance issues.
Local authorities hold a similar duty to ICBs, previous court judgments suggest.
Chelsea Pettitt, 25, and her parents, have been in dispute with Lancashire council over her entitlement to care on holiday.
Chelsea, who has cerebral palsy, quadriplegia and learning difficulties, wants to return to Spain where she had a week-long break in 2022 accompanied by two assistants. Like other twentysomethings, she loved the sun, the swimming, food and culture. “I felt like I belonged there,” she said.
But her parents, Barbara and Alison Pettitt, said they were told by a social worker that she was no longer eligible for care abroad as she now lived in supported accommodation.
Her care plan specifies two-to-one care for seven nights a year for trips outside Lancashire – but the council stipulates the care must be used by Chelsea to “maintain … important relationships” with her birth family and friends.
A lack of national guidelines means the family is unsure where this leaves Chelsea’s right to choose whether – or where – to travel. All Chelsea can do is savour her memories of Spain. “She had an absolute blast,” said Barbara, “and she’d like to do it again.”
The council said it did not object in principle to Chelsea using her care package on a holiday abroad and it was “working closely with the individual, their family and care provider to understand the issues that have been raised and support a positive resolution”.
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “This government is committed to making sure all those who are eligible for NHS continuing healthcare receive the support they need to live independent and fulfilling lives.
“Integrated care boards are responsible for planning a package of care that meets each individual’s needs. We expect them to fulfil this duty in line with national policy and legislation.”
Additional research by George Francis Lee

Poppy O’Toole’s midweek timesavers: spicy chicken and baked rice, and Thai-style lemongrass fishcakes – recipe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

I’ve called this spicy chicken and baked rice “midweek”, but you can enjoy this baby all week long. Juicy, spiced chicken, fluffy baked rice and enough flavour to make you bin that takeaway menu and raid your cupboards instead. Then some fragrant, delicate fishcakes with a lovely, bouncy texture, which are such a winner for the freezer. Taking only 10-ish minutes to cook from frozen, they save you from hunger and distraction on a busy WFH day.
Midweek spicy chicken and baked rice
Prep 10 min
Marinate 1 hr
 Cook 45 min
 Serves 8
200g Greek yoghurt 
  Zest and juice of 1 lemon 
  50g harissa paste 
  1 tbsp garlic granules 
  1 tbsp dried oregano 
  2 tsp ground turmeric 
  1 tbsp ras el hanout 
  2 tsp ground coriander 
  2 tsp ground cumin 
  Salt and pepper 
  16 skinless, boneless chicken thighs 
  Olive oil 
3 red onions, peeled and roughly chopped into large pieces 
2 red peppers, deseeded and roughly chopped into large pieces 
4 garlic cloves, peeled and minced or grated 
2 tbsp tomato puree 
  400g basmati rice 
  1 400g tin crushed tomatoes 
800ml chicken stock
Serving suggestions (optional) 
Sliced or pickled red onion 
  Crumbled feta 
  Flat-leaf parsley leaves
In a bowl, combine the yoghurt, lemon zest and juice, harissa, garlic granules, dried oregano, ground turmeric, ras el hanout, coriander and cumin with a large pinch each of salt and pepper. Add the chicken thighs, give them a good mix to coat, then pop them in the fridge to marinate for at least an hour.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Meanwhile, put a glug of olive oil in an oven-safe saute pan on a high heat. Chuck in the onions and peppers, fry for two to three minutes, until colooured and slightly blackened, then add the garlic and fry for a minute more, until fragrant.
Turn down the heat to medium, squeeze in the tomato puree and cook for one minute, until the mix darkens. Season generously, then tip in the rice and toast for a minute. Pour in the crushed tomatoes and chicken stock, and bring to a bubble.
Put the chicken thighs on top of the rice – you want about half of each chicken thigh sitting above the level of the stock – then put the pot in the oven for 30 minutes, until the chicken is slightly charred and cooked through and the rice is tender. Serve immediately, piping hot, with the pickled red onion, feta and parsley, if you like.
To eat later, freeze in an airtight container for up to three months. To reheat from frozen, heat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and reheat for 45–50 minutes, until piping hot throughout. Or defrost fully in the fridge overnight, then heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and reheat for 25–30 minutes, again until piping hot throughout.
Lemongrass and ginger Thai-style fishcakes
Prep 5 min
Chill 1 hr
 Cook 15 min
 Serves 8
500g skinless, boneless cod, or haddock 
  200g shelled raw king prawns 
  3 tbsp green Thai curry paste 
  2 lemongrass stalks, bashed and roughly chopped 
50g fresh ginger, peeled and roughly chopped 
4 garlic cloves, peeled 
1–2 tbsp fish sauce, to taste 
2 tsp palm sugar 
  1 tbsp light soy sauce 
  2 eggs 
  About 200g cornflour 
Olive oil
To serve (optional)
Sweet chilli sauce 
  Pickled veg 
  Cooked rice noodles 
  Thai basil and mint leaves 
  Lime wedges
Tip the fish, prawns, curry paste, lemongrass, ginger, garlic, fish sauce, palm sugar and soy sauce into a food processor. Crack in the eggs, then blitz to a paste. Tip the mixture into a bowl and stir through enough cornflour to make a wet dough (you may not need all of it, so add the cornflour in batches).
Wet your hands so the fishcake mixture won’t stick to them, then weigh out 16 equal balls of about 70g each. Shape these into 2cm-thick patties, then arrange on a well-oiled baking tray – they will feel really wet, but that’s normal! - and refrigerate for at least an hour, to firm up.
Put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium heat, then, working in batches, fry the fishcakes for three to four minutes on each side, until cooked through, piping hot and golden. Serve with sweet chilli sauce, rice noodles, herbs and lime, if you like.
To eat later, freeze the raw fishcakes on a tray until solid, then transfer to an airtight container and freeze for up to three months. To cook from frozen, put a little olive oil in a frying pan on a medium-low heat, then fry the fish cakes in batches for about five to six minutes on each side, turning carefully, until cooked through, piping hot and golden.
- 
  These reccipes are edited extracts from Poppy Cooks: The Actually Delicious Batch Cookbook, by Poppy O’Toole, published by Bloomsbury Publishing at £22. To order a copy for £19.80, visit guardianbookshop.com

====================================================================================================

Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

Damn the electorate. They’re so impatient. No sooner do they get a new leader than they want another one. Those ingrates are already starting to grumble about Andy Burnham. Maybe the country is becoming ungovernable. Perhaps it’s social media. Or a consumerist culture, always picking the next shiny thing. Perhaps we’re addicted to drama. As we’re on our sixth prime minister in 10 years, and as similar levels of discontent surface in many other countries, these claims are recited across the media. What’s wrong with us?
Yet our disgruntlement is entirely rational. We give up so quickly on our prime ministers because they give up so quickly on us. Though it may involve different issues, it is always the same betrayal: the public interest is sacrificed for the sake of a tiny number of immensely wealthy people. And it tends to happen almost immediately.
The latest example, which has triggered both fury and grim resignation, is Burnham’s backtracking on his intention to cap political donations. It was hardly a radical policy: he proposed that no person would be able to give more than £500,000 to a political party in one year. That would still have granted the very wealthy disproportionate influence over our politics. I have long believed that the only fair system is one in which there should be no private donations at all beyond a standard, fixed membership fee. Otherwise voters will always take second place to money. But at the moment there is no cap, which ensures that billionaires can buy political parties and their platforms. So a £500,000 maximum, pathetic as it is, is at least a start. In a subsequent pledge, Burnham suggested that it could gradually be lowered.
Now, we are told, even this high cap has been abandoned: the representation of the people bill will concentrate instead on introducing Keir Starmer’s risible proposals, which are intended to limit donations sent from abroad but not from within the UK: as if billionaire donors and their wealth managers have no expertise in transferring money from one account to another. The loopholes are designed in.
Burnham’s buckling on this issue is not a small matter. It cuts to the quick of what this country is and how it works. It has immense implications for democracy, for policy formation and for every other aspect of civic life. What it means is that the ultra-rich will continue to own our politics and our country. Succumb to the power of money and you will find yourself, like Starmer, tongue-tied and immobilised, unable to rise to any challenge that requires a confrontation with oligarchic might. In other words, get this wrong and every other wrong thing follows.
The official reason for Burnham’s U-turn is that trade unions objected: they have long channelled large sums into the Labour party. I doubt this is the real explanation; most of the donations Burnham received for his leadership campaign came from large private donors. Almost half was supplied by Lord Sainsbury, who was also a major funder of the Starmer project. Union money scarcely featured.
But even if Burnham has retreated from his promise for the sake of the unions, I believe trade union funding is also problematic. It ensures that sectoral interests are elevated above the general interest. For example, Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers. And if the unions believe that an uncapped system works for them, they are deluded. They can never match the spending power of billionaires, whose interests in most cases are diametrically opposed to those of their members.
The power of the ultra-rich is now manifest in every policy governments do adopt and the policies they don’t. We see it in the new protest laws and their applications, which become more absurd by the week. Labelling protesters “terrorists” is part of a long-running programme to ensure that no one dares protest about anything any more. This programme has been rolled out across the world, through model legislation drawn up by junktanks funded by some of the richest people on Earth. Just as it did in the 18th century, an ever more extreme defence of property keeps pace with a growing concentration of wealth.
We see it in the way that datacentres have been labelled “critical national infrastructure”, enabling the government to bypass the usual planning process and impose them on communities, regardless of their impacts on local people’s quality of life, on water resources, energy supply and climate breakdown. Again, similar measures are being imposed in other countries at the behest of the same billionaire-funded groups. The role of governments appears to have been reduced to nodding them through.
We see it in the Burnham government’s insistence this summer, in the midst of shattering droughts, heatwaves and fires, on launching a consultation that proposes radically curtailing the transition to electric vehicles. I believe there is only one possible explanation for this policy: lobbying by corporations and their shareholders. Their interests appear to outweigh those of the living planet and its 8 billion people.
If our country and many others are becoming ungovernable, it is not because of the people. It is because the ultra-rich have smashed the system. The electorate and the MPs who might seek to represent us pull the political levers, but nothing happens. They might replace the leader, but the new one promptly repeats the “mistakes” that caused the eviction of the old one. It makes you wonder: what threat do the oligarchs present that outweighs even the threat of losing power?
Whatever the reason may be, disillusionment is an inevitable result of such betrayals. I think most people want stability. I think most people want to be able to trust their governments. We don’t like in-built obsolescence in our leaders any more than like it in our phones. I don’t want to see Burnham go the way of Starmer. But I know he will succeed only if he defends the public interest against the power of money. So what’s stopping him?
- 
  George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

‘It smelled like dead people’: the plan to tackle England’s illegal waste problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

“There were parents dropping their children off and then heaving from the smell,” says Liz Thompson, 45, who runs Blessings Nursery in Bradford, West Yorkshire.
During the recent heatwaves, the smell from an illegal waste dump on Midland Road, just metres from the nursery, became so unbearable that staff had to keep the doors and windows shut and the children couldn’t play outside.
“It smelled like dead people, like really bad rotten food. It was horrible,” she says.
The smell, which lingered for weeks, started to impact Thompson’s business, with prospective parents put off from enrolling their children at the nursery. “It was embarrassing,” she says.
The situation Thompson faced is far from a one-off. The Environment Agency received 10,238 reports of suspected waste crime in England in 2025.
Yorkshire is a particular hotspot, with a new heatmap showing 1,068 reports in 2025, second only to the West Midlands, where a record 1,542 reports of waste crime were filed. These figures are probably underestimated, with just 27% of waste crimes thought to be reported.
It’s a problem that particularly exercises the public and it’s striking that in one of his first moves as prime minister, Andy Burnham visited the Midland Road waste dump, declaring that the “days of making easy money out of waste are over”.
The dump, which first came on to Bradford Council and the Environment Agency’s radar in June after reports of foul smells, had been building for months. HGVs had been entering the site in the dead of night and early hours, with a large excavator unloading and dumping thousands of tonnes of waste.
“There are really clear signs that this is linked to organised criminality,” says the Environment Agency’s area environment manager, Ben Hocking. Waste crime is profitable for the criminals involved, but costly for the public; approximately 20% of the waste in circulation in England is managed illegally, at a cost to the economy of about £1bn a year.
The clean-up is particularly expensive. Burnham has earmarked three illegal sites where waste needs to be removed: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road. But Hocking estimates the cost to the taxpayer of cleaning up the Midland Road site alone will be upwards of £250,000. The cost of cleaning up the Hoads Wood illegal waste dump in Kent came to £15m.
“The aim is to recoup the costs through the courts, but whether that will be possible for this site remains uncertain,” says Hocking. Criminal investigations are still taking place.
As part of Burnham’s plans to tackle waste crime, Tracy Brabin, the mayor of West Yorkshire, will be appointed to take a new region-led approach to the problem.
“We are cracking down on the criminals behind it and giving the Environment Agency the tools it needs to go further and faster,” said the environment secretary, Angela Eagle.
But just how well equipped mayoral authorities and the Environment Agency are to tackle organised criminality at this scale remains up for debate, with the House of Lords recently accusing the agency of “incompetence” when it comes to waste crime.
“We could always do with more funding,” says Hocking, “but we’re also looking to be more effective with the people that we have. We are really looking to get a better intelligence picture of what’s happening and where.”
With no set timeline for when the clean-up of the Midland Road waste dump will begin, one woman who works at a nearby youth centre but asked to remain anonymous worries that more hot weather could bring more devastating smells.
“It was really hard for us to work,” she says. The centre had to cancel its youth cooking and exercise classes because the flies and smell made working unbearable.
“Whoever did this wasn’t thinking about the local people and how it’s affecting them and their businesses,” she says. “It’s really unfair. Whoever dumped this waste needs to be held responsible.”

Off-grid UK-Australian couple given more access to children who were removed from home in Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:36:50 UTC
13:36:50 KST

A British-Australian couple will be allowed to spend more time with their three children after the youngsters were removed from the family’s off-grid woodland home in central Italy last year, their lawyer said on Tuesday.
The juvenile court of L’Aquila in Italy has approved a staged process under the supervision of social services that could ultimately allow the children to leave the residential care facility where they have been living since November.
Under the court’s plan, British father Nathan Trevallion and Australian mother Catherine Birmingham will gradually be able to spend more time with their children in a home environment.
“The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a gradual reunification process, allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend overnight stays with their family,” lawyer Simone Pillon said.
The decision marks a significant turning point in a case that sparked a national debate in Italy over alternative lifestyles and state intervention in family life.
Social services will monitor the process and assess the children’s reintegration before any permanent reunification can take place.
Pillon said the family planned an appeal in order to pursue a more rapid and complete process to bring the family back together.
The court suspended the couple’s parental responsibility in an order issued on 20 November last year.
Since then, the couple’s three children, a nine-year-old girl and twin boys aged seven, have been housed in a residential care facility.
Birmingham remained with the children until March when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling based on recommendations from social services.
The case first drew public attention last year after Italian authorities examined the family’s living conditions in a remote farmhouse in the Abruzzo region.
A court ruling issued in November said the family had no significant social interactions, no stable income and lacked adequate sanitary facilities. The children were being homeschooled.
The family’s situation first came to the attention of authorities after all five family members were taken to hospital following mushroom poisoning.

Prosecutor's Office investigating defense ministry's finances following audit reports

Prosecutor's Office investigating defense ministry's finances following audit reports
The Prosecutor's Office has opened criminal proceedings to investigate the Ministry of Defense's area of administration and its finances, which have been raised in several reports by the National Audit Office.
The criminal proceedings concern the Ministry of Defense's area of administration and the accuracy of the balance of inventories reported in the ministry's accounts as of December 31, 2024.
"Following the National Audit Office audit published in 2025, we analyzed both the information contained in it and a crime report that had been received. To examine additional circumstances, on October 13 we opened an investigation under the section concerning a breach of accounting obligations that has resulted in it becoming significantly more difficult to obtain an overview of the economic and financial position of the accounting entity (Penal Code § 381¹)," Prosecutor General Astrid Asi said.
"No separate criminal proceedings have been opened based on the National Audit Office audit published on August 28 this year, which concerns the 2025 report. We are analysing the circumstances and information presented in this year's audit as part of the criminal proceedings opened in 2025," she added.
No suspects have been named, and the Internal Security Service (KAPO) is leading the investigation.
Ministry of Defense Secretary General Kaimo Kuusk said the ministry is cooperating with the investigative authorities.
"We are aware of the ongoing proceedings. The case is currently being handled by the competent authorities, and we are cooperating fully within the framework of the proceedings. No one has been named a suspect. At present, we can only say that the matter concerns compliance with requirements for the organisation of accounting, which was addressed in the National Audit Office's report on the state's 2024 annual financial statements. The National Audit Office's observations are relevant, and we have since taken steps to remedy the shortcomings," Kuusk said.

How is the Mediterranean changing? 40 years of data reveal climate change impact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
04:00:24 UTC
13:00:24 KST

Spanish scientists and researchers from Europe and the US compiled data from 46 oceanographic campaigns carried out between 1976 and 2018 to study changes in the Mediterranean and the impact of climate change.
Temperature, oxygen, pH, carbon and even the age of water masses. More than 40 years of measurements now make it possible to look back and study how the Mediterranean is being transformed and to better understand what changes the climate crisis is bringing about in its waters.
Researchers at the La Coruña and Balearic oceanographic centres of the Spanish Institute of Oceanography (IEO-CSIC), together with scientists from European and US institutions, have compiled data from 46 oceanographic campaigns carried out between 1976 and 2018 across virtually the whole of the Mediterranean.
The result is Carimed (source in Spanish), a new database that makes it possible to compare measurements taken over four decades and track the evolution of indicators such as temperature, oxygen or pH. Until now, part of that information was scattered across different archives and had been collected during campaigns conducted at different times and using different methods.
Comparing today's Mediterranean with that of four decades ago can help to distinguish its natural variability from changes that persist over time and to better understand how it is responding to climate change. According to the IEO-CSIC, (source in Spanish) the data will make it possible to track these long-term trends and gain a better understanding of how a sea that is particularly sensitive to warming and to other environmental disturbances is evolving.
Recovering the past to understand the present
"A considerable part of the data was retrieved from fragmented historical records or archives held locally, thereby bringing together measurements that were previously not accessible," explains Marta Álvarez, a chemical oceanographer at the La Coruña Oceanographic Centre and coordinator of the research group, in comments released (source in Spanish) by the IEO-CSIC.
"Another part comes," Álvarez adds, "from international campaigns on board national and international research vessels that involved staff from the IEO's INOCEN group."
Recovering the data, however, was only the first step. There was another challenge: how do you compare a measurement taken in the 1970s with another taken decades later? Methods, instruments and survey conditions have changed over time and could introduce differences that do not necessarily mean that the Mediterranean itself has changed.
This is why the researchers reviewed and adjusted the measurements to identify possible differences arising from the way they were collected. That allows them to pinpoint, with greater confidence, the changes that really persist over the years.
What can 40 years of data reveal?
The Mediterranean is facing transformations that go beyond rising temperatures. The study itself highlights warming, acidification and the loss of oxygen among the main changes affecting the oceans, changes that can alter how they function and their ecosystems.
This is precisely why it is important to have observations that stretch back several decades. Looking at that long-term evolution can help to detect changes that would be hard to spot from isolated measurements.
To ensure that the measurements are comparable, the scientists subjected them to thorough quality control tailored to the specific characteristics of the Mediterranean. Put simply, the aim is to avoid a change in the way something is measured being mistaken for a real change in the sea.
"Thanks to the rigorous 2QC process systematic biases in biogeochemical variables were minimised and a more consistent dataset was obtained," explains Maribel García-Ibáñez, a researcher at the Balearic Oceanographic Centre.
What can all this information be used for now? Among other things, it makes it possible to see how processes linked to the acidification of the Mediterranean, the carbon stored in its waters or the renewal of deep waters have evolved over decades. The data can also be used to improve the models scientists use to try to understand how the Mediterranean will evolve under a changing climate.
Carimed is also open to the scientific community and will be able to incorporate new observations in future, expanding a snapshot of the Mediterranean that makes it possible to connect its past with the changes it is undergoing today.
